B. Mohenjodaro   2. Ravi
C. Kalibangan    3. Bhogavo
D. Lothal        4. Ghaggar
questions.exp: Harappa is on the Ravi, Mohenjodaro on the Indus, Kalibangan on the Ghaggar and Lothal on the Bhogavo. Alamgirpur, the eastern outpost, lies on the Hindon.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Harappan site)   List-II (Excavator)
A. Lothal       1. Daya Ram Sahni
B. Harappa      2. S.R. Rao
C. Dholavira    3. R.S. Bisht
D. Mohenjodaro  4. R.D. Banerji
questions.exp: Lothal was excavated by S.R. Rao, Harappa by Daya Ram Sahni, Dholavira by R.S. Bisht and Mohenjodaro was discovered by R.D. Banerji. Kalibangan was excavated by B.B. Lal and B.K. Thapar.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Harappan site)   List-II (State)
A. Banawali     1. Rajasthan
B. Kalibangan   2. Haryana
C. Ropar        3. Punjab
D. Alamgirpur   4. Uttar Pradesh
questions.exp: Banawali is in Fatehabad district (Haryana), Kalibangan in Hanumangarh (Rajasthan), Ropar in Rupnagar (Punjab) and Alamgirpur in Meerut (Uttar Pradesh).

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Harappan site)   List-II (Distinctive find)
A. Chanhudaro   1. Dockyard
B. Lothal       2. Bead-makers' workshop
C. Surkotada    3. Horse bones
D. Daimabad     4. Bronze chariot
questions.exp: Chanhudaro was a bead-making centre, Lothal has the dockyard, Surkotada yielded the disputed horse bones and Daimabad the bronze chariot group.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Theory of Harappan decline)   List-II (Scholar)
A. Aryan invasion          1. Gurdip Singh
B. Recurrent floods        2. Mortimer Wheeler
C. Increasing aridity      3. George F. Dales
D. Tectonic disturbance    4. Robert L. Raikes
questions.exp: Wheeler argued for an Aryan invasion, Raikes for repeated flooding, Gurdip Singh for growing aridity from pollen data, and Dales for tectonic disturbance. Most scholars now favour a gradual, multi-causal decline.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a Harappan site and its present-day location is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Rakhigarhi is in Hisar district of Haryana; Fatehabad district contains Banawali and Bhirrana. The other three pairs are correct.

questions.q: Which one of the following was NOT a feature of the Harappan civilisation?
opts: Use of burnt bricks in a standard ratio
A system of covered street drains
questions.exp: Iron was unknown to the Harappans, who worked copper, bronze, gold, silver and lead. Iron enters the Indian record only in the later Vedic period.

questions.q: Which one of the following Harappan sites is NOT located in Gujarat?
questions.exp: Banawali is in Fatehabad district of Haryana. Lothal, Rangpur, Surkotada, Dholavira, Rojdi and Desalpur are all Gujarat sites.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a Harappan find and its site is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: The inlaid ten-sign signboard belongs to Dholavira, not Kalibangan. Kalibangan is known instead for its ploughed field, fire altars and camel bones.

questions.q:
Arrange the following Harappan sites in the chronological order in which they were first excavated, beginning with the earliest:
I. Chanhudaro
II. Harappa
III. Lothal
IV. Mohenjodaro
questions.exp: Harappa was excavated in 1921, Mohenjodaro in 1922, Chanhudaro in 1931 and Lothal from 1955. Kalibangan followed in 1961 and Dholavira in 1989.

chapters.title: Vedic Age and the 6th Century BCE Religious Movements
factsheet: Rigveda - 10 mandalas and 1028 hymns (1017 plus 11 Valakhilya); mandalas II-VII are the 'family books' and are the oldest; mandalas I and X are the latest.
Mandala IX of the Rigveda is devoted entirely to Soma; the Gayatri mantra (Mandala III), addressed to the solar deity Savitri, is ascribed to Vishvamitra.
The Purusha Sukta (Rigveda X.90) contains the earliest reference to the four varnas; the Nadistuti Sukta of Mandala X lists the rivers.
Sindhu is the river most often named in the Rigveda; Saraswati is called naditama, 'best of rivers'. Ganga occurs once and Yamuna thrice.
The Battle of Ten Kings (Dasharajna) was fought on the Parushni (Ravi); Sudas of the Bharatas won, aided by the priest Vasishtha against Vishvamitra's confederacy.
Samaveda - musical chants, the earliest source of Indian music. Yajurveda - sacrificial formulae, the only Veda partly in prose; branches Shukla (Vajasaneyi) and Krishna (Taittiriya).
Atharvaveda - charms, spells and popular beliefs; also called the Brahmaveda; recensions Shaunaka and Paippalada.
Brahmanas: Aitareya and Kaushitaki (Rigveda), Panchavimsha/Tandya and Jaiminiya (Samaveda), Shatapatha (Shukla Yajurveda, the largest), Taittiriya (Krishna Yajurveda), Gopatha (Atharvaveda).
The Shatapatha Brahmana narrates the eastward migration of Videgha Mathava to the Sadanira (Gandak), marking the spread of Vedic culture into the middle Ganga plain.
Six Vedangas - Shiksha (phonetics), Kalpa (ritual), Vyakarana (grammar), Nirukta (etymology, by Yaska), Chhanda (metrics, by Pingala) and Jyotisha (astronomy).
'Satyameva Jayate' in the State Emblem of India is taken from the Mundaka Upanishad; Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya are the oldest Upanishads.
The dialogues of Yajnavalkya with Gargi and with Maitreyi occur in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.
Early Vedic assemblies: Sabha, Samiti, Vidatha (the oldest) and Gana; chief officials were the Purohita, Senani, Gramani and Vrajapati. There was no regular tax; bali was a voluntary offering.
Gavishti, literally 'search for cows', is the Rigvedic word for war; wealth was reckoned in cattle and the king is called gopati or gopa janasya.
Later Vedic period: iron appears as shyama ayas or krishna ayas; the culture is linked with Painted Grey Ware; rajasuya, ashvamedha and vajapeya sacrifices become prominent.
The word gotra first appears in the Atharvaveda; the four ashramas are fully listed only in later Vedic and post-Vedic texts.
The sixteen Mahajanapadas are listed in the Buddhist Anguttara Nikaya and in the Jain Bhagavati Sutra; Panini's Ashtadhyayi refers to many janapadas including the Yaudheyas and Salvas.
Mahajanapada capitals: Magadha-Girivraja/Rajagriha, Kosala-Shravasti, Kashi-Varanasi, Anga-Champa, Vatsa-Kaushambi, Avanti-Ujjain and Mahishmati, Vajji-Vaishali, Malla-Kushinara and Pava.
More capitals: Matsya-Viratnagar (Bairat), Surasena-Mathura, Gandhara-Taxila, Kamboja-Rajapura, Chedi-Shuktimati, Assaka-Potali, Kuru-Indraprastha, Panchala-Ahichhatra and Kampilya.
Matsya Mahajanapada covered the Jaipur-Alwar-Bharatpur tract of Rajasthan; its capital Viratnagar is modern Bairat in Jaipur district.
The Shivi janapada had its capital at Madhyamika (modern Nagari near Chittorgarh); Malava coins have been found in large numbers at Nagar in Tonk district.
Magadha's dynasties in order: Haryanka (Bimbisara, Ajatashatru, Udayin), Shishunaga, Nanda (Mahapadma, Dhana Nanda) and Maurya.
Ajatashatru used the rathamusala (mace-fitted chariot) and mahashilakantaka (stone-throwing engine) against the Vajjis; Udayin founded Pataliputra at the Ganga-Son confluence.
Mahapadma Nanda is called Ekarat and Sarvakshatrantaka in the Puranas; Dhana Nanda was the ruler of Magadha at the time of Alexander's invasion (326 BCE).
Mahavira - born c. 540 BCE at Kundagrama near Vaishali; father Siddhartha of the Jnatrika clan, mother Trishala; attained kaivalya at 42 on the bank of the Rijupalika; died at Pavapuri.
Jain Triratna: right faith, right knowledge, right conduct. Mahavira added brahmacharya to the four vows of Parshvanatha (ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha).
Jain doctrines: Anekantavada, that reality has many aspects, and Syadvada, that every judgement is only conditionally true ('may be'), expressed in seven-fold predication.

Jain councils: first at Pataliputra under Sthulabhadra (12 Angas compiled); second at Vallabhi under Devardhi Kshamashramana (canon written down in Ardhamagadhi). Sects: Digambara (Bhadrabahu) and Shvetambara (Sthulabhadra).

Buddha - born 563 BCE at Lumbini, enlightenment at Bodh Gaya on the Niranjana, first sermon at Sarnath, mahaparinirvana 483 BCE at Kushinagar. Buddhist councils: Rajagriha (Ajatashatru, Mahakassapa), Vaishali (Kalasoka, Sabakami), Pataliputra (Ashoka, Moggaliputta Tissa), Kashmir (Kanishka, Vasumitra).

Heterodox teachers: Makkhali Gosala of the Ajivikas (doctrine of niyati or destiny), Purana Kassapa (akriyavada), Ajita Kesakambalin (materialism), Pakudha Kachchayana (atomism), Sanjaya Belatthiputta (Ajnana or scepticism); Charvaka/Lokayata materialism is traced to Brihaspati.

questions.q: The Rigveda is divided into how many mandalas?
questions.exp: The Rigveda has 10 mandalas containing 1028 hymns. Mandalas II to VII, the 'family books', form its oldest core.

questions.q: The Gayatri mantra occurs in which mandala of the Rigveda and is addressed to which deity?
questions.exp: The Gayatri mantra is in the third mandala of the Rigveda and invokes the solar deity Savitri. It is ascribed to the sage Vishvamitra.

questions.q: The earliest reference to the four varnas is found in
opts: the Purusha Sukta of the Rigveda
questions.exp: The Purusha Sukta, hymn 90 of the tenth mandala, describes the four varnas as arising from the cosmic being. Mandala X is one of the latest parts of the Rigveda.

questions.q: Which mandala of the Rigveda is devoted entirely to Soma?
questions.exp: The whole of the ninth mandala consists of hymns to Soma Pavamana. Soma was both a plant-derived drink and a deity.

questions.q: Which river is described in the Rigveda as naditama, the best of rivers?
questions.exp: The Saraswati is called naditama in the Rigveda and is the most sacred river of the text. The Sindhu, however, is the river mentioned most frequently.

questions.q: The Battle of the Ten Kings (Dasharajna) was fought on the bank of which river?
questions.exp: The Dasharajna was fought on the Parushni, the modern Ravi. Sudas of the Bharata tribe, guided by the priest Vasishtha, defeated a confederacy of ten tribes.

questions.q: Which Veda contains sacrificial formulae and is composed partly in prose and partly in verse?
questions.exp: The Yajurveda gives the formulae to be recited by the adhvaryu priest during sacrifices and is the only Veda with substantial prose. It has Shukla and Krishna recensions.

questions.q: The Samaveda is important chiefly because it is
opts: the earliest source of Indian music
the first text to mention iron
questions.exp: The Samaveda sets Rigvedic verses to melody for the udgatri priest and is regarded as the earliest source of Indian music. Its Brahmanas are the Panchavimsha and the Jaiminiya.

questions.q: The Atharvaveda is also known as
questions.exp: The Atharvaveda, a compilation of charms, spells and popular beliefs, is called the Brahmaveda. It is the chief source for the non-Aryan and folk elements of Vedic society.

questions.q: The largest of the Brahmana texts, attached to the Shukla Yajurveda, is the
questions.exp: The Shatapatha Brahmana of the Shukla Yajurveda is the most extensive Brahmana. It records the eastward advance of Videgha Mathava to the Sadanira.

questions.q: The motto 'Satyameva Jayate' inscribed below the State Emblem of India is taken from the
questions.exp: The phrase comes from the Mundaka Upanishad, which belongs to the Atharvaveda. It was adopted along with the Sarnath lion capital as the national emblem.

questions.q: The Vedanga dealing with etymology, Nirukta, was composed by
questions.exp: Yaska's Nirukta is the earliest extant work on etymology and the oldest Indian glossary. Pingala wrote on Chhanda (metrics) and Panini on Vyakarana (grammar).

questions.q: In the Rigveda, the term gavishti, literally 'search for cows', is used to mean
questions.exp: Cattle were the chief measure of wealth, so conflicts were essentially cattle raids and war itself came to be called gavishti. The king was styled gopati, 'lord of cattle'.

questions.q: In later Vedic literature, iron is referred to as
questions.exp: Iron appears in later Vedic texts as shyama ayas or krishna ayas, literally 'dark metal', while copper was lohit ayas. The period is archaeologically linked with Painted Grey Ware.

questions.q: The list of sixteen Mahajanapadas is given in which Buddhist text?
questions.exp: The Anguttara Nikaya of the Sutta Pitaka enumerates the sixteen Mahajanapadas. The Jain Bhagavati Sutra gives a somewhat different list of sixteen.

questions.q: The capital of the Matsya Mahajanapada was
questions.exp: Matsya, covering the Jaipur-Alwar-Bharatpur region of Rajasthan, had its capital at Viratnagar, modern Bairat in Jaipur district. Mathura was the capital of Surasena.

questions.q: Which janapada of Rajasthan had its capital at Madhyamika, identified with modern Nagari near Chittorgarh?
questions.exp: The Shivi (Sibi) republic, which migrated from the Punjab, settled around Chittorgarh with its capital at Madhyamika. Shivi coins bearing the legend 'Majhamikaya Sibi janapadasa' have been found there.

questions.q: The city of Pataliputra was founded by the Haryanka ruler
questions.exp: Udayin, son of Ajatashatru, shifted the capital from Rajagriha to the new city of Pataliputra at the confluence of the Ganga and the Son. Ajatashatru had earlier fortified the village of Pataligrama.

questions.q: Mahavira attained kaivalya on the bank of which river?
questions.exp: Mahavira gained omniscience in his forty-second year under a sal tree at Jrimbhikagrama on the bank of the Rijupalika. The Buddha's enlightenment took place on the Niranjana at Bodh Gaya.

questions.q: The vow of brahmacharya was added to the four vows of Parshvanatha by
questions.exp: Parshvanatha prescribed four vows - non-injury, truth, non-stealing and non-possession - and Mahavira added celibacy as the fifth. Together they form the panchamahavrata of Jain ascetics.

questions.q: The second Jain council, at which the canon was finally written down in Ardhamagadhi, was held at
questions.exp: The second Jain council met at Vallabhi in Gujarat under Devardhi Kshamashramana. The first, at Pataliputra under Sthulabhadra, had compiled the twelve Angas.

questions.q: The Buddha delivered his first sermon, the Dharmachakrapravartana, at
questions.exp: The first sermon was preached in the deer park at Sarnath (Rishipatana or Isipatana) near Varanasi to five former companions. It set out the four noble truths and the eightfold path.

questions.q: The third Buddhist council, at which the Abhidhamma Pitaka was compiled, was presided over by
questions.exp: The third council was held at Pataliputra under the patronage of Ashoka and the presidency of Moggaliputta Tissa, who also composed the Kathavatthu. Missionaries, including Mahendra and Sanghamitra, were sent out after it.

questions.q: The Jataka stories form part of which section of the Pali canon?
opts: Khuddaka Nikaya of the Sutta Pitaka
questions.exp: The Jatakas, tales of the Buddha's previous births, belong to the Khuddaka Nikaya, one of the five nikayas of the Sutta Pitaka. They are a major source for the social life of the period.

questions.q: The doctrine of niyati, or destiny, was the central teaching of which school?
questions.exp: The Ajivikas, led by Makkhali Gosala, held that everything is fixed by niyati and that human effort cannot alter destiny. Ashoka and his grandson Dasharatha both donated caves to this sect.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about early Vedic polity:
I. Both the Sabha and the Samiti are mentioned in the Rigveda.
II. The Vidatha is the oldest of the Vedic assemblies.
III. A regular system of taxation existed and bali was a compulsory levy.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: There was no regular taxation in the early Vedic period; bali was a voluntary offering to the chief, so statement III is wrong. The chief's officials were the Purohita, Senani, Gramani and Vrajapati.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the later Vedic period:
I. It is associated archaeologically with Painted Grey Ware.
II. The rajasuya, ashvamedha and vajapeya sacrifices became prominent.
III. The Shatapatha Brahmana refers to the eastward migration of Videgha Mathava.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three statements are correct. The later Vedic period also saw the introduction of iron (shyama ayas) and the settlement of the Ganga-Yamuna doab.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Jainism:
I. Rishabhadeva, the first Tirthankara, is mentioned in the Rigveda.
II. Mahavira belonged to the Jnatrika clan.
III. The first Jain council at Pataliputra was presided over by Bhadrabahu.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The first Jain council at Pataliputra was presided over by Sthulabhadra; Bhadrabahu had by then migrated south with his followers, so statement III is wrong. That split produced the Shvetambara and Digambara sects.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Anekantavada is the Jain doctrine that reality has many aspects.
II. Syadvada holds that every proposition is true only in a limited or conditional sense.
III. Both doctrines were first propounded by the Buddha.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Anekantavada and Syadvada are distinctively Jain epistemological doctrines, not Buddhist, so statement III is wrong. Syadvada is elaborated through the saptabhangi or seven-fold predication.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Buddha:
I. He attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya on the bank of the Niranjana.
II. He passed away at Kushinagar in the Malla republic.
III. The first Buddhist council was held at Vaishali under the patronage of Ajatashatru.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The first council was held at Rajagriha under Ajatashatru with Mahakassapa presiding, so statement III is wrong. The second council met at Vaishali under Kalasoka.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Buddhist literature:
I. The Tripitaka is written in Pali.
II. The Milindapanho records a dialogue between the Indo-Greek king Menander and the monk Nagasena.
III. The Mahavamsa and the Dipavamsa are Buddhist chronicles of Sri Lanka.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three statements are correct. The Sanskrit Divyavadana, which contains the Ashokavadana, lies outside the Pali canon.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the janapadas:
I. Panini's Ashtadhyayi refers to a number of janapadas, including the Yaudheyas and the Salvas.
II. The list of sixteen Mahajanapadas occurs only in Buddhist literature.
III. Avanti had two capitals, Ujjain in the north and Mahishmati in the south.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: A list of sixteen Mahajanapadas is given by the Jain Bhagavati Sutra as well as by the Buddhist Anguttara Nikaya, so statement II is wrong. Panini's grammar is a key source for the janapadas of north-west India and Rajasthan.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the heterodox thinkers of the sixth century BCE:
I. Makkhali Gosala was the leader of the Ajivikas.
II. Ajita Kesakambalin was an early materialist thinker.
III. Sanjaya Belatthiputta founded the Charvaka school.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Sanjaya Belatthiputta represented Ajnana, the school of scepticism, not the Charvaka school, so statement III is wrong. Charvaka materialism is traditionally traced to Brihaspati.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Veda)   List-II (Principal content)
A. Rigveda      1. Charms and spells
B. Samaveda     2. Sacrificial formulae
C. Yajurveda    3. Hymns of praise
D. Atharvaveda  4. Musical chants
questions.exp: The Rigveda is a collection of hymns, the Samaveda of chants, the Yajurveda of sacrificial formulae and the Atharvaveda of charms. Only the Yajurveda contains substantial prose.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Brahmana)   List-II (Veda)
A. Aitareya      1. Atharvaveda
B. Panchavimsha  2. Rigveda
C. Taittiriya    3. Samaveda
D. Gopatha       4. Krishna Yajurveda
questions.exp: Aitareya belongs to the Rigveda, Panchavimsha (Tandya) to the Samaveda, Taittiriya to the Krishna Yajurveda and Gopatha to the Atharvaveda. The Shatapatha belongs to the Shukla Yajurveda.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Mahajanapada)   List-II (Capital)
A. Avanti   1. Champa
B. Anga     2. Kaushambi
C. Vatsa    3. Ujjain
D. Chedi    4. Shuktimati
questions.exp: Avanti's northern capital was Ujjain, Anga's was Champa, Vatsa's Kaushambi and Chedi's Shuktimati. Avanti also had a southern capital at Mahishmati.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Buddhist council)   List-II (Venue)
A. First Council   1. Vaishali
B. Second Council  2. Kashmir
C. Third Council   3. Rajagriha
D. Fourth Council  4. Pataliputra
questions.exp: The councils met at Rajagriha, Vaishali, Pataliputra and Kashmir respectively. Their patrons were Ajatashatru, Kalasoka, Ashoka and Kanishka.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Teacher)   List-II (Doctrine)
A. Makkhali Gosala        1. Materialism
B. Ajita Kesakambalin     2. Scepticism
C. Pakudha Kachchayana    3. Fatalism (niyati)
D. Sanjaya Belatthiputta  4. Atomism
questions.exp: Gosala preached niyati, Ajita Kesakambalin materialism, Pakudha Kachchayana an atomistic eternalism and Sanjaya Belatthiputta scepticism (Ajnana). All were contemporaries of the Buddha and Mahavira.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a Vedanga and its subject is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Chhanda is the Vedanga of metrics; etymology is the subject of Nirukta, composed by Yaska. The sixth Vedanga is Vyakarana or grammar.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT counted among the sixteen Mahajanapadas?
questions.exp: The Yaudheyas were a later republican tribe of the Sutlej-Yamuna region, not one of the sixteen Mahajanapadas. Assaka on the Godavari was the only Mahajanapada south of the Vindhyas.

questions.q: Which one of the following was NOT a feature of early Vedic society?
opts: A pastoral economy in which cattle were the chief measure of wealth
A rigid birth-based caste system with untouchability
Participation of women in assemblies such as the Sabha
Absence of a regular standing army
questions.exp: Social divisions in the early Vedic period were fluid and based mainly on occupation; a rigid, birth-based varna order hardened only in the later Vedic age. Untouchability is not attested in the Rigveda.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs relating to Jainism is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Bhadrabahu, who led the migration to the south, is associated with the Digambara sect; Sthulabhadra's followers who stayed behind became the Shvetambaras. The other three pairs are correct.

questions.q: Which one of the following texts does NOT belong to the Pali Tripitaka?
questions.exp: The Divyavadana is a Sanskrit collection of Buddhist legends, best known for the Ashokavadana, and lies outside the Pali canon. The Tripitaka consists of the Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma Pitakas.

questions.q:
Arrange the following dynasties that ruled Magadha in correct chronological order:
I. Nanda
II. Haryanka
III. Maurya
IV. Shishunaga
questions.exp: The order is Haryanka, Shishunaga, Nanda and then Maurya. The Shishunagas shifted the capital temporarily to Vaishali and destroyed the power of Avanti.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Magadha emerged as the most powerful of the sixteen Mahajanapadas.
Reason (R): Magadha commanded rich iron deposits and the fertile middle Ganga plain, and its capitals Rajagriha and Pataliputra were strategically placed.
Select the correct answer from the codes given below:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.exp: Iron from the Rajgir-Gaya region, agricultural surplus, elephants and river-fort capitals together explain Magadha's rise. Ambitious rulers from Bimbisara to Mahapadma Nanda exploited these advantages.

chapters.title: Mauryas and Post-Mauryan India
factsheet: Chandragupta Maurya founded the empire c. 322-321 BCE with the help of Kautilya (Chanakya/Vishnugupta), overthrowing Dhana Nanda of Magadha.
Treaty with Seleucus Nicator c. 305-303 BCE: Chandragupta obtained Aria, Arachosia, Gedrosia and the Paropanisadai in exchange for 500 elephants; Megasthenes came as Seleucid envoy.

Megasthenes' Indica survives only in fragments; it describes a seven-fold division of Indian society, denies the existence of slavery in India, and says Pataliputra was governed by six boards of five members each.
Kautilya's Arthashastra has 15 books (adhikaranas) and 180 prakaranas; the manuscript was found by R. Shamasastry in 1905 and published in 1909.
Junagadh rock: the Sudarshana lake was built by Pushyagupta, Chandragupta's governor; conduits were added by the Yavana Tushaspha under Ashoka; it was repaired by Rudradaman I in 150 CE.

Jain tradition holds that Chandragupta abdicated, followed Bhadrabahu to Shravanabelagola and died by sallekhana. Bindusara (Amitraghata) is the Greek 'Amitrochates'; Deimachus was Antiochus I's ambassador at his court.
Ashoka acceded c. 268 BCE; the Kalinga war was fought eight years after his consecration (c. 261 BCE) and is described in Major Rock Edict XIII, which also names five Greek kings.
Ashoka's edict titles are Devanampiya and Piyadasi; his personal name 'Ashoka' occurs at Maski, Gujarra, Nettur and Udegolam. James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi edicts in 1837.
The 14 Major Rock Edicts occur at Kalsi, Girnar, Sopara, Dhauli, Jaugada, Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra and Yerragudi, with later finds at Sannati and Kandahar.
Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra edicts are in Kharoshthi; the Kandahar edicts are in Greek and Aramaic; all the rest are in Brahmi. The two Separate (Kalinga) Rock Edicts occur only at Dhauli and Jaugada.
Pillar Edict VII, the longest, is found only on the Delhi-Topra pillar. Ashokan pillars are of Chunar sandstone and carry the distinctive Mauryan polish.

Bairat (Viratnagar, Jaipur district) has two Ashokan records - the Bairat minor rock edict on Bijak-ki-Pahari and the Bhabru or Calcutta-Bairat edict, found by Captain Burt and now in the Asiatic Society, Kolkata.
The Bhabru edict is the only edict in which Ashoka openly professes faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha and recommends named Buddhist texts.
Bairat also has India's earliest known free-standing circular Buddhist chaitya, a stupa within a colonnade of octagonal wooden pillars; the Buddhist remains there were excavated by Daya Ram Sahni.
The Rummindei (Lumbini) pillar exempted the village from bali and fixed its share of produce at one-eighth; the Nigalisagar pillar records the enlargement of the stupa of Konakamana.
Ashoka gave the Sudama, Vishvakarma and Karan Chaupar caves in the Barabar hills to the Ajivikas; his grandson Dasharatha gave the Nagarjuni hill caves (Gopika, Vadathika, Vapiyaka) to the same sect.
The Lomas Rishi cave has the famous carved elephant-frieze doorway but bears no Ashokan inscription; the Barabar caves are the earliest surviving rock-cut caves in India.
The Sarnath lion capital was adopted as the State Emblem of India on 26 January 1950; its abacus carries a lion, elephant, horse and bull separated by dharmachakras.
The Parkham yaksha near Mathura carries a Brahmi inscription naming the Manibhadra congregation and its maker Gomitaka, pupil of Kunika; the Didarganj chauri-bearer yakshi is in the Patna Museum.
Mauryan provinces and their headquarters: Uttarapatha-Taxila, Avantiratha-Ujjain, Kalinga-Tosali, Dakshinapatha-Suvarnagiri; the imperial capital was Pataliputra.

Mauryan officials: Samaharta (chief revenue collector), Sannidhata (treasurer), Rajuka (rural administration and justice), Pradeshika, Yukta, Nagaraka (city superintendent) and Dhamma Mahamatta (created in the 14th regnal year).
The last Maurya, Brihadratha, was killed in 185 BCE by his commander Pushyamitra Shunga; Vidisha was an important Shunga centre.

Patanjali's Mahabhashya and the Ayodhya inscription of Dhanadeva link Pushyamitra with two ashvamedha sacrifices; Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitram concerns his son Agnimitra. The Kanva dynasty was founded by Vasudeva c. 73 BCE after the last Shunga, Devabhuti.
Kharavela of Kalinga, of the Mahameghavahana (Chedi) line, is known from the Hathigumpha inscription in the Udayagiri hills; he was a patron of Jainism.
Satavahanas: founder Simuka; capital Pratishthana (Paithan) on the Godavari; kings used metronymics; they were the first Indian rulers to grant land to brahmanas.

The Nashik prashasti of Gautami Balashri praises her son Gautamiputra Satakarni as Ekabrahmana and destroyer of Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas; the Jogalthembi hoard contains Nahapana's coins restruck by him. The record was issued in the 19th regnal year of Vashishthiputra Pulumavi.

The Indo-Greeks were the first rulers in India to issue coins bearing the king's portrait and name and the first to issue gold coins; Menander (Milinda) was converted by Nagasena, as recorded in the Milindapanho.
The Heliodorus (Garuda) pillar at Besnagar near Vidisha was set up by Heliodorus, envoy of the Indo-Greek Antialcidas, at the court of Bhagabhadra. Maues (Moga) was the first Shaka king in India.

Kushana line: Kujula Kadphises, Vima Taktu, Vima Kadphises (gold coins, title Maheshvara), Kanishka (accession 78 CE, the Shaka era), Huvishka and Vasudeva I; capital Purushapura (Peshawar), second capital Mathura. Kanishka convened the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir under Vasumitra, which produced the Mahavibhasha.

Art and Sangam: Gandhara school used grey schist and Greco-Roman forms, Mathura school spotted red sandstone from Sikri, Amaravati school white limestone in the Krishna valley. Sangam kingdoms - Chera (Vanji, bow emblem, port Muziris), Chola (Uraiyur/Puhar, tiger emblem, Karikala built the Kallanai), Pandya (Madurai, fish emblem, port Korkai); Tolkappiyam is the oldest extant Tamil work.

questions.q: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya empire by overthrowing which Nanda ruler?
questions.exp: Chandragupta, guided by Kautilya, displaced Dhana Nanda of Magadha around 322-321 BCE. Greek writers call Dhana Nanda 'Agrammes' or 'Xandrames'.

questions.q: Megasthenes came to the Mauryan court as the ambassador of
questions.exp: Megasthenes was sent by Seleucus Nicator to the court of Chandragupta Maurya at Pataliputra. Deimachus later came from Antiochus I to the court of Bindusara.

questions.q: Kautilya's Arthashastra is divided into how many books (adhikaranas)?
questions.exp: The Arthashastra consists of 15 books containing 180 prakaranas. It is the most important source for Mauryan administration and statecraft.

questions.q: The manuscript of the Arthashastra was discovered in 1905 by
questions.exp: R. Shamasastry found the palm-leaf manuscript at the Oriental Research Institute, Mysore, in 1905, published the Sanskrit text in 1909 and an English translation in 1915.

questions.q: According to the Junagadh rock inscription, the Sudarshana lake was originally constructed by
questions.exp: Pushyagupta, Chandragupta Maurya's provincial governor in Saurashtra, built the Sudarshana lake; the Yavana governor Tushaspha added conduits under Ashoka. Rudradaman I repaired it in 150 CE and Skandagupta again in the fifth century.

questions.q: Bindusara was known to Greek writers as
questions.exp: Bindusara's title Amitraghata, 'slayer of foes', appears in Greek sources as Amitrochates. Sandrocottus is Chandragupta and Palibothra is Pataliputra.

questions.q: The Kalinga war and Ashoka's remorse are described in which of his Major Rock Edicts?
questions.exp: Major Rock Edict XIII describes the conquest of Kalinga in the eighth year after Ashoka's consecration and names five contemporary Greek kings. Rock Edict I prohibits animal slaughter and Rock Edict XII preaches religious tolerance.

questions.q: Ashoka's personal name, as distinct from his titles, occurs in which of the following?
questions.exp: The Maski edict in Raichur district, discovered in 1915, calls him 'Devanampiya Asoka' and settled the identification of Piyadasi with Ashoka. Gujarra, Nettur and Udegolam also name him.

questions.q: The Brahmi script of Ashoka's inscriptions was deciphered in 1837 by
questions.exp: James Prinsep, an officer of the Calcutta mint, deciphered Ashokan Brahmi in 1837, opening up the whole of early Indian epigraphy. The Bairat-Bhabru inscription was among the texts he worked on.

questions.q: The Ashokan edicts at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra are written in which script?
questions.exp: These two north-western sites use Kharoshthi, written right to left. The Kandahar edicts are in Greek and Aramaic; everywhere else Ashoka used Brahmi.

questions.q: The Bhabru (Calcutta-Bairat) edict of Ashoka is at present preserved in
questions.exp: The inscribed boulder was found at Bairat by Captain Burt and removed to Kolkata, where it is kept by the Asiatic Society. In it Ashoka addresses the Buddhist sangha of Magadha.

questions.q: India's earliest known free-standing circular Buddhist chaitya has been found at
questions.exp: The circular chaitya on Bijak-ki-Pahari at Bairat in Jaipur district enclosed a small stupa within a ring of octagonal wooden pillars. The Buddhist remains there were excavated by Daya Ram Sahni.

questions.q: The Rummindei pillar inscription of Ashoka fixed the revenue share of the village of Lumbini at
questions.exp: Ashoka exempted Lumbini from bali and reduced its share of produce to one-eighth (athabhagiya) because the Buddha was born there. The pillar also records his visit in the twentieth year of his reign.

questions.q: Ashoka donated the rock-cut caves of the Barabar hills to which sect?
questions.exp: The Sudama, Vishvakarma and Karan Chaupar caves were dedicated to the Ajivikas, the sect of Makkhali Gosala. They are the earliest surviving rock-cut caves in India and carry the Mauryan polish.

questions.q: The caves of the Nagarjuni hills were dedicated to the Ajivikas by
questions.exp: Dasharatha, Ashoka's grandson, gave the Gopika, Vadathika and Vapiyaka caves in the Nagarjuni hills to the Ajivikas around 230 BCE. The Barabar caves themselves were Ashoka's gift.

questions.q: Ashokan pillars were carved from sandstone quarried mainly at
questions.exp: The monolithic Ashokan pillars are of buff Chunar sandstone from near Mirzapur, finished with the characteristic mirror-like Mauryan polish. Sikri near Mathura supplied the spotted red sandstone of the Mathura school.

questions.q: The yaksha statue bearing an inscription that mentions the Manibhadra congregation was found at
questions.exp: The colossal Parkham yaksha, found near Mathura, is inscribed in Brahmi with a record of eight brothers of the Manibhadra congregation and names its maker Gomitaka, pupil of Kunika. It is displayed in the Government Museum, Mathura.

questions.q: The last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha was assassinated in 185 BCE by
questions.exp: Pushyamitra Shunga, the commander-in-chief, killed Brihadratha and founded the Shunga dynasty. Vasudeva Kanva later displaced the last Shunga, Devabhuti, around 73 BCE.

questions.q: The Hathigumpha inscription in the Udayagiri hills belongs to
questions.exp: Kharavela of the Mahameghavahana or Chedi line of Kalinga left this long Prakrit record near Bhubaneswar. It celebrates his military campaigns and his patronage of Jainism.

questions.q: The founder of the Satavahana dynasty was
questions.exp: Simuka founded the Satavahana line, whose capital was Pratishthana (Paithan) on the Godavari. Hala is remembered as the author of the Prakrit anthology Gathasaptashati.

questions.q: The Nashik prashasti praising Gautamiputra Satakarni was issued by
questions.exp: The record was set up by Gautami Balashri, mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni, in the nineteenth regnal year of her grandson Vashishthiputra Pulumavi. It calls the king Ekabrahmana and destroyer of Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas.

questions.q: The accession of Kanishka in 78 CE is generally taken to mark the beginning of which era?
questions.exp: The Shaka era of 78 CE is conventionally dated from Kanishka's accession and was adopted as India's national calendar in 1957. The Vikrama Samvat begins in 57 BCE.

questions.q: The Gandhara school of sculpture chiefly used
questions.exp: Gandhara sculptors worked in blue-grey mica schist and adopted Greco-Roman forms for Buddhist subjects. Mathura used spotted red sandstone and Amaravati white limestone.

questions.q: The oldest extant work in the Tamil language is
questions.exp: The Tolkappiyam of Tolkappiyar is a work on Tamil grammar and poetics and the earliest surviving Tamil text. Tirukkural belongs to the Pathinenkilkanakku group.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Chandragupta Maurya:
I. He founded the Maurya empire around 322 BCE.
II. He concluded a treaty with Seleucus Nicator about 305 BCE.
III. Jain tradition holds that he abdicated and ended his life at Shravanabelagola.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three statements are correct. Under the treaty Chandragupta gained Aria, Arachosia, Gedrosia and the Paropanisadai in exchange for 500 war elephants.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Indica of Megasthenes:
I. It survives only in fragments quoted by later classical writers.
II. It describes a seven-fold division of Indian society.
III. It states that slavery was widely prevalent in India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Megasthenes in fact denied the existence of slavery in India, a statement contradicted by the Arthashastra, so III is wrong. He also describes Pataliputra's administration by six boards of five members each.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Ashoka's inscriptions:
I. The two Separate (Kalinga) Rock Edicts are found only at Dhauli and Jaugada.
II. All seven Pillar Edicts occur on every Ashokan pillar.
III. The Kandahar edicts are inscribed in Greek and Aramaic.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Pillar Edict VII is found only on the Delhi-Topra pillar, so statement II is wrong. The Separate Rock Edicts replace Rock Edicts XI-XIII at the two Kalinga sites.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Bairat in Rajasthan:
I. It has yielded two separate Ashokan inscriptions.
II. The Bhabru edict was found here and later removed to Kolkata.
III. Bairat was the capital of the Surasena Mahajanapada.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Bairat, ancient Viratnagar, was the capital of Matsya, not Surasena, whose capital was Mathura, so III is wrong. Its two Ashokan records are the Bairat minor rock edict and the Bhabru edict.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Mauryan administration:
I. The Samaharta was the chief collector of revenue.
II. The Sannidhata was the treasurer.
III. The Rajukas were officers in charge of the royal household.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Rajukas were officers of rural administration and justice, comparable to modern district officers, so statement III is wrong. Ashoka created a new cadre of Dhamma Mahamattas in his fourteenth regnal year.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Shungas:
I. Pushyamitra Shunga is credited with performing two ashvamedha sacrifices.
II. Patanjali, author of the Mahabhashya, was his contemporary.
III. He was directly succeeded by Vasudeva, founder of the Kanva dynasty.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Pushyamitra was succeeded by his son Agnimitra; Vasudeva Kanva displaced the last Shunga, Devabhuti, about a century later, so III is wrong. Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitram is set in Agnimitra's reign.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The Indo-Greeks were the first rulers in India to issue coins bearing the portrait and name of the king.
II. Maues (Moga) was the first Shaka ruler in India.
III. The Junagadh rock inscription of Rudradaman I is the earliest long inscription in chaste Sanskrit.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three statements are correct. The Indo-Greeks were also the first to issue gold coins in India, a practice greatly expanded by the Kushanas.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Kanishka:
I. His capital was Purushapura, modern Peshawar.
II. Ashvaghosha, Nagarjuna and the physician Charaka are associated with his court.
III. His coins never carry an image of the Buddha.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Kanishka's coins do carry a standing Buddha with a Bactrian Greek legend, so statement III is wrong. He also convened the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir, presided over by Vasumitra.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Sangam age:
I. The Sangam corpus includes the Ettuthogai (eight anthologies) and the Pattuppattu (ten idylls).
II. The Silappadikaram was composed by Ilango Adigal.
III. The royal emblem of the Pandyas was the tiger.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The tiger was the Chola emblem; the Pandyas used the fish and the Cheras the bow, so III is wrong. Manimekalai, the companion epic to Silappadikaram, was written by Sattanar.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Mauryan province)   List-II (Provincial headquarters)
A. Uttarapatha    1. Tosali
B. Avantiratha    2. Suvarnagiri
C. Kalinga        3. Taxila
D. Dakshinapatha  4. Ujjain
questions.exp: Taxila governed the north-west, Ujjain the Avanti region, Tosali the newly conquered Kalinga and Suvarnagiri the Deccan. The imperial capital was Pataliputra.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Ashokan record)   List-II (Content)
A. Major Rock Edict XIII   1. Enlargement of the stupa of Konakamana
B. Rummindei pillar         2. The Kalinga war and its aftermath
C. Nigalisagar pillar       3. Faith in the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha
D. Bhabru edict             4. Tax concession to the village of Lumbini
questions.exp: Rock Edict XIII records the Kalinga war, the Rummindei pillar the Lumbini tax concession, the Nigalisagar pillar the enlargement of Konakamana's stupa, and the Bhabru edict Ashoka's Buddhist faith.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Dynasty)   List-II (Founder)
A. Shunga      1. Vasudeva
B. Kanva       2. Simuka
C. Satavahana  3. Kujula Kadphises
D. Kushana     4. Pushyamitra
questions.exp: Pushyamitra founded the Shungas, Vasudeva the Kanvas, Simuka the Satavahanas and Kujula Kadphises the Kushanas. Kanishka was the greatest of the Kushana rulers.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (School of sculpture)   List-II (Material and region)
A. Gandhara   1. White limestone, Krishna valley
B. Mathura    2. Grey schist, north-west
C. Amaravati  3. Chunar sandstone, middle Ganga
D. Sarnath    4. Spotted red sandstone
questions.exp: Gandhara used grey schist, Mathura the spotted red sandstone of Sikri, Amaravati white limestone in the Krishna valley and Sarnath the buff Chunar sandstone. Gandhara and Mathura were the first schools to represent the Buddha in human form.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Sangam dynasty)   List-II (Capital)
A. Chera    1. Uraiyur
B. Chola    2. Madurai
C. Pandya   3. Vanji
D. Pallava  4. Kanchipuram
questions.exp: Vanji was the Chera capital, Uraiyur the early Chola capital, Madurai the Pandya capital and Kanchipuram the later Pallava capital. Muziris and Korkai were the leading Chera and Pandya ports.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a Mauryan official and his function is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Rajuka - head of the royal household
questions.exp: The Rajuka was an officer of rural administration and justice, not of the royal household. Ashoka's Pillar Edict IV entrusts the Rajukas with wide judicial powers.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs relating to Mauryan art is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Lomas Rishi cave - an inscription of Ashoka
Sarnath Lion Capital - State Emblem of India
questions.exp: The Lomas Rishi cave is famous for its carved elephant-frieze doorway but carries no Ashokan inscription; the Sudama, Vishvakarma and Karan Chaupar caves do. The Sarnath capital was adopted as the national emblem on 26 January 1950.

questions.q: At which one of the following places has a set of Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts NOT been found?
questions.exp: Sarnath has a pillar edict, not the Major Rock Edicts. The 14 Major Rock Edicts are found at Kalsi, Girnar, Sopara, Dhauli, Jaugada, Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra and Yerragudi.

questions.q: Which one of the following was NOT associated with the court of Kanishka?
questions.exp: Bhavabhuti, the Sanskrit dramatist, belonged to the eighth-century court of Yashovarman of Kanauj. Kanishka's court included Ashvaghosha, Nagarjuna, Vasumitra, the physician Charaka and the engineer Agesilaus.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of an inscription and the ruler connected with it is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: The Besnagar Garuda pillar was set up by Heliodorus, envoy of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas, at the court of Bhagabhadra, and has nothing to do with Kanishka. The other three pairs are correct.

questions.q:
Arrange the following dynasties in correct chronological order of their rule:
I. Kanva
II. Maurya
III. Shunga
IV. Nanda
questions.exp: The sequence is Nanda, Maurya, Shunga and Kanva. The Kanvas were displaced in turn by the Satavahanas of the Deccan.

questions.q:
Arrange the following events in correct chronological order:
I. The Kalinga war
II. Chandragupta Maurya's treaty with Seleucus Nicator
III. Alexander's invasion of north-west India
IV. The accession of Kanishka
questions.exp: Alexander invaded in 326 BCE, the treaty with Seleucus followed about 305 BCE, the Kalinga war about 261 BCE, and Kanishka acceded in 78 CE.

chapters.title: Gupta, Post-Gupta and South Indian Dynasties
factsheet: Gupta dynasty founder — Sri Gupta (c. 240-280 CE), title only 'Maharaja'; son Ghatotkacha; Chandragupta I first to take 'Maharajadhiraja'.
Chandragupta I (c. 319-335 CE) married Licchavi princess Kumaradevi; 'King-Queen' type gold coins; Gupta era begins 319-320 CE.

Samudragupta (c. 335-375 CE) — Allahabad/Prayag Prashasti by court poet Harisena in champu (prose+verse) Sanskrit, engraved on an Ashokan pillar; titles Kaviraja, Ashvamedha-parakrama; called 'Napoleon of India' by V.A. Smith; lyrist (veena) type coins.
Prayag Prashasti policy: Aryavarta kings uprooted (prasabhoddharana); Dakshinapatha kings defeated then reinstated (grahana-moksha-anugraha).
Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (c. 375-415 CE) — title 'Sakari' after destroying the Western Kshatrapas of Malwa-Gujarat; first Gupta silver coinage; capital influence extended to Ujjain.

Vakataka alliance: daughter Prabhavati Gupta (mother Kuberanaga) married Vakataka king Rudrasena II; as widow she ruled c. 390-410 CE as regent for son Divakarasena — Poona copper plates call her 'mother of Yuvaraja Divakarasena'.
Fa-Hien (Faxian) visited India c. 399-414 CE under Chandragupta II; account Fo-Kuo-Ki (Record of Buddhist Kingdoms); silent on politics, wrote on Buddhism and society.
Navaratna traditionally of Chandragupta II's court: Kalidasa, Amarasimha (Amarakosha), Varahamihira, Dhanvantari, Vararuchi, Kshapanaka, Shanku, Ghatakarpara, Vetalabhatta.
Kumaragupta I (c. 415-455 CE) — title Mahendraditya; founded Nalanda Mahavihara; peacock-type coins (Kartikeya worship); Mandsaur silk-weavers' guild inscription of his reign.
Skandagupta (c. 455-467 CE) — repelled the Hunas; Junagadh rock inscription records repair of the Sudarshana lake; Bhitari pillar inscription records his victories over Pushyamitras and Hunas.

Gupta administration: Bhukti (province) under Uparika → Vishaya (district) under Vishayapati → Vithi/Grama; Kumaramatya = highest officer cadre; gold coin = dinara; land grants = agrahara/devagrahara.
Vardhana (Pushyabhuti) dynasty of Thanesar; Harshavardhana r. 606-647 CE, shifted capital to Kannauj; titles Siladitya, Rajaputra.
Harsha defeated by Chalukya Pulakeshin II on the Narmada (c. 618-619 CE) — Narmada became his southern limit.
Banabhatta wrote Harshacharita (biography) and Kadambari; Harsha himself wrote three Sanskrit plays — Nagananda, Ratnavali, Priyadarshika.
Hiuen Tsang (Xuanzang), the 'Prince of Pilgrims', account Si-yu-ki; Kannauj religious assembly 643 CE; Prayag Mahamoksha Parishad every 5 years; Harsha's Madhuban and Banskhera copper plates.
Palas of Bengal-Bihar: Gopala elected founder (c. 750 CE), built Odantapuri; Dharmapala founded Vikramshila and Somapura Mahavihara (Paharpur); Devapala the greatest.
Tripartite struggle for Kannauj — Palas vs Gurjara-Pratiharas vs Rashtrakutas (8th-9th century CE).
Senas replaced Palas: Samantasena/Vijayasena, Ballalasena (Danasagara, Adbhutasagara), Lakshmanasena — his court had Jayadeva, author of Gita Govinda.

Rashtrakutas — founder Dantidurga; Krishna I built the monolithic Kailasa temple (Cave 16) at Ellora; Amoghavarsha I wrote Kavirajamarga (earliest extant Kannada literary work) and founded Manyakheta.
Chalukyas of Badami (Vatapi): Pulakeshin II (610-642 CE); Aihole inscription by the Jain poet Ravikirti on the Meguti temple, Saka 556 (634-35 CE); defeated and killed by Pallava Narasimhavarman I.
Pattadakal Virupaksha temple built by queen Lokamahadevi for Vikramaditya II's victory over Kanchi; Pattadakal is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1987).
Chalukyas of Kalyani: Vikramaditya VI — court poet Bilhana (Vikramankadevacharita) and jurist Vijnaneshwara (Mitakshara); Someshvara III wrote Manasollasa.

Pallava architecture in four stages — Mahendra (Mandagapattu cave, 'without brick, timber, metal or mortar'), Mamalla (Pancha Rathas, Narasimhavarman I), Rajasimha (Shore Temple, Kailasanatha Kanchi), Nandivarman (Vaikuntha Perumal).
Narasimhavarman I Mamalla captured Vatapi (642 CE) and took the title 'Vatapikonda'; Mahendravarman I wrote the farce Mattavilasa Prahasana.
Imperial Cholas revived by Vijayalaya (c. 850 CE), capital Thanjavur; Rajaraja I built the Brihadeshwara (Rajarajeshwara) temple, consecrated 1010 CE.

Rajendra I — title Gangaikondachola, founded Gangaikonda Cholapuram, naval expedition against Srivijaya (Kadaram); Rajaraja II built Airavatesvara temple, Darasuram. The three are UNESCO's 'Great Living Chola Temples'.

Chola local self-government: Ur (ordinary village), Sabha/Mahasabha (brahmadeya village), Nagaram (merchants); Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I (c. 920 CE) detail the kudavolai (pot-ticket lottery) election of variyams.
Hoysalas — capital Dwarasamudra (Halebidu); Vishnuvardhana built Chennakeshava temple, Belur; Vesara style; 'Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas' inscribed by UNESCO in 2023.
Kakatiyas — capital Warangal (Orugallu); Rudramadevi (praised by Marco Polo); Prataparudra II defeated by Delhi in 1323; Ramappa (Rudreshwara) temple, Palampet, UNESCO 2021.
Sangam-age emblems: Chola — tiger; Pandya — fish (capital Madurai, port Korkai); Chera — bow and arrow (capital Vanji, port Muziris).

questions.q: Who is described in Gupta inscriptions as the founder of the Gupta dynasty?
questions.exp: Sri Gupta (c. 240-280 CE) is named as the founder and bore only the modest title Maharaja. Chandragupta I was the first Gupta to assume the imperial title Maharajadhiraja and to marry into the Licchavi family.

questions.q: The Allahabad Pillar Inscription (Prayag Prashasti), the principal source for the conquests of Samudragupta, was composed by
questions.exp: Harisena, Samudragupta's Sandhivigrahika (minister for war and peace) and court poet, composed it in champu style. It is engraved on a pillar that originally carried Ashokan edicts.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Allahabad Pillar Inscription of Samudragupta:
I. It is engraved on a pillar that originally bore the edicts of Ashoka.
II. It is composed in the champu style, mixing prose and verse.
III. It records that the kings of Dakshinapatha were defeated and their kingdoms permanently annexed.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The Dakshinapatha kings were captured and then released and reinstated (grahana-moksha-anugraha); only the Aryavarta kings were uprooted and annexed.

questions.q: Samudragupta was described as the 'Napoleon of India' by
questions.exp: Vincent A. Smith coined the description on account of his extensive campaigns. Samudragupta also performed the Ashvamedha, bore the title Kaviraja, and issued the celebrated lyrist (veena) type gold coins.

questions.q: Chandragupta II strengthened Gupta influence in the Deccan by marrying his daughter Prabhavati Gupta to the Vakataka ruler
questions.exp: Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II and Kuberanaga, was married to Rudrasena II of the Vakatakas. The alliance secured the Gupta flank during the campaign against the Western Kshatrapas.

questions.q: After the early death of her husband, Prabhavati Gupta administered the Vakataka kingdom as regent on behalf of her minor son
questions.exp: Her Poona copper-plate grant, issued in her thirteenth regnal year, styles her 'mother of the Yuvaraja Divakarasena'. She held power for roughly two decades (c. 390-410 CE) and retained her Gupta gotra in her charters.

questions.q: Chandragupta II assumed the title 'Sakari' after destroying which power?
opts: The Western Kshatrapas of Malwa and Gujarat
questions.exp: His conquest of the Western Kshatrapas (Shakas) gave the Guptas the ports of western India and led to the first Gupta silver coinage, modelled on Kshatrapa issues.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Chinese pilgrim Fa-Hien:
I. He visited India during the reign of Chandragupta II.
II. His travel account is known as Fo-Kuo-Ki, the Record of Buddhist Kingdoms.
III. His chief interest was the political administration of the Gupta empire.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Fa-Hien came to India c. 399-414 CE and wrote almost nothing about Gupta politics; he did not even name the reigning king. His concern was Buddhist sites, monasteries and monastic discipline.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Scholar)   List-II (Work / field)
A. Kalidasa    1. Amarakosha
B. Amarasimha    2. Brihat Samhita
C. Varahamihira    3. Abhijnanashakuntalam
D. Dhanvantari    4. Medicine
questions.exp: All four are counted among the 'Navaratna' traditionally associated with the court of Chandragupta II Vikramaditya at Ujjain.

questions.q: The Nalanda Mahavihara was founded during the reign of the Gupta emperor
questions.exp: Kumaragupta I (c. 415-455 CE), known in the Buddhist tradition as Shakraditya, founded Nalanda. He bore the title Mahendraditya and issued peacock-type coins associated with Kartikeya.

questions.q: The repair of the Sudarshana lake in Saurashtra by a Gupta ruler is recorded in the
questions.exp: The Junagadh (Girnar) rock, which also carries inscriptions of Ashoka and Rudradaman I, records Skandagupta's repair of the embankment through his governor Parnadatta and his son Chakrapalita.

questions.q: The Bhitari pillar inscription records the victories of which Gupta ruler over the Pushyamitras and the Hunas?
questions.exp: Skandagupta (c. 455-467 CE) checked the first Huna thrust into India. The sustained cost of these wars is generally regarded as a major cause of Gupta decline, reflected in the debasement of Gupta gold coinage.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Gupta administration:
I. The empire was divided into provinces called bhuktis, each under an uparika.
II. A bhukti was subdivided into districts called vishayas under a vishayapati.
III. Kumaramatya was the highest cadre of officers in the imperial service.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Gupta administration was markedly more decentralised than Mauryan, with hereditary offices and extensive land grants to Brahmanas and temples — the beginning of what historians call Indian feudalism.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a Gupta ruler and a gold-coin type associated with him is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: The lion-slayer (simhanihanta) type belongs to Chandragupta II. Skandagupta's issues are chiefly of the archer, king-and-queen and horseman types. Gupta gold coins were called dinaras.

questions.q:
Arrange the following Gupta rulers in correct chronological order:
I. Skandagupta
II. Chandragupta I
III. Kumaragupta I
IV. Samudragupta
questions.exp: Chandragupta I (c. 319-335) → Samudragupta (c. 335-375) → Chandragupta II (c. 375-415) → Kumaragupta I (c. 415-455) → Skandagupta (c. 455-467).

questions.q: Harshavardhana belonged to which dynasty?
questions.exp: The Pushyabhutis ruled from Thanesar. Harsha (606-647 CE) united Thanesar and Kannauj after the death of his brother Rajyavardhana and his sister Rajyashri's husband, the Maukhari ruler Grahavarman.

questions.q: Harshavardhana shifted his capital from Thanesar to
questions.exp: Kannauj replaced Pataliputra as the political centre of northern India and remained the prize of the later tripartite struggle among the Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas.

questions.q: The Harshacharita, a Sanskrit prose biography of Harshavardhana, was written by
questions.exp: Banabhatta was Harsha's court poet and also wrote the prose romance Kadambari. The Harshacharita is regarded as the first historical biography (akhyayika) in Sanskrit.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Work)   List-II (Author)
A. Nagananda    1. Hiuen Tsang
B. Harshacharita    2. Harshavardhana
C. Si-yu-ki    3. Bilhana
D. Vikramankadevacharita    4. Banabhatta
questions.exp: Harsha himself wrote Nagananda, Ratnavali and Priyadarshika. Bilhana's Vikramankadevacharita eulogises the Kalyani Chalukya king Vikramaditya VI.

questions.q: The travel account Si-yu-ki (Records of the Western World) was written by
questions.exp: Hiuen Tsang (Xuanzang), the 'Prince of Pilgrims', spent about fourteen years in India during Harsha's reign and studied at Nalanda under Shilabhadra.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Harshavardhana:
I. He convened a grand religious assembly at Kannauj in 643 CE in honour of Hiuen Tsang.
II. He held the Prayag Mahamoksha Parishad, a distribution of charity, every fifth year.
III. He was defeated by the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II on the banks of the Narmada.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The Narmada became the southern limit of Harsha's empire after that defeat, an event recorded in the Aihole inscription of Pulakeshin II.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about Harshavardhana is NOT correct?
opts: He was a patron of the Nalanda Mahavihara.
He composed the Sanskrit prose romance Kadambari.
His land grants are recorded in the Madhuban and Banskhera copper plates.
He wrote the Sanskrit plays Ratnavali and Priyadarshika.
questions.exp: Kadambari was written by Banabhatta and completed by his son Bhushanabhatta. Harsha's own compositions were the three plays Nagananda, Ratnavali and Priyadarshika.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Pala dynasty:
I. Its founder Gopala was elected king by the chiefs of Bengal.
II. Dharmapala founded the Vikramshila Mahavihara.
III. The Odantapuri Mahavihara was established by Devapala.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Odantapuri is credited to Gopala, the founder. Dharmapala also established the Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur, today a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Bangladesh.

questions.q: The tripartite struggle of the 8th-9th centuries CE for control of Kannauj was fought among the
questions.exp: Kannauj was finally retained by the Gurjara-Pratiharas under Nagabhata II and Mihir Bhoj. The Arab traveller Sulaiman described the Pratihara ruler as having the finest cavalry in India.

questions.q: Jayadeva, the author of the Gita Govinda, adorned the court of
questions.exp: Lakshmanasena was the last important Sena ruler of Bengal. His father Ballalasena wrote the Danasagara and the Adbhutasagara.

questions.q: The Rashtrakuta dynasty of the Deccan was founded by
questions.exp: Dantidurga overthrew the Badami Chalukyas around 753 CE. Amoghavarsha I later founded the capital Manyakheta (modern Malkhed).

questions.q: The monolithic Kailasa temple at Ellora (Cave 16) was excavated under the patronage of the Rashtrakuta ruler
questions.exp: Krishna I had the temple carved downward out of a single basalt rock in the Dravida style. It is the largest monolithic rock-cut temple in the world.

questions.q: The Kavirajamarga, the earliest extant literary work in Kannada, is attributed to the Rashtrakuta ruler
questions.exp: Amoghavarsha I, who also wrote the Sanskrit Prashnottara Ratnamalika, was a patron of Jainism and founded Manyakheta as the Rashtrakuta capital.

questions.q: The Aihole inscription, engraved on the wall of the Meguti Jain temple, was composed by
questions.exp: The Jain poet Ravikirti composed it in Sanskrit in Saka 556 (634-35 CE) in praise of his patron Pulakeshin II, and it records the defeat of Harshavardhana.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Pulakeshin II:
I. He belonged to the Chalukyas of Badami (Vatapi).
II. He defeated Harshavardhana on the banks of the Narmada.
III. He was finally defeated and killed by the Pallava ruler Mahendravarman I.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Pulakeshin II was defeated and killed when the Pallava ruler Narasimhavarman I sacked Vatapi in 642 CE. Hiuen Tsang visited his kingdom and left an admiring account of it.

questions.q: The Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal was built by queen Lokamahadevi to commemorate the victory over Kanchi of her husband
questions.exp: Vikramaditya II thrice overran the Pallava capital Kanchipuram. Pattadakal, with its mix of Nagara and Dravida shrines, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Work)   List-II (Author)
A. Vikramankadevacharita    1. Vijnaneshwara
B. Mitakshara    2. Someshvara III
C. Manasollasa    3. Amoghavarsha I
D. Kavirajamarga    4. Bilhana
questions.exp: Bilhana and Vijnaneshwara both adorned the court of the Kalyani Chalukya king Vikramaditya VI; the Mitakshara remains a foundational text of Hindu law.

questions.q: The Sanskrit farce Mattavilasa Prahasana was written by the Pallava ruler
questions.exp: Mahendravarman I bore the titles Vichitrachitta and Mattavilasa. His Mandagapattu inscription boasts of a temple made 'without brick, timber, metal or mortar' — the start of Pallava rock-cut architecture.

questions.q: The Pallava ruler who captured the Chalukyan capital Vatapi and assumed the title 'Vatapikonda' was
questions.exp: Narasimhavarman I Mamalla took Vatapi in 642 CE, killing Pulakeshin II. Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram) and its Pancha Rathas are named after him.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Monument)   List-II (Pallava ruler)
A. Mandagapattu cave temple    1. Narasimhavarman II
B. Pancha Rathas, Mamallapuram    2. Nandivarman II
C. Shore Temple, Mamallapuram    3. Mahendravarman I
D. Vaikuntha Perumal temple, Kanchipuram    4. Narasimhavarman I
questions.exp: Pallava architecture evolved through the Mahendra, Mamalla, Rajasimha and Nandivarman stages. Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha built both the Shore Temple and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a monument and the dynasty that built it is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Virupaksha temple, Pattadakal — Chalukyas of Badami
questions.exp: The Dashavatara temple at Deogarh (Uttar Pradesh) is a Gupta-period shrine and one of the earliest surviving examples of the Nagara style with a shikhara.

questions.q: The imperial Chola line of Thanjavur was revived in the 9th century CE by
questions.exp: Vijayalaya (c. 850 CE) captured Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyars, ending Pallava-Pandya dominance. His successors Aditya I and Parantaka I consolidated the kingdom.

questions.q: The Brihadeshwara (Rajarajeshwara) temple at Thanjavur was built by
questions.exp: Rajaraja I consecrated it in 1010 CE; its vimana is among the tallest in India. With the temples at Gangaikonda Cholapuram and Darasuram it forms the UNESCO 'Great Living Chola Temples'.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Rajendra I:
I. He took the title Gangaikondachola after his campaign towards the Ganga.
II. He despatched a naval expedition against the Srivijaya kingdom (Kadaram).
III. He built the Brihadeshwara temple at Thanjavur.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The Thanjavur temple was built by his father Rajaraja I; Rajendra I built his own great temple at his new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram.

questions.q: The Uttaramerur inscriptions, which describe in detail the working of the Chola village assembly, belong to the reign of
questions.exp: Dated to about 920 CE, they have been called a written constitution for the village assembly, prescribing qualifications, disqualifications and the term of office of committee members.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Chola local self-government:
I. The Sabha was the assembly of a brahmadeya village.
II. Members of the village committees (variyams) were selected by lot under the kudavolai system.
III. The Nagaram was the assembly of non-Brahmin landholding cultivators.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The Nagaram was the assembly of merchants; the assembly of ordinary non-Brahmin landholders was the Ur. Under kudavolai, name-tickets were drawn from a pot by a young boy.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Dynasty)   List-II (Capital)
A. Hoysalas    1. Warangal
B. Kakatiyas    2. Dwarasamudra
C. Chalukyas of Kalyani    3. Manyakheta
D. Rashtrakutas    4. Kalyani
questions.exp: Dwarasamudra is the modern Halebidu in Karnataka; Warangal (Orugallu) is in present-day Telangana; Manyakheta is modern Malkhed.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the Kakatiya dynasty is NOT correct?
opts: Its capital was Warangal (Orugallu) in present-day Telangana.
Rudramadevi, one of its rulers, was a woman whose rule Marco Polo praised.
Prataparudra II was defeated by the forces of the Delhi Sultanate.
The dynasty was finally overthrown by the Hoysala ruler Vishnuvardhana.
questions.exp: The Kakatiyas fell to the Delhi Sultanate in 1323, not to the Hoysalas. The Ramappa (Rudreshwara) temple at Palampet, built under Ganapatideva, was inscribed by UNESCO in 2021.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the Hoysalas is NOT correct?
opts: Their capital Dwarasamudra is the modern Halebidu.
Vishnuvardhana built the Chennakeshava temple at Belur.
Their temples are the finest examples of the Vesara style.
Their ruler Ballala III defeated Malik Kafur and preserved the kingdom intact.
questions.exp: Malik Kafur sacked Dwarasamudra in 1311 and Ballala III was repeatedly forced into submission. The 'Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas' at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the early kingdoms of the far south:
I. The Pandya capital was Madurai and their chief port was Korkai.
II. The Chera capital was Vanji and their chief port was Muziris.
III. The royal emblem of the Pallavas was the fish.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The fish was the Pandya emblem; the Chola emblem was the tiger and the Chera emblem the bow and arrow.

chapters.title: Ancient Indian Art, Science and the Indian Knowledge & Value System
factsheet: Stupa parts — medhi (drum/base), anda (hemispherical dome), harmika (railed square above the dome), yashti (mast), chhatra (umbrella tiers), vedika (railing), torana (gateway), pradakshina patha (circumambulatory path).

Bharhut stupa (Satna, Madhya Pradesh) — railings c. 125-100 BCE, torana c. 100-75 BCE, Shunga period; chief donor King Dhanabhuti; discovered by Alexander Cunningham in 1873; sculptures now in the Indian Museum, Kolkata.

Sanchi (Raisen, MP) — original brick stupa by Ashoka; doubled in size and cased in stone under the Shungas; four carved toranas added under the Satavahanas; Ashokan pillar there carries the Schism Edict; UNESCO site 1989.
Amaravati stupa (Andhra Pradesh) — on the Krishna river, Satavahana period, white limestone ('Palnad marble'); Amaravati school of sculpture. Sarnath's Dhamek stupa is Gupta period.

Ajanta (Aurangabad, Maharashtra) — 30 caves, exclusively Buddhist, in the Waghora river gorge; phase I Satavahana/Hinayana, phase II under Vakataka Harisena (c. 460-480 CE); rediscovered 1819 by Captain John Smith; UNESCO 1983.
Ajanta paintings: Padmapani and Vajrapani Bodhisattvas in Cave 1; Mahajanaka and Chhadanta Jataka scenes; tempera on a lime-plaster ground (not true fresco).
Ellora (Maharashtra) — 34 caves: Caves 1-12 Buddhist, 13-29 Hindu, 30-34 Jain; Cave 16 is Krishna I's monolithic Kailasa temple; Cave 10 Vishvakarma chaitya; UNESCO 1983.

Other rock-cut sites: Karle (largest chaitya hall, Maharashtra, Satavahana), Bhaja and Bedsa, Bagh caves (MP, painted), Barabar caves (Bihar, Ashoka, gifted to the Ajivikas), Udayagiri-Khandagiri (Odisha, Kharavela, Hathigumpha inscription), Udayagiri near Vidisha (Gupta, Varaha panel), Elephanta (Trimurti).

Temple styles — Nagara (North; curvilinear shikhara, no boundary walls or gateways), Dravida (South; pyramidal vimana inside a walled enclosure with towering gopurams), Vesara (Deccan hybrid; Chalukyas of Kalyani and Hoysalas).

Nagara sub-types: Latina/rekha-prasada, Phamsana, Valabhi; Odisha idiom uses deul (shikhara) and jagamohana (assembly hall); Khajuraho by the Chandelas; Modhera Sun temple and Dilwara by the Solankis.

Sculpture schools — Gandhara: grey schist, Greco-Roman/Hellenistic realism, wavy hair, patron Kushanas; Mathura: spotted red sandstone, indigenous idiom, first Buddha images alongside Gandhara; Amaravati: white limestone, narrative panels, Satavahana.
Gupta art: Sarnath Buddha (Dharmachakra-pravartana), Dashavatara temple Deogarh, Bhitargaon brick temple, Sultanganj bronze Buddha, Ajanta Cave 16/17 paintings.

Coinage: punch-marked karshapana (earliest); Indo-Greeks first issued coins bearing the king's portrait and name; Kushanas issued the first large gold coins; Gupta gold coin = dinara; Gupta silver began after the Shaka conquest.
Aryabhata (b. 476 CE) — Aryabhatiya, 499 CE; earth rotates on its axis; eclipses caused by shadows, not Rahu-Ketu; value of pi as 3.1416; place-value system.
Varahamihira (6th century) — Brihat Samhita (encyclopaedic), Panchasiddhantika (five astronomical systems), Brihat Jataka (astrology); one of Chandragupta II's 'Navaratna'.

Brahmagupta — Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 CE), first systematic rules for arithmetic with zero and negative numbers; Khandakhadyaka. Bhaskara II — Siddhanta Shiromani, whose four parts include Lilavati and Bijaganita.

Medicine: Charaka Samhita (medicine; Charaka traditionally at Kanishka's court), Sushruta Samhita (surgery; rhinoplasty, cataract, 8 branches of Ayurveda), Vagbhata's Ashtanga Hridaya, Nagarjuna's Rasaratnakara (alchemy/metallurgy).
Metallurgy: the Mehrauli iron pillar in the Qutb complex, Delhi, bears a Sanskrit praise of King Chandra (identified with Chandragupta II) and has resisted rust for about 1600 years.
Sulbasutras (part of the Kalpa Vedanga) contain the earliest Indian geometry, developed for the construction of Vedic fire altars.
Purushartha — the four aims of life: Dharma, Artha, Kama, Moksha. Dharma regulates the pursuit of Artha and Kama; Moksha is the ultimate goal.
Ashrama — four stages, ideally 25 years each: Brahmacharya (student), Grihastha (householder), Vanaprastha (forest-dweller), Sannyasa (renunciant). Grihastha supports all the others.

Varna — the fourfold order first mentioned in the Purusha Sukta of the tenth mandala of the Rigveda: Brahmana (mouth), Kshatriya (arms), Vaishya (thighs), Shudra (feet). Varna is fourfold and theoretical; jati is the local birth-group and runs into thousands.

Shodasha Samskara — the 16 sacraments, laid down in the Grihya Sutras: Garbhadhana, Pumsavana, Simantonnayana, Jatakarma, Namakarana, Nishkramana, Annaprashana, Chudakarana, Karnavedha, Vidyarambha, Upanayana, Vedarambha, Keshanta, Samavartana, Vivaha, Antyeshti.

Key sanskaras: Namakarana (naming, 10th-12th day), Nishkramana (first outing), Annaprashana (first solid food, ~6 months), Chudakarana (tonsure), Upanayana (sacred thread, entry to studentship), Samavartana (graduation), Antyeshti (last rites, the only posthumous one).
Rina (debts) — three, from the Taittiriya Samhita: Deva-rina (repaid by yajna), Rishi/Brahma-rina (repaid by svadhyaya, study and teaching), Pitri-rina (repaid by raising progeny).

Pancha Mahayajna, the householder's five daily duties — Brahma yajna (study), Deva yajna (offering to gods), Pitri yajna (to ancestors), Bhuta yajna (to all beings), Nri/Manushya yajna (hospitality to guests).
Shad-darshana (six astika schools) with founders: Nyaya-Gautama (Akshapada), Vaisheshika-Kanada, Samkhya-Kapila, Yoga-Patanjali, Purva Mimamsa-Jaimini, Uttara Mimamsa/Vedanta-Badarayana.

Darshana core ideas: Nyaya's four pramanas (pratyaksha, anumana, upamana, shabda); Vaisheshika's paramanuvada (atomism) and padarthas; Samkhya's Purusha-Prakriti dualism and 25 tattvas; Patanjali's ashtanga yoga; Mimamsa on ritual (dharma); Vedanta on Brahman. Nastika schools: Charvaka, Buddhism, Jainism.

Ancient centres of learning — Takshashila (Gandhara; Panini, Chanakya, Charaka, Jivaka), Nalanda (founded under Kumaragupta I; head Shilabhadra; Xuanzang and I-tsing studied there; sacked by Bakhtiyar Khalji c. 1193; UNESCO 2016), Vikramshila and Somapura (Dharmapala), Odantapuri (Gopala), Valabhi (Maitrakas of Gujarat).
Vedangas, the six limbs of Vedic study — Shiksha (phonetics), Kalpa (ritual), Vyakarana (grammar; Panini's Ashtadhyayi), Nirukta (etymology; Yaska), Chhanda (metre), Jyotisha (astronomy).

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Part of a stupa)   List-II (Description)
A. Anda    1. Railed square platform above the dome
B. Harmika    2. Hemispherical dome
C. Yashti    3. Gateway
D. Torana    4. Central mast bearing the umbrellas
questions.exp: The medhi is the drum on which the anda rests, the vedika is the surrounding railing, and the path between them is the pradakshina patha.

questions.q: The Bharhut stupa was discovered in 1873 by
questions.exp: Alexander Cunningham, the first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India, located the Bharhut stupa in Satna district, Madhya Pradesh. Its railings and gateway were removed to the Indian Museum, Kolkata.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Great Stupa at Sanchi:
I. The original brick stupa was built by Ashoka.
II. It was enlarged and encased in dressed stone during the Shunga period.
III. The four carved gateways (toranas) were added under the Satavahanas.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Sanchi is in Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh, and was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1989. Its Ashokan pillar carries the Schism Edict warning against division in the sangha.

questions.q: The railings and gateway of the Bharhut stupa are assigned to which period, and its principal donor named in an inscription was
questions.exp: The Bharhut railings date to about 125-100 BCE and the torana slightly later. The reliefs carry labels in Brahmi identifying Jataka scenes, making them among the earliest 'captioned' narrative art in India.

questions.q: The Amaravati stupa, noted for its white limestone narrative panels, is situated on the banks of which river?
questions.exp: Amaravati in Andhra Pradesh flourished under the Satavahanas. Its sculptural idiom, using the local 'Palnad marble', forms the third great early school alongside Gandhara and Mathura.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a stupa site and its present-day state is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Sarnath, where the Dhamek stupa stands, is near Varanasi in Uttar Pradesh. The Dhamek stupa in its present form is a Gupta-period structure.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Ajanta caves:
I. All the surviving caves at Ajanta are Buddhist.
II. The second phase of excavation took place under the patronage of the Vakataka ruler Harisena.
III. The caves are cut into a gorge of the Waghora river.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Ajanta has 30 caves in Aurangabad district, Maharashtra, and was inscribed by UNESCO in 1983. Unlike Ellora, it has no Hindu or Jain excavations.

questions.q: The Ajanta caves were brought to modern notice in 1819 by
opts: Captain John Smith of the British army
questions.exp: Captain John Smith came upon them while on a tiger hunt and left his name scratched on a pillar of Cave 10.

questions.q: The celebrated paintings of the Bodhisattvas Padmapani and Vajrapani are found in which cave at Ajanta?
questions.exp: Both flank the shrine doorway in Cave 1, a Vakataka-period vihara. The Ajanta paintings were executed in tempera on a lime-plaster ground rather than as true fresco.

questions.q: The 34 caves at Ellora are distributed among the religions as follows:
questions.exp: Caves 1-12 are Buddhist, 13-29 Hindu and 30-34 Jain. Cave 16 is the monolithic Kailasa temple; Ellora is unique in housing all three faiths at one site.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Rock-cut site)   List-II (State)
A. Bagh caves    1. Odisha
B. Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves    2. Bihar
C. Barabar caves    3. Maharashtra
D. Karle chaitya    4. Madhya Pradesh
questions.exp: Karle has the largest rock-cut chaitya hall in India. The Barabar caves in Bihar were excavated under Ashoka and granted to the Ajivika sect.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Temple style)   List-II (Characteristic)
A. Nagara    1. Hybrid form associated with the Hoysalas
B. Dravida    2. Curvilinear shikhara, usually without a boundary wall
C. Vesara    3. Pyramidal vimana within a walled enclosure with gopurams
