questions.exp: The Nagara style dominates north India, the Dravida the Tamil country, and the Vesara the Deccan under the Chalukyas of Kalyani and the Hoysalas.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the early schools of Indian sculpture:
I. The Gandhara school worked mainly in grey schist and shows strong Hellenistic influence.
II. The Mathura school used spotted red sandstone and developed an indigenous idiom.
III. The Amaravati school is characterised by the use of black basalt.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Amaravati sculpture is in white limestone, often called Palnad marble. All three schools flourished largely in the Kushana and Satavahana centuries.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about Gupta-period art is NOT correct?
opts: The seated Buddha of Sarnath depicts the Dharmachakra-pravartana mudra.
The Dashavatara temple at Deogarh is an early example of the Nagara style.
The Bhitargaon temple is a Gupta brick temple.
The Trimurti sculpture at Elephanta is the finest example of Gupta workmanship.
questions.exp: The Elephanta caves near Mumbai, with the celebrated Trimurti (Sadashiva), belong to the post-Gupta period and are usually attributed to Kalachuri or early Chalukya patronage.

questions.q: The Aryabhatiya, written in 499 CE, was composed by
questions.exp: Aryabhata was born in 476 CE and worked at Kusumapura (Pataliputra). The Aryabhatiya is in four sections and is written in terse Sanskrit verse.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Aryabhata:
I. He held that the apparent daily motion of the stars is caused by the rotation of the earth on its axis.
II. He explained eclipses as the effect of shadows cast by the earth and the moon.
III. He gave the value of pi as approximately 3.1416.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: His rejection of the Rahu-Ketu explanation of eclipses and his statement of the earth's rotation were both radical departures from the orthodox astronomy of his day.

questions.q: The Brihat Samhita and the Panchasiddhantika were written by
questions.exp: Varahamihira, one of the 'Navaratna' traditionally associated with Chandragupta II, also wrote the Brihat Jataka. The Panchasiddhantika summarises five earlier astronomical systems.

questions.q: Which ancient Indian mathematician, in a work of 628 CE, gave the first systematic rules for arithmetic involving zero and negative numbers?
questions.exp: Brahmagupta's Brahmasphutasiddhanta treated zero as a number in its own right rather than a mere placeholder. He also wrote the Khandakhadyaka.

questions.q: The Lilavati and the Bijaganita are sections of which mathematical work?
questions.exp: Bhaskara II (12th century) wrote the Siddhanta Shiromani in four parts — Lilavati (arithmetic), Bijaganita (algebra), Grahaganita and Goladhyaya (astronomy).

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Text)   List-II (Author)
A. Sushruta Samhita    1. Vagbhata
B. Ashtanga Hridaya    2. Nagarjuna
C. Rasaratnakara    3. Charaka
D. Charaka Samhita    4. Sushruta
questions.exp: The Sushruta Samhita is the classic text of surgery, describing rhinoplasty and cataract operations; the Charaka Samhita is the classic text of internal medicine.

questions.q: The rust-resistant iron pillar in the Qutb complex at Mehrauli, Delhi, carries a Sanskrit inscription praising a king named
questions.exp: King Chandra is generally identified with Chandragupta II. The pillar has resisted corrosion for about 1600 years, a celebrated testimony to ancient Indian metallurgy.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: The Ashtanga Hridaya was written by Vagbhata. Sushruta's work is the Sushruta Samhita.

questions.q: The four Purusharthas, the aims of human life in the Indian tradition, are
questions.exp: Dharma regulates the pursuit of Artha (wealth) and Kama (desire), with Moksha as the final goal. The second option lists Jain vows and the fourth the four ashramas.

questions.q: The correct sequence of the four Ashramas of life is
questions.exp: Each stage was idealised as 25 years of a 100-year life. Entry into Brahmacharya was marked by the Upanayana sanskara and its completion by Samavartana.

questions.q: In the Ashrama scheme, which stage is regarded as the support of all the other three?
questions.exp: The householder alone produces wealth and food and performs the Pancha Mahayajna, sustaining students, forest-dwellers and renunciants. Manusmriti calls Grihastha the best of the ashramas for this reason.

questions.q: The earliest reference to the fourfold varna order occurs in which hymn of the Rigveda?
opts: Nasadiya Sukta of the tenth mandala
Purusha Sukta of the tenth mandala
Gayatri Mantra of the third mandala
Apri Sukta of the first mandala
questions.exp: The Purusha Sukta (Rigveda 10.90) derives the Brahmana from the mouth, the Kshatriya from the arms, the Vaishya from the thighs and the Shudra from the feet of the cosmic Purusha. The tenth mandala is a later addition to the Rigveda.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about varna and jati:
I. The varna order is fourfold, while jatis number in the thousands.
II. Jati is a locally defined birth-group associated with occupation and endogamy.
III. The varna order in the Vedic texts included the untouchable castes as a fifth varna.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Vedic literature recognises only four varnas; groups treated as untouchable stood outside the scheme and are described in later texts as avarna or panchama.

questions.q: According to the Grihya Sutras, the total number of sanskaras (sacraments) prescribed for an individual's life is
questions.exp: These are the Shodasha Samskara, running from Garbhadhana before conception to Antyeshti after death. They mark the passage from one stage of life to the next.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Sanskara)   List-II (Occasion)
A. Namakarana    1. First feeding of solid food
B. Annaprashana    2. Ceremonial tonsure of the head
C. Chudakarana    3. Naming of the child
D. Samavartana    4. Completion of studentship
questions.exp: Antyeshti, the funeral rite, is the sixteenth and only posthumous sanskara. Nishkramana marks the infant's first outing and Karnavedha the piercing of the ears.

questions.q: The sanskara that marked the investiture with the sacred thread and the beginning of formal education was
questions.exp: Upanayana admitted the boy to the Brahmacharya ashrama under a guru; the prescribed ages were traditionally eight for a Brahmana, eleven for a Kshatriya and twelve for a Vaishya. Vedarambha, the start of Vedic study proper, followed it.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the sanskaras:
I. Garbhadhana, Pumsavana and Simantonnayana are performed before birth.
II. Namakarana is normally performed on the tenth to twelfth day after birth.
III. Antyeshti is the sixteenth and last sanskara.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The sixteen sanskaras fall into prenatal, childhood, educational, marriage and funerary groups, of which Vivaha and Antyeshti are the last two.

questions.q: The three Rinas (debts) that a person is traditionally said to be born with are the debts to the
opts: gods, the sages and the ancestors
gods, the king and the guru
ancestors, the guests and all beings
sages, the guests and the gods
questions.exp: The Taittiriya Samhita names Deva-rina, Rishi (Brahma)-rina and Pitri-rina. Discharging them is one of the classic justifications of the householder's life.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the three Rinas:
I. Deva-rina is discharged by the performance of yajna.
II. Rishi-rina is discharged through svadhyaya, the study and transmission of the Vedas.
III. Pitri-rina is discharged by raising progeny and continuing the lineage.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The three debts explain why the tradition treats Grihastha as obligatory before renunciation. They correspond closely to three of the Pancha Mahayajna.

questions.q: Which one of the following is counted among the Pancha Mahayajna, the five daily duties of a householder?
questions.exp: The five great daily sacrifices are Brahma yajna (study), Deva yajna, Pitri yajna, Bhuta yajna (offering to all beings) and Nri or Manushya yajna (hospitality). Rajasuya, Vajapeya and Ashvamedha were royal sacrifices, not household duties.

questions.q: The six systems of orthodox Indian philosophy are collectively known as
questions.exp: They are called astika because they accept the authority of the Vedas. The nastika schools that reject it are Charvaka, Buddhism and Jainism.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Darshana)   List-II (Founder)
A. Nyaya    1. Kanada
B. Vaisheshika    2. Jaimini
C. Purva Mimamsa    3. Gautama
D. Vedanta    4. Badarayana
questions.exp: Samkhya is attributed to Kapila and Yoga to Patanjali. Vedanta, also called Uttara Mimamsa, is founded on Badarayana's Brahma Sutra.

questions.q: The dualism of Purusha (consciousness) and Prakriti (matter) is the central doctrine of which darshana?
questions.exp: Samkhya, attributed to Kapila and expounded in Ishvarakrishna's Samkhyakarika, is the oldest of the six systems and derives twenty-five tattvas from this dualism. Yoga adopts its metaphysics and adds Ishvara.

questions.q: The atomic theory (paramanuvada) and the doctrine of categories (padarthas) belong to which school of Indian philosophy?
questions.exp: Vaisheshika, founded by Kanada, holds that the material world is composed of indivisible eternal atoms. It is traditionally paired with Nyaya, whose strength is logic and epistemology.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Purva Mimamsa, founded by Jaimini, is concerned chiefly with the interpretation of Vedic ritual injunctions.
II. Uttara Mimamsa, or Vedanta, is based on Badarayana's Brahma Sutra.
III. Advaita, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita are sub-schools of Vedanta.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Advaita is associated with Shankaracharya, Vishishtadvaita with Ramanuja and Dvaita with Madhvacharya.

questions.q: The eight limbs (ashtanga) of yoga — yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana and samadhi — are set out in the
questions.exp: Patanjali's Yoga Sutras accept the Samkhya account of Purusha and Prakriti but add Ishvara and a practical discipline for liberation.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a darshana and its basic text is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: The Mimamsa Sutras belong to Jaimini's Purva Mimamsa. The classical text of Samkhya is Ishvarakrishna's Samkhyakarika.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Nalanda Mahavihara:
I. It was founded during the reign of the Gupta emperor Kumaragupta I.
II. Shilabhadra was its head when the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang studied there.
III. It was destroyed by the forces of Bakhtiyar Khalji towards the close of the 12th century.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Nalanda, in present-day Nalanda district of Bihar, was also patronised by Harshavardhana and the Palas. Its archaeological remains were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of an ancient centre of learning and its founder or patron dynasty is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Vikramshila — Dharmapala of the Pala dynasty
Odantapuri — Gopala of the Pala dynasty
questions.exp: Takshashila lay in Gandhara, in the north-west, far from the Maukhari domain; Panini, Chanakya, Charaka and the physician Jivaka are all associated with it.

questions.q: Which of the six Vedangas deals with grammar?
questions.exp: The six Vedangas are Shiksha (phonetics), Kalpa (ritual), Vyakarana (grammar), Nirukta (etymology), Chhanda (metre) and Jyotisha (astronomy). Panini's Ashtadhyayi is the classic work of Vyakarana and Yaska's Nirukta of etymology.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the classical Indian scheme, the Grihastha ashrama was regarded as indispensable rather than as a stage that could be skipped.
Reason (R): It is in the householder stage that the three Rinas — to the gods, the sages and the ancestors — are discharged.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.exp: The householder repays Deva-rina by yajna, Rishi-rina by study and teaching, and Pitri-rina by progeny; he also performs the Pancha Mahayajna that sustains the other ashramas.

chapters.title: Delhi Sultanate
factsheet: First Battle of Tarain (1191) — Prithviraj Chauhan III defeated Muhammad Ghori; Second Battle of Tarain (1192) — Ghori defeated Prithviraj; Battle of Chandawar (1194) — Ghori defeated Jaichandra of Kannauj.
Delhi Sultanate 1206-1526, five dynasties: Mamluk/Slave (1206-1290), Khalji (1290-1320), Tughlaq (1320-1414), Sayyid (1414-1451), Lodi (1451-1526).

Qutbuddin Aibak (1206-1210) — founder, called Lakh Baksh for his charity; began the Qutb Minar; built the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque at Delhi and the Adhai Din ka Jhonpra at Ajmer; died at Lahore falling from his horse while playing chaugan (polo).

Iltutmish (1211-1236) — the real consolidator; shifted the capital from Lahore to Delhi; created the Iqta system and the Turkan-i-Chahalgani (Chalisa, corps of forty); issued the silver tanka and copper jital; completed the Qutb Minar; received investiture from the Abbasid Caliph in 1229.
Raziya (1236-1240) — the only woman to rule the Delhi Sultanate; nominated by Iltutmish over his sons; elevated the Abyssinian Jamal-ud-din Yaqut as Amir-i-Akhur; overthrown by the Turkish nobility.

Balban (1266-1287) — theory of kingship as Zill-i-Ilahi (Shadow of God); introduced sijda (prostration) and paibos (kissing the feet) and the Persian Nauroz; destroyed the Chalisa; 'blood and iron' policy; created the Diwan-i-Arz (military department) and an espionage network of barids.
Khalji dynasty founded by Jalaluddin Firoz Khalji (1290); his nephew and son-in-law Alauddin raided Devagiri in 1296 and then seized the throne.

Alauddin Khalji (1296-1316) — first Sultan to attempt systematic price control; markets: the grain mandi, the Sarai Adl for cloth and manufactures, a market for horses/slaves/cattle, and a general market.

Market-control officials — Diwan-i-Riyasat (controller of markets), Shahna-i-Mandi (superintendent of the grain market), barids (intelligence officers) and munhiyans (secret spies) reporting directly to the Sultan; principal source is Ziauddin Barani's Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi.

Alauddin's revenue reforms — kharaj raised to 50% of produce, assessed by measurement (masahat) on the yield per biswa; house tax (ghari) and grazing tax (charai) added; privileges of khuts, muqaddams and chaudharis abolished; Diwan-i-Mustakhraj created to recover arrears; milk, inam and waqf grants resumed.
Alauddin's conquests — Gujarat 1299, Ranthambore 1301 (Hammiradeva), Chittor 1303, Malwa 1305; Malik Kafur's Deccan campaigns against Devagiri, Warangal, Dwarasamudra and Madurai.
Alauddin built the Alai Darwaza (1311), the Siri fort and Hauz-i-Alai (Hauz Khas); the Alai Minar was left unfinished. Amir Khusrau, 'Tuti-i-Hind', wrote Khazain-ul-Futuh and Qiran-us-Sadain.
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq (1320-1325) founded the dynasty and built Tughlaqabad; Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325-1351); Firoz Shah Tughlaq (1351-1388).

Muhammad bin Tughlaq's experiments — increase of taxation in the Doab, transfer of the capital to Devagiri (renamed Daulatabad), introduction of a token currency in copper/brass, the Khurasan project and the Qarachil expedition; Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi created to promote agriculture.
Ibn Battuta, the Moroccan traveller, was made qazi of Delhi by Muhammad bin Tughlaq and sent as envoy to China; his account is the Rihla.

Firoz Shah Tughlaq — dug the largest canal network of the Sultanate; levied four taxes on the Islamic model (kharaj, zakat, jizya, khams) and added the irrigation cess haqq-i-sharb at one-tenth; first to impose jizya on Brahmanas; founded Firozabad, Hisar, Fatehabad and Jaunpur; set up Diwan-i-Khairat (charity) and Dar-ul-Shafa (free hospital); brought Ashokan pillars from Topra and Meerut to Delhi; his memoir is the Futuhat-i-Firozshahi.
Timur invaded and sacked Delhi in 1398 during the reign of Nasiruddin Mahmud Tughlaq.
Sayyid dynasty founded by Khizr Khan (1414), Timur's deputy at Multan; last ruler Alam Shah. Lodi dynasty founded by Bahlul Lodi (1451) — the first Afghan dynasty of Delhi.

Sikandar Lodi founded the city of Agra in 1504, introduced the Gaz-i-Sikandari measure and wrote Persian verse under the pen-name Gulrukhi; Ibrahim Lodi was defeated and killed by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat, 21 April 1526.
Central departments — Diwan-i-Wizarat (finance, under the Wazir), Diwan-i-Arz (military), Diwan-i-Insha (correspondence), Diwan-i-Risalat (religious affairs/appeals), Diwan-i-Qaza (justice).

Iqta — a revenue assignment, not land ownership; the holder was the muqti or iqtadar, obliged to maintain troops and remit the surplus (fawazil); formalised by Iltutmish, made transferable and audited under Alauddin and Firoz Shah made it hereditary.

Provincial kingdoms — Jaunpur under the Sharqis (Atala Masjid; called the 'Shiraz of the East'), Bengal, Malwa (Mandu, Jahaz Mahal), Gujarat (Ahmad Shah founded Ahmedabad), Kashmir under Zain-ul-Abidin, 'Budshah'.

Vijayanagara founded in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty, traditionally inspired by the sage Vidyaranya; capital Hampi on the Tungabhadra. Four dynasties: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu.

Krishnadevaraya (1509-1529) of the Tuluva dynasty — titles Andhra Bhoja and Abhinava Bhoja; wrote Amuktamalyada in Telugu and Jambavati Kalyanam in Sanskrit; built the Vitthalaswamy and Hazara Rama temples at Hampi and the town of Nagalapuram.

Ashtadiggajas, the eight Telugu poets of Krishnadevaraya's court — Allasani Peddana ('Andhra Kavita Pitamaha', Manucharitramu/Swarochisha Manu Sambhavam), Nandi Thimmana (Parijatapaharanam), Tenali Ramakrishna, Dhurjati, Madayyagari Mallana, Ayyalaraju Ramabhadrudu, Pingali Surana, Ramarajabhushanudu. The Kannada poet Mallanarya was also patronised by him.

Vijayanagara administration — the Nayankara system of military assignments and the Ayagar system of twelve hereditary village functionaries; foreign visitors Nicolo Conti, Abdur Razzaq, Domingo Paes, Fernao Nuniz and Duarte Barbosa.
Battle of Talikota (Rakshasa-Tangadi), 1565 — the allied Deccan sultanates defeated Rama Raya and sacked Hampi; the Aravidu dynasty then ruled from Penukonda and Chandragiri.

Bahmani kingdom founded 1347 by Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu); first capital Gulbarga, shifted to Bidar by Ahmad Shah Wali; Mahmud Gawan was wazir under Muhammad Shah III, divided the kingdom into eight tarafs, built the madrasa at Bidar, and was executed in 1481.
Bahmani successor states — Adil Shahi (Bijapur), Nizam Shahi (Ahmadnagar), Imad Shahi (Berar), Qutb Shahi (Golconda) and Barid Shahi (Bidar).

questions.q: In the Second Battle of Tarain (1192), Muhammad Ghori defeated
questions.exp: Prithviraj Chauhan III had defeated Ghori at the First Battle of Tarain in 1191. Two years later, in 1194, Ghori defeated Jaichandra of Kannauj at the Battle of Chandawar.

questions.q: The founder of the Delhi Sultanate, who is known in the chronicles as 'Lakh Baksh' for his lavish charity, was
questions.exp: Qutbuddin Aibak ruled 1206-1210 from Lahore and died there after falling from his horse during a game of chaugan (polo).

questions.q: The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque at Delhi and the Adhai Din ka Jhonpra at Ajmer were built by
questions.exp: Both were raised by Aibak from the materials of demolished temples and are the earliest surviving Indo-Islamic buildings in India. Aibak also began the Qutb Minar, which Iltutmish completed.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Iltutmish:
I. He organised the Turkan-i-Chahalgani, the corps of forty nobles.
II. He introduced the silver tanka and the copper jital.
III. He received a letter of investiture from the Abbasid Caliph in 1229.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Iltutmish also shifted the capital from Lahore to Delhi, gave the Iqta system its regular form, and completed the Qutb Minar.

questions.q: The only woman ever to sit on the throne of the Delhi Sultanate was
questions.exp: Raziya (1236-1240) was nominated by her father Iltutmish in preference to his sons. Her elevation of the Abyssinian Jamal-ud-din Yaqut as Amir-i-Akhur antagonised the Turkish nobility.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Balban:
I. He described the Sultan as Zill-i-Ilahi, the Shadow of God on earth.
II. He introduced the court practices of sijda and paibos.
III. He strengthened the Turkan-i-Chahalgani to secure the support of the nobility.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Balban systematically destroyed the Chalisa rather than strengthening it. He also revived the Persian Nauroz at court and reorganised the Diwan-i-Arz.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Ruler)   List-II (Associated with)
A. Qutbuddin Aibak    1. Blood and iron policy
B. Iltutmish    2. Adhai Din ka Jhonpra
C. Raziya    3. Silver tanka
D. Balban    4. Amir-i-Akhur Yaqut
questions.exp: Balban's 'blood and iron' policy was directed against internal rebels and the Turkish nobility alike.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the Slave (Mamluk) dynasty is NOT correct?
opts: Qutbuddin Aibak made Lahore his principal seat of government.
Iltutmish shifted the capital of the Sultanate to Delhi.
Balban was the last ruler of the dynasty.
Nasiruddin Mahmud ruled while Balban held effective power as his deputy.
questions.exp: The last Mamluk ruler was Muiz-ud-din Kaiqubad, after whose fall the Khaljis took power in 1290. Balban ruled 1266-1287.

questions.q: The Khalji dynasty of Delhi was founded in 1290 by
questions.exp: Jalaluddin Firoz Khalji was murdered in 1296 by his nephew and son-in-law Alauddin, who had just returned from a plundering raid on Devagiri.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the market control system of Alauddin Khalji:
I. The officer in overall charge of the markets was the Diwan-i-Riyasat.
II. The grain market was supervised by the Shahna-i-Mandi.
III. Barids and munhiyans reported on the working of the markets directly to the Sultan.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Alauddin fixed prices for grain, cloth, horses, slaves and cattle, banned hoarding and regrating, and registered merchants and carriers. The chief aim was to maintain a large standing army at low cost against Mongol invasions.

questions.q: Our fullest account of Alauddin Khalji's market regulations comes from which contemporary or near-contemporary work?
questions.exp: Barani wrote about half a century after Alauddin's death and set out the regulations as a connected series. Amir Khusrau's Khazain-ul-Futuh corroborates parts of the account.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the revenue reforms of Alauddin Khalji:
I. He raised the land tax (kharaj) to half the produce.
II. Revenue was assessed by measurement of the cultivated area and the yield per biswa.
III. He confirmed the traditional privileges of the khuts, muqaddams and chaudharis.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Alauddin abolished the intermediaries' privileges and made them pay at the same rate as ordinary cultivators. He also levied a house tax (ghari) and a grazing tax (charai) and set up the Diwan-i-Mustakhraj to recover arrears.

questions.q:
Arrange the following conquests of Alauddin Khalji in correct chronological order:
I. Chittor
II. Gujarat
III. Malwa
IV. Ranthambore
questions.exp: Gujarat 1299, Ranthambore 1301 (defeat of Hammiradeva), Chittor 1303 and Malwa 1305. The Deccan was then overrun by his general Malik Kafur.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about Alauddin Khalji is NOT correct?
opts: He built the Alai Darwaza and the fort of Siri.
He left the Alai Minar unfinished.
He was the first Sultan to shift the capital of the Sultanate to Daulatabad.
His general Malik Kafur led campaigns as far south as Madurai.
questions.exp: The transfer of the capital to Devagiri, renamed Daulatabad, was an experiment of Muhammad bin Tughlaq, not of Alauddin Khalji.

questions.q: The Tughlaq dynasty was founded in 1320 by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, who also built the fortified city of
questions.exp: Tughlaqabad was the third of Delhi's medieval cities. Jahanpanah was built by Muhammad bin Tughlaq and Firozabad by Firoz Shah Tughlaq.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the experiments of Muhammad bin Tughlaq:
I. He increased the rate of taxation in the Doab.
II. He transferred the capital from Delhi to Devagiri, which he renamed Daulatabad.
III. He set up the Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi to promote agriculture.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: His other two much-discussed projects were the token currency and the Khurasan and Qarachil expeditions. Barani, hostile to the Sultan, is the main source for all of them.

questions.q: The token currency introduced by Muhammad bin Tughlaq failed chiefly because
opts: the coins were made of gold that was quickly hoarded
the coins were easily and widely counterfeited
foreign merchants refused to accept any Indian coinage
the mints could not produce them in sufficient numbers
questions.exp: The tokens were of copper and brass but circulated at the value of silver; since the state did not monopolise their manufacture, forgery became widespread and the Sultan had to redeem them in silver.

questions.q: Muhammad bin Tughlaq shifted his capital from Delhi to
questions.exp: Devagiri was renamed Daulatabad. The move was intended to give better control over the Deccan, but the hardship of the migration and the shortage of water forced its abandonment.

questions.q: The Moroccan traveller who was appointed qazi of Delhi by Muhammad bin Tughlaq and later sent as his envoy to China was
questions.exp: Ibn Battuta's travel account is the Rihla. Abdur Razzaq was a Persian envoy to Vijayanagara and Nicolo Conti an Italian traveller there.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Firoz Shah Tughlaq:
I. He was the first Sultan of Delhi to levy jizya on Brahmanas.
II. He imposed an irrigation cess called haqq-i-sharb on lands watered by his canals.
III. He had two Ashokan pillars brought to Delhi from Topra and Meerut.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Firoz Shah also founded Firozabad, Hisar, Fatehabad and Jaunpur, and established the Diwan-i-Khairat and the free hospital Dar-ul-Shafa. His memoir is the Futuhat-i-Firozshahi.

questions.q: Delhi was invaded and sacked by Timur in the year
questions.exp: The invasion came during the reign of Nasiruddin Mahmud Tughlaq and shattered what remained of Tughlaq authority. Timur's deputy at Multan, Khizr Khan, later founded the Sayyid dynasty.

questions.q: The Sayyid dynasty of Delhi was founded in 1414 by
questions.exp: Khizr Khan had been Timur's governor of Multan and never assumed the title of Sultan, ruling nominally as a deputy. The last Sayyid ruler was Alam Shah.

questions.q: The Lodi dynasty, the first Afghan dynasty to rule Delhi, was founded by
questions.exp: Bahlul Lodi took the throne in 1451 after displacing the last Sayyid ruler. His son Sikandar Lodi founded Agra in 1504.

questions.q: The city of Agra was founded in 1504 by the Sultan of Delhi
questions.exp: Sikandar Lodi shifted his capital there, introduced the Gaz-i-Sikandari as a standard measure and wrote Persian verse under the pen-name Gulrukhi.

questions.q: The Delhi Sultanate came to an end when Ibrahim Lodi was defeated and killed at
questions.exp: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat on 21 April 1526, using field artillery and the tulughma tactic. Khanwa (1527) was against Rana Sanga and Ghaghra (1529) against the Afghans of Bihar and Bengal.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Department)   List-II (Function)
A. Diwan-i-Wizarat    1. Military affairs
B. Diwan-i-Arz    2. Royal correspondence
C. Diwan-i-Insha    3. Finance and revenue
D. Diwan-i-Risalat    4. Religious matters and appeals
questions.exp: The Wazir headed the Diwan-i-Wizarat and was the chief minister. Justice was administered through the Diwan-i-Qaza under the Sadr-us-Sudur and the Qazi-ul-Quzat.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Iqta system of the Delhi Sultanate:
I. The iqta was an assignment of revenue and not a grant of proprietary rights in land.
II. The holder of an iqta, called the muqti, was required to maintain troops from its income.
III. Iqtas were made hereditary by Alauddin Khalji.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Alauddin tightened control over iqtas and audited accounts strictly; it was Firoz Shah Tughlaq who allowed iqtas to become hereditary. The surplus that a muqti had to remit to the centre was called fawazil.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Tax)   List-II (Nature)
A. Kharaj    1. Tax on non-Muslims
B. Zakat    2. State share of the spoils of war
C. Jizya    3. Land tax
D. Khams    4. Religious tax on Muslims
questions.exp: Firoz Shah Tughlaq confined state levies to these four Islamic taxes and added only the irrigation cess haqq-i-sharb. The state's share of war booty (khams) was usually one-fifth.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Provincial kingdom)   List-II (Ruler or feature)
A. Jaunpur    1. Zain-ul-Abidin, called Budshah
B. Kashmir    2. Ahmad Shah, founder of Ahmedabad
C. Gujarat    3. Jahaz Mahal at Mandu
D. Malwa    4. Sharqi dynasty and the Atala Masjid
questions.exp: Jaunpur under the Sharqis was called the 'Shiraz of the East' for its learning. Zain-ul-Abidin of Kashmir is remembered for religious tolerance and for encouraging shawl weaving and papier mache.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the provincial kingdoms of the Sultanate period is NOT correct?
opts: Jaunpur was ruled by the Sharqi dynasty.
Ahmedabad was founded by Ahmad Shah of Gujarat.
Mandu was the capital of the Sultans of Malwa.
Zain-ul-Abidin was a ruler of Bengal.
questions.exp: Zain-ul-Abidin, popularly called Budshah, ruled Kashmir in the fifteenth century. Bengal's most notable independent ruler of the period was Alauddin Husain Shah.

questions.q:
Arrange the following dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate in correct chronological order:
I. Sayyid
II. Khalji
III. Tughlaq
IV. Lodi
The Vijayanagara empire was founded in 1336 by
questions.exp: The brothers Harihara and Bukka founded the Sangama dynasty, traditionally at the inspiration of the sage Vidyaranya. Their capital Hampi stood on the Tungabhadra.

questions.q: The Telugu work Amuktamalyada was composed by
questions.exp: Krishnadevaraya (1509-1529) of the Tuluva dynasty wrote Amuktamalyada in Telugu and Jambavati Kalyanam in Sanskrit, and bore the title Andhra Bhoja.

questions.q: The poet of Krishnadevaraya's court who bore the title 'Andhra Kavita Pitamaha' was
questions.exp: Allasani Peddana, first among the Ashtadiggajas, wrote Manucharitramu, also called Swarochisha Manu Sambhavam. Krishnadevaraya is said to have honoured him with the Kanakabhishekam.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Poet of the Ashtadiggajas)   List-II (Work)
A. Allasani Peddana    1. Parijatapaharanam
B. Nandi Thimmana    2. Panduranga Mahatmyamu
C. Tenali Ramakrishna    3. Raghavapandaveeyamu
D. Pingali Surana    4. Manucharitramu
questions.exp: The Ashtadiggajas, the 'eight elephants of the quarters', were the eight Telugu poets of Krishnadevaraya's court. Their age is regarded as the classical age of Telugu literature.

questions.q: Mallanarya, a poet patronised by Krishnadevaraya, composed his works in which language?
questions.exp: Krishnadevaraya's patronage extended beyond Telugu: the Kannada poet Mallanarya of Gubbi and Sanskrit scholars also flourished at his court, and he wrote in Sanskrit himself.

questions.q: In the Battle of Talikota (1565), the allied Deccan sultanates defeated the Vijayanagara forces commanded by
questions.exp: Rama Raya, the effective ruler behind the nominal king Sadashiva Raya, was killed and Hampi was sacked. Tirumala then founded the Aravidu dynasty, ruling from Penukonda.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the Vijayanagara empire is NOT correct?
opts: Its capital Hampi stood on the Tungabhadra river.
Nayankara was a system of assigning territory to military chiefs.
Abdur Razzaq and Domingo Paes left accounts of the empire.
It was ruled successively by the Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Bahmani dynasties.
questions.exp: The four Vijayanagara dynasties were Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu. The Bahmani kingdom was Vijayanagara's rival in the Deccan, not one of its dynasties.

questions.q: The Bahmani kingdom was founded in 1347 by
questions.exp: Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah, better known as Hasan Gangu, rebelled against Muhammad bin Tughlaq. Gulbarga was the first capital; Ahmad Shah Wali later moved it to Bidar.

questions.q: Mahmud Gawan, who divided the Bahmani kingdom into eight tarafs and built a celebrated madrasa at Bidar, served as wazir under
questions.exp: Gawan, a Persian merchant by origin, was executed in 1481 on a forged charge of treason; the kingdom broke up soon afterwards into the five Deccan sultanates.

chapters.title: Mughal Empire and the Marathas
factsheet: First Battle of Panipat, 21 April 1526 - Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi; first large-scale use of field artillery in India.
Khanwa 17 Mar 1527 (Rana Sanga), Chanderi 1528 (Medini Rai), Ghaghra 1529 (Afghans) - Babur takes the title Ghazi after Khanwa.
Babur's memoir Tuzuk-i-Baburi is in Chaghatai Turkish; Persian translation (Baburnama) by Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan.
Sher Shah Suri = Farid Khan; title 'Sher Khan' from Bahar Khan Lohani of Bihar. Chausa 1539, Kannauj/Bilgram 1540.
Sher Shah died 22 May 1545 at the siege of Kalinjar; tomb at Sasaram (Bihar) - octagonal, in an artificial lake, architect Aliwal Khan.
Sher Shah built the Purana Qila complex at Delhi with the Qila-i-Kuhna Masjid (1541) and Rohtasgarh fort; revived the Sadak-i-Azam (Grand Trunk Road).
Sher Shah's silver rupiya = 178 grains; copper coin = dam. Pargana officials: Shiqdar (law & order), Amin (assessment), Fotedar (treasurer), Karkun (clerk).
Humayun built Din Panah; died 1556 falling from the Sher Mandal staircase. Humayun-nama by Gulbadan Begum; Tazkirat-ul-Waqiat by Jauhar Aftabchi.
Second Battle of Panipat, 5 Nov 1556 - Bairam Khan defeats Hemu (Hemchandra Vikramaditya).
Akbar abolished the pilgrimage tax 1563 and jizya 1564; Ibadat Khana 1575; Mahzar 1579; Din-i-Ilahi (Tauhid-i-Ilahi) 1582 - Birbal the only Hindu adherent.
Mansabdari: zat = personal rank/status and pay; sawar = cavalry contingent. Du-aspa sih-aspa introduced by Jahangir.
Dahsala / Ain-i-Dahsala (Zabti), 1580, by Raja Todar Mal - averages produce and prices of the previous ten years; state share about one-third.
Other systems: Kankut (crop estimate), Ghalla-bakhshi/Batai (crop sharing), Nasaq (lump-sum on past collections).
Karori experiment 1574; khalisa = crown land, jagir = revenue assignment for salary, paibaqi = land reserved for future assignment.
Razmnama = Persian Mahabharata (Naqib Khan and others); Ramayana translated by Badauni; Lilavati by Faizi; Panchatantra as Ayar Danish by Abul Fazl.
Fatehpur Sikri founded 1571; Panch Mahal - five storeys, entirely columnar, 176 pillars. Buland Darwaza 1601, commemorating the Gujarat conquest.
Akbar created 12 subas in 1580 (15 by the end of the reign). Ain-i-Akbari = third volume of Abul Fazl's Akbarnama.
Central offices: Diwan-i-Ala (revenue), Mir Bakhshi (military pay/mansab), Mir Saman (household & karkhanas), Sadr-us-Sudur (charity & endowments), Qazi-ul-Quzat (justice).
Provincial: Subedar (suba), Faujdar (sarkar, law & order), Amil/Amalguzar (pargana revenue), Kotwal (city), Qanungo (records), Qazi (justice).
Jahangir: zanjir-i-adl at Agra Fort; Nur Jahan had coins struck in her name; Hawkins 1608, Sir Thomas Roe 1615-19.
War of succession: Dharmat (Apr 1658) - Samugarh (May 1658) - Khajwa (Jan 1659) - Deorai (1659).
Aurangzeb (Alamgir): jizya reimposed 1679; Bijapur annexed 1686, Golconda 1687; died 1707, buried at Khuldabad; Fatawa-i-Alamgiri compiled under him.
Nadir Shah defeated Muhammad Shah at Karnal, 1739, and carried off the Peacock Throne and the Kohinoor. Farrukhsiyar's farman of 1717 to the English Company.
Shivaji: Afzal Khan killed at Pratapgarh 1659; Shaista Khan attacked 1663; Surat sacked 1664 and 1670; Treaty of Purandar 1665 with Mirza Raja Jai Singh.
Shivaji crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad, 6 June 1674, by Gaga Bhatt; died 1680. Ashtapradhan of eight ministers; Chauth = 1/4, Sardeshmukhi = 1/10.
Peshwas: Balaji Vishwanath (1713, office made hereditary), Baji Rao I (Palkhed 1728), Balaji Baji Rao, Madhav Rao I, Baji Rao II (last).
Third Battle of Panipat, 14 Jan 1761 - Sadashivrao Bhau and Ibrahim Khan Gardi defeated by Ahmad Shah Abdali; Vishwasrao killed.
Confederacy: Gaekwad-Baroda, Holkar-Indore, Scindia-Gwalior, Bhonsle-Nagpur, Peshwa-Poona.

Anglo-Maratha Wars: I (1775-82, Treaty of Surat 1775, Convention of Wadgaon 1779, Treaty of Salbai 1782); II (1803-05, Treaty of Bassein 1802, Assaye 1803); III (1817-19, Peshwa deposed 1818, pensioned at Bithur).

questions.q: Babur's memoirs, the Tuzuk-i-Baburi, were originally composed in which language?
questions.exp: Babur wrote in his mother tongue, Chaghatai Turkish. Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan later rendered it into Persian as the Baburnama.

questions.q: Babur assumed the title of 'Ghazi' after his victory in the Battle of:
questions.exp: Khanwa (17 March 1527) was fought against Rana Sanga of Mewar, after which Babur took the title Ghazi. Panipat (1526) had been fought against Ibrahim Lodi.

questions.q: The battle of 1540 that finally drove Humayun out of India and made Sher Shah master of Delhi was fought at:
questions.exp: Sher Shah defeated Humayun at Kannauj, also called Bilgram, in 1540; the earlier defeat at Chausa was in 1539. Humayun regained Delhi only in 1555.

questions.q: Humayun died in 1556 after falling from the staircase of which structure?
opts: Sher Mandal in the Purana Qila
questions.exp: Humayun used the Sher Mandal octagonal pavilion inside the Purana Qila as his library and fell from its steps. He was succeeded by the thirteen-year-old Akbar.

questions.q: The Humayun-nama, an eyewitness account of Humayun's reign, was written by:
questions.exp: Gulbadan Begum, Babur's daughter and Humayun's half-sister, wrote the Humayun-nama at Akbar's request. Jauhar Aftabchi, Humayun's ewer-bearer, wrote the Tazkirat-ul-Waqiat.

questions.q: The original name of Sher Shah Suri was:
questions.exp: He was born Farid Khan, son of Hasan Khan Sur of Sasaram. The title 'Sher Khan' was conferred on him by Bahar Khan Lohani of Bihar.

questions.q: The tomb of Sher Shah Suri, built on an octagonal plan and standing in the middle of an artificial lake, is located at:
questions.exp: The mausoleum at Sasaram in Bihar is attributed to the architect Aliwal Khan and was completed in 1545. It is the finest example of Indo-Islamic architecture of the Sur period.

questions.q: The Qila-i-Kuhna Masjid, built by Sher Shah Suri, stands inside:
questions.exp: Sher Shah raised the Qila-i-Kuhna mosque in 1541 within the Purana Qila at Delhi. Its five-arched red sandstone facade is a landmark of pre-Mughal architecture.

questions.q: The silver coin introduced by Sher Shah Suri, weighing 178 grains, was called the:
questions.exp: Sher Shah standardised the silver rupiya at 178 grains; the corresponding copper coin was the dam. The rupiya is the direct ancestor of the modern rupee.

questions.q: Sher Shah Suri died in 1545 during the siege of which fort?
questions.exp: He was fatally injured by a gunpowder explosion at Kalinjar on 22 May 1545 and was succeeded by his son Islam Shah.

questions.q: The Second Battle of Panipat (1556) was fought between the Mughal forces led by Bairam Khan and:
questions.exp: Hemu, who had assumed the title Vikramaditya after capturing Delhi, was defeated and killed on 5 November 1556, securing Akbar's throne.

questions.q: Which noble of Akbar's court is generally regarded as the only Hindu to have accepted the Din-i-Ilahi?
questions.exp: Birbal is traditionally named as the only Hindu follower of the Din-i-Ilahi, proclaimed in 1582. Todar Mal and Man Singh remained orthodox Hindus.

questions.q: The Dahsala system of revenue assessment introduced in 1580 was based on the average produce and prices of the preceding:
questions.exp: Raja Todar Mal's Ain-i-Dahsala averaged the yields and prices of ten years (1570-71 to 1579-80) to fix a permanent cash demand per bigha.

questions.q: The Razmnama, prepared at Akbar's court, is a Persian translation of the:
questions.exp: Razmnama literally means 'Book of War' and renders the Mahabharata into Persian; Abul Fazl wrote its preface. The Ramayana was translated separately by Badauni.

questions.q: The Panch Mahal, a five-storeyed columnar structure at Fatehpur Sikri, was built by:
questions.exp: Akbar built the Panch Mahal near the zenana quarters at Fatehpur Sikri as a pleasure pavilion. Each of its five storeys is smaller than the one below.

questions.q: Akbar erected the Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri to commemorate his conquest of:
questions.exp: The Buland Darwaza was raised in 1601 in memory of the Gujarat campaign of 1572-73. It is the loftiest gateway in India.

questions.q: In 1580 Akbar divided his empire into how many subas (provinces)?
questions.exp: Twelve subas were created in 1580; the number rose to fifteen by the close of the reign with the Deccan acquisitions of Berar, Khandesh and Ahmadnagar.

questions.q: The additional cavalry rank 'du-aspa sih-aspa', under which a mansabdar maintained double the normal number of troopers, was introduced by:
questions.exp: Jahangir devised the du-aspa sih-aspa (two-horse, three-horse) rank to raise a favoured noble's contingent without raising his zat rank.

questions.q: Which Mughal empress had coins struck jointly in her name with the emperor's?
questions.exp: Nur Jahan's name appeared on coins and on royal farmans, an unprecedented position for a Mughal queen. Her family group is often called the Nur Jahan junta.

questions.q: Aurangzeb re-imposed the jizya on his non-Muslim subjects in the year:
questions.exp: The jizya, abolished by Akbar in 1564, was revived in 1679 and became a major grievance among Rajput and Maratha chiefs.

questions.q: Nadir Shah defeated the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah in 1739 in the Battle of:
questions.exp: After Karnal, Nadir Shah sacked Delhi and carried away the Peacock Throne and the Kohinoor diamond, exposing the hollowness of Mughal power.

questions.q: The farman of 1717 granting the English East India Company duty-free trade in Bengal was issued by:
questions.exp: Farrukhsiyar's farman, often called the Company's 'Magna Carta', allowed duty-free trade in Bengal for an annual payment of Rs 3,000.

questions.q: Shivaji's coronation as Chhatrapati at Raigad in June 1674 was performed by:
questions.exp: The Banaras scholar Gaga Bhatt conducted the Vedic coronation on 6 June 1674, legitimising Shivaji's kshatriya status and sovereign kingship.

questions.q: Shivaji killed Afzal Khan, the general of Bijapur, in 1659 at:
questions.exp: The encounter took place at the foot of Pratapgarh fort, after which the Bijapuri army was routed. Shaista Khan's night attack followed in 1663.

questions.q: Chauth, the levy imposed by the Marathas, amounted to what share of the standard revenue of a territory?
questions.exp: Chauth was one-fourth of the assessed revenue; Sardeshmukhi was an additional one-tenth claimed as the hereditary right of the sardeshmukh.

questions.q: Who was appointed Peshwa by Chhatrapati Shahu in 1713 and made the office hereditary in his family?
questions.exp: Balaji Vishwanath, the first of the Chitpavan Brahmin Peshwas, secured the Mughal grant of chauth and sardeshmukhi over the Deccan in 1719.

questions.q: The First Anglo-Maratha War was brought to a close by the:
questions.exp: The Treaty of Salbai (1782) restored the pre-war position and gave the English about twenty years of peace with the Marathas. The war had begun with the Treaty of Surat (1775).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the administration of Sher Shah Suri:
I. He revived the ancient imperial highway running from Sonargaon in Bengal towards the north-west, calling it the Sadak-i-Azam.
II. He enforced the branding of horses (dagh) and the descriptive roll of soldiers (chehra).
III. He issued a purely copper currency and abolished silver coinage altogether.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Statements I and II are correct. Sher Shah struck a well-regulated silver rupiya alongside copper dams, so III is wrong.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Akbar's religious policy:
I. He abolished the pilgrimage tax in 1563 and the jizya in 1564.
II. The Ibadat Khana was set up at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575 for religious discussions.
III. The Din-i-Ilahi was proclaimed in 1582.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The Mahzar or so-called 'infallibility decree' of 1579 preceded the Din-i-Ilahi and made Akbar the final arbiter in disputed religious matters.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Panch Mahal at Fatehpur Sikri:
I. It is a five-storeyed structure in which each successive storey is smaller than the one below.
II. It is an entirely columnar building with 176 pillars in all.
III. Its uppermost storey is supported on eighty-four columns.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: I and II are correct. The eighty-four columns are on the ground floor; the topmost storey is a small kiosk resting on only four.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Ain-i-Akbari:
I. It forms the third and concluding volume of the Akbarnama.
II. It was written by Abul Fazl.
III. It contains statistical accounts of the subas of Akbar's empire.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The Ain-i-Akbari is the single richest source for Mughal administration, revenue rates and provincial geography.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Akbar's mansabdari system:
I. The zat rank determined a mansabdar's personal status and pay.
II. The sawar rank indicated the number of cavalrymen he was required to maintain.
III. Mansabs were hereditary and passed automatically to the holder's son.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: I and II are correct. Mansabs were neither hereditary nor permanent; on a mansabdar's death his assignment reverted to the emperor.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Aurangzeb:
I. He assumed the title of Alamgir on his accession.
II. He annexed Golconda in 1686 and Bijapur in 1687.
III. He died in 1707 and was buried at Khuldabad.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: I and III are correct. The order in II is reversed: Bijapur was annexed in 1686 and Golconda in 1687.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the jagirdari crisis of the later Mughal period:
I. The number of claimants to jagirs grew faster than the stock of assignable revenue-yielding land.
II. Land reserved for future assignment was known as khalisa.
III. The crisis is closely associated with the interpretation of Mughal decline offered by the historian Satish Chandra.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: I and III are correct. Land kept in reserve for future assignment was paibaqi; khalisa was crown land whose revenue went directly to the imperial treasury.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Baji Rao I:
I. He defeated the Nizam-ul-Mulk in the Battle of Palkhed in 1728.
II. He was defeated by the Nizam at Bhopal in 1737-38.
III. He was the son of Balaji Vishwanath.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: I and III are correct. At Bhopal it was Baji Rao I who defeated the Nizam, not the other way round; he is credited with the idea of Hindu Pad Padshahi.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Third Battle of Panipat (1761):
I. The Maratha army was commanded by Sadashivrao Bhau.
II. Vishwasrao, son of the Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao, was killed in the battle.
III. The Marathas were defeated by Ahmad Shah Abdali.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The battle was fought on 14 January 1761; the Maratha artillery was led by Ibrahim Khan Gardi.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Marathas after Shivaji:
I. Sambhaji was captured and executed by Aurangzeb in 1681.
II. Rajaram shifted the centre of Maratha resistance to Jinji after the fall of Raigad.
III. Shahu was released from Mughal captivity in 1707.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: II and III are correct. Sambhaji was captured and executed in 1689, not 1681; Tarabai then led the resistance in the name of Shivaji II.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Official under Sher Shah)   List-II (Function)
A. Shiqdar    1. Treasurer
B. Amin       2. Law and order of the pargana
C. Fotedar    3. Clerk and accountant
D. Karkun     4. Land measurement and revenue assessment
questions.exp: The shiqdar kept order, the amin assessed, the fotedar held the treasury and karkuns kept the records. At the sarkar level stood the shiqdar-i-shiqdaran and munsif-i-munsifan.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Mughal revenue system)   List-II (Method of assessment)
A. Zabti           1. Sharing of the actual harvested produce
B. Kankut          2. Estimate of the standing crop
C. Ghalla-bakhshi  3. Measurement of land with fixed cash rates per bigha
D. Nasaq           4. Lump-sum assessment based on past collections
questions.exp: Zabti (Todar Mal's system) rested on measurement; kankut on eye estimate; ghalla-bakhshi or batai on crop-sharing; nasaq on past figures. Nasaq was common in Bengal.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Sanskrit work translated into Persian)   List-II (Translator at Akbar's court)
A. Mahabharata               1. Faizi
B. Ramayana                  2. Naqib Khan and associates
C. Lilavati                  3. Abdul Qadir Badauni
D. Panchatantra (Ayar Danish) 4. Abul Fazl
questions.exp: The Razmnama team was headed by Naqib Khan; Badauni translated the Ramayana; Faizi rendered Bhaskaracharya's Lilavati; Abul Fazl produced the Ayar Danish.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Mughal central officer)   List-II (Department)
A. Diwan-i-Ala    1. Military pay and mansab records
B. Mir Bakhshi    2. Religious endowments and charity
C. Mir Saman      3. Revenue and finance
D. Sadr-us-Sudur  4. Imperial household and karkhanas
questions.exp: The diwan headed revenue, the mir bakhshi the military establishment, the mir saman the household workshops and the sadr-us-sudur charitable grants. Justice was under the qazi-ul-quzat.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Member of the Ashtapradhan)   List-II (Function)
A. Peshwa     1. Chief justice
B. Amatya     2. Prime minister
C. Sumant     3. Finance and revenue
D. Nyayadhish 4. Foreign affairs
questions.exp: Shivaji's council of eight also included the Sachiv (correspondence), Mantri (personal records), Senapati (army) and Panditrao (religious affairs). Moropant Trimbak Pingle was the first Peshwa.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Maratha house)   List-II (Seat of power)
A. Gaekwad   1. Gwalior
B. Holkar    2. Nagpur
C. Scindia   3. Baroda
D. Bhonsle   4. Indore
questions.exp: The Maratha confederacy grouped the Gaekwads of Baroda, Holkars of Indore, Scindias of Gwalior and Bhonsles of Nagpur under the Peshwa at Poona.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT associated with Sher Shah Suri?
questions.exp: The Jahangiri Mahal inside the Agra Fort was built by Akbar. The fort at Rohtasgarh, the Qila-i-Kuhna mosque and the Sadak-i-Azam are all works of Sher Shah.

questions.q: Which one of the following was NOT among the 'Navaratnas' of Akbar's court?
questions.exp: Abdul Hamid Lahori was the court historian of Shah Jahan and author of the Padshahnama, born long after Akbar's navaratnas.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a Mughal emperor and a European visitor to his court is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Francois Bernier, the French physician, was in India during the closing years of Shah Jahan and the reign of Aurangzeb, not under Akbar.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs relating to Mughal provincial administration is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Faujdar - officer of a sarkar responsible for law and order
Kotwal - chief officer of a city
Amil - chief judicial officer of a suba
questions.exp: The amil or amalguzar was the revenue collector of a pargana. Judicial work in a province was handled by the qazi.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: The Convention of Wadgaon was signed in 1779 during the First Anglo-Maratha War. The Treaty of Bassein of 1802 led directly to the Second Anglo-Maratha War.

questions.q:
Arrange the following battles fought by Babur in the correct chronological order:
I. Ghaghra
II. Panipat
III. Chanderi
IV. Khanwa
questions.exp: Panipat 1526, Khanwa 1527, Chanderi 1528 and Ghaghra 1529 mark the four stages by which Babur secured northern India.

questions.q:
Arrange the following battles of the Mughal war of succession (1658-59) in the correct chronological order:
I. Samugarh
II. Dharmat
III. Deorai
IV. Khajwa
questions.exp: Dharmat (April 1658) and Samugarh (May 1658) broke Dara Shukoh's power; Khajwa (January 1659) defeated Shuja and Deorai (1659) ended Dara's resistance.

chapters.title: Medieval Art, Architecture, Literature, Painting, Music; Bhakti & Sufi Movements
factsheet: Quwwat-ul-Islam Masjid, Delhi (1192-98) - first mosque of the Delhi Sultanate, built by Qutbuddin Aibak; Qutb Minar begun by Aibak and completed by Iltutmish.
Sultan Ghari (1231), built by Iltutmish for his son Nasiruddin Mahmud, is regarded as the first Islamic mausoleum in India.
Alai Darwaza (1311), added by Alauddin Khalji to the Qutb complex, is the first Indian building to use the true arch and true dome.
Tughlaq architecture: battered (sloping) walls, grey rubble, arch-and-lintel combination - Tughlaqabad (Ghiyasuddin), Jahanpanah, Firoz Shah Kotla.
Provincial styles: Adina Masjid at Pandua (Bengal), Atala Masjid at Jaunpur (Sharqi), Jahaz Mahal and Hindola Mahal at Mandu (Malwa), Sidi Saiyyed jali at Ahmedabad (Gujarat).
Humayun's tomb (1565-72), commissioned by Bega Begum, designed by Mirak Mirza Ghiyas - the first garden (charbagh) tomb in India; UNESCO site 1993.
Fatehpur Sikri (1571): Buland Darwaza, Panch Mahal, Diwan-i-Khas, Jama Masjid, tomb of Salim Chishti.
Itmad-ud-Daulah's tomb at Agra (1622-28), built by Nur Jahan for her father - first Mughal building entirely of white marble and the first large use of pietra dura.
Taj Mahal (1632-53), chief architect Ustad Ahmad Lahauri; Shah Jahan also built the Red Fort and Jama Masjid at Delhi and the Moti Masjid at Agra. UNESCO site 1983.
Gol Gumbaz, Bijapur - tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah (completed 1656), famous whispering gallery and one of the largest masonry domes in the world.
Char Minar, Hyderabad (1591), built by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah of Golconda.
Mughal painting begins with Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd-us-Samad, brought from Persia by Humayun.
Akbar's atelier: Hamzanama (about 1400 cloth paintings), Tutinama, Akbarnama; leading painters Daswanth, Basawan, Kesu Das, Miskin, Lal, Farrukh Beg.
Jahangir - zenith of Mughal painting; Ustad Mansur (title Nadir-ul-Asr) for birds and animals, Abul Hasan (Nadir-uz-Zaman), Bishandas for portraits, Manohar, Govardhan.
Shah Jahan's painting is formal and gold-laden; Aurangzeb withdrew patronage and artists dispersed to Rajasthan and the Punjab hills.
Pahari schools: Basohli (earliest, Kripal Pal, Rasamanjari), Guler, Kangra (Raja Sansar Chand, Gita Govinda), Chamba, Garhwal, Mandi, Nurpur.
Deccani painting: Ahmadnagar, Bijapur (Nujum-al-Ulum) and Golconda; Rajasthani/Rajput schools develop parallel to the Mughal.
Amir Khusrau (1253-1325) - 'Tuti-i-Hind', disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, credited with qawwali, the tarana and the sitar; buried at the Nizamuddin dargah.
Raja Man Singh Tomar of Gwalior was the great patron of dhrupad; the treatise Man Kautuhal is associated with his court.
Tansen (Ramtanu Pandey) served Raja Ramchandra of Rewa before joining Akbar; one of the navaratnas; ragas Miyan ki Malhar and Miyan ki Todi; buried at Gwalior.
Medieval literature: Padmavat by Malik Muhammad Jayasi (Awadhi), Akbarnama by Abul Fazl, Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh by Badauni, Padshahnama by Abdul Hamid Lahori, Muntakhab-ul-Lubab by Khafi Khan.
Dara Shukoh wrote Majma-ul-Bahrain and translated the Upanishads into Persian as Sirr-i-Akbar.
Bhakti in the south: Alvars (12, Vaishnava - Nalayira Divya Prabandham, Andal the only woman) and Nayanars (63, Shaiva - Tevaram).
Acharyas: Ramanuja - Vishishtadvaita (Sri sampradaya); Madhvacharya - Dvaita/Tattvavada (Brahma sampradaya, Udupi); Nimbarka - Dvaitadvaita; Vallabhacharya - Shuddhadvaita (Pushtimarg, Nathdwara).
Ramananda was the first to preach bhakti in the vernacular in the north; among his disciples were Kabir, Raidas, Dhanna, Pipa and Sena.
Kabir (nirguna, Bijak - Sakhi, Sabad, Ramaini, died at Maghar); Guru Nanak (b. 1469 Talwandi); Adi Granth compiled by Guru Arjan Dev in 1604.
Varkari sampradaya of Maharashtra worships Vitthala of Pandharpur; saints Dnyaneshwar (Jnaneshwari), Namdev, Chokhamela, Eknath and Tukaram; wari on Ashadhi Ekadashi.
Chaitanya Mahaprabhu (b. 1486, Nabadwip) - Gaudiya Vaishnavism, Achintya Bhedabheda, sankirtan; Basavanna founded the Lingayat/Virashaiva movement and the Anubhava Mantapa in Karnataka.
Sufi silsilas: Chishti (Moinuddin Chishti, Ajmer - Gharib Nawaz; Bakhtiyar Kaki, Baba Farid at Ajodhan, Nizamuddin Auliya, Gesu Daraz at Gulbarga, Salim Chishti at Fatehpur Sikri).

Suhrawardi (Bahauddin Zakariya, Multan - accepted state patronage), Qadiri (Miyan Mir of Lahore, guide of Dara Shukoh), Naqshbandi (Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi, Mujaddid-i-Alf-i-Sani, Wahdat-ul-Shuhud against Ibn Arabi's Wahdat-ul-Wujud). Terms: khanqah, sama, zikr, urs, pir, murid, futuh.

questions.q: The Qutb Minar at Delhi was begun by Qutbuddin Aibak and completed by:
questions.exp: Iltutmish added the upper storeys; Firoz Shah Tughlaq later repaired the topmost portion after lightning damage.

questions.q: Which structure of the Qutb complex is regarded as the first building in India to employ the true arch and the true dome?
questions.exp: The Alai Darwaza was added by Alauddin Khalji in 1311 and marks the arrival of genuine arcuate construction in Indian architecture.

questions.q: The fortress city of Tughlaqabad near Delhi was founded by:
questions.exp: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq raised Tughlaqabad, the third city of Delhi, with the massive sloping walls typical of Tughlaq building.

questions.q: The Gol Gumbaz, famous for its whispering gallery, is the mausoleum of:
questions.exp: The Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur, completed in 1656, houses the tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah and carries one of the largest masonry domes in the world.

questions.q: The Char Minar at Hyderabad was built in 1591 by:
questions.exp: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah of Golconda founded the city of Hyderabad and raised the Char Minar at its centre.

questions.q: Which monument is regarded as the first garden tomb (charbagh) built in the Indian subcontinent?
questions.exp: Humayun's tomb at Delhi was commissioned by his widow Bega Begum and designed by the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993.

questions.q: The architect traditionally credited with the design of the Taj Mahal is:
questions.exp: Ustad Ahmad Lahauri is named as the chief architect of the Taj Mahal, built between 1632 and 1653 for Mumtaz Mahal.

questions.q: The tomb of Itmad-ud-Daulah at Agra, the first Mughal building constructed entirely of white marble, was raised by:
questions.exp: Nur Jahan built it between 1622 and 1628 for her father Mirza Ghiyas Beg. Its extensive pietra dura inlay anticipates the Taj Mahal.

questions.q: The two Persian masters who founded the Mughal school of painting were brought to India by:
questions.exp: Humayun brought Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd-us-Samad from Persia; they later supervised the Hamzanama project under Akbar.

questions.q: The Hamzanama, the largest illustrated project of the Mughal atelier, was executed during the reign of:
questions.exp: Akbar's atelier produced about 1,400 large paintings on cloth for the Hamzanama, also called the Dastan-i-Amir Hamza.

questions.q: The painter honoured with the title 'Nadir-ul-Asr' for his studies of birds and animals was:
questions.exp: Ustad Mansur painted the Siberian crane, the dodo and the turkey cock for Jahangir. Abul Hasan received the parallel title Nadir-uz-Zaman.

questions.q: Which is regarded as the earliest of the Pahari schools of painting, known for its Rasamanjari series?
questions.exp: The Basohli school, patronised by Raja Kripal Pal, is marked by bold colour, beetle-wing inlay for jewellery and a strongly stylised face.

questions.q: The Kangra school of painting reached its height under the patronage of:
questions.exp: Under Sansar Chand the Kangra school produced its celebrated Gita Govinda, Bihari Satsai and Nala-Damayanti sets in a soft lyrical style.

questions.q: Before joining Akbar's court, the musician Tansen was in the service of the ruler of:
questions.exp: Tansen, born Ramtanu Pandey, served Raja Ramchandra of Rewa before Akbar summoned him in 1562. He was one of the navaratnas and is buried at Gwalior.

questions.q: Amir Khusrau, who bore the epithet 'Tuti-i-Hind', was the disciple of which Sufi saint?
questions.exp: Khusrau was the devoted murid of Nizamuddin Auliya and is buried beside him at the Nizamuddin dargah in Delhi.

questions.q: Which ruler of Gwalior is remembered as the greatest medieval patron of dhrupad music?
questions.exp: Raja Man Singh Tomar of Gwalior (late 15th century) systematised dhrupad; the musical treatise Man Kautuhal is associated with his court.

questions.q: The Padmavat, composed in the Awadhi dialect, was written by:
questions.exp: Jayasi wrote the Padmavat around 1540, during the reign of Sher Shah Suri, as a Sufi allegory around the siege of Chittor.

questions.q: The Persian translation of the Upanishads titled 'Sirr-i-Akbar' was prepared by:
questions.exp: Dara Shukoh, Shah Jahan's eldest son, also wrote the Majma-ul-Bahrain, seeking common ground between Hindu Vedanta and Sufi thought.

questions.q: The Dvaita school of Vedanta, also called Tattvavada, was propounded by:
questions.exp: Madhvacharya, also known as Ananda Tirtha, taught the absolute distinction between the individual soul and Brahman and established the Krishna Mutt and the Ashta Mathas at Udupi.

questions.q: Which saint is generally regarded as the first to preach bhakti in the vernacular in northern India, and counted Kabir and Raidas among his disciples?
questions.exp: Ramananda, a follower of the Ramanuja tradition, opened his order to all castes and preached in Hindi rather than Sanskrit.

questions.q: The compositions of Kabir are collected in which work?
questions.exp: The Bijak, arranged as Sakhi, Sabad and Ramaini, preserves Kabir's nirguna verse. He is believed to have died at Maghar.

questions.q: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, who popularised congregational singing (sankirtan), is associated with which school of Vaishnavism?
questions.exp: Born at Nabadwip in Bengal in 1486, Chaitanya taught Achintya Bhedabheda and made Krishna-bhakti a mass movement in eastern India.

questions.q: The Lingayat or Virashaiva movement of Karnataka, with its assembly known as the Anubhava Mantapa, was founded by:
questions.exp: Basavanna, a minister of the Kalachuri king Bijjala, rejected caste and ritual; the movement's teachings survive as vachanas in Kannada.

questions.q: Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti, who introduced the Chishti silsila into India, has his dargah at:
questions.exp: Popularly called Gharib Nawaz, Moinuddin Chishti settled at Ajmer in the late twelfth century; his urs draws pilgrims of all faiths.

questions.q: The Suhrawardi silsila was established in India by Shaikh Bahauddin Zakariya, whose centre was at:
questions.exp: Unlike the Chishtis, the Suhrawardis of Multan accepted state offices, land grants and wealth. Ajodhan (Pakpattan) was the seat of the Chishti Baba Farid.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the early bhakti saints of the Tamil country:
I. The Alvars were devotees of Vishnu.
II. The Nayanars were devotees of Shiva.
III. The hymns of the Alvars are collected in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. Andal was the only woman among the twelve Alvars, and the Nayanar hymns form the Tevaram.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Varkari sampradaya:
I. Its devotees worship Vitthala of Pandharpur.
II. Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, Eknath and Tukaram are among its revered saints.
III. Its principal pilgrimage, the wari, culminates on Ashadhi Ekadashi.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The Varkari movement made Marathi abhanga poetry the vehicle of bhakti and drew followers from every caste, including Chokhamela.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Vallabhacharya:
I. He propounded the philosophy of Shuddhadvaita.
II. His sect, the Pushtimarg, has its principal seat at Nathdwara.
III. He personally organised the group of eight devotional poets known as the Ashtachhap.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: I and II are correct. The Ashtachhap, which included Surdas, was constituted by Vallabhacharya's son Vitthalnath.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi:
I. He belonged to the Naqshbandi silsila.
II. He was given the title Mujaddid-i-Alf-i-Sani.
III. He was the foremost exponent of the doctrine of Wahdat-ul-Wujud.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: I and II are correct. Sirhindi opposed Ibn Arabi's Wahdat-ul-Wujud (unity of being) and advanced Wahdat-ul-Shuhud (apparentism).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Mughal painting:
I. Mughal painting reached its zenith under Akbar and declined sharply during Jahangir's reign.
II. Abul Hasan received the title Nadir-uz-Zaman from Jahangir.
III. Ustad Mansur specialised in the painting of birds and animals.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: II and III are correct. It was under Jahangir, himself a connoisseur, that Mughal painting attained its finest quality; decline set in under Aurangzeb.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Amir Khusrau:
I. He served as a court poet under several sultans of Delhi.
II. He is credited with the development of qawwali and the tarana.
III. He is buried at the Nizamuddin dargah in Delhi.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. Khusrau is also credited with modifying the three-stringed veena into the sitar and wrote in Persian as well as Hindavi.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Guru Nanak:
I. He was born in 1469 at Talwandi.
II. The Adi Granth was compiled by Guru Angad.
III. Nanak's hymns form part of the Guru Granth Sahib.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: I and III are correct. The Adi Granth was compiled by the fifth Guru, Arjan Dev, at Amritsar in 1604.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Tughlaq architecture:
I. It is marked by lavish ornamentation and the extensive use of white marble.
II. Sloping or battered walls are among its distinctive features.
III. It combines the arch with the lintel-and-beam.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: II and III are correct. Tughlaq buildings are severe and austere, using grey rubble and stone rather than marble; ornament belongs to the Mughal phase.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Acharya)      List-II (School of Vedanta)
A. Ramanuja       1. Dvaitadvaita
B. Madhvacharya   2. Vishishtadvaita
C. Nimbarka       3. Shuddhadvaita
D. Vallabhacharya 4. Dvaita
questions.exp: Ramanuja taught qualified non-dualism, Madhva outright dualism, Nimbarka dualistic non-dualism and Vallabha pure non-dualism. Each founded a distinct Vaishnava sampradaya.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Sufi saint)        List-II (Seat/dargah)
A. Nizamuddin Auliya   1. Gulbarga
B. Baba Farid          2. Fatehpur Sikri
C. Gesu Daraz          3. Delhi
D. Salim Chishti       4. Ajodhan
questions.exp: All four belonged to the Chishti order. Baba Farid's Ajodhan is the modern Pakpattan, and Gesu Daraz carried the Chishti silsila into the Deccan at Gulbarga.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Monument)          List-II (Place)
A. Adina Masjid        1. Ahmedabad
B. Atala Masjid        2. Mandu
C. Jahaz Mahal         3. Jaunpur
D. Sidi Saiyyed Mosque 4. Pandua
questions.exp: These are the classic provincial styles: Bengal at Pandua, the Sharqis at Jaunpur, Malwa at Mandu and Gujarat at Ahmedabad, whose Sidi Saiyyed jali is world famous.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Saint/poet)   List-II (Work)
A. Tulsidas      1. Sursagar
B. Surdas        2. Ramcharitmanas
C. Jayadeva      3. Jnaneshwari
D. Dnyaneshwar   4. Gita Govinda
questions.exp: Tulsidas wrote the Awadhi Ramcharitmanas, Surdas the Brajbhasha Sursagar, Jayadeva the Sanskrit Gita Govinda and Dnyaneshwar the Marathi commentary on the Gita.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Medieval chronicle)   List-II (Author)
A. Tarikh-i-Firozshahi   1. Minhaj-us-Siraj
B. Tabaqat-i-Nasiri      2. Abul Fazl
C. Akbarnama             3. Ziauddin Barani
D. Padshahnama           4. Abdul Hamid Lahori
questions.exp: Barani wrote under Firoz Shah Tughlaq, Minhaj under Nasiruddin Mahmud, Abul Fazl under Akbar and Lahori under Shah Jahan.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a Sufi saint and his silsila is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Miyan Mir of Lahore belonged to the Qadiri silsila and was the spiritual guide of Dara Shukoh.

questions.q: Which one of the following monuments was NOT built during the reign of Shah Jahan?
questions.exp: The Agra Fort was built by Akbar from 1565; Shah Jahan only added marble palaces such as the Khas Mahal and the Moti Masjid within it.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a painting school and its patron or centre is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Guler is a Pahari state of the Punjab hills, patronised by its own Rajput chiefs; the Adil Shahis ruled Bijapur in the Deccan.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a bhakti saint and his region is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Vidyapati was a Maithili poet of Mithila in present-day Bihar. Shankaradeva founded the Ekasarana dharma and the sattra institution in Assam.

questions.q: Which one of the following terms is NOT associated with Sufism?
questions.exp: Ashtachhap refers to the eight poets of the Vallabhite Pushtimarg. Khanqah is the hospice, sama the devotional music assembly and futuh the unasked-for offering.

questions.q:
Arrange the following monuments in the correct chronological order of their construction:
I. Alai Darwaza
II. Quwwat-ul-Islam Masjid
III. Gol Gumbaz
IV. Tughlaqabad Fort
questions.exp: Quwwat-ul-Islam 1192-98, Alai Darwaza 1311, Tughlaqabad 1321-25 and Gol Gumbaz completed in 1656.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Chishti silsila became the most widely followed Sufi order in medieval India.
Reason (R): The Chishtis lived among the common people and refused grants and offices from the state.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.exp: The Chishti insistence on poverty, service and distance from the court gave the order a popular base that the state-linked Suhrawardis never acquired.

chapters.title: British Expansion, Policies, 1857 and Socio-Religious Reform
factsheet: Battle of Plassey — 23 June 1757; Robert Clive defeated Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah through Mir Jafar's betrayal; Mir Jafar made Nawab of Bengal.
Battle of Buxar — 22 October 1764; Hector Munro defeated the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah (Awadh) and Emperor Shah Alam II.
Treaty of Allahabad, 1765 — Shah Alam II granted the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa (12 August 1765) against an annual pension of Rs 26 lakh.
Dual Government in Bengal (1765-72) — devised by Robert Clive; abolished by Warren Hastings in 1772.
Regulating Act 1773 — Governor of Bengal became Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings first); Supreme Court at Calcutta, 1774.
Pitt's India Act 1784 — created the Board of Control; system of 'double government' of Company and Crown.
Charter Act 1813 — ended the Company's trade monopoly except tea and trade with China; Rs 1 lakh a year for education.
Charter Act 1833 — Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India (Bentinck first); Law Member (Macaulay) added; Company's commercial functions ended.
Charter Act 1853 — open competition for the covenanted civil service; separate legislative machinery.
Government of India Act 1858 — East India Company abolished; Secretary of State for India with a 15-member Council; Governor-General became Viceroy (Canning first).
Permanent Settlement 1793 — Cornwallis (with John Shore); Bengal, Bihar, Orissa; zamindar kept 1/11th and paid 10/11th; 'Sunset Law' auctioned defaulting estates.
Ryotwari Settlement — Thomas Munro and Captain Alexander Read; Madras (1820) and Bombay; revenue settled directly with the cultivator.
Mahalwari Settlement — Holt Mackenzie, Regulation VII of 1822; revised 1833 under Bentinck (R.M. Bird); North-Western Provinces, Punjab, Central India; village/mahal as unit.
Subsidiary Alliance — Lord Wellesley; first accepted by the Nizam of Hyderabad (1798); Awadh 1801; Peshwa by the Treaty of Bassein 1802.
Doctrine of Lapse — Lord Dalhousie; Satara 1848 (first), Jaitpur and Sambalpur 1849, Udaipur 1852, Jhansi 1853, Nagpur 1854; Awadh annexed 1856 on the plea of misgovernance.
Anglo-Mysore Wars — I 1767-69 (Treaty of Madras); II 1780-84 (Treaty of Mangalore); III 1790-92 (Treaty of Seringapatam); IV 1799 — Tipu Sultan killed at Seringapatam, 4 May 1799.
Anglo-Maratha Wars — I 1775-82 (Treaty of Salbai); II 1803-05 (after the Treaty of Bassein, 1802); III 1817-18 — Peshwaship abolished.
Anglo-Sikh Wars — I 1845-46 (Treaty of Lahore); II 1848-49 — Punjab annexed by Dalhousie in 1849. Anglo-Burmese — I 1824-26 (Treaty of Yandabo); III 1885 — Burma annexed.
Macaulay's Minute, 2 February 1835 — English as the medium of higher education; 'downward filtration theory'.
Wood's Despatch 1854 — the 'Magna Carta of English education in India'; universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras founded 1857.
Education commissions — Hunter Commission 1882 (W.W. Hunter, under Ripon); Raleigh Commission 1902 leading to the Indian Universities Act 1904; Sadler Commission 1917-19; Hartog Committee 1929.
Revolt of 1857 — Barrackpore, 29 March (Mangal Pandey); Meerut, 10 May; Delhi, 11 May under Bahadur Shah II with General Bakht Khan as commander.

1857 centres and leaders — Kanpur: Nana Saheb and Tatya Tope; Lucknow: Begum Hazrat Mahal; Jhansi: Rani Lakshmibai; Bareilly: Khan Bahadur Khan; Faizabad: Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah; Jagdishpur: Kunwar Singh; Allahabad: Liaquat Ali.

Revolt declared suppressed by Canning on 8 July 1858; Queen Victoria's Proclamation read at Allahabad, 1 November 1858; Bahadur Shah II exiled to Rangoon. V.D. Savarkar called it 'The Indian War of Independence, 1857'.
Raja Rammohan Roy — Atmiya Sabha 1815, Brahmo Samaj 1828; Sambad Kaumudi (Bengali) and Mirat-ul-Akhbar (Persian); title 'Raja' from Akbar II; died at Bristol, 1833.

Sati abolished by Regulation XVII of 1829 under Lord William Bentinck. Brahmo line — Debendranath Tagore (Tattvabodhini Sabha 1839), Keshab Chandra Sen (Brahmo Samaj of India 1866), Sadharan Brahmo Samaj 1878.
Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar — Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (Act XV of 1856). Kandukuri Veeresalingam — first widow remarriage in the Telugu country at Rajahmundry, 11 December 1881.
Arya Samaj — Dayanand Saraswati, Bombay, 10 April 1875; Satyarth Prakash; Shuddhi; DAV School, Lahore 1886; Gurukul Kangri 1902 (Swami Shraddhanand).

Reform bodies and founders — Prarthana Samaj 1867 (Atmaram Pandurang); Ramakrishna Mission 1897 (Vivekananda, Belur Math); Theosophical Society 1875 New York, Indian HQ Adyar 1882; Aligarh/MAO College 1875 (Syed Ahmad Khan); Satyashodhak Samaj 1873 (Jyotiba Phule); Servants of India Society 1905 (Gokhale); Self-Respect Movement 1925 (Periyar).

Ambedkar — Mooknayak 1920, Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha 1924, Mahad (Chavdar tank) Satyagraha 1927, Bahishkrit Bharat 1927, Kalaram temple entry 1930. Age of Consent Act 1891 (Behramji Malabari); Sarda Act 1929 — girls 14, boys 18.

questions.q: The Battle of Plassey (1757) was fought between the English East India Company and which Nawab of Bengal?
questions.exp: Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah at Plassey on 23 June 1757, largely through the treachery of the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar, who was then installed as Nawab.

questions.q: The English forces at the Battle of Buxar (1764) were commanded by:
questions.exp: Hector Munro defeated the combined armies of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah of Awadh and Emperor Shah Alam II on 22 October 1764. Buxar established British political supremacy in eastern India.
