Global deforestation has slowed from about 17.6 million hectares a year in the 1990s to about 10.9 million hectares a year in the most recent decade.

The largest direct driver of tropical deforestation is conversion of forest to agricultural land - shifting cultivation, cattle ranching in the Amazon and oil-palm and soy plantations in South-East Asia and Brazil.
The Amazon rainforest, largely in Brazil, is often called the 'lungs of the earth' and holds the world's largest area of tropical rainforest.
Biome wildlife: orangutan - Borneo and Sumatra; gorilla, okapi and bonobo - Congo basin; grizzly bear, moose, lynx and wolf - North American coniferous belt; kangaroo - Australian grassland.
Sequence of vegetation belts from the Equator poleward: equatorial rainforest, savanna, hot desert, Mediterranean, temperate grassland and deciduous forest, taiga, tundra, ice cap.
Vertical (altitudinal) zonation repeats the same sequence up a mountain, ending in alpine pastures above the tree line - the 'alps' of Europe and the bugyals of the Himalaya.
Coniferous softwood forests are the world's leading lumbering regions; equatorial hardwood forests are lumbered far less because of mixed stands and poor accessibility.
Grassland and vegetation names to memorise: Selva, Llanos, Campos, Pampas, Prairie, Steppe, Veld, Downs, Canterbury, Puszta, Taiga, Tundra, Maquis, Chaparral, Fynbos, Mallee, Matorral.

questions.q: The equatorial evergreen rainforest of the Amazon basin is locally known as:
questions.exp: 'Selva' is the name given to the dense equatorial rainforest of the Amazon. Llanos and Campos are savanna grasslands of the Orinoco basin and the Brazilian highlands respectively.

questions.q: The Prairies are the temperate grasslands of:
questions.exp: The Prairies stretch across the central plains of the United States and Canada and form one of the world's great wheat belts.

questions.q: The Pampas grassland is located in:
questions.exp: The Pampas of Argentina and Uruguay are famous for wheat, alfalfa and cattle ranching; the herdsmen of the region are called gauchos.

questions.q: 'Veld' is the name of the temperate grassland of:
questions.exp: The Veld, divided into high veld, middle veld and low veld, lies on the plateau of South Africa and supports large-scale maize cultivation and sheep and cattle rearing.

questions.q: The Canterbury grassland is found in:
questions.exp: The Canterbury Plains on the eastern side of South Island, New Zealand, are famous for sheep rearing and for lamb and wool exports.

questions.q: 'Chaparral' is the Mediterranean type of scrub vegetation of:
questions.exp: Chaparral is the Californian name for Mediterranean sclerophyll scrub. Its counterparts are maquis in the Mediterranean basin, matorral in Chile, fynbos in South Africa and mallee in Australia.

questions.q: Which of the following is the largest land biome of the earth?
questions.exp: The taiga sweeps in a broad belt across Siberia, Canada and Scandinavia and is the largest land biome. It supplies the world's chief stocks of softwood, pulp and newsprint.

questions.q: Reindeer moss and lichens are the characteristic vegetation of which biome?
questions.exp: The tundra, lying beyond the tree line and underlain by permafrost, supports only mosses, lichens and sedges. Reindeer or caribou graze on reindeer moss.

questions.q: At present the maximum deforestation in the world is taking place in which type of forest?
questions.exp: Tropical forests, particularly in the Amazon, the Congo basin and South-East Asia, account for the bulk of the world's forest loss, driven by clearing for agriculture, ranching and plantations.

questions.q: Which country has the largest forest area in the world?
questions.exp: Russia has about 832 million hectares of forest, roughly one-fifth of the world's total, followed by Brazil, Canada, the United States and China.

questions.q: The tropical grassland of the Orinoco basin in Venezuela is known as:
questions.exp: The Llanos are the savanna of the Orinoco basin, while the Campos are the savanna of the Brazilian highlands. Both are tropical, not temperate, grasslands.

questions.q: Baobab and acacia trees standing amid tall coarse grasses are typical of which biome?
questions.exp: The savanna or tropical grassland has tall grass with scattered drought-resistant trees such as acacia and baobab. It is called the 'big game country' for its lions, zebras, giraffes and elephants.

questions.q: The largest mangrove forest in the world is the:
questions.exp: The Sundarbans, in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta of India and Bangladesh, is the world's largest mangrove forest and the home of the Royal Bengal tiger.

questions.q: Mahogany, ebony and rosewood are characteristic hardwoods of which forest?
questions.exp: Equatorial rainforests yield heavy, durable hardwoods such as mahogany, ebony, rosewood and greenheart. Their scattered occurrence in mixed stands makes commercial exploitation difficult.

questions.q: Pine, fir, spruce and larch are the characteristic trees of the:
questions.exp: These conifers have needle-shaped leaves and a conical shape that sheds snow, and they supply the softwood used for paper pulp, matchwood and furniture.

questions.q: As per the Global Forest Resources Assessment of the FAO, forests cover approximately what proportion of the world's land area?
questions.exp: The world's forests extend over about 4.14 billion hectares, roughly 31 to 32 per cent of the global land area. Just five countries hold more than half of this area.

questions.q: Teak, sal and sandalwood are typical trees of which forest type?
questions.exp: Tropical deciduous or monsoon forests shed their leaves in the dry season to conserve water. They are commercially the most useful forests of the monsoon lands.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the equatorial rainforest:
I. It has a multi-storeyed structure with a dense canopy.
II. Its trees shed their leaves in a definite dry season.
III. Lianas and epiphytes are common in it.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Rainfall and temperature are high throughout the year in the equatorial belt, so there is no distinct leaf-shedding season and the forest remains evergreen.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about temperate grasslands:
I. They are practically treeless.
II. They are among the world's leading wheat-producing regions.
III. The Steppes are the temperate grassland of Eurasia.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three statements are correct. Temperate grasslands lie in continental interiors with 25 to 75 cm of rainfall and are the world's granaries as well as great ranching lands.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the taiga:
I. It occurs as a continuous belt in the Southern Hemisphere.
II. Its trees are mostly evergreen conifers with needle-shaped leaves.
III. It is the world's principal source of softwood.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: There is very little land in the corresponding latitudes of the Southern Hemisphere, so the taiga is confined almost entirely to the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about deforestation in the world:
I. Tropical forests record the maximum loss of forest area in the world.
II. Conversion of forest into agricultural land is the largest direct driver of deforestation.
III. The annual rate of global deforestation has risen steadily since 1990.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The rate of global deforestation has in fact declined, from about 17.6 million hectares a year in the 1990s to about 10.9 million hectares a year in the most recent decade, though tropical forests still bear the greatest loss.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Mediterranean vegetation:
I. The plants are adapted to hot dry summers and mild wet winters.
II. Leaves are usually small, thick and waxy to check transpiration.
III. Citrus fruits, olives and grapes are typical of the region.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three statements are correct. Mediterranean lands lie on the western margins of continents between about 30 and 40 degrees latitude and are often called the orchard lands of the world.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the tundra biome:
I. It has a permanently frozen sub-soil called permafrost.
II. It has a long growing season of more than six months.
III. Musk ox, arctic fox and polar bear are found in it.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The tundra's growing season lasts only about two months of the brief Arctic summer, when the surface thaws and mosses, lichens and sedges appear.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Temperate grassland)   List-II (Region)
A. Pampas  1. Australia
B. Downs   2. South Africa
C. Veld    3. Argentina
D. Steppe  4. Eurasia
questions.exp: The Pampas are in Argentina, the Downs in Australia, the Veld in South Africa and the Steppes in Eurasia. Canterbury in New Zealand and Puszta in Hungary complete the list.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Mediterranean scrub)   List-II (Region)
A. Maquis    1. Chile
B. Fynbos    2. South-western Australia
C. Mallee    3. Mediterranean basin
D. Matorral  4. South Africa
questions.exp: The five Mediterranean climate regions are the Mediterranean basin (maquis and garrigue), California (chaparral), central Chile (matorral), the Cape region of South Africa (fynbos) and south-western Australia (mallee).

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Biome)   List-II (Characteristic animal)
A. Tundra                1. Kangaroo
B. Savanna               2. Caribou
C. Taiga                 3. Zebra
D. Australian grassland  4. Lynx
questions.exp: Caribou or reindeer graze the tundra, zebra the African savanna, lynx the coniferous taiga and kangaroos the grasslands of Australia.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a temperate grassland and its region is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: The Pampas are the temperate grassland of Argentina and Uruguay in South America. The temperate grassland of South Africa is the Veld.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a vegetation name and its description is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Campos is the tropical savanna grassland of the Brazilian highlands. The Mediterranean scrub of central Chile is called matorral.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements regarding the forests of the world is NOT correct?
opts: Russia has the largest forest area of any country
Nearly half of the world's forests are tropical
Temperate forests are recording the maximum deforestation in the world
Forests cover about one-third of the world's land area
questions.exp: Tropical forests, not temperate forests, record the maximum deforestation. Temperate and boreal forest areas have in fact been broadly stable or expanding in recent decades.

questions.q:
Arrange the following natural vegetation belts in the correct sequence from the Equator towards the North Pole:
I. Tundra
II. Savanna
III. Equatorial rainforest
IV. Taiga
questions.exp: Moving poleward from the Equator the sequence is equatorial rainforest, savanna, hot desert, Mediterranean, temperate grassland and deciduous forest, taiga and finally tundra.

chapters.title: World Agriculture
factsheet: Mediterranean agriculture is confined to five belts: the Mediterranean basin, central California, central Chile, the south-western Cape of South Africa and south-western/southern Australia.
Mediterranean lands = 'orchard lands of the world' - citrus, olives, figs, grapes; viticulture (grape growing) is their most distinctive commercial activity.

Shifting cultivation local names: Jhum (NE India), Milpa (Mexico/Central America), Ladang (Indonesia-Malaysia), Chena (Sri Lanka), Roca (Brazil), Ray (Vietnam), Taungya (Myanmar), Conuco (Venezuela), Masole (Congo), Humah (Java).

Nomadic herders: Bedouin (Arabia-Sahara, camel), Masai (East Africa, cattle), Lapps/Sami (European tundra, reindeer), Chukchi (Siberian tundra), Kirghiz & Kazakh (Central Asian steppe), Fulani (West Africa).
Transhumance = seasonal movement of herders between highland summer and lowland winter pastures; Gujjars and Bakarwals in the western Himalayas.
Intensive subsistence farming: monsoon Asia, wet paddy dominant, tiny holdings, high yield per hectare but very low output per worker.
Extensive commercial grain farming regions: Prairie (USA-Canada), Pampas (Argentina), Steppe (Russia-Ukraine), Veld (South Africa), Downs (Australia), Canterbury (New Zealand).

Plantation agriculture: introduced by Europeans in the tropics; single cash crop, large estate, hired labour, heavy capital in processing and transport - rubber (Malaysia), tea (Sri Lanka), coffee (Brazil), cocoa (Ghana), banana (Central America).
Kolkhoz = collective farm of the erstwhile USSR (collectivisation from 1929); Sovkhoz = state farm with wage labour; Denmark is the classic case of co-operative farming.
Market gardening / truck farming: intensive growing of vegetables, fruit and flowers near big cities; 'factory farming' for stall-fed livestock.
Von Thunen's isolated-state model (1826): market gardening and dairying in the innermost ring, forestry next, crop rotation and grain, ranching in the outermost ring.
Leading producers (FAO 2023): rice - China then India; wheat - China then India then Russia; maize - USA then China then Brazil; soybean - Brazil then USA then Argentina.
Sugarcane - Brazil (about 40 per cent of world output) then India; potato - China then India; groundnut - China then India.
Coffee - Brazil is No. 1, Vietnam No. 2 and the largest producer of Robusta; coffee originated in the Ethiopian highlands.
Tea - China No. 1, India No. 2, Kenya No. 3, Sri Lanka No. 4; Kenya is the largest exporter of black tea.
Cocoa - Cote d'Ivoire No. 1, Ghana No. 2; concentrated on the Gulf of Guinea coast of West Africa.
Natural rubber - Thailand No. 1, Indonesia No. 2, Vietnam No. 3; Hevea brasiliensis is native to the Amazon basin.
Palm oil - Indonesia No. 1 and Malaysia No. 2 together supply about 85 per cent of world output; oil palm is native to West Africa.
Olives and olive oil - Spain No. 1, Italy No. 2; jute - India is the largest producer, Bangladesh the largest exporter.
Milk - India is the world's largest producer (Operation Flood, Verghese Kurien); New Zealand is the largest exporter of dairy products.
Largest exporters: rice - India; wheat - Russia; maize - USA and Brazil; soybean - Brazil; wool - Australia.
Fish - China is the largest producer (capture plus aquaculture) and the largest exporter of fishery products.

Major fishing grounds: North-West Pacific (world's most productive), North-East Atlantic, Grand Banks off Newfoundland (Labrador Current meets Gulf Stream), Dogger Bank (North Sea), Georges Bank, Peru-Chile coast.
The Peruvian anchoveta fishery depends on upwelling caused by the Peru (Humboldt) Current; catches collapse in El Nino years.
Norman Borlaug - father of the Green Revolution, Nobel Peace Prize 1970 for dwarf wheat; M. S. Swaminathan led its Indian adaptation from 1966-67.

Colour revolutions in India: Green - foodgrains, White - milk, Blue - fish, Yellow - oilseeds, Golden - horticulture/honey, Pink - prawn/onion, Silver - eggs, Red - meat/tomato, Brown - leather/cocoa, Round - potato.
FAO was founded on 16 October 1945 with headquarters at Rome; World Food Day is observed on 16 October.

questions.q: Which one of the following regions is NOT associated with the Mediterranean type of agriculture?
opts: The south-western Cape of South Africa
questions.exp: Mediterranean agriculture is confined to the five Mediterranean-climate belts - the Mediterranean basin, central California, central Chile, the south-western Cape of South Africa and south-western/southern Australia. The Pampas is a temperate grassland of extensive commercial grain farming and cattle ranching.

questions.q: Mediterranean agriculture is characteristically associated with the cultivation of
questions.exp: Mediterranean lands specialise in citrus fruits, olives, figs and grapes and are called the 'orchard lands of the world'. Viticulture, or grape growing for wine, is their most distinctive commercial activity.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Local name of shifting cultivation)   List-II (Region)
A. Milpa   1. Sri Lanka
B. Ladang   2. Mexico
C. Chena   3. Brazil
D. Roca   4. Indonesia
questions.exp: Shifting cultivation is called Milpa in Mexico and Central America, Ladang in Indonesia and Malaysia, Chena in Sri Lanka and Roca in Brazil. In north-eastern India it is known as Jhum.

questions.q: Which one of the following countries is the world's largest producer of natural rubber?
questions.exp: Thailand has been the world's leading producer of natural rubber for decades, ahead of Indonesia and Vietnam. The rubber tree, Hevea brasiliensis, is native to the Amazon basin.

questions.q: The world's largest producer of coffee is
questions.exp: Brazil has been the world's largest coffee producer for over a century and a half; Vietnam is second and is the largest producer of Robusta coffee. The plant itself originated in the Ethiopian highlands.

questions.q: Which country leads the world in the production of cocoa beans?
questions.exp: Cote d'Ivoire produces roughly two-fifths of the world's cocoa, ahead of Ghana. Cocoa cultivation is concentrated along the Gulf of Guinea coast of West Africa.

questions.q: The world's largest producer of palm oil is
questions.exp: Indonesia and Malaysia together account for about 85 per cent of world palm oil output, with Indonesia far ahead. The oil palm, Elaeis guineensis, is native to West Africa.

questions.q: In the erstwhile Soviet Union, the term 'Kolkhoz' referred to a
opts: state-owned farm on which workers drew wages
collective farm run jointly by its member households
large private estate held by a landlord
co-operative society for the marketing of grain
questions.exp: The Kolkhoz was the collective farm formed by pooling the land, implements and livestock of member households; the Sovkhoz was the state farm worked by wage labour. Collectivisation in the USSR began in 1929.

questions.q: Which country is the world's largest producer of milk?
questions.exp: India has been the world's largest milk producer since the 1990s, an outcome of Operation Flood led by Verghese Kurien. New Zealand, though a modest producer, is the largest exporter of dairy products.

questions.q: Which country is at present the world's largest exporter of rice?
questions.exp: India is the world's largest rice exporter, followed by Thailand and Vietnam. China, though the biggest producer of rice, consumes almost its entire output at home.

questions.q: The world's largest producer of wheat is
questions.exp: China is the largest wheat producer, followed by India and Russia; the three together account for well over 40 per cent of world output. Wheat is a rabi crop of the temperate and sub-tropical lands.

questions.q: Which country is the world's largest producer of maize?
questions.exp: The United States produces roughly a third of the world's maize, ahead of China and Brazil. The American Corn Belt centres on Iowa and Illinois in the Middle West.

questions.q: Which country is at present the world's largest producer of soybean?
questions.exp: Brazil overtook the United States as the largest soybean producer around 2019-20 and has held first place since; Argentina is third and leads in exports of soybean oil and meal.

questions.q: The world's largest producer of sugarcane is
questions.exp: Brazil grows about 40 per cent of the world's sugarcane, with India second. A large share of the Brazilian crop is converted into ethanol rather than sugar.

questions.q: The Grand Banks, one of the world's richest fishing grounds, lie off the coast of
questions.exp: The Grand Banks lie off Newfoundland in Canada, where the cold Labrador Current meets the warm Gulf Stream and the resulting plankton bloom supports huge cod stocks. The Dogger Bank is the corresponding shallow bank in the North Sea.

questions.q: Market gardening, also known as truck farming, is best described as the
opts: cultivation of a single crop on a large estate for export
growing of high-value vegetables, fruits and flowers close to urban markets
rearing of livestock on natural pasture over vast areas
temporary cultivation of food crops on freshly cleared forest land
questions.exp: Market gardening is an intensive, capital- and labour-intensive form of cultivation of vegetables, fruits and flowers for nearby city markets. In the United States it is called truck farming because the produce is trucked in daily.

questions.q: Which country is the world's largest producer of fish, counting both capture fisheries and aquaculture?
questions.exp: China accounts for well over a third of world fish production and is also the largest exporter of fish and fishery products. Peru's output, by contrast, is dominated by a single species, the anchoveta.

questions.q: Which country is at present the world's largest exporter of wheat?
questions.exp: Russia has been the world's largest wheat exporter since the mid-2010s, shipping mainly through its Black Sea ports. The European Union, the United States, Canada and Australia follow.

questions.q: Transhumance refers to the
opts: permanent migration of herders and their families to towns
cultivation of fodder crops for stall-fed cattle
clearing of forest by burning for temporary cultivation
seasonal movement of herders and their livestock between highland and lowland pastures
questions.exp: Transhumance is the regular seasonal movement of pastoralists with their animals between summer pastures on high ground and winter pastures in the valleys - as practised by the Gujjars and Bakarwals of the western Himalayas.

questions.q: The scientist regarded as the father of the Green Revolution, who received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970 for developing high-yielding dwarf varieties of wheat, was
questions.exp: Norman Borlaug developed semi-dwarf, rust-resistant wheat in Mexico and won the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize. M. S. Swaminathan led the adaptation of these varieties in India from 1966-67.

questions.q: Which European country, famous for the co-operative organisation of its dairy industry, is popularly described as the 'Dairy of Europe'?
questions.exp: Denmark's dairying is organised almost wholly through producers' co-operatives, which makes the country the standard textbook example both of co-operative farming and of commercial dairy farming.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about plantation agriculture:
I. It was introduced in the tropics largely by European settlers.
II. It is characterised by the cultivation of a single cash crop on a large estate.
III. It requires very little capital investment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Plantations are large, single-crop, export-oriented estates set up by Europeans in tropical colonies. They are highly capital-intensive, needing heavy investment in processing plants, transport and management, so statement III is wrong.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about intensive subsistence agriculture:
I. It is practised mainly in the densely populated monsoon lands of Asia.
II. Holdings are small and the use of human labour is very high.
III. Output per hectare is low but output per worker is high.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Intensive subsistence farming in monsoon Asia yields a high output per hectare but a very low output per worker, because a large labour force works tiny holdings. Statement III reverses this relationship.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about nomadic herding:
I. It is practised in the semi-arid and arid lands of Africa and Asia and in the tundra.
II. The Masai of East Africa and the Bedouin of Arabia are nomadic herders.
III. It is an intensive, market-oriented form of animal rearing.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Nomadic herding is an extensive, largely subsistence activity carried on in harsh environments - the Sahara-Arabia belt, Central Asia and the tundra. Commercial livestock ranching is its market-oriented counterpart.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about von Thunen's model of agricultural land use:
I. It was put forward in 1826 for an 'isolated state' served by a single central market.
II. Market gardening and dairying occupy the zone nearest the market.
III. Extensive ranching occupies the zone farthest from the market.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Von Thunen's concentric-ring model (Der isolierte Staat, 1826) places perishable and bulky produce - market gardening and dairying - closest to the market and ranching in the outermost ring, because transport cost rises with distance.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about shifting cultivation:
I. It involves clearing a patch of forest by cutting and burning the vegetation.
II. The same plot is cultivated continuously for several decades.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.exp: Shifting or slash-and-burn cultivation clears and burns a forest patch, crops it for two or three years until fertility falls and then abandons it for a long fallow. It is called Jhum in north-eastern India.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about commercial dairy farming:
I. It is most highly developed in north-western Europe, north-eastern North America and New Zealand.
II. Nearness to urban markets and an efficient transport system are essential to it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.exp: Milk is bulky and perishable, so dairy belts develop close to large urban markets and depend on refrigerated transport. Denmark, the Netherlands, north-eastern USA, Canada, New Zealand and south-eastern Australia are the leading dairy regions.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the fishery off the coast of Peru:
I. Its richness is due to the upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water associated with the Peru (Humboldt) Current.
II. The anchoveta catch collapses during El Nino years.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.exp: Upwelling along the Peruvian coast brings nutrients to the surface and sustains the world's largest single-species fishery, the anchoveta. During El Nino the intrusion of warm water suppresses upwelling and the catch collapses.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Crop)   List-II (Leading producing country)
A. Tea   1. Brazil
B. Coffee   2. Thailand
C. Cocoa   3. Cote d'Ivoire
D. Natural rubber   4. China
questions.exp: China leads in tea, Brazil in coffee, Cote d'Ivoire in cocoa and Thailand in natural rubber. India is second in tea and Vietnam second in coffee.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Temperate grassland)   List-II (Country)
A. Prairie   1. Australia
B. Pampas   2. United States of America
C. Veld   3. South Africa
D. Downs   4. Argentina
questions.exp: The Prairies (USA and Canada), Pampas (Argentina), Veld (South Africa) and Downs (Australia) are the great temperate grasslands where extensive commercial grain farming and livestock ranching are carried on.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Pastoral community)   List-II (Region)
A. Bedouin   1. Steppes of Central Asia
B. Masai   2. East Africa
C. Lapps (Sami)   3. Tundra of northern Europe
D. Kirghiz   4. Arabian desert
questions.exp: The Bedouin herd camels and goats in the Arabian desert, the Masai cattle in East Africa, the Lapps or Sami reindeer in the European tundra and the Kirghiz sheep and horses on the Central Asian steppes.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of crop and leading producing country is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: India, not Bangladesh, is the world's largest producer of jute; Bangladesh is the largest exporter of jute and jute goods. Spain leads in olives and olive oil, Indonesia in palm oil and Brazil in sugarcane.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT a characteristic feature of plantation agriculture?
opts: Large estates worked by hired labour
Cultivation of a wide variety of food crops for local consumption
Production of a single crop mainly for export
Heavy investment in processing and transport
questions.exp: Plantations are monocultures grown for distant export markets, not diversified food farms. Rubber in Malaysia, tea in Sri Lanka, coffee in Brazil and cocoa in Ghana are the classic examples.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of fishing ground and its location is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Georges Bank - north-eastern coast of North America
questions.exp: The Grand Banks lie off Newfoundland in Canada, not off Norway. The north-west Pacific, which includes the Sea of Okhotsk and the seas around Japan, is the world's most productive fishing region.

questions.q:
Arrange the following countries in descending order of their annual production of tea:
I. India
II. Kenya
III. China
IV. Sri Lanka
questions.exp: China is the world's largest tea producer, followed by India, Kenya and Sri Lanka. Kenya is, however, the world's largest exporter of black tea.

chapters.title: World Industry, Transport and Environmental Issues
factsheet: Ruhr (Germany) - Europe's foremost coal-based iron and steel region; cities Essen, Dortmund, Duisburg (Rhine inland port); the Saar is the other German coalfield.
Lorraine (France) - 'minette' iron ore, Western Europe's largest ore reserve; Nord-Pas-de-Calais is the French coalfield.

United Kingdom - Midlands/Black Country (Birmingham, engineering), Lancashire (Manchester, cotton - 'Cottonopolis'), Yorkshire (Leeds-Bradford, wool), Clydeside (Glasgow, shipbuilding), Sheffield (cutlery and special steels).
Donbas or Donetsk Basin - Ukraine (coal and steel); Kuzbas (Kuznetsk Basin) and the Urals with Magnitogorsk - Russia; Silesia with Katowice - Poland; Sambre-Meuse - Belgium; Po valley - Italy.

Japan - Keihin (Tokyo-Yokohama, largest), Hanshin (Osaka-Kobe), Chukyo (Nagoya), Kitakyushu/Yawata (steel). USA - New England (cotton textiles), Pittsburgh-Lake Erie (steel), Great Lakes with Detroit (automobiles), Silicon Valley in California (electronics and IT). China - Anshan (Manchuria, steel), Shanghai (largest industrial city), Wuhan, Beijing-Tianjin.
China makes more than half the world's crude steel; India is second and Japan third. Australia is the largest producer and exporter of iron ore, Brazil (Carajas, Itabira) second.

Chile leads world copper output (Chuquicamata, Escondida) and reserves; Kazakhstan leads uranium; China leads coal and gold; Indonesia leads nickel; Guinea holds the largest bauxite reserves. USA is the largest crude oil producer and Saudi Arabia the largest exporter; OPEC was founded at Baghdad in 1960 with headquarters at Vienna.
Trans-Siberian Railway - Moscow to Vladivostok, about 9,289 km, the longest railway line in the world, completed 1916, crossing eight time zones.

Trans-Australian Railway (Indian Pacific, Perth-Sydney) carries the world's longest dead-straight stretch of track, about 478 km across the Nullarbor Plain; the Canadian Pacific crosses Canada from Montreal to Vancouver. The Pan-American Highway, the longest motorable road, runs from Alaska to southern Argentina and is broken only by the Darien Gap.
Suez Canal - opened 1869, 193 km, Port Said to Suez, links the Mediterranean with the Red Sea, sea-level and lock-free; nationalised by Egypt in 1956.

Panama Canal - opened 1914, about 82 km, links the Atlantic with the Pacific through the Gatun, Pedro Miguel and Miraflores locks and Gatun Lake. Kiel Canal joins the North Sea to the Baltic; the Grand Canal of China is the world's longest canal.

Shanghai is the world's busiest container port, Singapore second, Rotterdam the largest in Europe; Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta is the busiest airport by total passengers, Dubai by international passengers, Hong Kong by air cargo.

Ozone: Vienna Convention 1985; Montreal Protocol adopted 16 September 1987, in force 1 January 1989 - the first UN treaty with universal ratification. World Ozone Day is 16 September. Ozone lies in the stratosphere and is measured in Dobson Units.
Kigali Amendment adopted at Kigali, Rwanda in 2016, in force 1 January 2019 - phase-down of hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), which are greenhouse gases but not ozone-depleting; India ratified it in 2021.
Acid rain - sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen form sulphuric and nitric acid; rain with pH below 5.6; damage to the Taj Mahal ('marble cancer'), the Black Forest and Scandinavian lakes.

Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment 1972 created UNEP (headquarters Nairobi) and gave us World Environment Day on 5 June; the UNFCCC was adopted at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992, came into force in 1994 and rests on the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities.

Kyoto Protocol adopted at COP3 in 1997, in force 16 February 2005, first commitment period 2008-12; flexible mechanisms - Clean Development Mechanism, Joint Implementation, Emissions Trading; Doha Amendment 2012 extended it to 2020.

Kyoto basket of gases - carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, HFCs, PFCs and sulphur hexafluoride, with nitrogen trifluoride added by the Doha Amendment; sulphur hexafluoride has the highest global warming potential.

Conventional order of contribution to the enhanced greenhouse effect: carbon dioxide (about 60 per cent) > methane (about 20 per cent) > chlorofluorocarbons (about 14 per cent) > nitrous oxide (about 6 per cent).

Paris Agreement adopted at COP21 on 12 December 2015, in force 4 November 2016 - hold warming well below 2 degrees Celsius and pursue 1.5 degrees Celsius, through Nationally Determined Contributions and a global stocktake every five years.

COP hosts and outcomes: COP21 Paris 2015 (Paris Agreement); COP26 Glasgow 2021 (Glasgow Climate Pact, 'phase-down' of unabated coal, India's net-zero 2070 Panchamrit); COP27 Sharm el-Sheikh 2022 (Loss and Damage Fund created); COP28 Dubai 2023 (first Global Stocktake, 'transitioning away from fossil fuels', treble renewables).

COP29 Baku 2024 - New Collective Quantified Goal of at least 300 billion US dollars a year by 2035 within a 1.3 trillion dollar 'Baku Finance Goal'; Article 6 carbon market rules finalised. COP30 Belem 2025 - the 'Global Mutirao' decision, adaptation finance to be trebled by 2035, no fossil-fuel roadmap in the text. COP31 is to be at Antalya, Turkiye, with Australia holding the presidency.

Net-zero target years: India 2070, China 2060, the European Union, United Kingdom, United States and Japan 2050. India's updated NDC - cut the emission intensity of GDP by 45 per cent by 2030 over 2005 and reach 50 per cent non-fossil installed power capacity by 2030.
IPCC was set up in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization and UNEP; it shared the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize with Al Gore; the AR6 Synthesis Report appeared in 2023.
UNCCD adopted at Paris on 17 June 1994, in force 1996; World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought is 17 June; UNCCD COP16 met at Riyadh in 2024; Land Degradation Neutrality is SDG target 15.3.
Great Green Wall - launched by the African Union in 2007 to create an 8,000 km belt of restored land across the Sahel from Senegal to Djibouti.

Biodiversity hotspots - concept of Norman Myers (1988); 36 hotspots at present; criteria are at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and loss of at least 70 per cent of original vegetation; India has four - Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (Nicobar Islands).

Ramsar Convention on Wetlands 1971 (Ramsar, Iran), in force 1975, World Wetlands Day 2 February; CITES 1973 (Washington), in force 1975; CBD 1992 (Rio); Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety 2000; Nagoya Protocol on access and benefit sharing 2010; Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, CBD COP15 Montreal 2022, 23 targets including '30x30'.

Chemicals and waste treaties - Basel 1989 (trans-boundary movement of hazardous wastes), Rotterdam 1998 (prior informed consent), Stockholm 2001 (persistent organic pollutants), Minamata 2013 (mercury).

Plastics - UNEA-5.2 at Nairobi adopted resolution 5/14 'End Plastic Pollution' in March 2022; negotiating sessions at Busan (2024) and Geneva (2025) ended without a treaty. The Great Pacific Garbage Patch lies in the North Pacific gyre between Hawaii and California.

questions.q: Essen, Dortmund and Duisburg are the principal industrial cities of which industrial region?
questions.exp: These cities lie in the Ruhr basin of western Germany, Europe's foremost coal-based iron and steel region, served by the Rhine waterway and the great inland port of Duisburg.

questions.q: The Kuzbas (Kuznetsk Basin), one of the world's great coal-based industrial regions, lies in
questions.exp: The Kuznetsk basin in western Siberia is Russia's largest coalfield and the base of the Kuzbas iron and steel region. Magnitogorsk in the Urals is the other great Russian steel centre.

questions.q: Silicon Valley, the world's best known concentration of electronics and information technology industries, lies in
questions.exp: Silicon Valley occupies the Santa Clara Valley of California around San Jose. The Route 128 belt near Boston in New England is the other major American high-technology cluster.

questions.q: The Keihin industrial region, the largest manufacturing belt of Japan, is centred on
questions.exp: Keihin (Tokyo-Yokohama) on the Kanto plain is Japan's leading industrial region. Hanshin is Osaka-Kobe, Chukyo is Nagoya and Kitakyushu on Kyushu is the old iron and steel belt.

questions.q: Which country is the world's largest producer of crude steel?
questions.exp: China produces more than half of the world's crude steel. India is second, having overtaken Japan in 2018, and Japan third.

questions.q: Which country is the world's largest exporter of iron ore?
questions.exp: Australia, drawing mainly on the Pilbara ranges of Western Australia, is both the largest producer and the largest exporter of iron ore; Brazil, with Carajas and Itabira, is second.

questions.q: The world's leading producer of copper is
questions.exp: Chile, with the Chuquicamata and Escondida mines in the Atacama region, leads world copper production and also holds the largest reserves; Peru is second.

questions.q: The Trans-Siberian Railway, the longest railway line in the world, runs from Moscow to
questions.exp: The Trans-Siberian Railway links Moscow with the Pacific port of Vladivostok over about 9,289 km, crossing eight time zones. It was completed in 1916.

questions.q: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch, the largest known accumulation of floating marine plastic debris, lies between
questions.exp: The patch lies in the North Pacific subtropical gyre between Hawaii and California, where circulating currents concentrate plastic waste. A global treaty on plastic pollution, mandated by the UN Environment Assembly in 2022, is still under negotiation.

questions.q: Which country is at present the world's largest producer of crude oil?
questions.exp: The United States has been the largest crude oil producer since 2018, ahead of Saudi Arabia and Russia. Saudi Arabia remains the largest exporter; OPEC, founded at Baghdad in 1960, has its headquarters at Vienna.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the Suez and Panama Canals is correct?
opts: Both canals are provided with locks
The Suez Canal has locks while the Panama Canal has none
The Panama Canal has locks while the Suez Canal has none
questions.exp: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869 and 193 km long, is a sea-level canal joining the Mediterranean and the Red Sea and needs no locks. The Panama Canal, opened in 1914 and about 82 km long, lifts ships through the Gatun, Pedro Miguel and Miraflores locks.

questions.q: Which is at present the world's busiest airport in terms of total passenger traffic?
questions.exp: Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta has been the world's busiest airport by total passenger numbers for most of the last quarter century. Dubai handles the most international passengers and Hong Kong the most air cargo.

questions.q: Which is at present the world's busiest container port?
questions.exp: Shanghai has been the world's busiest container port since 2010, with Singapore second. Rotterdam is the largest port in Europe.

questions.q: The Pan-American Highway, generally regarded as the longest motorable road in the world, is broken by a single unbridged stretch of forest and swamp known as the
questions.exp: The Darien Gap, on the Panama-Colombia border, is the only break in the Pan-American Highway, which otherwise runs from Alaska to southern Argentina.

questions.q: The Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer was adopted in the year
questions.exp: The Montreal Protocol was adopted on 16 September 1987 and entered into force on 1 January 1989. It implements the Vienna Convention of 1985 and is the first treaty in UN history to secure universal ratification.

questions.q: The Kigali Amendment of 2016 to the Montreal Protocol provides for the phase-down of
questions.exp: The Kigali Amendment, adopted in Rwanda in 2016 and in force from 1 January 2019, phases down hydrofluorocarbons. HFCs do not deplete ozone but are powerful greenhouse gases. India ratified the amendment in 2021.

questions.q: The International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer is observed every year on
questions.exp: 16 September marks the signing of the Montreal Protocol in 1987. World Environment Day is 5 June, World Wetlands Day 2 February and the World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought 17 June.

questions.q: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) was established in 1988 jointly by
opts: the World Meteorological Organization and the United Nations Environment Programme
the United Nations Development Programme and the World Bank
the Food and Agriculture Organization and UNESCO
the World Health Organization and the World Trade Organization
questions.exp: The IPCC was set up by WMO and UNEP to assess the science of climate change. It shared the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize with Al Gore, and its Sixth Assessment Synthesis Report was released in 2023.

questions.q: The Paris Agreement on climate change was adopted at which session of the Conference of the Parties to the UNFCCC?
questions.exp: The Paris Agreement was adopted at COP21 in Paris on 12 December 2015 and entered into force on 4 November 2016. It replaced the Kyoto Protocol's imposed targets with Nationally Determined Contributions.

questions.q: The long-term temperature goal of the Paris Agreement is to hold the rise in global average temperature to
opts: below 3 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels
well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees Celsius
questions.exp: Article 2 of the Paris Agreement sets the 'well below 2 degrees Celsius, pursuing 1.5 degrees Celsius' goal. Progress is reviewed through a global stocktake every five years, the first of which concluded at COP28 in 2023.

questions.q: At COP26 held in Glasgow, India announced that it would achieve net-zero emissions by the year
questions.exp: India announced the 2070 net-zero target at Glasgow in 2021 as part of the five-point 'Panchamrit' pledge. China's target year is 2060, and that of the European Union, the United Kingdom, the United States and Japan is 2050.

questions.q: The decision to establish a dedicated Loss and Damage Fund for countries hit by climate disasters was taken at
questions.exp: COP27 at Sharm el-Sheikh in Egypt in 2022 agreed to create the Loss and Damage Fund. It was operationalised with the first pledges at COP28 in Dubai the following year.

questions.q: The first Global Stocktake under the Paris Agreement was concluded at
questions.exp: COP28 at Dubai in 2023 concluded the first global stocktake, whose outcome for the first time called on countries to contribute to 'transitioning away from fossil fuels' and to treble renewable energy capacity by 2030.

questions.q: The New Collective Quantified Goal on climate finance agreed at COP29 in Baku commits developed countries to mobilise at least
opts: 100 billion US dollars a year by 2030
300 billion US dollars a year by 2035
500 billion US dollars a year by 2040
1.3 trillion US dollars a year by 2030
questions.exp: COP29 (Baku, 2024) set a core goal of at least 300 billion US dollars a year by 2035 for developing countries, inside a wider 'Baku Finance Goal' aspiration of scaling all sources of climate finance to 1.3 trillion dollars a year by 2035.

questions.q: COP30 of the UNFCCC, held in November 2025, was hosted by which city?
questions.exp: COP30 met at Belem in the Brazilian Amazon; its main outcome decision is known as the 'Global Mutirao', which called for adaptation finance to be trebled by 2035. COP31 is to be held at Antalya in Turkiye with Australia holding the presidency.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the industrial regions of the United States of America:
I. New England was the earliest centre of cotton textile manufacture in the country.
II. Detroit in the Great Lakes region is the leading centre of the automobile industry.
III. Pittsburgh grew as an iron and steel centre on the Appalachian coalfield.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. New England around Boston pioneered American cotton textiles, Detroit is the automobile capital, and Pittsburgh grew where Appalachian coking coal met iron ore brought by the Great Lakes waterway.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about acid rain:
I. Sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen are its principal precursors.
II. It is caused mainly by the release of chlorofluorocarbons from refrigerators and air-conditioners.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.exp: Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides released by burning fossil fuels form sulphuric and nitric acid in the atmosphere and bring down rain with a pH below 5.6. Chlorofluorocarbons cause ozone depletion, not acid rain.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Montreal Protocol:
I. It was preceded by the Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer.
II. It is the first treaty in the history of the United Nations to be ratified by every member state.
III. It sets binding targets for the reduction of carbon dioxide emissions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The Montreal Protocol of 1987 implements the Vienna Convention of 1985 and has achieved universal ratification. Carbon dioxide is dealt with under the UNFCCC and its Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement, not under the Montreal Protocol.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Kyoto Protocol:
I. It was adopted in 1997 and entered into force in 2005.
II. It placed legally binding emission reduction targets on the developed countries listed in Annexure I.
III. Clean Development Mechanism, Joint Implementation and Emissions Trading were its three flexible mechanisms.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The Kyoto Protocol was adopted at COP3 in 1997, entered into force on 16 February 2005 and covered the first commitment period 2008-2012; the Doha Amendment of 2012 extended it to 2020.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Paris Agreement:
I. Every party is required to prepare and communicate a Nationally Determined Contribution.
II. It obliges developing countries to accept legally binding absolute cuts in emissions.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.exp: The Paris Agreement rests on self-determined national pledges; the targets themselves are not legally binding and no absolute cut is imposed on developing countries. India's updated NDC promises a 45 per cent cut in the emission intensity of GDP by 2030 over 2005 levels.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification was adopted in 1994.
II. The Great Green Wall initiative to check desertification is being implemented across the Sahel region of Africa.
III. The World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought is observed on 5 June.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The UNCCD was adopted at Paris on 17 June 1994 and the day is therefore observed on 17 June, not 5 June. The Great Green Wall, launched by the African Union in 2007, aims to create an 8,000 km belt of restored land from Senegal to Djibouti.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about biodiversity hotspots:
I. The concept was first put forward by Norman Myers.
II. A region must have at least 1,500 endemic species of vascular plants to qualify as a hotspot.
III. There are at present 36 recognised biodiversity hotspots in the world.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. A hotspot must in addition have lost at least 70 per cent of its original natural vegetation. Four hotspots extend into India - the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (the Nicobar Islands).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about deforestation in the world:
I. Tropical forests record the highest rate of deforestation among all forest types.
II. Conversion of forest to cropland and pasture is the single largest driver of deforestation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.exp: Tropical forests, chiefly in the Amazon basin, the Congo basin and South-East Asia, lose far more area each year than temperate or boreal forests, and agricultural expansion - cattle ranching, soybean and oil palm - is the main cause.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of industrial region and country is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: The Donbas or Donetsk basin, a great coal and steel region, lies in eastern Ukraine and not in Poland. Poland's corresponding coal-and-steel region is Silesia, centred on Katowice.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT an ozone-depleting substance?
questions.exp: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas but does not destroy stratospheric ozone. Chlorofluorocarbons, halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform and methyl bromide are the controlled ozone-depleting substances under the Montreal Protocol.

questions.q: Which one of the following gases is NOT included in the basket of greenhouse gases regulated under the Kyoto Protocol?
questions.exp: The Kyoto basket covers carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons and sulphur hexafluoride, with nitrogen trifluoride added by the Doha Amendment. Chlorofluorocarbons are controlled instead under the Montreal Protocol.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of trans-continental railway and country is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Union Pacific Railway - United States of America
questions.exp: The Canadian Pacific Railway runs across Canada from Montreal to Vancouver. Australia's great east-west line is the Trans-Australian Railway, on which the Indian Pacific service runs from Perth to Sydney.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the greenhouse effect is NOT correct?
opts: Water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas in the atmosphere
Methane has a much higher global warming potential than carbon dioxide over a hundred-year horizon
Nitrogen is a major greenhouse gas
The natural greenhouse effect keeps the earth's mean surface temperature well above what it would otherwise be
questions.exp: Nitrogen and oxygen, though they make up about 99 per cent of the atmosphere, are not greenhouse gases because their molecules do not absorb infra-red radiation. Without the natural greenhouse effect the earth's mean surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Industrial region)   List-II (Country)
A. Lorraine   1. Ukraine
B. Midlands   2. Germany
C. Ruhr   3. France
D. Donbas   4. United Kingdom
questions.exp: Lorraine is in France, the Midlands or Black Country around Birmingham in the United Kingdom, the Ruhr in Germany and the Donbas in Ukraine.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Convention)   List-II (Year of adoption)
A. Ramsar Convention   1. 1992
B. CITES   2. 2013
C. Convention on Biological Diversity   3. 1973
D. Minamata Convention   4. 1971
questions.exp: Ramsar 1971 (Ramsar, Iran), CITES 1973 (Washington), the Convention on Biological Diversity 1992 (Rio Earth Summit) and the Minamata Convention on Mercury 2013 (Kumamoto, Japan). Ramsar and CITES both entered into force in 1975.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Conference of the Parties)   List-II (Host city)
A. COP26   1. Sharm el-Sheikh
B. COP27   2. Baku
C. COP28   3. Glasgow
D. COP29   4. Dubai
questions.exp: COP26 met at Glasgow in 2021, COP27 at Sharm el-Sheikh in 2022, COP28 at Dubai in 2023 and COP29 at Baku in 2024. COP30 was held at Belem in Brazil in 2025.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Mineral)   List-II (Leading producing country)
A. Copper   1. Kazakhstan
B. Uranium   2. Chile
C. Coal   3. China
D. Nickel   4. Indonesia
questions.exp: Chile leads world copper output, Kazakhstan supplies about two-fifths of the world's uranium, China is the largest coal producer and Indonesia now dominates world nickel supply. India is the second largest producer of coal.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Industrial city)   List-II (Country)
A. Magnitogorsk   1. Japan
B. Anshan   2. Russia
C. Kitakyushu   3. China
D. Katowice   4. Poland
questions.exp: Magnitogorsk is the great Ural steel city of Russia, Anshan in Manchuria is China's oldest major steel centre, Kitakyushu (Yawata) is Japan's classic steel town and Katowice lies in the Upper Silesian industrial region of Poland.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Convention)   List-II (Subject)
A. Basel Convention   1. Mercury
B. Rotterdam Convention   2. Trans-boundary movement of hazardous wastes
C. Stockholm Convention   3. Prior informed consent for hazardous chemicals
D. Minamata Convention   4. Persistent organic pollutants
questions.exp: Basel (1989) governs the trans-boundary movement of hazardous wastes, Rotterdam (1998) the prior informed consent procedure for hazardous chemicals and pesticides, Stockholm (2001) persistent organic pollutants and Minamata (2013) mercury.

questions.q:
Arrange the following greenhouse gases in decreasing order of their conventionally estimated contribution to the enhanced greenhouse effect:
I. Methane
II. Carbon dioxide
III. Nitrous oxide
IV. Chlorofluorocarbons
questions.exp: The standard ordering is carbon dioxide (about 60 per cent), methane (about 20 per cent), chlorofluorocarbons (about 14 per cent) and nitrous oxide (about 6 per cent). Ranked by global warming potential per molecule, however, the order is very nearly reversed.

chapters.title: Physiographic Divisions of India
factsheet: India lies between 8°4'N-37°6'N and 68°7'E-97°25'E; area 32.87 lakh sq km; 7th largest country; about 2.4% of the world's land area.
Indira Point in Great Nicobar (6°45'N) is India's southernmost point; Kanniyakumari (8°4'N) is the southernmost point of the mainland.
Standard Meridian 82°30'E passes through Mirzapur (UP) and five states — UP, MP, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh; IST = GMT + 5:30.
Tropic of Cancer crosses eight states — Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, Mizoram.
Land frontier 15,106.7 km; longest border with Bangladesh (4,096.7 km), shortest with Afghanistan (106 km).
Coastline re-assessed by the National Hydrographic Office to 11,098.81 km (earlier official figure 7,516.6 km); Gujarat longest at 2,340.62 km.
Three geological divisions — the Peninsular block (Archaean gneiss and granite), the Himalaya (folded Tethyan sediments) and the Indo-Ganga plain (alluvium).
North-to-south sequence of Himalayan ranges: Karakoram – Ladakh – Zaskar – Great Himalaya (Himadri) – Lesser Himalaya (Himachal) – Shivalik.
Himadri averages about 6,000 m and carries all the great peaks; Himachal 3,700–4,500 m (Pir Panjal, Dhauladhar, Mahabharat); Shivalik only 900–1,100 m.
Duns are longitudinal valleys between the Shivalik and the Lesser Himalaya — Dehra Dun, Kotli Dun, Patli Dun; Karewas are lacustrine deposits of the Kashmir valley.
Kangchenjunga (8,586 m, Sikkim) — highest peak of India and third highest in the world; K2/Godwin Austen (8,611 m) lies in the Karakoram.
Nanda Devi (7,816 m, Chamoli, Uttarakhand) — highest peak lying entirely within Indian territory; Kamet 7,756 m.
Burrard's regional divisions: Punjab Himalaya (Indus–Satluj), Kumaon Himalaya (Satluj–Kali), Nepal Himalaya (Kali–Teesta), Assam Himalaya (Teesta–Dihang).
Purvanchal hills: Patkai Bum, Naga, Manipur, Mizo (Lushai), Barail, Mikir and the Garo–Khasi–Jaintia group.

Passes — Zoji La and Khardung La (Ladakh), Banihal (J&K), Rohtang, Shipki La, Bara Lacha La and Kunzum (HP), Mana, Niti and Lipulekh (Uttarakhand), Nathu La and Jelep La (Sikkim), Bomdi La, Se La, Diphu and Pangsau (Arunachal Pradesh).
Northern Plain belts north to south: Bhabar (porous pebbles, streams vanish) → Terai (marshy, streams re-emerge) → Bhangar (old alluvium with kankar) → Khadar (new alluvium of flood plains).
Punjab doabs: Bist (Beas–Satluj), Bari (Beas–Ravi), Rechna (Ravi–Chenab), Chaj (Chenab–Jhelum), Sindh Sagar (Jhelum–Indus).
Aravalli — oldest fold mountain system of India, running north-east to south-west from Delhi to Gujarat; highest peak Guru Shikhar (1,722 m, Mount Abu, Sirohi).
Deccan Trap is basaltic lava of Cretaceous–Eocene age; its weathering yields black regur (cotton) soil.
Malwa plateau lies between the Aravalli and the Vindhya; the Chotanagpur plateau is drained by the Damodar; the Meghalaya plateau is cut off from the main block by the Malda (Garo–Rajmahal) gap.
Dhupgarh (1,350 m) near Pachmarhi is the highest point of the Satpura; the Maikal range links Satpura to Chotanagpur; Amarkantak is the Narmada–Son–Johilla source area.
Western Ghats (Sahyadri) are continuous and crossed only by passes; the Eastern Ghats are discontinuous and dissected by the east-flowing rivers.
Anamudi (2,695 m, Idukki–Ernakulam, Kerala) — highest peak of the Western Ghats, of South India and of the whole of India south of the Himalaya.
Doddabetta (2,637 m) is the highest peak of the Nilgiri hills; Arma Konda (1,680 m, Alluri Sitharama Raju district, Andhra Pradesh) is the highest peak of the Eastern Ghats.
The Eastern and Western Ghats meet at the Nilgiris; the Palghat (Palakkad) gap separates the Nilgiri from the Anaimalai hills; Thal Ghat and Bhor Ghat cross the Sahyadri in Maharashtra.
Western coastal plain — narrow, submergent: Kachchh–Kathiawar, Gujarat, Konkan, Kanara and Malabar (backwaters called kayals).
Eastern coastal plain — wide, emergent and deltaic: Utkal, Northern Circars/Andhra and Coromandel; Chilika and Pulicat lie along it.
Andaman & Nicobar: Ten Degree Channel separates Little Andaman from Car Nicobar; Duncan Passage separates South Andaman from Little Andaman; Coco Channel lies towards Myanmar.
Barren Island is India's only active volcano and Narcondam is dormant; Saddle Peak (732 m, North Andaman) is the highest point of the group.
Lakshadweep is of coral origin with headquarters at Kavaratti; the Nine Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the main group and the Eight Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the Maldives.

questions.q: Which mountain peak, the third highest in the world, lies on the India–Nepal border in Sikkim?
questions.exp: Kangchenjunga (8,586 m) is the highest peak of India and the third highest in the world after Mount Everest and K2.

questions.q: Which one of the following is the highest mountain peak lying entirely within Indian territory?
questions.exp: Nanda Devi (7,816 m) in Chamoli district, Uttarakhand, is the highest peak wholly within India. Kangchenjunga is higher but straddles the India–Nepal border.

questions.q: Anamudi, the highest peak of peninsular India, is located in which state?
questions.exp: Anamudi (2,695 m) stands at the junction of the Anaimalai, Cardamom and Palani hills in Idukki–Ernakulam districts of Kerala. It is the highest point in India south of the Himalaya.

questions.q: Arma Konda, the highest peak of the Eastern Ghats, lies in which state?
questions.exp: Arma Konda (1,680 m) in Alluri Sitharama Raju district of Andhra Pradesh is the highest peak of the Eastern Ghats. Mahendragiri in Odisha is another prominent Eastern Ghats peak.

questions.q: Doddabetta (2,637 m) is the highest peak of which hills?
questions.exp: Doddabetta near Udhagamandalam (Ooty) in Tamil Nadu is the highest peak of the Nilgiris, the block where the Eastern and Western Ghats converge.

questions.q: The Eastern Ghats and the Western Ghats meet at the:
questions.exp: The two Ghats converge in the Nilgiri hills. South of the Nilgiris the Palghat gap breaks the continuity of the Western Ghats.

questions.q: India's only active volcano is situated on:
questions.exp: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is the only active volcano in Indian territory; Narcondam Island nearby is dormant.

questions.q: The Ten Degree Channel separates:
opts: Minicoy from the main Lakshadweep group
questions.exp: The Ten Degree Channel divides the Andaman group from the Nicobar group, i.e. Little Andaman from Car Nicobar. The Duncan Passage lies between South Andaman and Little Andaman.

questions.q: Indira Point, the southernmost point of India, is located in:
questions.exp: Indira Point (6°45'N) lies at the southern tip of Great Nicobar. It was earlier called Pygmalion Point and subsided during the 2004 tsunami.

questions.q: The Standard Meridian of India (82°30' E) passes through which city?
questions.exp: The 82°30'E meridian passes through Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh and fixes Indian Standard Time at GMT + 5:30.

questions.q: The Tropic of Cancer passes through how many Indian states?
questions.exp: It crosses Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram — eight states.

questions.q: India shares its longest land boundary with:
questions.exp: The India–Bangladesh boundary is 4,096.7 km long, the longest; the shortest is with Afghanistan (106 km).

questions.q: The narrow belt of porous pebbly deposits along the Himalayan foothills, in which the descending streams disappear underground, is called the:
questions.exp: The Bhabar is an 8–16 km wide pebble belt at the foot of the Shivalik. South of it the streams re-emerge in the marshy Terai.

questions.q: The newer alluvium deposited on the flood plains of the northern plains is known as:
questions.exp: Khadar is the new alluvium renewed almost every year by floods; Bhangar is the older alluvium and often contains calcareous kankar nodules.

questions.q: The longitudinal valleys lying between the Shivalik and the Lesser Himalaya are known as:
questions.exp: Dehra Dun, Kotli Dun and Patli Dun are such valleys. Karewas are lacustrine deposits of the Kashmir valley and bugyals are alpine meadows.

questions.q: Guru Shikhar, the highest peak of the Aravalli range, lies in which district of Rajasthan?
questions.exp: Guru Shikhar (1,722 m) is on the Mount Abu plateau in Sirohi district.

questions.q: The Deccan Trap is composed mainly of:
questions.exp: The Deccan Trap was formed by fissure eruptions of basaltic lava of Cretaceous–Eocene age; its weathering produces black regur soil.

questions.q: The Meghalaya plateau is separated from the main block of the Peninsular Plateau by the:
questions.exp: The Malda gap, also called the Garo–Rajmahal gap, was filled by later Ganga–Brahmaputra alluvium and detaches the Meghalaya plateau from the Chotanagpur block.

questions.q: Which Indian state has the longest coastline?
questions.exp: Gujarat has the longest coastline of any Indian state — 2,340.62 km in the revised National Hydrographic Office assessment.

questions.q: According to the re-assessment carried out by the National Hydrographic Office, the length of India's coastline is:
questions.exp: The earlier official figure of 7,516.6 km was revised to 11,098.81 km using high-resolution mapping. 15,106.7 km is the length of India's land frontier.

questions.q: The Zoji La pass provides a road link between:
questions.exp: Zoji La on NH-1 crosses the Great Himalaya and links the Kashmir valley with Kargil and Leh.

questions.q: Which one of the following ranges lies immediately to the north of the Great Himalaya (Himadri)?
questions.exp: The trans-Himalayan sequence from north to south is Karakoram – Ladakh – Zaskar, and then the Great Himalaya. The Pir Panjal and Dhauladhar belong to the Lesser Himalaya, south of the Himadri.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Shivalik range:
I. It is the southernmost and geologically youngest range of the Himalaya.
II. It is built largely of unconsolidated sediments brought down by rivers from the main Himalaya.
III. Its average elevation exceeds 3,000 metres.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The Shivalik averages only 900–1,100 m, so statement III is wrong. Its outer, unconsolidated character makes it highly prone to landslides and erosion.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. In the Bhabar belt the streams descending from the Himalaya disappear into porous pebble beds.
II. The Terai lies south of the Bhabar and is a marshy, damp and thickly forested belt where the streams re-emerge.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.exp: Both are correct. Much of the Terai in Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh was cleared for agriculture after Partition.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Peninsular Plateau of India:
I. It is composed mainly of ancient crystalline, igneous and metamorphic rocks.
II. The Deccan Trap of the north-western Deccan is of volcanic origin.
III. The Chotanagpur plateau is drained by the Damodar river.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The Peninsular block is one of the oldest and most stable landmasses on earth.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Andaman and Nicobar Islands:
I. Saddle Peak in North Andaman is the highest point of the island group.
II. Barren Island is the only active volcano in Indian territory.
III. The Duncan Passage separates Little Andaman from Car Nicobar.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The Duncan Passage separates South Andaman from Little Andaman; it is the Ten Degree Channel that separates Little Andaman from Car Nicobar, so III is wrong.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Lakshadweep islands:
I. They are of coral origin.
II. Kavaratti is the administrative headquarters.
III. The Eight Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the Maldives.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The Nine Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the rest of the Lakshadweep group.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The western coastal plain is narrow and is an example of a submerged coast.
II. The eastern coastal plain is wider and carries the well-developed deltas of the major east-flowing rivers.
III. The Malabar coast is noted for its lagoons known as kayals.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The submerged western coast provides natural harbours such as Mumbai and Marmagao, while the emergent eastern coast has few good ports.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Aravalli range:
I. It is one of the oldest fold mountain systems in the world.
II. It runs in a north-east to south-west direction from Delhi to Gujarat.
III. Its highest peak is Guru Shikhar.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The Aravalli survives today as a heavily denuded relict range, with detached Vindhyan outliers to its east.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the regional divisions of the Himalaya:
I. The Punjab Himalaya lies between the Indus and the Satluj.
II. The Kumaon Himalaya lies between the Satluj and the Kali.
III. The Assam Himalaya lies between the Teesta and the Dihang.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct in Sydney Burrard's fourfold division; the Nepal Himalaya lies between the Kali and the Teesta.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Pass)   List-II (State/UT)
A. Shipki La   1. Sikkim
B. Nathu La   2. Himachal Pradesh
C. Se La   3. Uttarakhand
D. Lipulekh   4. Arunachal Pradesh
questions.exp: Shipki La is in Kinnaur (HP) and admits the Satluj into India; Nathu La is in Sikkim; Se La lies on the road to Tawang in Arunachal Pradesh; Lipulekh is in Pithoragarh, Uttarakhand.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Peak)   List-II (Range/Hills)
A. Anamudi   1. Nilgiri hills
B. Doddabetta   2. Aravalli range
C. Guru Shikhar   3. Satpura range
D. Dhupgarh   4. Anaimalai hills
questions.exp: Anamudi (2,695 m) belongs to the Anaimalai group, Doddabetta (2,637 m) to the Nilgiris, Guru Shikhar (1,722 m) to the Aravalli and Dhupgarh (1,350 m) to the Satpura.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Hills)   List-II (State)
A. Cardamom hills   1. Rajasthan
B. Javadi hills   2. Kerala
C. Rajmahal hills   3. Tamil Nadu
D. Mukundara hills   4. Jharkhand
questions.exp: The Cardamom hills lie in Kerala, the Javadi hills of the Eastern Ghats in Tamil Nadu, the Rajmahal hills in Jharkhand and the Mukundara hills near Kota in Rajasthan.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Water body)   List-II (Separates)
A. Ten Degree Channel   1. Minicoy and the Maldives
B. Duncan Passage   2. Little Andaman and Car Nicobar
C. Nine Degree Channel   3. South Andaman and Little Andaman
D. Eight Degree Channel   4. Minicoy and the main Lakshadweep group
questions.exp: The Ten Degree Channel divides the Andaman and Nicobar groups; the Duncan Passage lies within the Andamans; the Nine and Eight Degree Channels lie in the Lakshadweep sea.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Doab)   List-II (Rivers between which it lies)
A. Bist Doab   1. Beas and Ravi
B. Bari Doab   2. Ravi and Chenab
C. Rechna Doab   3. Chenab and Jhelum
D. Chaj Doab   4. Beas and Satluj
questions.exp: The Punjab doabs from east to west are Bist, Bari, Rechna, Chaj and Sindh Sagar; the last lies between the Jhelum and the Indus.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Anamudi is in Kerala, at the meeting point of the Anaimalai, Cardamom and Palani hills; Doddabetta is the highest peak in Tamil Nadu.

questions.q: Which one of the following hill ranges is NOT a part of the Purvanchal?
questions.exp: The Kaimur hills belong to the Vindhyan system of the Peninsular Plateau. The Purvanchal comprises the Patkai Bum, Naga, Manipur, Mizo, Barail and Garo–Khasi–Jaintia hills.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the Northern Plains of India is NOT correct?
opts: The Khadar belt lies away from the flood plains and is not renewed by fresh silt.
They have been built by the alluvium of the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra systems.
Bhangar represents the older alluvium and often contains calcareous kankar nodules.
The Bhabar belt lies immediately south of the Shivalik foothills.
questions.exp: It is the Bhangar that lies above the flood level and is not renewed; the Khadar is the new alluvium of the flood plains, enriched almost every year.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a gap or ghat and its location is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Palghat gap — between the Nilgiri and Anaimalai hills
questions.exp: The Bhor Ghat is in Maharashtra and carries the Mumbai–Pune route; the Thal Ghat carries the Mumbai–Nashik route.

questions.q:
Arrange the following ranges in the correct sequence from north to south:
I. Shivalik
II. Karakoram
III. Zaskar
IV. Ladakh
questions.exp: The correct order is Karakoram – Ladakh – Zaskar – Great Himalaya – Lesser Himalaya – Shivalik, i.e. II, IV, III, I.

chapters.title: Climate of India
factsheet: India has a tropical monsoon climate; the Himalaya shuts out cold Central Asian air and the Tropic of Cancer divides the country into a tropical south and a sub-tropical north.
IMD's four seasons: Winter (January–February), Pre-monsoon or hot weather (March–May), South-west monsoon (June–September), Post-monsoon or retreating monsoon (October–December).
Western disturbances are extra-tropical cyclones that originate over the Mediterranean region and are carried to India by the subtropical westerly jet stream.
Winter rain from western disturbances (locally mahawat) is small in amount but vital for the rabi wheat crop of Punjab, Haryana, western UP and northern Rajasthan.
The subtropical westerly jet stream lies south of the Himalaya in winter; its withdrawal north of the Tibetan plateau in early June is a precondition for the monsoon burst.
The tropical easterly jet stream develops over peninsular India in summer above the intensely heated Tibetan plateau.
The Somali (Findlater) jet is a low-level cross-equatorial jet off the East African coast that strengthens the Arabian Sea branch of the south-west monsoon.
The ITCZ shifts north in summer as the monsoon trough; the south-east trades cross the equator, are deflected right by the Coriolis force and arrive as south-west monsoon winds.
Normal onset of the south-west monsoon over Kerala is 1 June; it covers the whole country by about 8 July (IMD normal dates).
IMD's revised normal date for the start of withdrawal from west Rajasthan is 17 September (earlier 1 September); withdrawal from the country is complete by 15 October.
The south-west monsoon has two branches — the Arabian Sea branch and the Bay of Bengal branch — which converge over the north-western plains.
The Arabian Sea branch gives heavy rain on the windward (western) slopes of the Western Ghats and leaves a rain-shadow on the Deccan plateau.
Mawsynram in the Khasi hills of Meghalaya records the world's highest average annual rainfall; funnel-shaped valleys trap the Bay branch.
West Rajasthan (Jaisalmer, Barmer) and Ladakh receive less than 20 cm of rainfall; Leh is a cold desert.
A 'break' in the monsoon is a spell of dry weather during the rainy season, caused by shifts in the position of the monsoon trough.
The retreating monsoon season brings the oppressive 'October heat' — high temperature with high humidity and clear skies.
The north-east or retreating monsoon gives the Coromandel (Tamil Nadu) coast its main rainfall in October–December, the winds picking up moisture over the Bay of Bengal.
The Tamil Nadu coast stays dry in the south-west monsoon because it lies in the rain-shadow of the Western Ghats and runs parallel to the Bay of Bengal branch.
Rainfall variability is inversely related to rainfall amount — above 50% in west Rajasthan, Ladakh and the interior Deccan, below 25% on the west coast, the north-east and the Himalaya.
Mumbai receives over 2,000 mm of rain concentrated in June–September; Chennai receives about 1,200–1,400 mm with its maximum in October–November.
El Nino (warm eastern Pacific) is associated with weak or deficient Indian monsoons; La Nina with stronger ones; ENSO is tracked by the Southern Oscillation Index (Tahiti minus Darwin pressure).
A positive Indian Ocean Dipole (warmer western Indian Ocean) favours a good monsoon and can offset the effect of an El Nino.

MONEX (Monsoon Experiment) was an international field programme under the Global Weather Experiment — Winter MONEX in December 1978 and Summer MONEX in May–July 1979 over the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal.

Koppen's Indian types: Amw (west coast), As (Coromandel coast), Aw (tropical savanna of the peninsula), BShw (semi-arid steppe), BWhw (hot desert, west Rajasthan), Cwg (Ganga plain), Dfc (Arunachal Pradesh), E (polar, high Himalaya).

Local winds and showers: Loo (northern plains, May–June), Kal Baisakhi (West Bengal), Bardoli Chheerha (Assam), Mango showers (Kerala and coastal Karnataka), Blossom showers (coffee areas of Karnataka).
Tropical cyclones of the Bay of Bengal are about four times as frequent as those of the Arabian Sea, with peaks before and after the monsoon; the Odisha–Andhra coast is the most vulnerable.
Cyclones of the North Indian Ocean are named by IMD as the Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre, New Delhi, on behalf of thirteen WMO/ESCAP member countries.
IMD was established in 1875 and is headquartered at New Delhi; it is the national meteorological service of India.
IMD drought scale: rainfall deficiency of 26–50% of normal is a moderate drought, more than 50% a severe drought.
The Brahmaputra valley of Assam, the Kosi belt of north Bihar and the Damodar basin of West Bengal are among India's most flood-prone regions.

questions.q: The western disturbances that bring winter rainfall to north-western India originate over the:
questions.exp: Western disturbances are extra-tropical cyclones formed over the Mediterranean region and steered into India by the subtropical westerly jet stream.

questions.q: The winter rainfall of north-western India brought by western disturbances is locally known as:
questions.exp: Mahawat is small in amount but extremely important for the rabi wheat crop of Punjab, Haryana and adjoining Rajasthan.

questions.q: The normal date of onset of the south-west monsoon over Kerala is:
questions.exp: IMD's normal onset date over Kerala is 1 June; the monsoon normally covers the whole country by about 8 July.

questions.q: As per IMD's revised normal dates, the withdrawal of the south-west monsoon begins from west Rajasthan around:
questions.exp: In 2020 IMD revised the date from 1 September to 17 September; final withdrawal from the country is complete by 15 October.

questions.q: The Tamil Nadu coast receives the bulk of its annual rainfall during October–December from the:
questions.exp: During the retreating monsoon the north-east winds pick up moisture while crossing the Bay of Bengal and shed it on the Coromandel coast.

questions.q: The Coromandel coast remains comparatively dry during the south-west monsoon season mainly because:
