opts: It lies in the rain-shadow of the Western Ghats and runs parallel to the Bay of Bengal branch
It lies too far from the sea
The ITCZ does not shift northward over it
The Eastern Ghats are too high for the monsoon winds to cross
questions.exp: The Arabian Sea branch has already shed its moisture on the Western Ghats, while the Bay branch moves parallel to the coast without striking it.

questions.q: Which place records the highest average annual rainfall in India?
questions.exp: Mawsynram in the Khasi hills of Meghalaya receives the highest average annual rainfall in India and in the world; Cherrapunji (Sohra) lies close by.

questions.q: The 'Loo' is:
opts: A hot, dry westerly wind of the northern plains in May and June
A pre-monsoon shower of the Malabar coast
A thunderstorm of West Bengal in March
A cold wind of the Kashmir valley in January
questions.exp: The Loo blows in the afternoons of May–June across the northern plains and can raise temperatures to 45–47 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: 'Kal Baisakhi', the violent pre-monsoon thunderstorm, is associated with which state?
questions.exp: Kal Baisakhi (the nor'wester) strikes West Bengal in April–May; the same storms are called Bardoli Chheerha in Assam.

questions.q: 'Mango showers' are pre-monsoon showers that occur in:
questions.exp: These April–May showers help the early ripening of mangoes; in the coffee areas of Karnataka they are called blossom showers.

questions.q: The tropical easterly jet stream over peninsular India in summer develops mainly because of the:
opts: Intense heating of the Tibetan plateau
questions.exp: Heating of the Tibetan plateau creates a high-level anticyclone from which the tropical easterly jet flows out over peninsular India, aiding the monsoon.

questions.q: The low-level cross-equatorial jet stream that strengthens the Arabian Sea branch of the south-west monsoon is known as the:
questions.exp: The Somali or Findlater jet flows past the East African coast and turns into the Arabian Sea, feeding moisture into the monsoon current.

questions.q: El Nino conditions in the Pacific Ocean are generally associated with:
opts: Early onset of the monsoon over Kerala
Increased cyclone frequency in the Arabian Sea
questions.exp: El Nino, the warming of the eastern equatorial Pacific, weakens the Indian monsoon, while La Nina generally strengthens it.

questions.q: The Southern Oscillation Index is computed from the sea-level pressure difference between:
questions.exp: A persistently negative SOI (lower pressure at Tahiti than Darwin) indicates El Nino conditions and a likely weak Indian monsoon.

questions.q: MONEX, the international field programme of 1978–79, was undertaken to study:
opts: El Nino in the Pacific Ocean
questions.exp: The Monsoon Experiment was carried out under the Global Weather Experiment — Winter MONEX in December 1978 and Summer MONEX in May–July 1979 over the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal.

questions.q: In Koppen's classification, western Rajasthan is placed under which climatic type?
questions.exp: BWhw denotes a hot desert climate with dry winters, covering Barmer, Jaisalmer and adjoining western Rajasthan; BShw is the semi-arid steppe around it.

questions.q: The coefficient of variability of annual rainfall in India is highest in:
questions.exp: Variability exceeds 50% in west Rajasthan, Ladakh and parts of the interior Deccan; it is under 25% where rainfall is heavy, such as the west coast and the north-east.

questions.q: The India Meteorological Department was established in the year:
questions.exp: IMD was set up in 1875 and is the national meteorological service of India, headquartered at New Delhi.

questions.q: Cyclones forming in the North Indian Ocean are named by the Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre located at:
questions.exp: IMD, New Delhi, acts as the RSMC for tropical cyclones over the North Indian Ocean and issues names on behalf of thirteen WMO/ESCAP member countries.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about western disturbances:
I. They are extra-tropical cyclones originating over the Mediterranean region.
II. They are carried into India by the subtropical westerly jet stream.
III. The rainfall they bring is important for the rabi wheat crop.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. Western disturbances also cause snowfall in the western Himalaya and occasional hailstorms in Rajasthan.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the mechanism of the south-west monsoon:
I. The ITCZ shifts northward in summer and lies over the Ganga plain as the monsoon trough.
II. The south-east trade winds cross the equator and are deflected to their right to become south-west winds.
III. The withdrawal of the subtropical westerly jet from south of the Himalaya precedes the burst of the monsoon.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The deflection in statement II is caused by the Coriolis force in the northern hemisphere.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the retreating monsoon season in India:
I. The withdrawal of the monsoon begins from north-western India.
II. October and November bring rainfall to the Coromandel coast.
III. The season is marked by high temperature with high humidity, popularly called 'October heat'.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The retreating monsoon season also sees frequent tropical cyclones over the Bay of Bengal.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. El Nino conditions are generally associated with a weak Indian summer monsoon.
II. A positive Indian Ocean Dipole generally favours a good monsoon over India.
III. La Nina conditions are generally associated with above-normal monsoon rainfall over India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. A strong positive IOD can partly offset the drying effect of an El Nino year.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Mumbai receives the bulk of its annual rainfall between June and September.
II. Chennai receives its maximum rainfall in October and November.
III. The variability of rainfall is generally higher in regions of low rainfall than in regions of heavy rainfall.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. Mumbai is fed by the Arabian Sea branch in the south-west monsoon, while Chennai depends largely on the north-east monsoon.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about tropical cyclones affecting India:
I. Cyclones of the Bay of Bengal are about four times as frequent as those of the Arabian Sea.
II. The Odisha–Andhra Pradesh coast is the most cyclone-prone stretch of the Indian coast.
III. Cyclones over the Bay of Bengal are most frequent just before and just after the south-west monsoon season.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The pre-monsoon (April–June) and post-monsoon (October–December) periods are the two cyclone peaks.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. IMD classifies a rainfall deficiency of 10–25% of normal as a moderate drought.
II. The Kosi is known as the 'Sorrow of Bihar' because of its recurrent floods.
III. The Brahmaputra valley of Assam is among the most flood-prone regions of India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Statement I is wrong: a deficiency of 26–50% of normal rainfall is a moderate drought and more than 50% a severe drought.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Local wind/shower)   List-II (Region)
A. Loo   1. Assam
B. Kal Baisakhi   2. Kerala and coastal Karnataka
C. Mango showers   3. Northern plains
D. Bardoli Chheerha   4. West Bengal
questions.exp: The Loo is a hot summer wind of the northern plains, Kal Baisakhi a nor'wester of West Bengal, mango showers pre-monsoon rain of Kerala and coastal Karnataka, and Bardoli Chheerha the nor'wester of Assam.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Koppen's climatic type)   List-II (Region of India)
A. Amw   1. Western Rajasthan
B. As   2. Malabar (west) coast
C. BWhw   3. Arunachal Pradesh
D. Dfc   4. Coromandel coast
questions.exp: Amw is the monsoon type with a short dry season on the west coast, As the monsoon type with dry summer on the Coromandel coast, BWhw the hot desert of west Rajasthan and Dfc the cold humid winter type of Arunachal Pradesh.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Season as classified by IMD)   List-II (Months)
A. Winter   1. March to May
B. Pre-monsoon   2. October to December
C. South-west monsoon   3. January and February
D. Post-monsoon   4. June to September
questions.exp: IMD divides the year into winter (January–February), pre-monsoon (March–May), south-west monsoon (June–September) and post-monsoon (October–December).

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Wind system)   List-II (Characteristic)
A. Subtropical westerly jet   1. Blows over peninsular India in summer above the heated Tibetan plateau
B. Tropical easterly jet   2. Low-level cross-equatorial jet off the East African coast
C. Somali jet   3. Lies south of the Himalaya in winter and shifts north in early June
D. Monsoon trough   4. Northward-shifted position of the ITCZ over the Ganga plain in July
questions.exp: The northward shift of the subtropical westerly jet, the establishment of the tropical easterly jet and the strengthening of the Somali jet together mark the onset of the monsoon.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a local wind or shower and its region is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Bardoli Chheerha is the nor'wester of Assam, not of Punjab.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the south-west monsoon is NOT correct?
opts: The Arabian Sea branch causes heavy rainfall on the windward western side of the Western Ghats.
The Bay of Bengal branch is deflected westward along the Ganga plain by the Himalaya.
The Arabian Sea branch causes maximum rainfall over the Coromandel coast.
The two branches converge over the north-western plains of India.
questions.exp: The Coromandel coast lies in the rain-shadow of the Western Ghats and gets little rain in the south-west monsoon; it is watered mainly by the retreating monsoon.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about western disturbances is NOT correct?
opts: They are extra-tropical cyclones that originate over the Mediterranean region.
They reach India along with the tropical easterly jet stream.
They give winter rainfall to Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.
The winter rain they bring is beneficial for the rabi wheat crop.
questions.exp: Western disturbances are steered by the subtropical westerly jet stream, not the tropical easterly jet, which is a summer feature of peninsular India.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of Koppen's climatic type and Indian region is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Arunachal Pradesh falls under Dfc, the cold humid winter type with a short summer. Aw is the tropical savanna type of most of the peninsula.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Tamil Nadu coast receives most of its annual rainfall during October to December.
Reason (R): During this period the north-east monsoon winds pick up moisture while crossing the Bay of Bengal.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.exp: The retreating monsoon blows offshore over most of India, but over the Bay of Bengal it gathers moisture and sheds it on the Coromandel coast.

chapters.title: Rivers, Lakes and Drainage of India
factsheet: Himalayan rivers are perennial, snow- and rain-fed, antecedent in places and cut deep gorges; peninsular rivers are seasonal, rain-fed and flow in broad, shallow, graded valleys.
The Ganga basin is the largest river basin of India (about a quarter of the country's area); the Godavari basin is the largest peninsular basin.
Indus rises near the Bokhar Chu glacier in the Kailash range of Tibet and enters India in Ladakh; its Himalayan tributaries include the Zaskar, Shyok, Nubra, Hunza and Gilgit.
Indus Waters Treaty signed at Karachi on 19 September 1960 by Jawaharlal Nehru and Ayub Khan with the World Bank as a signatory; the Permanent Indus Commission implements it.
Under the treaty the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Satluj) are for India and the western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) for Pakistan; India held the treaty in abeyance in April 2025.
Jhelum rises from a spring at Verinag (Anantnag) and flows through Wular lake; Chenab is formed by the union of the Chandra and Bhaga at Tandi in Himachal Pradesh.
Ganga (2,525 km) is formed at Devprayag by the Bhagirathi (from Gaumukh, Gangotri glacier) and the Alaknanda (from Satopanth); it enters the plains at Haridwar.
Panch Prayag on the Alaknanda: Vishnuprayag (Dhauliganga), Nandprayag (Nandakini), Karnaprayag (Pindar), Rudraprayag (Mandakini), Devprayag (Bhagirathi).
Left-bank tributaries of the Ganga: Ramganga, Gomti, Ghaghara, Gandak, Burhi Gandak, Kosi, Mahananda. Right-bank: Yamuna, Son, Punpun.
Yamuna rises from the Yamunotri glacier on Bandarpunch; its longest tributary is the Tons; its peninsular tributaries are the Chambal, Sind, Betwa and Ken.
Ghaghara is the Karnali in Nepal; the Rapti and the Sarda (Kali) are its tributaries. The Kosi, 'Sorrow of Bihar', is formed by the Sun Kosi, Arun and Tamur (Sapta Kosi).
Damodar, the 'Sorrow of Bengal', drains the Chotanagpur plateau and joins the Hooghly; the Damodar Valley Corporation (1948) was India's first multipurpose river valley project.
Brahmaputra is the Tsangpo in Tibet, enters Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang/Dihang, is joined by the Dibang and Lohit, is called the Jamuna in Bangladesh and merges with the Padma to form the Meghna.
Brahmaputra tributaries: Subansiri (antecedent), Kameng, Manas, Sankosh, Teesta, Dhansiri and Kopili; Majuli in Assam is the largest river island of India.
Narmada (1,312 km) rises at Amarkantak and flows west through a rift valley between the Vindhya and the Satpura; Dhuandhar falls and the Marble Rocks are at Jabalpur.
Narmada tributaries: Hiran, Burhner, Banjar, Tawa (largest), Sher, Shakkar, Barna, Kolar and Orsang.
Tapi (724 km) rises at Multai in Betul district of Madhya Pradesh and also occupies a rift valley; its tributaries are the Purna, Girna, Panjhra, Waghur and Bori.
Narmada and Tapi form estuaries in the Gulf of Khambhat instead of deltas because they flow through rift valleys.
Mahi crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice; the Sabarmati and the Luni rise in the Aravalli; the Luni turns saline below Balotra and ends in the Rann of Kachchh.
Godavari (1,465 km), the 'Dakshin Ganga', rises at Trimbakeshwar near Nashik; tributaries Penganga, Wardha, Wainganga (jointly Pranhita), Indravati, Manjra, Sabari, Purna and Pravara.
Krishna (1,400 km) rises near Mahabaleshwar; tributaries Koyna, Bhima, Ghataprabha, Malaprabha, Tungabhadra and Musi.
Kaveri (800 km) rises at Talakaveri in the Brahmagiri hills of Kodagu, Karnataka; tributaries Hemavati, Kabini, Bhavani, Noyyal and Amaravati; Shivanasamudram falls lie on it.
Mahanadi rises near Sihawa in Dhamtari district of Chhattisgarh and is dammed at Hirakud; Odisha's other rivers are the Subarnarekha, Brahmani and Baitarani.

Waterfalls: Kunchikal on the Varahi and Jog (Gersoppa) on the Sharavathi in Karnataka; Dudhsagar on the Mandovi (Goa); Chitrakote on the Indravati (Chhattisgarh); Hundru on the Subarnarekha (Jharkhand); Athirappilly on the Chalakudy (Kerala); Nohkalikai in Meghalaya.
Wular (Bandipora, J&K) on the Jhelum is India's largest freshwater lake; Vembanad in Kerala is the longest lake in India.
Chilika (Odisha) is India's largest brackish-water lagoon and contains the Nalabana Bird Sanctuary; Pulicat (Andhra Pradesh–Tamil Nadu), behind which lies Sriharikota, is the second largest.
Loktak (Manipur) carries floating phumdi mats and holds Keibul Lamjao, the only floating national park, home of the sangai deer.

Kolleru lies between the Krishna and Godavari deltas in Andhra Pradesh; Sambhar in Rajasthan is India's largest inland saline lake; Lonar in Buldhana district, Maharashtra, is a meteorite-impact crater lake in Deccan basalt.
Roopkund, the 'Skeleton Lake', is a glacial lake at about 5,029 m in Chamoli district of Uttarakhand, below the Trisul massif.

Ramsar Convention 1971 (Ramsar, Iran); India acceded in 1982; Chilika (Odisha) and Keoladeo Ghana (Rajasthan) were designated in 1981 as India's first sites; Sundarban Wetland is the largest and Renuka (HP) among the smallest; Tamil Nadu has the largest number.
National Perspective Plan (1980) proposes 30 links — 16 peninsular and 14 Himalayan; NWDA was set up in 1982; the Ken–Betwa link with the Daudhan dam is the first project taken up.
Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 governs tribunals — Kaveri, Krishna, Godavari, Narmada (award 1979), Ravi–Beas (Eradi), Mahadayi and Vansadhara.

questions.q: The Rapti river is a tributary of the:
questions.exp: The Rapti rises in Nepal and joins the Ghaghara in eastern Uttar Pradesh. The Ghaghara itself is the Karnali in Nepal and is a left-bank tributary of the Ganga.

questions.q: The Teesta river is a tributary of the:
questions.exp: The Teesta drains Sikkim and northern West Bengal and joins the Brahmaputra in Bangladesh. It once flowed into the Ganga but shifted course after the flood of 1787.

questions.q: The Hiran river is a tributary of the:
questions.exp: The Hiran joins the Narmada in Madhya Pradesh. Other Narmada tributaries are the Burhner, Banjar, Tawa, Sher, Barna, Kolar and Orsang.

questions.q: The Purna river, which rises in the Ajanta hills of Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad) district and meets its main stream near Purna town in Parbhani district, is a tributary of the:
questions.exp: This Purna is a right-bank tributary of the Godavari in Marathwada. A different river of the same name in Vidarbha joins the Tapi, which is why the district is specified.

questions.q: The Ganga is formed by the confluence of the Bhagirathi and the Alaknanda at:
questions.exp: The two headstreams meet at Devprayag in Tehri Garhwal, below which the river is called the Ganga. It debouches on to the plains at Haridwar.

questions.q: The Chenab is formed by the union of the Chandra and the Bhaga at:
questions.exp: The two streams meet at Tandi in Lahaul, Himachal Pradesh. The Chenab is the largest tributary of the Indus in India by volume.

questions.q: The Jhelum river rises from a spring at:
questions.exp: The Jhelum rises at Verinag in Anantnag district, flows through the Kashmir valley and Wular lake, and enters Pakistan through the Baramulla gorge.

questions.q: The Indus Waters Treaty between India and Pakistan was signed in 1960 at:
questions.exp: It was signed at Karachi on 19 September 1960 by Jawaharlal Nehru and Ayub Khan, with the World Bank as a signatory.

questions.q: Under the Indus Waters Treaty, the waters of which group of rivers were allotted to India?
questions.exp: The three eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas and Satluj — were allotted to India and the three western rivers — Indus, Jhelum and Chenab — to Pakistan.

questions.q: Which is the longest river of peninsular India?
questions.exp: The Godavari (about 1,465 km) is the longest peninsular river and is called the Dakshin Ganga; its basin is also the largest in peninsular India.

questions.q: The Kaveri river rises at Talakaveri in which hills?
questions.exp: Talakaveri lies in the Brahmagiri range of Kodagu district, Karnataka. The Kaveri flows through Karnataka and Tamil Nadu into the Bay of Bengal.

questions.q: Which pair of peninsular rivers flows through rift valleys and forms estuaries instead of deltas?
questions.exp: The Narmada and the Tapi flow west through fault troughs and discharge into the Gulf of Khambhat as estuaries, carrying too little silt in suspension to build deltas.

questions.q: Which Indian river crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice?
questions.exp: The Mahi rises in the Vindhyan hills of Madhya Pradesh, loops north into Rajasthan and turns south-west into Gujarat, cutting the Tropic of Cancer twice.

questions.q: Which is the largest freshwater lake of India?
questions.exp: Wular lake in Bandipora district of Jammu and Kashmir, fed by the Jhelum, is India's largest freshwater lake and a Ramsar site.

questions.q: Which is the longest lake in India?
questions.exp: Vembanad in Kerala stretches about 96 km and is the longest lake in India; the Nehru Trophy boat race is held on it and the Vembanad-Kol wetland is a Ramsar site.

questions.q: Keibul Lamjao, the only floating national park in the world, is situated on which lake?
questions.exp: Keibul Lamjao lies on the floating phumdi mats of Loktak lake in Manipur and protects the sangai or brow-antlered deer.

questions.q: Roopkund, the high-altitude 'Skeleton Lake', is located in which state?
questions.exp: Roopkund lies at about 5,029 m in Chamoli district of Uttarakhand, below the Trisul massif, and is famous for the human skeletal remains found in and around it.

questions.q: Chilika, the largest brackish-water lagoon of India, lies in which state?
questions.exp: Chilika lies along the Odisha coast, holds the Nalabana Bird Sanctuary and shelters Irrawaddy dolphins.

questions.q: Majuli, the largest river island of India, lies on which river?
questions.exp: Majuli in Assam lies in the Brahmaputra and is also a centre of the Vaishnavite satras founded in the tradition of Srimanta Sankardeva.

questions.q: Which two wetlands were designated as India's first Ramsar sites in 1981?
questions.exp: Chilika in Odisha and Keoladeo Ghana in Bharatpur, Rajasthan, were designated in 1981. Sambhar, Rajasthan's other early site, was designated in 1990.

questions.q: The first project taken up under the National Perspective Plan for interlinking of rivers is the link between the:
questions.exp: The Ken–Betwa Link Project in Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh, centred on the Daudhan dam, is the first project under the National Perspective Plan of 1980.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Himalayan rivers are perennial because they are fed by both snowmelt and rainfall.
II. Peninsular rivers generally flow in broad, shallow valleys with a nearly graded profile.
III. The Himalayan rivers build large deltas where they reach the sea.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The Ganga–Brahmaputra delta, the largest in the world, is the classic example of statement III.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Indus Waters Treaty:
I. It was signed in 1960 with the World Bank as a signatory.
II. The waters of the Ravi, Beas and Satluj were allotted to India.
III. A Permanent Indus Commission was constituted under the treaty.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. India placed the treaty in abeyance in April 2025 following the Pahalgam terror attack.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Brahmaputra:
I. It is known as the Tsangpo in Tibet.
II. It enters India in Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang or Dihang.
III. It is called the Padma in Bangladesh.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Statement III is wrong: in Bangladesh the Brahmaputra is called the Jamuna; the Padma is the name of the Ganga there, and the combined stream below their junction is the Meghna.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Narmada:
I. It rises at Amarkantak in Madhya Pradesh.
II. It flows westward through a rift valley between the Vindhya and the Satpura.
III. It forms the Dhuandhar falls near Jabalpur.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The Marble Rocks gorge at Bhedaghat near Jabalpur lies immediately below the Dhuandhar falls.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Chilika lake:
I. It is the largest brackish-water lagoon in India.
II. It was designated a Ramsar site in 1981.
III. The Nalabana Bird Sanctuary lies within it.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. Chilika is separated from the Bay of Bengal by a sandbar and supports a resident population of Irrawaddy dolphins.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Lonar is a meteorite-impact crater lake formed in the basalt of the Deccan Trap in Maharashtra.
II. Sambhar is the largest inland saline lake of India.
III. Pulicat is the second largest brackish-water lagoon of India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. Sriharikota island, which carries India's spaceport, separates Pulicat lagoon from the Bay of Bengal.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the interlinking of rivers in India:
I. The National Perspective Plan of 1980 envisages 30 links, 16 peninsular and 14 Himalayan.
II. The National Water Development Agency was set up in 1982.
III. The Ken–Betwa link involves the construction of the Daudhan dam.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The Daudhan dam on the Ken lies close to the Panna Tiger Reserve, which is why the project has been environmentally contested.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Tributary)   List-II (Main river)
A. Rapti   1. Brahmaputra
B. Teesta   2. Godavari
C. Hiran   3. Ghaghara
D. Purna   4. Narmada
questions.exp: The Rapti joins the Ghaghara, the Teesta the Brahmaputra, the Hiran the Narmada and the Marathwada Purna the Godavari.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (River)   List-II (Place of origin)
A. Godavari   1. Multai (Betul)
B. Krishna   2. Trimbakeshwar (Nashik)
C. Mahanadi   3. Mahabaleshwar
D. Tapi   4. Sihawa (Dhamtari)
questions.exp: The Godavari rises at Trimbakeshwar, the Krishna near Mahabaleshwar, the Mahanadi near Sihawa in Chhattisgarh and the Tapi at Multai in Madhya Pradesh.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Lake)   List-II (State/UT)
A. Kolleru   1. Manipur
B. Loktak   2. Andhra Pradesh
C. Lonar   3. Uttarakhand
D. Roopkund   4. Maharashtra
questions.exp: Kolleru lies between the Krishna and Godavari deltas in Andhra Pradesh, Loktak in Manipur, Lonar in Buldhana district of Maharashtra and Roopkund in Chamoli district of Uttarakhand.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Waterfall)   List-II (River)
A. Jog   1. Indravati
B. Dudhsagar   2. Sharavathi
C. Chitrakote   3. Subarnarekha
D. Hundru   4. Mandovi
questions.exp: Jog falls lie on the Sharavathi in Karnataka, Dudhsagar on the Mandovi in Goa, Chitrakote on the Indravati in Chhattisgarh and Hundru on the Subarnarekha in Jharkhand.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Confluence)   List-II (River meeting the Alaknanda there)
A. Vishnuprayag   1. Pindar
B. Nandprayag   2. Mandakini
C. Karnaprayag   3. Dhauliganga
D. Rudraprayag   4. Nandakini
questions.exp: The Panch Prayag in order are Vishnuprayag (Dhauliganga), Nandprayag (Nandakini), Karnaprayag (Pindar), Rudraprayag (Mandakini) and Devprayag (Bhagirathi).

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a river and its tributary is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: The Sabari is a tributary of the Godavari, not of the Krishna. Major Krishna tributaries are the Bhima, Koyna, Ghataprabha, Malaprabha, Tungabhadra and Musi.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a lake and its state is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Kanwar or Kabartal lake is in Begusarai district of Bihar and is one of the largest freshwater oxbow lakes in the region.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT a left-bank tributary of the Ganga?
questions.exp: The Son is a right-bank tributary rising at Amarkantak. The Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi, Ramganga, Gomti and Mahananda join the Ganga from the left.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the peninsular rivers of India is NOT correct?
opts: Most of them rise in the Western Ghats and flow eastward into the Bay of Bengal.
They generally have broad and shallow valleys with a nearly graded profile.
The Narmada and the Tapi build large deltas at their mouths.
They are largely seasonal and depend on rainfall.
questions.exp: The Narmada and the Tapi flow through rift valleys and form estuaries, not deltas.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a waterfall and its state is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Chitrakote falls lie on the Indravati river in the Bastar region of Chhattisgarh and are the widest falls in India.

questions.q:
Arrange the following rivers in descending order of their length:
I. Godavari
II. Ganga
III. Narmada
IV. Krishna
questions.exp: Ganga about 2,525 km, Godavari about 1,465 km, Krishna about 1,400 km and Narmada about 1,312 km.

questions.q:
Arrange the following confluences on the Alaknanda in order from upstream to downstream:
I. Karnaprayag
II. Devprayag
III. Vishnuprayag
IV. Rudraprayag
questions.exp: Going downstream the order is Vishnuprayag, Nandprayag, Karnaprayag, Rudraprayag and Devprayag.

chapters.title: Irrigation and Multipurpose Projects of India
factsheet: Sources of irrigation (net irrigated area): tube wells ~45%, canals ~25%, other wells ~16%, other sources ~11%, tanks ~3% — wells+tube wells together irrigate over 60%.
Uttar Pradesh has the largest net irrigated area of any state; Punjab has the highest share of its net sown area irrigated (about 98%).
Rice takes the largest share of India's irrigated area, followed by wheat; canal irrigation dominates the northern plains, tank irrigation the peninsular plateau.
Bhakra Dam — Sutlej — Bilaspur (Himachal Pradesh); 226 m, highest straight gravity dam in India; reservoir Gobind Sagar; Nangal dam lies downstream.
Bhakra-Nangal is a joint venture of Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Himachal Pradesh; Nangal Hydel Channel feeds the Bhakra main line.
Tehri Dam — Bhagirathi and Bhilangana — Uttarakhand; 260.5 m, the tallest dam in India.
Hirakud Dam — Mahanadi — Odisha (1957); with its dykes it is among the longest dams in the world (about 25.8 km).

Damodar Valley Corporation (1948) — first multipurpose river valley project of independent India, modelled on the Tennessee Valley Authority; dams Tilaiya and Maithon (Barakar), Konar, Panchet (Damodar); Jharkhand and West Bengal.
Nagarjuna Sagar — Krishna — Telangana/Andhra Pradesh; one of the largest masonry dams; canals Jawahar (right bank) and Lal Bahadur (left bank).
Rihand Dam — Rihand river (Son tributary), Sonbhadra, Uttar Pradesh; its reservoir, Govind Ballabh Pant Sagar, is one of the largest artificial lakes in India.
Sardar Sarovar — Narmada — Gujarat; benefits Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Rajasthan; Narmada main canal is among the world's largest irrigation canals.
Farakka Barrage (1975) — Ganga, West Bengal; diverts water into the Bhagirathi-Hooghly to flush silt and keep Kolkata port navigable.
Indira Gandhi Canal (formerly Rajasthan Canal) — off-takes from Harike barrage below the Sutlej-Beas confluence; Rajasthan feeder 204 km + main canal 445 km; longest canal in India.
Kosi project — joint Indo-Nepal venture, tames the 'Sorrow of Bihar'; Gandak project — Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Nepal.
Chambal Valley project — joint Madhya Pradesh–Rajasthan: Gandhi Sagar, Rana Pratap Sagar, Jawahar Sagar and Kota barrage.
Tungabhadra project — Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh; Parambikulam-Aliyar — Tamil Nadu and Kerala; Bansagar (Son) — Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

Other key pairs: Ukai–Tapi (Gujarat), Koyna–Koyna (Maharashtra), Idukki–Periyar arch dam (Kerala), Mettur/Stanley–Kaveri (Tamil Nadu), Sriramsagar–Godavari (Telangana), Nathpa Jhakri–Satluj (Himachal), Ranjit Sagar (Thein)–Ravi, Pong (Maharana Pratap Sagar)–Beas.
PMKSY launched 1 July 2015 with the motto 'Har Khet Ko Pani'; 2021-26 phase outlay Rs 93,068.56 crore; components — AIBP, Har Khet Ko Pani and Watershed Development.

'Per Drop More Crop' (micro-irrigation: drip and sprinkler) was a PMKSY component till 2021-22; from 2022-23 it is implemented under the Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana; Micro Irrigation Fund is with NABARD.
Command Area Development Programme launched 1974-75; now Command Area Development and Water Management under PMKSY.

Atal Bhujal Yojana — launched 25 December 2019 (Vajpayee's birth anniversary), Ministry of Jal Shakti; Rs 6,000 crore, 50% World Bank loan and 50% Central share; demand-side, community-led groundwater management.
Atal Bhujal Yojana covers seven water-stressed states — Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh; water security plans are made by gram panchayats.
Dynamic Ground Water Resource Assessment 2024 (CGWB): annual recharge 446.90 BCM, extractable resource 406.19 BCM, extraction 245.64 BCM, stage of extraction 60.47%.
Of 6,746 assessment units in 2024, 4,951 are 'safe' (73.4%), 751 'over-exploited' (11.1%), 206 'critical' and 711 'semi-critical'.

Traditional water harvesting: khadin and tanka (Rajasthan), johad (Alwar), kuhl (Himachal), zabo (Nagaland), apatani (Arunachal), ahar-pyne (Bihar), eri tanks (Tamil Nadu), surangam (Kerala), phad (Maharashtra), bamboo drip (Meghalaya).

National Perspective Plan (1980) is executed by the National Water Development Agency (1982); the Ken-Betwa Link (Daudhan dam on the Ken, Panna) is the first river-link project taken up, in Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
National Water Policy first framed in 1987 (revised 2002 and 2012); the National Water Mission under NAPCC targets a 20% improvement in water-use efficiency.
Jal Jeevan Mission (2019) aims at functional household tap connections ('Har Ghar Jal'); Namami Gange is the umbrella Ganga rejuvenation programme.

questions.q: The Bhakra Dam, the highest straight gravity dam in India, is built on which river?
questions.exp: Bhakra Dam (226 m) stands in Bilaspur district of Himachal Pradesh on the Sutlej; its reservoir is Gobind Sagar and the Nangal dam lies downstream.

questions.q: Tehri Dam, the tallest dam in India, is built at the confluence of the Bhagirathi with which river?
questions.exp: The 260.5 m Tehri Dam in Uttarakhand is a rock-fill dam at the Bhagirathi-Bhilangana confluence.

questions.q: The Hirakud Dam, one of the longest dams in the world, is built on the Mahanadi in which state?
questions.exp: Hirakud (Sambalpur, Odisha) was commissioned in 1957; with its dykes it stretches about 25.8 km.

questions.q: Which was the first multipurpose river valley project of independent India, modelled on the Tennessee Valley Authority?
questions.exp: The Damodar Valley Corporation was set up in 1948 by an Act of Parliament for Jharkhand and West Bengal, on the TVA model.

questions.q: Nagarjuna Sagar, one of the largest masonry dams in the world, is built across which river?
questions.exp: Nagarjuna Sagar lies on the Krishna at Nandikonda on the Telangana-Andhra Pradesh border; its canals are named Jawahar and Lal Bahadur.

questions.q: Govind Ballabh Pant Sagar, one of India's largest artificial lakes, is the reservoir of which dam?
questions.exp: The Rihand Dam in Sonbhadra district of Uttar Pradesh impounds Govind Ballabh Pant Sagar on the Rihand, a tributary of the Son.

questions.q: The Farakka Barrage on the Ganga was built primarily to
opts: divert water into the Bhagirathi-Hooghly to keep Kolkata port navigable
control floods of the Kosi river
supply irrigation water to the Damodar valley
questions.exp: Commissioned in 1975 in West Bengal, Farakka diverts Ganga water through a feeder canal into the Bhagirathi-Hooghly to flush silt from Kolkata port.

questions.q: The Indira Gandhi Canal, the longest canal in India, takes off from which barrage?
questions.exp: It off-takes from the Harike barrage just below the Sutlej-Beas confluence; the Rajasthan feeder (204 km) is followed by the main canal (445 km). It was earlier called the Rajasthan Canal.

questions.q: Which of the following is the largest source of irrigation in India in terms of net irrigated area?
questions.exp: Wells and tube wells together irrigate over 60% of the net irrigated area, tube wells alone about 45%; canals account for roughly a quarter and tanks only about 3%.

questions.q: Which crop accounts for the largest share of India's irrigated area?
questions.exp: Rice is the most heavily irrigated crop in India, followed by wheat; together they take the bulk of irrigation water.

questions.q: The Atal Bhujal Yojana, launched on 25 December 2019, is implemented by which ministry?
opts: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
questions.exp: Atal Jal is a Rs 6,000 crore central sector scheme of the Ministry of Jal Shakti, half of it funded by a World Bank loan, for community-led groundwater management.

questions.q: Under the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana, which component promotes drip and sprinkler (micro) irrigation?
questions.exp: 'Per Drop More Crop' covers micro-irrigation; from 2022-23 it has been implemented under the Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana rather than PMKSY.

questions.q: The Command Area Development Programme was launched in which year?
questions.exp: Launched in 1974-75 to bridge the gap between irrigation potential created and utilised, it now continues as Command Area Development and Water Management under PMKSY.

questions.q: Besides Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra, which state is a beneficiary of the Sardar Sarovar Project?
questions.exp: The Sardar Sarovar dam on the Narmada in Gujarat supplies water to four states, Rajasthan receiving water through the Narmada main canal in Jalore and Barmer.

questions.q: The Tungabhadra multipurpose project is a joint undertaking of which states?
questions.exp: The Tungabhadra dam at Hospet is shared by Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh; the Tungabhadra is a tributary of the Krishna.

questions.q: The Ken-Betwa Link Project, the first river-linking project taken up under the National Perspective Plan, involves which two states?
questions.exp: Water surplus in the Ken is to be transferred to the Betwa through the Daudhan dam in Panna district; the National Water Development Agency (1982) prepares such link proposals.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Damodar Valley Corporation:
I. It was set up in 1948 on the model of the Tennessee Valley Authority.
II. Maithon and Panchet are among its dams.
III. It serves the states of Jharkhand and West Bengal.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The DVC also operates Tilaiya and Konar dams and the Durgapur barrage, and was India's first multipurpose river valley project.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Atal Bhujal Yojana:
I. Half of its outlay is met by a World Bank loan.
II. It is being implemented in all the states of India.
III. It stresses demand-side management of groundwater through community participation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Statement II is wrong — Atal Jal covers only seven water-stressed states: Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Indira Gandhi Canal:
I. It off-takes from the Harike barrage.
II. It carries the waters of the Sutlej and the Beas.
III. Its main canal terminates at Sriganganagar.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Statement III is wrong — the main canal runs south-west up to Mohangarh in Jaisalmer; Sriganganagar lies on the earlier Gang Canal system.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Dynamic Ground Water Resource Assessment, 2024:
I. The average stage of groundwater extraction for the country is about 60 per cent.
II. Less than half of the assessment units fall in the 'safe' category.
III. The assessment is carried out by the Central Ground Water Board along with the states.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The stage of extraction was 60.47%, and 4,951 of 6,746 units (about 73%) were 'safe', so statement II is wrong; 751 units were over-exploited.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about irrigation in India:
I. Tanks account for nearly one-fourth of India's net irrigated area.
II. Canal irrigation is dominant in the northern plains.
III. Punjab has the highest proportion of its net sown area under irrigation among the major states.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Tanks irrigate only about 3% of the net irrigated area and matter mainly in the peninsular plateau, so statement I is wrong. Nearly 98% of Punjab's net sown area is irrigated.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana:
I. It was launched in 2015 with the motto 'Har Khet Ko Pani'.
II. The Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme is one of its components.
III. From 2022-23 'Per Drop More Crop' is implemented under the Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct; the 2021-26 phase of PMKSY has an outlay of Rs 93,068.56 crore covering AIBP, Har Khet Ko Pani and Watershed Development.

chapters.title: Agriculture and Crops of India
factsheet: Kharif crops are sown with the onset of the south-west monsoon (June-July) and harvested in September-October: rice, jowar, bajra, maize, cotton, jute, groundnut, tur, soybean.
Rabi crops are sown in October-December and harvested in April-June: wheat, barley, gram, mustard, peas, linseed. Zaid is the short summer season: watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, moong, fodder.
Leading producer states: wheat and sugarcane — Uttar Pradesh; jute — West Bengal; tea — Assam; coffee — Karnataka; rubber — Kerala; cotton — Gujarat (largest area under cotton is in Maharashtra).

Leading producer states: rapeseed-mustard, bajra and barley — Rajasthan; soybean, gram and total pulses — Madhya Pradesh; groundnut — Gujarat; jowar — Maharashtra; onion — Maharashtra; potato and mango — Uttar Pradesh.
India is the world's largest producer of milk, pulses, jute and spices, and the second largest producer of rice, wheat, sugarcane, groundnut, fruits and vegetables.
Rice needs over 100 cm rainfall and 25 degrees C; West Bengal grows three crops — aus, aman and boro; Punjab has the highest rice yield per hectare among major states.
Wheat is a rabi crop of 50-75 cm rainfall and a cool growing season with bright sunshine at ripening; Punjab has the highest wheat productivity.
Sugarcane belt: Uttar Pradesh leads in area and production; sugar recovery is higher in the tropical belt of Maharashtra and Karnataka; sugarcane gets a Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP), not MSP.
Jute, the 'golden fibre', needs 150-200 cm rainfall and grows in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta; the first jute mill was set up at Rishra (1855).
Plantation crops: tea introduced in Assam in the 1830s (Darjeeling, Nilgiris); coffee (Arabica and Robusta) began in the Baba Budan hills of Karnataka; rubber needs over 200 cm rainfall.
Soils of India: alluvial (largest area, northern plains and deltas), black/regur, red and yellow, laterite, arid, forest-mountain, saline-alkaline and peaty.
Black (regur) soil forms from the basaltic lava of the Deccan trap; it is rich in lime, iron, magnesia and potash but poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and humus, and self-ploughs by cracking in summer.
Laterite soil is the product of intense leaching under high rainfall and high temperature; poor in fertility but good for tea, coffee, cashew and rubber; used as building brick.
Red soils form from crystalline igneous rocks; they are reddish from iron oxide and deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus and humus.
The Planning Commission divided India into 15 agro-climatic zones; ICAR/NARP recognises 127 agro-climatic zones and NBSS&LUP 20 agro-ecological regions.

Green Revolution began in 1966-67 with HYV wheat (Mexican dwarf varieties of Norman Borlaug); M. S. Swaminathan is called the father of India's Green Revolution; Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh gained most; IR-8 was the miracle rice of IRRI.

White Revolution — Operation Flood (1970), NDDB, Verghese Kurien, Anand pattern cooperatives; Yellow Revolution — oilseeds, Technology Mission on Oilseeds (1986); Blue — fisheries; Silver — eggs/poultry; Round — potato; Pink — prawns; Grey — fertilisers.

Minimum Support Price is recommended by the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (set up 1965) and announced by the CCEA for 22 crops, plus FRP for sugarcane; since 2018-19 MSP is at least 1.5 times the A2+FL cost.
Food Corporation of India (1965) is the central procurement, storage and distribution agency; buffer stocking norms are fixed by the government.
e-NAM, the electronic National Agriculture Market, was launched on 14 April 2016 and is run by the Small Farmers' Agribusiness Consortium (SFAC), linking APMC mandis online.
PM-KISAN (announced 24 February 2019, effective from 1 December 2018) pays Rs 6,000 a year in three equal instalments of Rs 2,000.
Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (kharif 2016) caps farmer premium at 2% for kharif, 1.5% for rabi food and oilseed crops and 5% for commercial and horticultural crops; it replaced NAIS and MNAIS.

Soil Health Card Scheme was launched on 19 February 2015 from Suratgarh in Rajasthan; Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana promotes organic farming; Sikkim became India's first fully organic state in 2016.
National Food Security Mission started in 2007-08; Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana in 2007; Kisan Credit Card in 1998; Operation Greens (2018) covers tomato, onion and potato (TOP).
Shifting cultivation is called jhum in the north-east, podu in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, bewar and dahiya in Madhya Pradesh, kumari in Kerala and walra among the Bhils of Rajasthan.
Net sown area is about 46% of the reporting area — the largest single land use in India; cropping intensity is the ratio of gross cropped area to net sown area.

Crop research institutes: rice — Cuttack (ICAR-NRRI), sugarcane — Lucknow (IISR), potato — Shimla (CPRI), pulses — Kanpur (IIPR), wheat and barley — Karnal (IIWBR), arid horticulture — Bikaner, seed spices — Ajmer, camel — Bikaner.
Agriculture and allied sectors contribute roughly 18% of gross value added but support nearly half the workforce; the National Agriculture Policy, 2000 set a 4% annual growth target.

questions.q: Which one of the following is a rabi crop?
questions.exp: Mustard is sown in October-December and harvested in spring. Bajra, cotton and jute are kharif crops.

questions.q: West Bengal accounts for the largest share of India's production of which crop, known as the 'golden fibre'?
questions.exp: West Bengal produces roughly four-fifths of India's jute, grown in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta; Bihar and Assam follow.

questions.q: Which state is the largest producer of tea in India?
questions.exp: Assam alone produces about half of India's tea; the Brahmaputra and Barak valleys are the main belts, with West Bengal (Darjeeling, Dooars) second.

questions.q: Karnataka accounts for the bulk of India's production of which plantation crop?
questions.exp: Karnataka produces about 70% of India's coffee (Chikkamagaluru, Kodagu, Hassan), followed by Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Coffee cultivation in India began in the Baba Budan hills.

questions.q: Which state is the largest producer of natural rubber in India?
questions.exp: Kerala produces the overwhelming share of India's natural rubber; Tripura is the second largest producer.

questions.q: Uttar Pradesh is the leading producing state of which of the following crops?
questions.exp: Uttar Pradesh leads in both area and production of sugarcane, and is also the largest producer of wheat; sugarcane receives a Fair and Remunerative Price rather than an MSP.

questions.q: Which state is the largest producer of rapeseed and mustard in India?
questions.exp: Rajasthan produces close to half of India's rapeseed-mustard and is also the leading producer of bajra and barley.

questions.q: Madhya Pradesh is India's leading producer of which oilseed?
questions.exp: Madhya Pradesh, the 'soya state', leads in soybean; Gujarat leads in groundnut and Rajasthan in rapeseed-mustard.

questions.q: Which state is the largest producer of raw cotton in India?
questions.exp: Gujarat leads in cotton production, while Maharashtra has the largest area under the crop; cotton is a kharif crop of the black soil region.

questions.q: Which state is the largest producer of total pulses in India?
questions.exp: Madhya Pradesh leads in total pulses and in gram; Maharashtra leads in tur (arhar). India is the world's largest producer and consumer of pulses.

questions.q: Which state is the largest producer of bajra (pearl millet) in India?
questions.exp: Rajasthan leads in bajra, a hardy kharif millet of light sandy soils; jowar is led by Maharashtra and Karnataka.

questions.q: Which soil type covers the largest area in India?
questions.exp: Alluvial soils cover the northern plains, the coastal plains and the deltas and are the most extensive and most fertile soil group of India.

questions.q: Regur or black cotton soil is formed by the weathering of
opts: basaltic lava of the Deccan trap
questions.exp: Regur develops on the Deccan trap basalt of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and adjoining areas; it is clayey, moisture-retentive and cracks in summer.

questions.q: Laterite soil is formed mainly by which process?
opts: Intense leaching under high rainfall and high temperature
questions.exp: Alternating wet and dry spells leach away silica, leaving iron and aluminium oxides. Laterite is poor in fertility but supports tea, coffee, cashew and rubber, and is cut into building bricks.

questions.q: Who is regarded as the father of India's Green Revolution?
questions.exp: M. S. Swaminathan led the introduction of high-yielding dwarf wheat varieties from 1966-67; Norman Borlaug bred those Mexican varieties and Verghese Kurien led the White Revolution.

questions.q: Operation Flood, launched in 1970, is associated with which product?
questions.exp: Operation Flood, run by the National Dairy Development Board under Verghese Kurien on the Anand cooperative pattern, made India the world's largest milk producer.

questions.q: Into how many agro-climatic zones did the Planning Commission divide India?
questions.exp: The Planning Commission's 15 agro-climatic zones are used for agricultural planning; ICAR's NARP recognises 127 zones and NBSS&LUP 20 agro-ecological regions.

questions.q: Minimum Support Prices for crops are recommended by
opts: the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices
the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution
questions.exp: CACP (1965) recommends MSPs, which are announced by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs for 22 crops; the FCI is the procurement agency.

questions.q: The e-NAM (National Agriculture Market) electronic trading portal was launched in which year?
questions.exp: e-NAM was launched on 14 April 2016 and is implemented by the Small Farmers' Agribusiness Consortium, integrating APMC mandis into a single online market.

questions.q: Under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana, the maximum premium payable by a farmer for rabi food and oilseed crops is
opts: 1.5 per cent of the sum insured
2 per cent of the sum insured
5 per cent of the sum insured
10 per cent of the sum insured
questions.exp: Farmer premium is capped at 2% for kharif, 1.5% for rabi food and oilseed crops and 5% for commercial and horticultural crops; the balance is shared by the Centre and the states.

questions.q: Under PM-KISAN, how much income support does an eligible farmer family receive in a year?
questions.exp: PM-KISAN pays Rs 6,000 a year in three equal instalments of Rs 2,000; it took effect from 1 December 2018 and was formally launched in February 2019.

questions.q: The Soil Health Card Scheme was launched in February 2015 from which place?
questions.exp: Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched the Soil Health Card Scheme on 19 February 2015 at Suratgarh in Sriganganagar district of Rajasthan.

questions.q: Which state became India's first fully organic state?
questions.exp: Sikkim was declared India's first fully organic state in 2016 and won the FAO's Future Policy Gold Award for it.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about rice cultivation in India:
I. Rice is a kharif crop requiring high temperature and rainfall above 100 cm.
II. In West Bengal three crops of rice — aus, aman and boro — are raised.
III. Punjab has the highest yield of rice per hectare among the major states.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. In areas of lower rainfall, such as Punjab and Haryana, rice is grown with canal and tube-well irrigation.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Green Revolution in India:
I. It began with the introduction of high-yielding varieties of wheat in the mid-1960s.
II. Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh were its main beneficiaries.
III. It was based on IR-8, a dwarf wheat variety developed in Mexico.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Statement III is wrong — IR-8 is a rice variety developed at the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines; the wheat varieties came from Mexico.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about black soil:
I. It is also known as regur soil.
II. It is rich in nitrogen, phosphorus and organic matter.
III. It develops deep cracks in summer which help aeration of the soil.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Black soil is rich in lime, iron, magnesia and potash but poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and humus, so statement II is wrong.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Minimum Support Price system:
I. MSP is announced for 22 crops besides the Fair and Remunerative Price for sugarcane.
II. Since 2018-19 MSP has been fixed at not less than 1.5 times the A2+FL cost of production.
III. The Food Corporation of India is a principal central procurement agency.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. A2+FL covers paid-out costs plus the imputed value of family labour.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana:
I. It replaced the National Agricultural Insurance Scheme and the Modified NAIS.
II. It has been made voluntary for loanee farmers.
III. The farmer's premium for commercial and horticultural crops is capped at 5 per cent.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct; PMFBY started in the kharif season of 2016 and enrolment was made voluntary for loanee farmers in 2020.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about India's position in world agriculture:
I. India is the world's largest producer of milk.
II. India is the world's largest producer of pulses and jute.
III. India is the world's largest producer of wheat.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: India is the second largest producer of wheat after China, so statement III is wrong; India also ranks second in rice, sugarcane and groundnut.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the zaid season:
I. Zaid crops are grown in the short season between the rabi harvest and the kharif sowing.
II. Watermelon, muskmelon and cucumber are zaid crops.
III. Gram and mustard are typical zaid crops.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Gram and mustard are rabi crops, so statement III is wrong; zaid also includes fodder crops and summer moong.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Soil)   List-II (Typical region)

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Research institute)   List-II (Headquarters)
A. National Rice Research Institute   1. Cuttack
B. Indian Institute of Sugarcane Research   2. Lucknow

questions.exp: The rice institute at Cuttack was formerly the Central Rice Research Institute; wheat and barley research is centred at Karnal.

questions.q: Which one of the following crop-state pairs is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Coffee is grown in the hills of Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu; Assam is the leading tea producer. Saffron is grown at Pampore in Kashmir.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT a kharif crop?
questions.exp: Barley is a rabi crop sown in winter; jowar, bajra and cotton are sown with the south-west monsoon.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about laterite soil is NOT correct?
opts: It forms under high rainfall with alternating wet and dry periods
It is rich in humus and nitrogen
It is suited to tea, coffee and cashew cultivation
It is rich in iron and aluminium oxides
questions.exp: Leaching removes lime and silica and washes away organic matter, leaving laterite poor in humus, nitrogen, phosphate and calcium.

questions.q: Which one of the following scheme-year pairs is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: The National Food Security Mission was launched in 2007-08 to raise the output of rice, wheat and pulses; the other three pairs are correct.

questions.q:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their launch:
I. Operation Flood
II. National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development
III. National Food Security Mission
IV. Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana
questions.exp: Operation Flood began in 1970, NABARD was set up in 1982, the National Food Security Mission in 2007-08 and PMFBY in 2016.

chapters.title: Minerals, Industries and Transport of India
factsheet: Iron ore: Odisha is the largest producer; belts are Odisha-Jharkhand (Badampahar, Gua, Noamundi), Durg-Bastar-Chandrapur (Bailadila, Dalli-Rajhara), Bellary-Chitradurga-Tumakuru (Kudremukh) and Maharashtra-Goa.
Bailadila (Dantewada, Chhattisgarh) haematite is exported to Japan through Visakhapatnam; Kudremukh (Karnataka) magnetite moved through New Mangalore.

Manganese: Madhya Pradesh is the leading producer (about 31% as per the Indian Bureau of Mines), followed by Maharashtra and Odisha; Odisha holds the largest reserves (about 34%). Belt: Balaghat (MP) and Nagpur-Bhandara (Maharashtra).
Copper: Madhya Pradesh (Malanjkhand, Balaghat) is the largest producer; Rajasthan (Khetri) holds over half the country's copper reserves; Singhbhum (Jharkhand) is the third belt.
Bauxite: Odisha leads (Panchpatmali in Koraput, Kalahandi); other areas are Lohardaga (Jharkhand), Amarkantak plateau and Gujarat. NALCO has its refinery at Damanjodi and smelter at Angul.
Lead-zinc: almost the entire output is from Rajasthan — Rampura Agucha (Bhilwara), Zawar (Udaipur) and Rajpura-Dariba, worked by Hindustan Zinc.

Gold: Karnataka — Hutti and Kolar (KGF closed in 2001) — plus Ramagiri in Andhra Pradesh. Chromite: Odisha's Sukinda valley yields nearly all of India's output. Uranium: Jaduguda (Jharkhand) and Tummalapalle (Andhra Pradesh).

Limestone: Rajasthan is the largest producer (about 22%) while Karnataka holds the largest reserves; rock phosphate — Jhamarkotra (Udaipur); gypsum — Nagaur and Bikaner; mica — Koderma-Giridih (Jharkhand), Nellore (Andhra Pradesh), Bhilwara.

Coal: about 96% of reserves are Gondwana coal; Jharia is the largest coalfield and the chief source of prime coking coal; Raniganj (1774) is the oldest; others are Bokaro, Karanpura, Korba, Singrauli and Talcher. Jharkhand has the largest reserves; Odisha has led production in recent years.
Lignite (brown coal): Neyveli in Tamil Nadu is the largest field; others are Kapurdi-Jalipa and Barsingsar (Rajasthan) and Panandhro (Gujarat).

Petroleum: Mumbai High (found 1974, drilled by Sagar Samrat) is the largest field; Rajasthan's Barmer basin (Mangala field, 2004) makes it the leading onshore crude producer; Gujarat has Ankleshwar and Kalol; Assam has Digboi, Naharkatiya and Moran.

Refineries: Digboi (1901) is the oldest; Jamnagar in Gujarat is the world's largest refining complex; the HPCL Rajasthan Refinery is at Pachpadra in Balotra (erstwhile Barmer). Natural gas moves through the Hazira-Vijaipur-Jagdishpur (HVJ) pipeline of GAIL.

Nuclear power: Tarapur (Maharashtra, 1969) is the oldest; Rawatbhata (Rajasthan) was built with Canadian help; Kalpakkam and Kudankulam (largest, Russian-aided) are in Tamil Nadu; Kakrapar (Gujarat) has India's first indigenous 700 MWe PHWR; also Narora (UP) and Kaiga (Karnataka).

Steel: the Tata plant at Jamshedpur (founded 1907, production from 1912) on the Subarnarekha was India's first modern steel plant; SAIL plants — Bhilai and Bokaro (USSR), Rourkela (West Germany), Durgapur (United Kingdom); Visakhapatnam (RINL) is the only shore-based integrated plant.
Aluminium: Odisha leads; NALCO (Angul/Damanjodi), BALCO (Korba) and HINDALCO (Renukoot) are the main producers.

Cotton textiles: the first mill was set up at Mumbai in 1854; Ahmedabad is the 'Manchester of India' and Coimbatore the 'Manchester of South India'. The first jute mill came up at Rishra on the Hooghly in 1855.

Sugar: Uttar Pradesh has the most mills and cane area; Maharashtra has higher recovery. Cement: the first plant was set up at Chennai in 1904; India is the world's second largest cement producer. Sindri (1951) was the first large fertiliser plant.
Automobiles: Chennai is the 'Detroit of India'; other hubs are Gurugram-Manesar, Pune-Chakan, Sanand and Pithampur. Bengaluru is the 'Silicon Valley of India'.
Eight major industrial regions: Mumbai-Pune, Hugli (oldest), Bengaluru-Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Chotanagpur, Vishakhapatnam-Guntur, Gurugram-Delhi-Meerut and Kollam-Thiruvananthapuram.

Dedicated Freight Corridors: Western DFC Dadri (UP) to JNPT Mumbai, about 1,506 km, with Japanese assistance; Eastern DFC Sahnewal (Ludhiana) to Sonnagar (Bihar), about 1,337 km, with World Bank assistance. The Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor runs along the Western DFC and about 39% of its alignment lies in Rajasthan.

Roads: India's road network is the second largest in the world; national highways are about 1.46 lakh km (2024-25), roughly 2% of road length but carrying about 40% of traffic. NHAI was constituted under an Act of 1988 and became operational in 1995; Bharatmala Pariyojana (2017) Phase-I covers 34,800 km.
Golden Quadrilateral: 5,846 km linking Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Mumbai under NHDP Phase-I, completed in 2012; Delhi-Kolkata is NH-19, Kolkata-Chennai NH-16, Chennai-Mumbai and Mumbai-Delhi NH-48.

North-South Corridor: Srinagar to Kanniyakumari (with a Salem-Kochi spur), largely NH-44; East-West Corridor: Silchar to Porbandar, largely NH-27. The two corridors cross at Jhansi in Uttar Pradesh; both are NHDP Phase-II.

NH-44 (4,113 km) is the longest national highway and NH-27 (about 3,507 km) the second longest; NH-66 runs along the west coast. Under the 2010 renumbering, north-south highways get even numbers increasing from east to west and east-west highways odd numbers increasing from north to south.

Railways: the first passenger train ran from Bori Bunder to Thane (34 km) on 16 April 1853; Indian Railways now has 19 zones, the newest being South Coast Railway with headquarters at Visakhapatnam, functional from 1 June 2026; Kolkata Metro is counted as a zone.

Ports: there are 12 major ports, with Vadhavan (Palghar, Maharashtra) approved in 2024 as a new one. Jawaharlal Nehru Port (Nhava Sheva) is the largest container-handling major port, Kolkata (Syama Prasad Mookerjee) the only major riverine port, Kamarajar (Ennore) the first corporatised major port and Kandla is now Deendayal Port.

Inland waterways: NW-1 Ganga, Haldia to Prayagraj (1,620 km); NW-2 Brahmaputra, Dhubri to Sadiya (891 km); NW-3 West Coast Canal, Kollam to Kottapuram (205 km). The National Waterways Act, 2016 declared 111 national waterways; the Inland Waterways Authority of India (1986) has its headquarters at Noida.

Industrial corridors and programmes: DMIC (Japan-aided), Chennai-Bengaluru, Amritsar-Kolkata and Vizag-Chennai corridors; Sagarmala (2015) for port-led development; Make in India (2014) and PM Gati Shakti (2021) for multimodal connectivity.

questions.q: Which state is the largest producer of iron ore in India?
questions.exp: Odisha accounts for over half of India's iron ore output, mainly haematite from Keonjhar, Sundargarh and Mayurbhanj districts.

questions.q: The Bailadila iron ore mines are located in which state?
questions.exp: Bailadila lies in Dantewada district of Chhattisgarh in the Durg-Bastar-Chandrapur belt; its high-grade haematite is exported to Japan through Visakhapatnam port.

questions.q: As per the Indian Bureau of Mines, which state is the leading producer of manganese ore in India?
questions.exp: Madhya Pradesh accounts for about 31% of manganese ore production, ahead of Maharashtra and Odisha; Odisha, however, holds the largest reserves of manganese in the country.

questions.q: The Balaghat and Nagpur-Bhandara manganese belt lies in which two states?
questions.exp: Balaghat is in Madhya Pradesh and Nagpur-Bhandara in Maharashtra; together they form India's most productive manganese belt. Manganese is used mainly in making steel and dry batteries.

questions.q: The Malanjkhand copper project is located in which state?
questions.exp: Malanjkhand in Balaghat district makes Madhya Pradesh the largest copper-producing state; Khetri in Rajasthan and Ghatsila in Jharkhand are the other Hindustan Copper units.

questions.q: Panchpatmali, India's most important bauxite mining area, is located in which state?
questions.exp: Panchpatmali in Koraput district of Odisha feeds NALCO's alumina refinery at Damanjodi and smelter at Angul; Odisha is the leading bauxite producer.

questions.q: Rampura Agucha, India's largest lead-zinc mine, is located in which state?
questions.exp: Rampura Agucha in Bhilwara district, along with Zawar and Rajpura-Dariba, makes Rajasthan the source of almost all of India's lead and zinc.

questions.q: Under the national highway numbering system notified in 2010, highways running north-south are given
opts: odd numbers increasing from north to south
even numbers increasing from east to west
odd numbers increasing from east to west
even numbers increasing from north to south
questions.exp: North-south highways carry even numbers rising from east to west (NH-44, NH-48, NH-66) and east-west highways carry odd numbers rising from north to south (NH-19, NH-27).

questions.q: Which is the oldest coalfield of India, where mining began in 1774?
questions.exp: Coal mining in India started at Raniganj in West Bengal in 1774; Jharia in Jharkhand is the largest coalfield and the main source of coking coal.

questions.q: The Jharia coalfield is especially important because it produces
questions.exp: Jharia supplies most of India's prime coking coal, essential for metallurgical use in the steel industry; it lies in the Damodar valley in Jharkhand.

questions.q: Which one of the following lignite fields is located in Rajasthan?
questions.exp: Kapurdi and Jalipa in Barmer district feed the Barmer lignite-based thermal plant; Neyveli (Tamil Nadu) is India's largest lignite field, Panandhro is in Gujarat and Talcher in Odisha is a coalfield.

questions.q: The Mangala oil field, India's biggest onshore oil discovery in recent decades, lies in which basin?
questions.exp: Mangala in the Barmer basin was discovered in 2004 and has made Rajasthan the largest onshore crude oil producing state; the HPCL Rajasthan Refinery at Pachpadra was commissioned in 2026.

questions.q: Which is the largest oil field of India?
questions.exp: Mumbai High, about 176 km off the Maharashtra coast, was discovered in 1974 and drilled by the rig Sagar Samrat; it remains India's largest producing field.

questions.q: India's oldest oil refinery, set up in 1901, is located at
questions.exp: The Digboi refinery in Assam is the oldest in India and among the oldest in the world; Jamnagar in Gujarat is today the world's largest refining complex.

questions.q: India's first nuclear power station, commissioned in 1969, is located at
questions.exp: Tarapur in Maharashtra began operating in 1969 with boiling water reactors built with American help; Rawatbhata in Rajasthan followed with Canadian collaboration.

questions.q: India's first indigenously designed 700 MWe pressurised heavy water reactor was commissioned at
questions.exp: Unit 3 of the Kakrapar Atomic Power Station in Gujarat is the first indigenous 700 MWe PHWR; Kudankulam in Tamil Nadu, built with Russian help, is India's largest nuclear station by capacity.

questions.q: The Rourkela steel plant was set up with the collaboration of which country?
questions.exp: Rourkela (Odisha) was built with West German collaboration, Bhilai and Bokaro with Soviet help and Durgapur with British help.

questions.q: The first cotton textile mill of India was set up in 1854 at
questions.exp: The first successful cotton mill was established at Mumbai in 1854; Ahmedabad, which followed in 1861, came to be called the 'Manchester of India'.

questions.q: Which city is known as the 'Detroit of India' because of its automobile industry?
questions.exp: Chennai and its neighbourhood host a large share of India's car and commercial vehicle output; other hubs are Gurugram-Manesar, Pune-Chakan, Sanand and Pithampur.

questions.q: The Golden Quadrilateral highway network connects which four cities?
questions.exp: The Golden Quadrilateral was taken up as Phase-I of the National Highways Development Project and was completed in 2012.

questions.q: The North-South and East-West corridors of the national highway network intersect at
questions.exp: The Srinagar-Kanniyakumari corridor (NH-44) and the Silchar-Porbandar corridor (NH-27) cross each other at Jhansi in Uttar Pradesh.

questions.q: The East-West Corridor of the National Highways Development Project connects
questions.exp: The East-West Corridor runs from Silchar in Assam to Porbandar in Gujarat, largely along NH-27; the North-South Corridor runs from Srinagar to Kanniyakumari.

questions.q: What is the approximate total length of the Golden Quadrilateral?
questions.exp: The Golden Quadrilateral is about 5,846 km long; its Kolkata-Chennai arm is the longest side and Chennai-Mumbai the shortest.

questions.q: Which is the longest national highway of India?
questions.exp: NH-44, running from Srinagar to Kanniyakumari, is about 4,113 km long; NH-27 from Porbandar to Silchar is the second longest.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the highway corridors of India:
I. The North-South Corridor connects Srinagar with Kanniyakumari.
II. The East-West Corridor connects Silchar with Porbandar.
III. Both corridors were taken up under Phase-II of the National Highways Development Project.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct; the North-South Corridor also has a spur from Salem to Kochi, and the two corridors meet at Jhansi.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about national highways in India:
I. They form about 2 per cent of the total road length but carry about 40 per cent of road traffic.
II. The national highway network of the country exceeds one lakh kilometres.
III. The National Highways Authority of India was constituted under an Act of 1988.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct; the national highway network stood at about 1.46 lakh km in 2024-25 and the NHAI became operational in 1995.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Indian Railways:
I. India's first passenger train ran between Bori Bunder and Thane in 1853.
II. Kolkata Metro is counted as a zone of Indian Railways.
III. The headquarters of the newly created South Coast Railway zone is at Vijayawada.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The South Coast Railway zone, functional from 1 June 2026, has its headquarters at Visakhapatnam, so statement III is wrong; with it Indian Railways has 19 zones.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the ports of India:
I. Jawaharlal Nehru Port is the largest container-handling major port of the country.
II. Kolkata (Syama Prasad Mookerjee) Port is India's only major riverine port.
III. Vadhavan in Maharashtra has been approved as a new major port.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. India has 12 major ports under the Centre, and Vadhavan in Palghar district was cleared in 2024.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about coal in India:
I. Gondwana coal accounts for the bulk of India's coal reserves.
II. Rajasthan has the largest coal reserves in the country.
III. Tertiary coal is found in the north-eastern states.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Jharkhand holds the largest coal reserves, so statement II is wrong; Rajasthan's fossil fuel wealth is lignite, not coal.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the national waterways of India:
I. National Waterway-1 lies on the Ganga between Haldia and Prayagraj.
II. National Waterway-2 lies on the Brahmaputra between Dhubri and Sadiya.
III. The Inland Waterways Authority of India has its headquarters at Kolkata.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The IWAI, set up in 1986, has its headquarters at Noida, so statement III is wrong; the National Waterways Act, 2016 declared 111 national waterways.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the industrial regions of India:
I. The Hugli region is the oldest industrial region of India.
II. The Chotanagpur region is noted for heavy metallurgical industries.
III. The Kollam-Thiruvananthapuram region is based mainly on iron and steel.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The Kollam-Thiruvananthapuram region rests on plantation produce and agricultural raw materials — coir, rubber, cashew, sugar and aluminium — not iron and steel.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Dedicated Freight Corridors:
I. The Western Corridor runs from Dadri to Jawaharlal Nehru Port.
II. The Eastern Corridor runs from Sahnewal (Ludhiana) to Sonnagar.
III. The Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor is being developed along the Western Corridor.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct; the Western DFC (about 1,506 km) was built with Japanese assistance and the Eastern DFC (about 1,337 km) with World Bank support.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Segment of the Golden Quadrilateral)   List-II (National Highway)
A. Delhi-Kolkata   1. NH-19
B. Kolkata-Chennai   2. NH-16
C. Chennai-Mumbai   3. NH-48
D. Srinagar-Kanniyakumari   4. NH-44
questions.exp: Delhi-Kolkata is NH-19 (old NH-2), Kolkata-Chennai NH-16 (old NH-5), Chennai-Mumbai NH-48 (old NH-4) and the North-South Corridor NH-44.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Mineral)   List-II (Mining area)
A. Rock phosphate   1. Jhamarkotra
B. Chromite   2. Sukinda
C. Diamond   3. Panna
D. Uranium   4. Jaduguda
questions.exp: Jhamarkotra (Udaipur) is India's chief rock phosphate mine, Sukinda in Odisha supplies most of its chromite, Panna in Madhya Pradesh its diamonds and Jaduguda in Jharkhand was its first uranium mine.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Steel plant)   List-II (State)
A. Bhilai   1. Chhattisgarh
B. Rourkela   2. Odisha
C. Durgapur   3. West Bengal
D. Bokaro   4. Jharkhand
questions.exp: All four are public sector SAIL plants; Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh is the only shore-based integrated steel plant.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Port)   List-II (State)
A. Paradip   1. Odisha
B. Mormugao   2. Goa
C. Deendayal   3. Gujarat
D. V. O. Chidambaranar   4. Tamil Nadu
questions.exp: Deendayal is the renamed Kandla port in Gujarat and V. O. Chidambaranar the renamed Tuticorin port; Mormugao handles iron ore exports.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Industrial region)   List-II (Characteristic industry)
A. Hugli   1. Jute
B. Chotanagpur   2. Iron and steel
C. Gujarat   3. Cotton textiles and petrochemicals
D. Vishakhapatnam-Guntur   4. Shipbuilding
questions.exp: The Hugli region grew around jute mills, Chotanagpur around coal and iron ore, Gujarat around cotton and petrochemicals, and Vishakhapatnam around shipbuilding and petroleum refining.

questions.q: Which one of the following mineral-state pairs is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Punjab has virtually no metallic minerals; bauxite comes mainly from Odisha, Jharkhand, Gujarat and Chhattisgarh.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT a nuclear power station of India?
questions.exp: Neyveli in Tamil Nadu is a lignite-based thermal power complex, not a nuclear station; Kaiga is in Karnataka, Narora in Uttar Pradesh and Kakrapar in Gujarat.

questions.q: Which one of the following national highway-route pairs is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: NH-48 runs from Delhi to Chennai through Mumbai; the Delhi-Kolkata highway of the Golden Quadrilateral is NH-19.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT a major port of India?
questions.exp: Mundra in Gujarat is a privately developed non-major port and the largest privately operated port of the country; Kamarajar (Ennore) was the first corporatised major port.

questions.q: Which one of the following industrial region-state pairs is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: The Chotanagpur industrial region lies mainly in Jharkhand with extensions into Odisha and West Bengal.

questions.q: Which one of the following coalfield-state pairs is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: The Bokaro coalfield lies in Jharkhand in the Damodar valley; Raniganj is the major coalfield of West Bengal.

questions.q:
Arrange the following steel plants in the chronological order in which they started production:
I. Jamshedpur
II. Bhilai
III. Bokaro
IV. Visakhapatnam
questions.exp: The Tata plant at Sakchi (Jamshedpur) was set up in 1907 and began production in 1912, Bhilai started in 1959, Bokaro in the early 1970s and Visakhapatnam in 1992.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Odisha is the leading producer of manganese ore in India.
Reason (R): Odisha holds the largest share of the country's manganese ore reserves.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
