Officials: B. N. Rau - Constitutional Adviser (prepared the initial draft, October 1947); H. V. R. Iyengar - Secretary; S. N. Mukherjee - Chief Draftsman. The Drafting Committee's Draft Constitution was published in February 1948 and submitted to the President of the Assembly on 21 February 1948.
Objectives Resolution moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947; it became the basis of the Preamble.
Drafting Committee constituted on 29 August 1947 with seven members under Dr. B. R. Ambedkar.

Drafting Committee: Ambedkar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, K. M. Munshi, Syed Mohammad Saadullah, N. Madhava Rau (replaced B. L. Mitter) and T. T. Krishnamachari (replaced D. P. Khaitan, who died in 1948).
Committees chaired by Nehru: Union Powers, Union Constitution, States (Negotiating with States) Committee.
Committees chaired by Sardar Patel: Provincial Constitution Committee, and the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas.
Committees chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad: Steering Committee, Rules of Procedure Committee, Finance and Staff Committee, and the Ad hoc Committee on the National Flag.

Minor committees: Credentials - Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar; House - B. Pattabhi Sitaramayya; Order of Business - K. M. Munshi; Functions of the Constituent Assembly - G. V. Mavalankar; Chief Commissioners' Provinces - B. Pattabhi Sitaramayya; Press Gallery - Usha Nath Sen.

Sub-committees under the Advisory Committee: Fundamental Rights - J. B. Kripalani; Minorities - H. C. Mukherjee; North-East Frontier Tribal Areas and Assam Excluded Areas - Gopinath Bardoloi; Excluded and Partially Excluded Areas (other than Assam) - A. V. Thakkar.
11 sessions spread over 165 days; 114 days spent on considering the Draft Constitution; total time taken 2 years, 11 months and 18 days.

Constitution adopted 26 November 1949 (observed as Constitution Day / Samvidhan Divas since 2015); it came into force on 26 January 1950, the date chosen because Purna Swaraj Day had been observed on 26 January since 1930.
Articles 5-9 (citizenship) and a few other provisions came into force on 26 November 1949 itself; the rest of the Constitution on 26 January 1950.
Last (eleventh) session, 24 January 1950: members signed the Constitution and Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected the first President of India.
The manuscript was handwritten in flowing italic calligraphy by Prem Behari Narain Raizada; decorations by Nandalal Bose and Beohar Rammanohar Sinha of Shantiniketan.
Original Constitution: 395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules. At present: about 448 Articles, 25 Parts and 12 Schedules - the lengthiest written constitution in the world.

Preamble keywords: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic; Justice (social, economic, political); Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; Equality of status and opportunity; Fraternity assuring dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the Nation.
The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 - the only amendment to the Preamble so far - added the words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity'.

Berubari Union case (1960): Preamble is not a part of the Constitution. Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Preamble IS a part of the Constitution and can be amended without damaging the basic structure; reaffirmed in LIC of India case (1995).

Sources - Britain: parliamentary government, rule of law, single citizenship, prerogative writs, bicameralism, cabinet system. USA: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independence of judiciary, impeachment of President, post of Vice-President.

Sources - Ireland: Directive Principles, nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha, method of election of the President. Canada: federation with a strong Centre, residuary powers with the Union, appointment of Governors, advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.

Sources - Australia: Concurrent List, joint sitting of the two Houses, freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse. Weimar Germany: suspension of Fundamental Rights during an emergency. Japan: 'procedure established by law'.

Sources - USSR: Fundamental Duties and the ideal of justice (social, economic and political) in the Preamble. France: republic and the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity. South Africa: procedure for amendment and election of Rajya Sabha members. Government of India Act, 1935: federal scheme, office of Governor, judiciary, public service commissions, emergency provisions.

Articles 1-4: Art. 1 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States'; Art. 2 admission or establishment of new States; Art. 3 formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names; Art. 4 such laws are not deemed amendments under Art. 368.

Schedules: 1 States and UTs; 2 emoluments and allowances; 3 forms of oaths; 4 allocation of Rajya Sabha seats; 5 Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes; 6 tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram; 7 Union, State and Concurrent Lists; 8 languages (22 at present); 9 laws immune from challenge (1st Amendment, 1951); 10 anti-defection (52nd Amendment, 1985); 11 panchayats, 29 subjects (73rd Amendment); 12 municipalities, 18 subjects (74th Amendment).

Seventh Schedule as originally enacted: Union List 97 subjects, State List 66, Concurrent List 47. Eighth Schedule: Sindhi added by the 21st Amendment (1967); Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali by the 92nd Amendment (2003).

questions.q: The idea of a Constituent Assembly for India was first put forward in 1934 by:
questions.exp: M. N. Roy, a pioneer of the communist movement in India, first mooted the idea in 1934. The Indian National Congress adopted it as an official demand in 1935.

questions.q: The Constituent Assembly of India was constituted in November 1946 under the scheme of the:
questions.exp: The Assembly was constituted under the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946; its members were elected indirectly by the provincial legislative assemblies through proportional representation with a single transferable vote.

questions.q: The first meeting of the Constituent Assembly of India was held on:
questions.exp: The first sitting took place on 9 December 1946 in the Constitution Hall, New Delhi. The Muslim League boycotted the sitting and demanded a separate constituent assembly.

questions.q: Who presided over the first sitting of the Constituent Assembly as its temporary (provisional) President?
questions.exp: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, the oldest member, was made provisional President following French practice. Dr. Rajendra Prasad was later elected the permanent President.

questions.q: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected the permanent President of the Constituent Assembly on:
questions.exp: He was elected on 11 December 1946, along with H. C. Mukherjee as Vice-President; V. T. Krishnamachari was later elected a second Vice-President.

questions.q: Who was appointed the Constitutional Adviser to the Constituent Assembly of India?
questions.exp: Sir B. N. Rau prepared the initial draft of the Constitution in October 1947. S. N. Mukherjee was the Chief Draftsman and H. V. R. Iyengar the Secretary of the Assembly.

questions.q: The Objectives Resolution was moved in the Constituent Assembly on 13 December 1946 by:
questions.exp: Nehru's Objectives Resolution laid down the philosophy and guiding principles of the Constitution and became the basis of the Preamble.

questions.q: The Objectives Resolution was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on:
questions.exp: Moved on 13 December 1946, it was adopted on 22 January 1947 after prolonged debate. Its substance was later reflected almost verbatim in the Preamble.

questions.q: The Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly, set up on 29 August 1947, consisted of how many members?
questions.exp: The seven-member Drafting Committee was chaired by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. It was the most important of all the committees of the Assembly.

questions.q: Who was inducted into the Drafting Committee in place of D. P. Khaitan after the latter's death in 1948?
questions.exp: T. T. Krishnamachari replaced D. P. Khaitan; earlier N. Madhava Rau had replaced B. L. Mitter, who resigned on grounds of ill-health.

questions.q: The Constitution of India was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on:
questions.exp: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949, now observed as Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas). It came into force on 26 January 1950.

questions.q: The Constituent Assembly took how long to frame the Constitution of India?
questions.exp: From 9 December 1946 to 26 November 1949 the Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days, holding 11 sessions over 165 days.

questions.q: The Constituent Assembly held its last session, at which the members signed the Constitution, on:
questions.exp: At the final session on 24 January 1950 the members signed the Constitution and also elected Dr. Rajendra Prasad as the first President of India.

questions.q: As originally enacted, the Constitution of India contained:
questions.exp: The original Constitution had 395 Articles in 22 Parts and 8 Schedules. At present it has about 448 Articles, 25 Parts and 12 Schedules.

questions.q: The words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' were inserted in the Preamble by the:
questions.exp: The 42nd Amendment is the only amendment so far to have amended the Preamble. It changed 'Sovereign Democratic Republic' to 'Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic' and 'unity of the Nation' to 'unity and integrity of the Nation'.

questions.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution?
questions.exp: In the Berubari Union case (1960) the Court held that the Preamble was not part of the Constitution, though it was a key to the minds of the makers.

questions.q: The view that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution and can be amended under Article 368 was laid down in:
questions.exp: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) reversed the Berubari view and held the Preamble to be part of the Constitution, amendable so long as the basic structure is not destroyed. This was reaffirmed in the LIC of India case (1995).

questions.q: The Preamble of the Constitution mentions the date of its adoption as:
questions.exp: The Preamble ends with the words 'this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949'. Commencement, however, was on 26 January 1950.

questions.q: The Directive Principles of State Policy in the Indian Constitution have been borrowed from the Constitution of:
questions.exp: The Directive Principles, the method of election of the President and the nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha were all drawn from Ireland.

questions.q: The provision for the suspension of Fundamental Rights during an emergency has been borrowed from the constitution of:
questions.exp: The suspension of Fundamental Rights during an emergency was taken from the Weimar Constitution of Germany.

questions.q: The expression 'procedure established by law' used in Article 21 has been drawn from the Constitution of:
questions.exp: 'Procedure established by law' comes from Japan, in contrast to the American 'due process of law'. Maneka Gandhi (1978) later infused due-process content into Article 21.

questions.q: Under Article 1 of the Constitution, India is described as:
questions.exp: Article 1 says 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States'. Dr. Ambedkar explained that the term 'Union' signifies that the federation is not the result of an agreement and that no State has a right to secede.

questions.q: The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution of India contains:
opts: Allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha
The languages recognised by the Constitution
questions.exp: The Eighth Schedule now lists 22 languages. Sindhi was added by the 21st Amendment (1967) and Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali by the 92nd Amendment (2003).

questions.q: The original manuscript of the Constitution of India was handwritten in flowing italic calligraphy by:
questions.exp: Prem Behari Narain Raizada penned the manuscript; its decorative borders and illustrations were done by Nandalal Bose and his students at Shantiniketan.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Constituent Assembly of India:
I. It was constituted in November 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan.
II. Its members were directly elected by the people of India on the basis of adult franchise.
III. Its total strength before Partition was fixed at 389.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Members were elected indirectly by the provincial legislative assemblies, not directly by the people, so II is wrong. The 389 seats comprised 296 for British India and 93 for the princely states.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Preamble to the Constitution of India:
I. Its provisions are enforceable in a court of law.
II. It has been amended only once so far.
III. It declares India to be a Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The Preamble is non-justiciable and is not a source of any substantive power. Only the 42nd Amendment (1976) has amended it so far.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Objectives Resolution:
I. It was moved by Jawaharlal Nehru.
II. It formed the basis of the Preamble of the Constitution.
III. It was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The Objectives Resolution was moved on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947, not in 1949.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly:
I. It was constituted on 29 August 1947.
II. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar was its chairman.
III. Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar and K. M. Munshi were among its members.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The other members were N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, Syed Mohammad Saadullah, N. Madhava Rau and T. T. Krishnamachari.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Articles 1 to 4 of the Constitution:
I. Article 1 describes India as a Union of States.
II. A Bill under Article 3 for the formation of a new State can be introduced in Parliament only on the prior recommendation of the President.
III. A law made under Article 3 is deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution under Article 368.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Article 4 expressly provides that laws made under Articles 2 and 3 are not to be deemed amendments under Article 368; they are passed by simple majority.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the salient features of the Constitution of India:
I. It provides for dual citizenship - of the Union and of the State.
II. It is the lengthiest written constitution in the world.
III. It establishes a parliamentary form of government both at the Centre and in the States.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: India has single citizenship for the whole country, unlike the United States. Statements II and III are correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the sources of the Indian Constitution:
I. The system of single citizenship has been borrowed from Britain.
II. The procedure for amendment of the Constitution has been drawn from South Africa.
III. The Directive Principles of State Policy have been borrowed from the Constitution of Canada.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The Directive Principles came from Ireland, not Canada. From Canada came the federation with a strong Centre and residuary powers with the Union.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Schedules of the Constitution:
I. The Eleventh Schedule contains 18 subjects relating to municipalities.
II. The Ninth Schedule was added by the First Amendment Act, 1951.
III. The Tenth Schedule was inserted by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The Eleventh Schedule contains 29 subjects of panchayats (73rd Amendment); the 18 municipal subjects are in the Twelfth Schedule (74th Amendment).

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Committee of the Constituent Assembly)   List-II (Chairman)
A. Union Powers Committee   1. Jawaharlal Nehru
B. Provincial Constitution Committee   2. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
C. Steering Committee   3. Dr. Rajendra Prasad
D. Drafting Committee   4. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar
questions.exp: Nehru chaired the Union Powers, Union Constitution and States Committees; Patel the Provincial Constitution and the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities; Rajendra Prasad the Steering and Rules of Procedure Committees.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Committee)   List-II (Chairman)
A. Order of Business Committee   1. Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar
B. Credentials Committee   2. B. Pattabhi Sitaramayya
C. Committee on the Functions of the Constituent Assembly   3. K. M. Munshi
D. House Committee   4. G. V. Mavalankar
questions.exp: K. M. Munshi headed the Order of Business Committee, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar the Credentials Committee, G. V. Mavalankar the Committee on the Functions of the Assembly and B. Pattabhi Sitaramayya the House Committee.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Sub-committee of the Advisory Committee)   List-II (Chairman)
A. Minorities Sub-Committee   1. J. B. Kripalani
B. Excluded and Partially Excluded Areas (other than Assam) Sub-Committee   2. H. C. Mukherjee
C. Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee   3. Gopinath Bardoloi
D. North-East Frontier Tribal Areas and Assam Excluded Areas Sub-Committee   4. A. V. Thakkar
questions.exp: The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas, chaired by Sardar Patel, worked through these five sub-committees.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Country)   List-II (Feature borrowed)
A. Ireland   1. Rule of law
B. Australia   2. Judicial review
C. Britain   3. Nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha
D. USA   4. Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse
questions.exp: Ireland gave the nomination of Rajya Sabha members and the Directive Principles; Australia the Concurrent List and freedom of trade; Britain the rule of law; the USA judicial review.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Schedule)   List-II (Subject)
A. Fourth Schedule   1. Emoluments and allowances of the President, Governors and Judges
B. Second Schedule   2. Allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha
C. Seventh Schedule   3. Administration of tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram
D. Sixth Schedule   4. Division of legislative powers between the Union and the States
questions.exp: The Fourth Schedule allocates Rajya Sabha seats, the Second lists emoluments, the Seventh contains the three Lists and the Sixth deals with the tribal areas of the four north-eastern States.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Person)   List-II (Role in the making of the Constitution)
A. S. N. Mukherjee   1. Constitutional Adviser
B. Nandalal Bose   2. Secretary to the Constituent Assembly
C. H. V. R. Iyengar   3. Chief Draftsman
D. B. N. Rau   4. Decoration and illustration of the manuscript
questions.exp: S. N. Mukherjee was Chief Draftsman, Nandalal Bose decorated the manuscript, H. V. R. Iyengar was Secretary and B. N. Rau the Constitutional Adviser.

questions.q: Who among the following was NOT a member of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
questions.exp: Nehru chaired the Union Powers, Union Constitution and States Committees but was never on the Drafting Committee, which was headed by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a country and a feature borrowed from its constitution is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Canada - Appointment of State Governors by the Centre
Ireland - Method of election of the President
France - Ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity
questions.exp: Fundamental Duties were borrowed from the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR, not the USA. From the USA came Fundamental Rights, judicial review and the office of Vice-President.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the Preamble of the Constitution is NOT correct?
opts: It declares India to be a Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic
It is a source of legislative power for the Government
It was amended by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976
It mentions 26 November 1949 as the date of adoption
questions.exp: The Preamble is neither a source of power nor a source of limitation on power; it is non-justiciable. The other three statements are correct.

questions.q: Which one of the following Schedules is NOT correctly matched with its subject?
opts: Third Schedule - Forms of oaths and affirmations
Fifth Schedule - Administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes
questions.exp: The Twelfth Schedule lists 18 subjects of municipalities, added by the 74th Amendment. The anti-defection provisions are in the Tenth Schedule.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the Constituent Assembly of India is NOT correct?
opts: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha presided over its first sitting
It held 11 sessions spread over 165 days
Its total membership after Partition was 299
Dr. B. R. Ambedkar was elected its permanent Chairman
questions.exp: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the permanent President of the Assembly; Dr. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.

questions.q:
Arrange the following events in the correct chronological order:
I. First meeting of the Constituent Assembly
II. Adoption of the Objectives Resolution
III. Constitution of the Drafting Committee
IV. Adoption of the Constitution by the Constituent Assembly
questions.exp: 9 December 1946 (first meeting), 22 January 1947 (Objectives Resolution adopted), 29 August 1947 (Drafting Committee), 26 November 1949 (adoption).

questions.q:
Arrange the following in the correct chronological order:
I. Commencement of the Constitution of India
II. Signing of the Constitution by the members at the last session of the Constituent Assembly
III. Adoption of the Constitution by the Constituent Assembly
IV. Submission of the Draft Constitution by the Drafting Committee to the President of the Assembly
questions.exp: 21 February 1948 (Draft submitted), 26 November 1949 (adoption), 24 January 1950 (signing at the last session), 26 January 1950 (commencement).

chapters.title: Citizenship and Fundamental Rights
factsheet: Citizenship - Part II, Articles 5-11. Art. 5 citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution; Art. 6 rights of persons who migrated to India from Pakistan; Art. 7 rights of persons who migrated to Pakistan; Art. 8 persons of Indian origin residing outside India; Art. 9 voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship ends Indian citizenship; Art. 10 continuance of rights; Art. 11 Parliament's power to regulate citizenship by law.
India provides for single citizenship only - there is no separate citizenship of a State.

Citizenship Act, 1955: five modes of acquisition - by birth, by descent, by registration, by naturalisation and by incorporation of territory; three modes of loss - renunciation, termination and deprivation.

Citizenship Act amendments: 1986, 1992, 2003, 2005, 2015 and 2019. The 1992 amendment allowed citizenship by descent through the mother; the 2003 amendment defined 'illegal migrant'; the 2015 amendment merged the PIO card scheme into the OCI card scheme.

Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019: Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Christians from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered India on or before 31 December 2014; naturalisation period cut from 11 years to 5 years.

Fundamental Rights - Part III, Articles 12-35, called the 'Magna Carta of India'. Originally seven; the right to property was deleted by the 44th Amendment (1978) and is now a constitutional/legal right under Article 300A.

Art. 12 - 'State' means the Government and Parliament of India, the Government and legislature of each State, and all local and other authorities within India or under the control of the Government of India.
Art. 13 - laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void; the express basis of judicial review. Art. 13(4), added by the 24th Amendment, keeps constitutional amendments outside Article 13.

Right to Equality: Art. 14 equality before law and equal protection of the laws; Art. 15 prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; Art. 16 equality of opportunity in public employment; Art. 17 abolition of untouchability; Art. 18 abolition of titles.

Art. 15(4) inserted by the 1st Amendment (1951); Art. 15(5) on private educational institutions by the 93rd Amendment (2005); Art. 15(6) and 16(6) on EWS reservation by the 103rd Amendment (2019); Art. 16(4A) reservation in promotion by the 77th Amendment (1995); Art. 16(4B) backlog vacancies by the 81st Amendment (2000).

Art. 17 is enforced through the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 (originally the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955). Art. 18 exempts military and academic distinctions; national awards were upheld in Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996).

Art. 19 - six freedoms: speech and expression; assembly without arms; association or unions or co-operative societies (the last added by the 97th Amendment, 2011); free movement; residence; profession, occupation, trade or business. The seventh freedom - property - was removed by the 44th Amendment.
Art. 20 - no ex post facto criminal law, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination. Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during a National Emergency (44th Amendment, 1978).
Art. 21 - protection of life and personal liberty. A. K. Gopalan (1950) took a narrow view; Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) held that the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable.

Judicial expansion of Art. 21: right to livelihood - Olga Tellis (1985); clean environment - Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991); speedy trial and free legal aid - Hussainara Khatoon (1979); education - Unni Krishnan (1993); privacy - K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017, nine-judge bench); death with dignity - Common Cause (2018). Gian Kaur (1996) held the right to life does not include the right to die.
Art. 21A - free and compulsory education for children of 6-14 years; inserted by the 86th Amendment, 2002; the RTE Act, 2009 came into force on 1 April 2010.

Art. 22 - grounds of arrest to be communicated, right to consult a lawyer, production before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours (excluding journey time); these do not apply to enemy aliens or to preventive detention. Preventive detention beyond three months requires the opinion of an advisory board.
Art. 23 - prohibition of traffic in human beings, begar and other forms of forced labour. Art. 24 - no child below 14 years to be employed in any factory, mine or hazardous employment.

Freedom of religion: Art. 25 conscience and free profession, practice and propagation; Art. 26 management of religious affairs; Art. 27 no tax for the promotion of any religion; Art. 28 no religious instruction in wholly State-funded educational institutions.

Cultural and educational rights: Art. 29 protection of the language, script and culture of any section of citizens; Art. 30 right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

Art. 32 - right to constitutional remedies; Dr. Ambedkar called it 'the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it'. It is itself a Fundamental Right and cannot be suspended except as provided by Article 359.
Five writs: habeas corpus ('to have the body'), mandamus ('we command'), prohibition, certiorari ('to be certified') and quo warranto ('by what authority').
Article 32 can be invoked only for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights; Article 226, which empowers High Courts, is wider - it covers Fundamental Rights 'and for any other purpose'.

Art. 33 - Parliament may restrict the Fundamental Rights of the armed forces, paramilitary forces, police, intelligence agencies and analogous services. Art. 34 - restriction while martial law is in force. Art. 35 - only Parliament may legislate on certain Fundamental Rights matters.

Fundamental Rights available only to citizens: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30. All other Fundamental Rights - including Articles 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 23, 24 and 25-28 - are available to citizens and foreigners alike.

Doctrines: eclipse (Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 1955), severability, non-waiver of Fundamental Rights (Basheshar Nath v. CIT, 1959) and basic structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973).

Articles 31A, 31B and 31C save certain laws; Art. 31B protects laws placed in the Ninth Schedule. In I. R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) the Supreme Court held that laws added to the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to judicial review.
Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan upheld the 17th Amendment and reaffirmed Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights - a view reversed two years later in Golaknath (1967).

questions.q: The provisions relating to citizenship are contained in which Part of the Constitution of India?
questions.exp: Part II covers Articles 5 to 11. The Constitution deals only with citizenship at its commencement; later matters are governed by the Citizenship Act, 1955.

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution empowers Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law?
questions.exp: Article 11 gives Parliament plenary power over citizenship, in exercise of which it enacted the Citizenship Act, 1955.

questions.q: The Citizenship Act, which lays down the modes of acquisition and loss of Indian citizenship, was enacted in the year:
questions.exp: The Citizenship Act, 1955 provides five modes of acquisition - birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory - and three modes of loss.

questions.q: The Person of Indian Origin (PIO) card scheme was merged with the Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card scheme by the Citizenship (Amendment) Act of:
questions.exp: The 2015 amendment created a single 'Overseas Citizen of India Cardholder' category. OCI cardholders have no right to vote, no right to hold constitutional office and no right to government employment.

questions.q: The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 reduces the period of residence required for naturalisation of the specified communities from eleven years to:
questions.exp: The Act relaxes the naturalisation requirement to five years for Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Christians from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan.

questions.q: Under the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, the cut-off date of entry into India for the specified communities is:
questions.exp: Migrants of the six specified communities from the three neighbouring countries who entered India on or before 31 December 2014 are not to be treated as illegal migrants.

questions.q: Article 12 of the Constitution of India defines the term:
questions.exp: For Part III, 'State' includes the Government and Parliament of India, the Government and legislature of each State, and all local and other authorities within India or under the control of the Government of India.

questions.q: Article 13 of the Constitution provides for:
opts: Judicial review of laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights
questions.exp: Article 13 declares that any law inconsistent with the Fundamental Rights shall be void, and is the express constitutional basis of judicial review.

questions.q: The abolition of titles is dealt with in which Article of the Constitution?
questions.exp: Article 18 prohibits the State from conferring titles, except military and academic distinctions. National awards such as Bharat Ratna were upheld in Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996).

questions.q: How many freedoms are guaranteed to citizens under Article 19 of the Constitution at present?
questions.exp: Article 19 originally guaranteed seven freedoms; the freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property under Article 19(1)(f) was deleted by the 44th Amendment, 1978.

questions.q: The right to property was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by the:
questions.exp: The 44th Amendment repealed Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 and inserted Article 300A in Part XII, making property a constitutional or legal right.

questions.q: At present, the right to property is a constitutional (legal) right under:
questions.exp: Article 300A provides that no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law. It is not a Fundamental Right, so Article 32 cannot be invoked for its enforcement.

questions.q: Article 20(2) of the Constitution embodies the principle of:
questions.exp: Article 20(2) says no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. Clause (1) bars ex post facto criminal laws and clause (3) bars compelled self-incrimination.

questions.q: Under Article 22, a person who is arrested must be produced before the nearest magistrate within:
questions.exp: The period of 24 hours excludes the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court. This protection is not available to enemy aliens or to persons under preventive detention.

questions.q: Under Article 22, a person may be kept under preventive detention without obtaining the opinion of an advisory board for a maximum period of:
questions.exp: Detention beyond three months requires the report of an advisory board. The 44th Amendment sought to reduce this to two months, but that provision was never brought into force.

questions.q: Article 23 of the Constitution prohibits:
opts: Traffic in human beings and forced labour
questions.exp: Article 23 forbids traffic in human beings, begar and other similar forms of forced labour. It is available against the State as well as private persons.

questions.q: Article 24 prohibits the employment of children below which age in any factory, mine or hazardous employment?
questions.exp: Article 24 sets the bar at 14 years. It is reinforced by the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986.

questions.q: Article 21A, which makes elementary education a Fundamental Right, was inserted by the:
questions.exp: The 86th Amendment inserted Article 21A, substituted Article 45 and added Article 51A(k). It covers children of the age of six to fourteen years.

questions.q: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 came into force on:
questions.exp: The RTE Act operationalised Article 21A from 1 April 2010, reserving 25 per cent of entry-level seats in specified private schools for disadvantaged children.

questions.q: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar described which Article of the Constitution as 'the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it'?
questions.exp: Article 32, the right to constitutional remedies, is itself a Fundamental Right. It can be suspended only as provided by Article 359 during a National Emergency.

questions.q: The writ issued by a court directing a public official or a public body to perform a public duty which it has failed to perform is:
questions.exp: Mandamus means 'we command'. It does not lie against a private individual, against the President or a Governor, or to enforce a purely discretionary duty.

questions.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable?
opts: A. K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
questions.exp: Maneka Gandhi (1978) overruled the narrow reading in A. K. Gopalan (1950) and introduced substantive due process into Article 21, opening the way for its later judicial expansion.

questions.q: The right to privacy was declared a Fundamental Right flowing from Article 21 in:
opts: K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)
questions.exp: A nine-judge bench in Puttaswamy (2017) unanimously held privacy to be intrinsic to life and personal liberty under Article 21, overruling M. P. Sharma and Kharak Singh on that point.

questions.q: The right to livelihood was read into the right to life under Article 21 in:
opts: Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar
Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar
Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh
questions.exp: Olga Tellis (1985), the pavement-dwellers case, held that the right to livelihood is an integral facet of the right to life. Subhash Kumar (1991) read in the right to a pollution-free environment.

questions.q: Article 30 of the Constitution confers on minorities the right to:
opts: Conserve their language, script and culture
Establish and administer educational institutions of their choice
questions.exp: Article 30 covers both religious and linguistic minorities. The right to conserve language, script and culture is guaranteed separately by Article 29.

questions.q: Article 33 of the Constitution empowers Parliament to restrict or abrogate the Fundamental Rights of:
opts: Members of Parliament and State legislatures
Members of the armed forces and forces charged with the maintenance of public order
questions.exp: Article 33 covers the armed forces, paramilitary forces, police, intelligence agencies and analogous services. Only Parliament, not a State legislature, can make such a law.

questions.q: The doctrine under which a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with a Fundamental Right becomes operative again once the inconsistency is removed is known as the doctrine of:
questions.exp: The doctrine of eclipse was applied in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955); such a law is dormant, not dead.

questions.q: Articles 15(6) and 16(6), providing reservation for the economically weaker sections, were inserted by the:
questions.exp: The 103rd Amendment enables up to 10 per cent reservation for economically weaker sections in education and public employment; it was upheld in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about citizenship under the Constitution of India:
I. Article 5 deals with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution.
II. Article 11 empowers Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law.
III. The Constitution provides for dual citizenship - of the Union and of the State.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: India follows single citizenship. Articles 5 to 11 deal only with citizenship as it stood at the commencement of the Constitution.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Citizenship Act, 1955:
I. An Overseas Citizen of India cardholder has the right to vote in elections in India.
II. It provides five modes of acquisition of Indian citizenship.
III. It provides three modes of loss of Indian citizenship.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: OCI cardholders have no right to vote, no right to hold constitutional posts and no right to ordinary government employment. Acquisition is by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory; loss by renunciation, termination and deprivation.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the term 'State' as defined in Article 12:
I. It includes all local and other authorities within the territory of India.
II. It is confined to the Union and State Governments only.
III. It includes bodies which are under the control of the Government of India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Article 12 is deliberately wide - it takes in local bodies such as municipalities and panchayats and 'other authorities' such as statutory and non-statutory bodies under government control.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Article 14 of the Constitution:
I. It is available to all persons, including foreigners.
II. The expression 'equality before the law' is of British origin, while 'equal protection of the laws' is of American origin.
III. It permits reasonable classification but forbids class legislation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. 'Equality before the law' is a negative concept of the absence of privilege; 'equal protection of the laws' is a positive concept of equal treatment in like circumstances.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Article 19:
I. The freedom to form co-operative societies was added to Article 19(1)(c) by the 97th Amendment.
II. The freedoms under Article 19 are available only to citizens of India.
III. The right to strike is a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(c).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The Supreme Court has consistently held that the right to strike is a legal right, not a Fundamental Right. The 97th Amendment (2011) added the words 'or co-operative societies' to Article 19(1)(c).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the judicial expansion of Article 21:
I. The right to a clean and pollution-free environment was recognised in Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar.
II. In Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab the Supreme Court held that the right to life includes the right to die.
III. The right to a speedy trial was recognised in Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Gian Kaur (1996) held that the right to life does not include the right to die. Passive euthanasia with a living will was later permitted in Common Cause (2018).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Article 22 of the Constitution:
I. The protection under Article 22 is not available to an enemy alien.
II. An arrested person must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours, excluding the time of the journey.
III. The protection under clauses (1) and (2) of Article 22 is available to persons detained under a preventive detention law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Article 22(3) expressly denies the safeguards of clauses (1) and (2) to enemy aliens and to persons detained under preventive detention laws.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the writ jurisdiction of the courts in India:
I. The writ of habeas corpus can be issued against private individuals also.
II. The writ of mandamus cannot be issued against the President of India or the Governor of a State.
III. The writ jurisdiction of a High Court under Article 226 is wider than that of the Supreme Court under Article 32.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. Article 32 is confined to the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, while Article 226 extends to Fundamental Rights 'and for any other purpose'.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The freedoms guaranteed by Article 19 are available only to citizens of India.
II. The protection of life and personal liberty under Article 21 is available to foreigners also.
III. The prohibition of discrimination under Article 15 is available to foreigners also.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Fundamental Rights available only to citizens are those under Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30; all the rest are available to citizens and foreigners alike.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Article 32 of the Constitution:
I. Article 32 empowers only the Supreme Court to issue writs.
II. It can be invoked only for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
III. The right guaranteed by Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: High Courts also issue writs, under Article 226. Article 32 is placed in Part III and is therefore itself a Fundamental Right.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Article)   List-II (Subject)
A. Article 24   1. Equality before the law
B. Article 28   2. Abolition of untouchability
C. Article 14   3. Prohibition of employment of children in factories
D. Article 17   4. Freedom from attending religious instruction in State-funded institutions
questions.exp: Article 24 bars child labour below 14 years, Article 28 deals with religious instruction, Article 14 with equality before the law and Article 17 with untouchability.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Writ)   List-II (Purpose)
A. Quo warranto   1. Release of a person unlawfully detained
B. Prohibition   2. Command to a public authority to perform its legal duty
C. Habeas corpus   3. Preventing a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction
D. Mandamus   4. Enquiry into the legality of a claim to a public office
questions.exp: Prohibition is issued before a decision, to a judicial or quasi-judicial body only; certiorari is issued after a decision, to quash it.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Case)   List-II (Principle laid down)
A. Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan   1. Procedure established by law must be fair, just and reasonable
B. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India   2. Right to livelihood is part of the right to life
C. K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India   3. Right to privacy is a Fundamental Right
D. Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation   4. Guidelines against sexual harassment of women at the workplace
questions.exp: Vishaka (1997) arose from Rajasthan and framed binding guidelines under Articles 14, 19 and 21 until Parliament enacted the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Amendment)   List-II (Provision inserted)
A. 93rd Amendment Act, 2005   1. Article 15(4)
B. First Amendment Act, 1951   2. Article 21A
C. 103rd Amendment Act, 2019   3. Article 15(5)
D. 86th Amendment Act, 2002   4. Article 15(6)
questions.exp: The 93rd Amendment extended reservation to private unaided educational institutions, the First inserted Article 15(4), the 103rd created EWS reservation and the 86th made education a Fundamental Right.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Article)   List-II (Subject)
A. Article 9   1. Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution
B. Article 8   2. Rights of citizenship of certain persons who migrated to India from Pakistan
C. Article 6   3. Rights of citizenship of certain persons of Indian origin residing outside India
D. Article 5   4. Persons voluntarily acquiring citizenship of a foreign State not to be citizens
questions.exp: Article 7 (not listed here) deals with the rights of citizenship of persons who migrated to Pakistan and later returned under a permit for resettlement.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Category of Fundamental Rights)   List-II (Articles)
A. Cultural and Educational Rights   1. Articles 14-18
B. Right to Equality   2. Articles 19-22
C. Right to Freedom   3. Articles 23-24
D. Right against Exploitation   4. Articles 29-30
questions.exp: Part III also contains the Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28) and the Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32).

questions.q: Which one of the following Fundamental Rights is NOT available to foreigners in India?
opts: Right to equality before the law under Article 14
Protection of life and personal liberty under Article 21
Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19
Freedom of conscience and religion under Article 25
questions.exp: The rights under Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30 are confined to citizens. Articles 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 23, 24 and 25-28 are available to all persons.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT a mode of acquiring Indian citizenship under the Citizenship Act, 1955?
questions.exp: The five modes are birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory. A foreign spouse of an Indian citizen acquires citizenship by registration, not by the fact of marriage.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Article 15 - Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
Article 16 - Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment
Article 20 - Protection in respect of conviction for offences
questions.exp: Article 18 abolishes titles; untouchability is abolished by Article 17 and is enforced through the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT a writ that the Supreme Court may issue under Article 32?
questions.exp: Article 32 names five writs - habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto. An injunction is an ordinary civil remedy, not a constitutional writ.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about Article 21A is NOT correct?
opts: It was inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002
It covers children of the age of six to fourteen years
It makes elementary education a Fundamental Right
It is enforceable only against the Union Government
questions.exp: Article 21A binds the State as defined in Article 12, which includes State Governments and local authorities. The RTE Act, 2009 gave it statutory shape from 1 April 2010.

questions.q:
Arrange the following judgments of the Supreme Court in the correct chronological order:
I. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
II. A. K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
III. K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
IV. Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
questions.exp: A. K. Gopalan (1950), Maneka Gandhi (1978), Olga Tellis (1985) and Puttaswamy (2017) mark the successive stages in the widening of Article 21.

chapters.title: Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties
factsheet: Directive Principles of State Policy - Part IV, Articles 36-51; borrowed from the Constitution of Ireland (which had itself taken the idea from Spain).

Art. 36 defines 'State' for Part IV in the same terms as Art. 12. Art. 37 - the Directive Principles are NOT enforceable by any court, but are 'fundamental in the governance of the country' and it is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws.

Dr. B. R. Ambedkar called the Directive Principles a 'novel feature'; K. T. Shah called them 'pious superfluities'; Sir Ivor Jennings called them 'pious aspirations'; Granville Austin saw Part III and Part IV together as the 'conscience of the Constitution'.

Art. 38 - State to promote the welfare of the people by securing a social order in which justice (social, economic and political) informs all institutions. Art. 38(2), added by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978, directs the State to minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities.

Art. 39 - six directives: (a) adequate means of livelihood; (b) distribution of the material resources of the community for the common good; (c) prevention of concentration of wealth; (d) equal pay for equal work for men and women; (e) health and strength of workers and children not abused; (f) children given opportunities to develop in a healthy manner (clause (f) recast by the 42nd Amendment).

Art. 39A - equal justice and free legal aid; inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976; given statutory form by the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 (NALSA, State and District Legal Services Authorities, Lok Adalats).
Art. 40 - organisation of village panchayats as units of self-government. Art. 41 - right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement.

Art. 42 - just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. Art. 43 - living wage, decent standard of life and promotion of cottage industries. Art. 43A - participation of workers in the management of industries (42nd Amendment, 1976). Art. 43B - promotion of co-operative societies (97th Amendment, 2011).
Art. 44 - uniform civil code for the citizens throughout the territory of India.

Art. 45 - as substituted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, directs the State to provide early childhood care and education to all children until they complete the age of six years. (Originally it directed free and compulsory education for all children up to 14 years within 10 years.)
Art. 46 - promotion of the educational and economic interests of the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other weaker sections, and their protection from social injustice and exploitation.
Art. 47 - raise the level of nutrition and the standard of living, improve public health, and bring about prohibition of intoxicating drinks and of drugs injurious to health.

Art. 48 - organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines; prohibition of the slaughter of cows, calves and other milch and draught cattle. Art. 48A - protection and improvement of the environment and safeguarding of forests and wildlife (42nd Amendment, 1976).

Art. 49 - protection of monuments and places and objects of artistic or historic interest declared to be of national importance. Art. 50 - separation of the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.

Art. 51 - promotion of international peace and security: (a) promote international peace and security; (b) maintain just and honourable relations between nations; (c) foster respect for international law and treaty obligations; (d) encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration.
Classification (Laxmikanth): Socialistic - Arts. 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47; Gandhian - Arts. 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48; Liberal-intellectual - Arts. 44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51.
Directives outside Part IV: Art. 335 (claims of SCs and STs to services), Art. 350A (instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage), Art. 351 (promotion and development of Hindi).
New Directive Principles added by amendment: 42nd Amendment 1976 - Arts. 39A, 43A and 48A; 44th Amendment 1978 - Art. 38(2); 86th Amendment 2002 - substituted Art. 45; 97th Amendment 2011 - Art. 43B.
Champakam Dorairajan (1951): Fundamental Rights prevail; the Directive Principles must run subsidiary to them - this led directly to the 1st Amendment Act, 1951.
Golaknath (1967): Parliament cannot abridge or take away any Fundamental Right. Reversed by the 24th Amendment Act, 1971.
Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Amendment Act, 1971: laws giving effect to Art. 39(b) and 39(c) cannot be challenged as violating Arts. 14, 19 (and then 31).
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): upheld the first part of Art. 31C but struck down the second part (which barred judicial review of such laws); propounded the basic structure doctrine.

The 42nd Amendment, 1976 extended Art. 31C's protection to laws implementing ANY Directive Principle; Minerva Mills (1980) struck down that extension and held that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is an essential feature of the basic structure.

Fundamental Duties - Part IVA, single Article 51A, added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 on the recommendation of the Sardar Swaran Singh Committee (1976), set up during the internal emergency; the idea was borrowed from the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR.
The Swaran Singh Committee recommended EIGHT duties; the 42nd Amendment incorporated TEN. Its recommendations of a penalty for non-compliance and of a duty to pay taxes were NOT accepted.
The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 added the eleventh duty - Art. 51A(k): a parent or guardian shall provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between the ages of six and fourteen years.

The eleven duties, Art. 51A(a)-(k): (a) abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals, institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem; (b) cherish the noble ideals of the freedom struggle; (c) uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; (d) defend the country and render national service; (e) promote harmony and common brotherhood and renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women; (f) value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture; (g) protect and improve the natural environment and have compassion for living creatures; (h) develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform; (i) safeguard public property and abjure violence; (j) strive towards excellence in all spheres; (k) provide education to one's child or ward aged 6-14.
Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable and apply only to CITIZENS, not to foreigners; unlike some Directive Principles, no writ lies for their enforcement.

Justice J. S. Verma Committee (1999) was set up to work out a strategy for the operationalisation of the Fundamental Duties; it listed existing laws such as the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act 1971, the Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955, the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 and the Representation of the People Act 1951.

In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (July 2021) the Supreme Court struck down Part IXB of the Constitution insofar as it applied to co-operative societies within a State, but Article 43B remains intact.

questions.q: The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in which Part of the Constitution of India?
questions.exp: Part IV, Articles 36 to 51, contains the Directive Principles. Part IVA (Article 51A) contains the Fundamental Duties.

questions.q: Article 36 defines the term 'State' for the purposes of the Directive Principles in the same terms as which other Article of the Constitution?
questions.exp: Article 36 adopts the definition of 'State' given in Article 12, so the Directive Principles bind the Union, the States, local bodies and other authorities under government control.

questions.q: Article 39A, which directs the State to secure equal justice and to provide free legal aid, was inserted into the Constitution by which Amendment Act?
questions.exp: Article 39A was added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976. It was given statutory shape by the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, under which NALSA and the Lok Adalats function.

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution directs the State to organise village panchayats as units of self-government?
questions.exp: Article 40 is the Gandhian directive on village panchayats; it was the constitutional inspiration for the 73rd Amendment Act, 1992.

questions.q: The directive to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India is contained in:
questions.exp: Article 44 is a liberal-intellectual directive. The Supreme Court referred to it in the Shah Bano case (1985) and in Sarla Mudgal (1995).

questions.q: Article 48A, directing the State to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wildlife of the country, was added by:
questions.exp: Article 48A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976. Its counterpart among the Fundamental Duties is Article 51A(g).

questions.q: The separation of the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State is directed by which Article?
questions.exp: Article 50 is a liberal-intellectual directive. It was implemented largely through the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

questions.q: Which one of the following Articles directs the State to promote international peace and security?
questions.exp: Article 51 has four elements: promoting international peace and security, maintaining just and honourable relations between nations, fostering respect for international law and treaty obligations, and encouraging settlement of international disputes by arbitration.

questions.q: The directive to raise the level of nutrition and the standard of living, to improve public health and to bring about prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs injurious to health is contained in:
questions.exp: Article 47 is the constitutional basis of state prohibition policies. Article 48 deals with agriculture, animal husbandry and the prohibition of cow slaughter.

questions.q: Article 43B, which directs the State to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operative societies, was inserted by:
questions.exp: The 97th Amendment Act, 2011 added Article 43B and Part IXB. In 2021 the Supreme Court struck down Part IXB so far as it applied to co-operative societies within a State, but Article 43B survives.

questions.q: As substituted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, Article 45 now directs the State to provide:
opts: early childhood care and education to all children until they complete the age of six years
free and compulsory education to all children up to the age of fourteen years
free legal aid to the weaker sections of society
a living wage to all industrial workers
questions.exp: The original Article 45 (free and compulsory education up to 14 years) was converted into the Fundamental Right in Article 21A; Article 45 now covers children below six years.

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution declares that the Directive Principles shall not be enforceable by any court but are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country?
questions.exp: Article 37 also lays down that it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws. Article 36 merely defines 'State' for Part IV.

questions.q: The Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution of India by which Amendment Act?
questions.exp: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 added Part IVA containing the single Article 51A, with ten Fundamental Duties.

questions.q: The Fundamental Duties were incorporated in the Constitution on the recommendation of:
opts: The Justice J. S. Verma Committee
questions.exp: The Sardar Swaran Singh Committee was set up by the Congress party in 1976, during the internal emergency, to study the question of amending the Constitution.

questions.q: How many Fundamental Duties did the Sardar Swaran Singh Committee recommend for inclusion in the Constitution?
questions.exp: The Committee recommended eight duties, but the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 actually incorporated ten. The number rose to eleven with the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.

questions.q: The eleventh Fundamental Duty, added by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, casts a duty on a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between the ages of:
questions.exp: Article 51A(k) matches the age group of Article 21A, which makes elementary education a Fundamental Right for children of six to fourteen years.

questions.q: 'To develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform' is a Fundamental Duty listed under:
questions.exp: Clause (f) is about valuing the composite culture, clause (i) about safeguarding public property and abjuring violence, and clause (j) about striving towards excellence.

questions.q: The committee set up in 1999 to work out a strategy for the operationalisation of the Fundamental Duties was headed by:
questions.exp: The Justice J. S. Verma Committee (1999) identified existing legal provisions - such as the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 - through which several duties are already enforced.

questions.q: The promotion of the educational and economic interests of the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes and other weaker sections is directed by:
questions.exp: Article 46 also requires the State to protect these sections from social injustice and all forms of exploitation. It is classified as a Gandhian directive.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Directive Principles of State Policy:
I. They are enforceable by the courts.
II. They are fundamental in the governance of the country.
III. It is the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Article 37 expressly makes the Directive Principles non-justiciable while declaring them fundamental in governance and binding on the State in law-making.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Fundamental Duties:
I. They are contained in Part IVA of the Constitution.
II. They are enforceable in a court of law through a writ petition.
III. They apply only to the citizens of India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Like the Directive Principles, the Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable; no writ lies to enforce them. They bind citizens alone, not foreigners.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Sardar Swaran Singh Committee:
I. It was constituted in 1976, during the operation of the internal emergency.
II. It recommended the incorporation of eleven Fundamental Duties.
III. It recommended that a duty to pay taxes should be included among the Fundamental Duties.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The Committee recommended eight duties, not eleven. Its suggestions of a duty to pay taxes and of a penalty for non-compliance were not accepted by Parliament.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Minerva Mills case (1980):
I. It struck down the provision of the 42nd Amendment that had given all Directive Principles primacy over the Fundamental Rights conferred by Articles 14 and 19.
II. It held that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is an essential feature of the basic structure of the Constitution.
III. It restored the scope of Article 31C to laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and 39(c) only.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three propositions were laid down in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), which also struck down the 42nd Amendment's attempt to make Parliament's amending power unlimited.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Article 31C of the Constitution:
I. It was inserted by the 25th Amendment Act, 1971.
II. As it stands today, it protects laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
III. Its second provision, which barred courts from questioning such laws, was struck down in the Kesavananda Bharati case.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Article 31C thus survives only in its original, narrower form after Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Minerva Mills (1980).

questions.q:
Consider the following Directive Principles:
I. Article 39A - equal justice and free legal aid
II. Article 43A - participation of workers in the management of industries
III. Article 43B - promotion of co-operative societies
Which of the above were added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976?
questions.exp: The 42nd Amendment added Articles 39A, 43A and 48A. Article 43B was inserted much later, by the 97th Amendment Act, 2011.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Article 39 of the Constitution:
I. It directs the State to secure a uniform civil code for the citizens.
II. It directs the State to secure equal pay for equal work for both men and women.
III. It directs the State to ensure that the ownership and control of the material resources of the community are so distributed as best to subserve the common good.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Equal pay for equal work is Article 39(d) and the distribution of material resources is Article 39(b). A uniform civil code is directed by Article 44.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Article)   List-II (Directive Principle)
A. Article 39A   1. Organisation of village panchayats
B. Article 40   2. Uniform civil code
C. Article 44   3. Protection and improvement of the environment
D. Article 48A   4. Equal justice and free legal aid
questions.exp: Articles 39A and 48A were both inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976; Articles 40 and 44 are part of the original Constitution.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Article)   List-II (Subject)
A. Article 41   1. Separation of the judiciary from the executive
B. Article 43   2. Right to work, to education and to public assistance
C. Article 46   3. Living wage and promotion of cottage industries
D. Article 50   4. Promotion of the interests of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
questions.exp: Article 41 also covers public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Amendment Act)   List-II (Change made in Part IV)
A. 42nd Amendment, 1976   1. Inserted Article 38(2) on minimising inequalities in income
B. 44th Amendment, 1978   2. Inserted Article 43B on co-operative societies
C. 86th Amendment, 2002   3. Inserted Article 48A on protection of the environment
D. 97th Amendment, 2011   4. Substituted Article 45 with early childhood care and education
questions.exp: The 42nd Amendment also added Articles 39A and 43A; the 86th Amendment simultaneously inserted Article 21A and the eleventh Fundamental Duty.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Case)   List-II (Principle laid down)
A. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)   1. Parliament cannot abridge or take away a Fundamental Right
B. Golaknath (1967)   2. Harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is part of the basic structure
C. Kesavananda Bharati (1973)   3. Directive Principles must run subsidiary to the Fundamental Rights
D. Minerva Mills (1980)   4. Basic structure doctrine; the second part of Article 31C held unconstitutional
questions.exp: The Champakam Dorairajan judgment led to the 1st Amendment Act, 1951; Golaknath was reversed by the 24th Amendment Act, 1971.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of an Article and its Directive Principle is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Article 42 - Just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief
Article 47 - Prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs injurious to health
Article 49 - Protection of monuments and places of national importance
questions.exp: Article 43A deals with the participation of workers in the management of industries. The uniform civil code is directed by Article 44.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A of the Constitution?
opts: To pay taxes to the State honestly and in time
To safeguard public property and to abjure violence
To develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform
To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture
questions.exp: The Swaran Singh Committee had recommended a duty to pay taxes, but it was not incorporated in Article 51A by the 42nd Amendment.

questions.q: Which one of the following Directive Principles was NOT inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976?
questions.exp: Article 38(2), which directs the State to minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities, was added by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the relationship between the Directive Principles and the Fundamental Rights is NOT correct?
opts: In Champakam Dorairajan (1951) the Supreme Court held that the Directive Principles override the Fundamental Rights
The 1st Amendment Act, 1951 was passed in the wake of the Champakam Dorairajan judgment
Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Amendment Act, 1971
After Minerva Mills (1980) Article 31C protects only laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and 39(c)
questions.exp: Champakam Dorairajan held exactly the opposite - that the Fundamental Rights prevail and the Directive Principles must run subsidiary to them.

questions.q:
Arrange the following judgments of the Supreme Court in the correct chronological order:
I. Champakam Dorairajan case
II. Kesavananda Bharati case
III. Golaknath case
IV. Minerva Mills case
questions.exp: Champakam Dorairajan (1951), Golaknath (1967), Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Minerva Mills (1980) mark the successive stages of the Fundamental Rights versus Directive Principles debate.

chapters.title: Union Executive: President, Vice-President, PM and Council of Ministers
factsheet: Article 52 — there shall be a President of India; Article 53 — the executive power of the Union is vested in the President and exercised by him directly or through officers subordinate to him.

Article 54 — electoral college for the President: elected members of both Houses of Parliament + elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States + elected members of the Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry (added by the 70th Amendment Act, 1992). Nominated MPs/MLAs and all MLCs are excluded.
Article 55 — election by proportional representation through a single transferable vote by secret ballot; uniformity of representation among States is to be secured.

Value of an MLA's vote = (population of the State as per the 1971 census / number of elected MLAs) / 1000. Value of an MP's vote = (total value of the votes of all MLAs) / (total number of elected MPs).
Nomination of a presidential candidate needs 50 proposers and 50 seconders; security deposit Rs 15,000. For the Vice-President it is 20 proposers, 20 seconders and Rs 15,000.

Article 56 — term of five years; resignation is addressed to the Vice-President; the President continues in office until his successor enters upon office. Article 57 — eligible for re-election any number of times.
Article 58 — qualifications: citizen of India, completed 35 years of age, qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha, and not holding any office of profit.
Article 60 — the oath is administered by the Chief Justice of India, and in his absence by the senior-most available judge of the Supreme Court.

Article 61 — impeachment: the sole ground is 'violation of the Constitution'; the charge may be preferred by either House; the resolution must be signed by not less than one-fourth of the total members of that House; 14 days' notice; passed by not less than two-thirds of the total membership of the House.

In impeachment, nominated members of Parliament participate but elected members of State Legislative Assemblies do not — the reverse of the presidential election. No President of India has ever been impeached.
Article 62 — a vacancy caused by death, resignation or removal must be filled by an election held within six months; the new incumbent gets a fresh full term of five years.

Article 65 — the Vice-President acts as President during a vacancy. For a simultaneous vacancy in both offices, the Presidential (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969 puts the Chief Justice of India first — Justice M. Hidayatullah so acted in 1969.

Article 71 — all doubts and disputes arising out of the election of the President or the Vice-President are inquired into and decided by the Supreme Court, whose decision is final; the election is not invalidated by a vacancy in the electoral college.

Three vetoes are available to the President — absolute, suspensive and pocket. There is NO qualified veto in India (that exists in the USA). Over a State Bill reserved under Article 201 the President enjoys an absolute veto.
Pocket veto: Article 111 prescribes no time limit for the President to act on a Bill. Famously used by President Giani Zail Singh on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986.

Article 72 — pardoning power: pardon, commutation, remission, respite and reprieve. Only the President can pardon a death sentence or a sentence by a court martial; the Governor under Article 161 can do neither.

Article 123 — ordinance-making power; the ordinance is co-extensive with Parliament's legislative power, must be laid before both Houses and ceases to operate six weeks after the reassembly of Parliament. It cannot amend the Constitution.
D. C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987) — repeated re-promulgation of ordinances is a fraud on the Constitution; reaffirmed in Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017).
Article 63 — there shall be a Vice-President of India; Article 64 — the Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States and draws the salary payable to the Chairman.

Article 66 — the Vice-President is elected by an electoral college of the members of BOTH Houses of Parliament, including the nominated members, by proportional representation with a single transferable vote. No State legislature takes part.
Article 66(3) — qualifications for Vice-President: citizen of India, 35 years of age, and qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha (not the Lok Sabha).

Article 67(b) — removal of the Vice-President: a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Rajya Sabha (effective majority) and agreed to by the Lok Sabha, after 14 days' notice. The Constitution states no ground. Resignation is addressed to the President.

Article 74 — a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President; the advice was made binding by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, and the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 allowed the President to require reconsideration once. The advice is not enquirable in any court.

Article 75 — the PM is appointed by the President and other Ministers on the PM's advice; Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President; the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the House of the People alone.
Article 75(5) — a Minister who is not a member of either House for six consecutive months ceases to be a Minister.

91st Amendment Act, 2003 — Article 75(1A): total Ministers including the PM cannot exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha; Article 164(1A): 15% of the Legislative Assembly for a State, subject to a minimum of 12.
Article 77 — conduct of the business of the Government of India; Article 78 — duties of the Prime Minister to communicate the decisions of the Council of Ministers to the President.

The Cabinet, Cabinet Committees and the 'Kitchen Cabinet' are extra-constitutional; the word 'Cabinet' entered the Constitution only through Article 352 as amended by the 44th Amendment (written recommendation of the Cabinet required for a National Emergency).

Article 76 — the Attorney General of India is appointed by the President, must be qualified to be a judge of the Supreme Court, holds office during the President's pleasure, has a right of audience in all courts, and under Article 88 may speak in either House without a right to vote. He is not barred from private practice.
The Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General are NOT constitutional posts — the Constitution mentions only the Attorney General (Article 165 is the Advocate General of a State).

questions.q: Under which Article of the Constitution is the executive power of the Union vested in the President?
questions.exp: Article 53(1) vests the executive power of the Union in the President, to be exercised by him directly or through officers subordinate to him. Article 52 merely declares that there shall be a President of India.

questions.q: The oath of office to the President of India is administered by
opts: the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court
