questions.exp: Under Article 60 the oath is administered by the Chief Justice of India, and in his absence by the senior-most available judge of the Supreme Court.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the electoral college for the election of the President of India:
I. It consists of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States.
II. The elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry were included in it by the 70th Constitutional Amendment Act.
III. Members of the State Legislative Councils also take part in the election.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Article 54. Nominated members of Parliament and of State Assemblies, and all members of Legislative Councils, are excluded. The 70th Amendment Act, 1992 added the Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry.

questions.q: The value of the vote of a member of a State Legislative Assembly in the presidential election is determined with reference to the population of the State as per which census?
questions.exp: Article 55 read with the 84th Amendment freezes the population figure at the 1971 census until the first census taken after 2026. Value of an MLA's vote = (State population / elected MLAs) / 1000.

questions.q: The President of India is elected in accordance with the system of
opts: direct election by secret ballot of all adult citizens
proportional representation by means of a single transferable vote
first-past-the-post voting in a joint sitting of Parliament
a simple majority of the members of the electoral college
questions.exp: Article 55(3) prescribes proportional representation by means of a single transferable vote, the voting being by secret ballot. The winner must secure a prescribed quota, not merely the largest number of first preferences.

questions.q: A person is qualified for election as President of India only if he has completed the age of
questions.exp: Article 58. He must also be a citizen of India, qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha, and must not hold any office of profit.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Article)   List-II (Subject)
A. Article 56   1. Pardoning power of the President
B. Article 61   2. Term of office of the President
C. Article 72   3. Ordinance-making power of the President
D. Article 123   4. Procedure for impeachment of the President
questions.exp: Article 56 fixes the five-year term, Article 61 lays down the impeachment procedure, Article 72 confers the pardoning power and Article 123 the ordinance-making power.

questions.q: The only ground on which the President of India can be removed by impeachment is
opts: incapacity to discharge the functions of the office
questions.exp: Article 61 permits impeachment only for 'violation of the Constitution', an expression the Constitution leaves undefined. 'Proved misbehaviour or incapacity' is the ground for removing judges under Article 124(4).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the impeachment of the President of India:
I. The charge may be preferred by either House of Parliament.
II. The resolution containing the charge must be signed by not less than one-fourth of the total number of members of that House.
III. A notice of 14 days must be given to the President.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three requirements are laid down in Article 61. The resolution must then be passed by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of that House before the other House investigates the charge.

questions.q: A resolution containing a charge for the impeachment of the President must be passed by the House in which it is introduced by a majority of
opts: not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting
not less than two-thirds of the total membership of that House
an absolute majority of that House
three-fourths of the members present and voting
questions.exp: Article 61(2) requires a special majority of not less than two-thirds of the TOTAL membership of the House — a stricter requirement than two-thirds of those present and voting.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the impeachment of the President is NOT correct?
opts: Nominated members of Parliament can participate in the impeachment process
Elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies can participate in the impeachment process
The President has the right to appear and be represented at the investigation of the charge
The charge, when investigated by the other House, must also be passed by a two-thirds majority of its total membership
questions.exp: State legislators take part in the ELECTION of the President but not in his impeachment; nominated members of Parliament do the opposite — they cannot vote in the election but can vote on impeachment.

questions.q: If the office of the President falls vacant on account of death, resignation or removal, a fresh election must be held within
questions.exp: Article 62(2). The person so elected holds office for a fresh full term of five years, not merely for the unexpired portion of the predecessor's term.

questions.q: The President of India addresses his resignation to
opts: the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
questions.exp: Article 56(1)(a). The Vice-President must forthwith communicate the resignation to the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

questions.q: All doubts and disputes arising out of or in connection with the election of the President are inquired into and decided by
opts: a tribunal appointed by the Vice-President
questions.exp: Article 71; the decision of the Supreme Court is final. The election cannot be challenged on the ground that the electoral college was incomplete because of a vacancy.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the veto powers of the President of India:
I. The President enjoys a pocket veto because the Constitution prescribes no time limit within which he must act on a Bill.
II. The President cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration.
III. The President enjoys a qualified veto over ordinary Bills.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: A qualified veto — one that can be overridden by a lower majority — exists in the USA, not in India. The Indian President has only the absolute, suspensive and pocket vetoes.

questions.q: The pocket veto was notably exercised by President Giani Zail Singh in respect of
questions.exp: President Zail Singh neither assented to nor returned the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986. The other three Bills listed were passed at joint sittings of the two Houses.

questions.q: In respect of a State Bill reserved for his consideration by the Governor, the President enjoys
questions.exp: Under Article 201 no time limit is prescribed and the President is not bound to give assent even if the State Legislature passes the Bill again — an absolute veto in substance.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT a form of veto power available to the President of India?
questions.exp: The qualified veto, which can be overridden by the legislature by a higher-than-ordinary majority, is a feature of the American presidency and is unknown to the Indian Constitution.

questions.q: Under Article 72, the pardoning power of the President extends to a sentence of death and also to
opts: a sentence awarded by a court martial
a sentence awarded under a State law only
a sentence of imprisonment for life only
a sentence awarded by a High Court only
questions.exp: Article 72 covers punishment by a court martial, punishment for an offence against a law relating to a Union subject, and all death sentences. A Governor under Article 161 can pardon neither a court-martial sentence nor a death sentence.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Term)   List-II (Meaning)
A. Commutation   1. Substituting one form of punishment with a lighter form
B. Remission   2. Reducing the period of a sentence without changing its character
C. Respite   3. Awarding a lesser sentence on account of some special fact, such as the physical disability of the convict
D. Reprieve   4. A temporary stay of the execution of a sentence
questions.exp: A pardon, the fifth form, absolves the convict of the sentence, the conviction and all disqualifications.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The President can pardon a sentence awarded by a court martial, but the Governor cannot.
II. The President can pardon a death sentence, but the Governor cannot.
III. The pardoning power of the President extends only to offences against Union laws.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Statement III is wrong: besides offences against Union laws and court-martial sentences, the President's power under Article 72 covers every case where the sentence is one of death, even under a State law.

questions.q: The ordinance-making power of the President is provided for under
questions.exp: Article 123. Article 213 confers the corresponding power on a Governor, and Article 143 deals with the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.

questions.q: An ordinance promulgated by the President ceases to operate on the expiry of
opts: six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament
six months from the date of promulgation
six weeks from the date of promulgation
three months from the reassembly of Parliament
questions.exp: Article 123(2)(a). If the two Houses reassemble on different dates, the six weeks are counted from the later date; the ordinance may lapse earlier if disapproved by resolutions of both Houses.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the ordinance-making power of the President:
I. It is co-extensive with the legislative power of Parliament.
II. An ordinance can be promulgated only when both Houses of Parliament are not in session.
III. An ordinance can amend or repeal any provision of the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Statement III is wrong — an ordinance has the same force as an Act of Parliament and therefore cannot amend the Constitution. It also cannot take away or abridge fundamental rights.

questions.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the repeated re-promulgation of ordinances amounts to a fraud on the Constitution?
opts: Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab
R. C. Cooper v. Union of India
D. C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar
A. K. Roy v. Union of India
questions.exp: D. C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987) struck down the Bihar practice of re-promulgating ordinances for years; the principle was reaffirmed in Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017).

questions.q: The Vice-President of India is the ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States under
questions.exp: Article 64. Article 63 declares that there shall be a Vice-President, Article 66 lays down the mode of his election and Article 89 provides for the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the election of the Vice-President of India:
I. The electoral college consists of the members of both Houses of Parliament, including the nominated members.
II. Members of the State Legislative Assemblies take part in the election.
III. The election is held in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of a single transferable vote.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Article 66(1). Unlike the presidential election, no State legislature participates and nominated members of Parliament are included in the electoral college.

questions.q: To be qualified for election as Vice-President, a person must be qualified for election as a member of
questions.exp: Article 66(3). The President, by contrast, must be qualified for election to the Lok Sabha. In both cases the minimum age is 35 years.

questions.q: A resolution for the removal of the Vice-President of India can be moved only in
opts: a joint sitting of both Houses
questions.exp: Article 67(b): the resolution must be passed by a majority of all the then members of the Rajya Sabha and then agreed to by the Lok Sabha, after 14 days' notice. No ground for removal is specified.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the Vice-President of India is NOT correct?
opts: The Constitution does not lay down any ground for his removal
He addresses his resignation to the President
While acting as President he continues to perform the duties of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
Nominated members of Parliament participate in his election
questions.exp: When the Vice-President acts as or discharges the functions of the President, he does not perform the duties of Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and is not entitled to the Chairman's salary (Articles 64 and 65).

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Article)   List-II (Provision)
A. Article 63   1. Vice-President to be ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States
B. Article 64   2. There shall be a Vice-President of India
C. Article 65   3. Election of the Vice-President
D. Article 66   4. Vice-President to act as President or discharge his functions
questions.exp: Article 67 deals with the term of office and removal of the Vice-President, and Article 68 with the timing of the election to fill a vacancy.

questions.q: In the event of a vacancy in the offices of both the President and the Vice-President, who discharges the functions of the President?
opts: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The senior-most Governor of a State
questions.exp: The Presidential (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969 places the Chief Justice of India first and, in his absence, the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court. Justice M. Hidayatullah discharged the functions of President in 1969.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. When the Vice-President acts as President he is not entitled to the salary of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
II. The Vice-President can act as President for a maximum period of six months.
III. Justice M. Hidayatullah discharged the functions of the President of India in 1969.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Article 62(2) requires the vacancy to be filled within six months, so the Vice-President cannot act as President for longer than that. During this period he draws the emoluments of the President.

questions.q: Article 74 of the Constitution provides for
opts: the appointment of the Prime Minister
the duties of the Prime Minister
a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President
questions.exp: Article 74(1). The 42nd Amendment made the advice binding on the President and the 44th Amendment allowed him to require reconsideration once, after which he must act in accordance with the advice tendered.

questions.q: The advice tendered by the Council of Ministers was made binding on the President by which Constitutional Amendment?
questions.exp: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 made the advice binding; the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 added the proviso permitting the President to require the Council of Ministers to reconsider its advice once.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Council of Ministers:
I. The Prime Minister is appointed by the President and the other Ministers are appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.
II. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to both Houses of Parliament.
III. A Minister who is not a member of either House of Parliament for six consecutive months ceases to be a Minister.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Article 75(3) makes the Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the House of the People alone, not to both Houses.

questions.q: The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 provides that the total number of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, shall not exceed
opts: 10 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
12 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
15 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
20 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
questions.exp: Article 75(1A). For a State, Article 164(1A) fixes the same 15 per cent ceiling on the strength of the Legislative Assembly, subject to a minimum of 12 Ministers.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Provision)   List-II (Article)
A. Ordinance-making power of the President   1. Article 111
B. Assent to Bills	   2. Article 123
C. Joint sitting of both Houses   3. Article 108
D. Summoning and prorogation of Parliament   4. Article 85
questions.exp: The President exercises all four powers on the advice of the Council of Ministers; only the summoning of a joint sitting under Article 108 and the dissolution of the Lok Sabha involve any element of situational discretion.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the Cabinet is NOT correct?
opts: The original text of Article 74 did not use the word 'Cabinet'
The word 'Cabinet' was inserted in Article 352 by the 44th Amendment Act
The Kitchen Cabinet is an extra-constitutional body
questions.exp: Cabinet Committees are extra-constitutional bodies created under the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules. The only mention of the 'Cabinet' in the Constitution is in Article 352, which requires its written recommendation for a National Emergency.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Article)   List-II (Subject)
A. Article 74   1. Duties of the Prime Minister
B. Article 75   2. Conduct of business of the Government of India
C. Article 77   3. Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President
D. Article 78   4. Other provisions as to Ministers
questions.exp: Article 78 obliges the Prime Minister to communicate to the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to the administration of the Union and to furnish information the President calls for.

questions.q: The Attorney General of India is appointed under which Article, and must possess the qualifications of
opts: Article 88; a judge of the Supreme Court
Article 165; a judge of the Supreme Court
Article 76; a judge of a High Court
Article 76; a judge of the Supreme Court
questions.exp: Article 76. Article 165 provides for the Advocate General of a State, and Article 88 gives Ministers and the Attorney General the right to speak in either House.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Attorney General of India:
I. He has the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of both Houses of Parliament but has no right to vote.
II. He holds office during the pleasure of the President.
III. He is a whole-time counsel of the Government and is barred from taking up private practice.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Article 88 gives him the right of audience in both Houses and their committees without a vote. He is not a whole-time government servant and may take up private practice, subject to the restriction that he cannot advise against the Government of India.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of Article and subject is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Article 77 — Conduct of business of the Government of India
Article 78 — Duties of the Prime Minister
questions.exp: Article 79 constitutes Parliament (the President and the two Houses). The Solicitor General is not a constitutional post and finds no mention anywhere in the Constitution.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Office-holder)   List-II (Distinction)
A. Dr. Rajendra Prasad   1. First President of India to die in office
B. Dr. Zakir Husain   2. Only person elected President of India twice
C. V. V. Giri   3. Elected President on the basis of second-preference votes
D. Dr. S. Radhakrishnan   4. First Vice-President of India
questions.exp: Dr. Rajendra Prasad served two full terms (1950-1962). Dr. Zakir Husain died in office in 1969, after which V. V. Giri resigned as Vice-President, contested and won on second preferences.

questions.q:
Arrange the following Presidents of India in the correct chronological order of their assumption of office:
I. V. V. Giri
II. Dr. Zakir Husain
III. Dr. S. Radhakrishnan
IV. Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed
questions.exp: Dr. S. Radhakrishnan (1962), Dr. Zakir Husain (1967), V. V. Giri (1969) and Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed (1974). Zakir Husain and Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed both died in office.

chapters.title: Parliament and the Legislative Process
factsheet: Article 79 — Parliament of India consists of the President and the two Houses, the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and the House of the People (Lok Sabha).

Article 80 — maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha is 250: 238 representatives of States and Union Territories elected indirectly + 12 nominated by the President for special knowledge in literature, science, art and social service. Present strength 245; allocation of seats is in the Fourth Schedule.

Article 81 — maximum strength of the Lok Sabha is 550: 530 from States + 20 from Union Territories. Present strength 543. The two nominated Anglo-Indian seats (Article 331) were discontinued by the 104th Amendment Act, 2019, with effect from 25 January 2020.
Article 82 — readjustment of seats after each census; the 42nd and 84th Amendments froze the allocation of seats on the basis of the 1971 census until the first census taken after 2026.

Article 83 — the Rajya Sabha is a permanent body not subject to dissolution; one-third of its members retire every second year, the term being six years. The Lok Sabha's term is five years, extendable by Parliament by one year at a time during a Proclamation of Emergency and not beyond six months after the Proclamation ceases.
Article 84 — qualifications: citizen of India; minimum age 30 years for the Rajya Sabha and 25 years for the Lok Sabha.

Article 85 — the gap between two sessions of Parliament must not exceed six months; by convention there are three sessions — Budget, Monsoon and Winter. Summoning, prorogation and dissolution are done by the President.
Article 100 — quorum is one-tenth of the total number of members of the House; the presiding officer has no ordinary vote but exercises a casting vote in a tie.

Article 93 — Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha; Article 89 — Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Removal is by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members (effective majority) after 14 days' notice.

The Speaker certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill (Article 110(4)), presides over a joint sitting (Article 118(4)) and decides questions of disqualification on the ground of defection; but disqualification under Article 102(1) is decided by the President on the opinion of the Election Commission (Article 103).

Article 105 — powers, privileges and immunities of the Houses and their members, including freedom of speech in Parliament and immunity from proceedings in any court for anything said or any vote given.

Article 108 — joint sitting to resolve a deadlock over an ordinary or a financial Bill; it is NOT available for a Money Bill or a Constitution Amendment Bill. Only three joint sittings have been held: Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill (1978) and Prevention of Terrorism Bill (2002).

Article 110 — a Money Bill may be introduced only in the Lok Sabha and only on the recommendation of the President; the Rajya Sabha must return it within 14 days and may only make recommendations; the Speaker's certificate is final and the President cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration.
Article 109 — special procedure for Money Bills; Article 117 — Financial Bills; every Money Bill is a Financial Bill but every Financial Bill is not a Money Bill.

Article 112 — the Annual Financial Statement (Budget); Article 113 — demands for grants, voted only by the Lok Sabha; Article 114 — Appropriation Bill; Article 115 — supplementary, additional and excess grants; Article 116 — vote on account, votes of credit and exceptional grants.
Cut motions: a policy cut reduces the demand to Re 1, an economy cut reduces it by a specified amount, and a token cut reduces it by Rs 100 to air a specific grievance.

Article 265 — no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law; Article 266 — Consolidated Fund of India and Public Account of India; Article 267 — Contingency Fund of India, whose corpus was raised from Rs 500 crore to Rs 30,000 crore by the Finance Act, 2021 and which is held by the Finance Secretary on behalf of the President.
Expenditure 'charged' on the Consolidated Fund of India (salaries of the President, Speaker, judges, CAG, debt charges) can be discussed but is not submitted to the vote of Parliament.

Question Hour is the first hour of a sitting and is regulated by the Rules — starred questions get an oral answer with supplementaries, unstarred questions a written answer, and short notice questions relate to urgent matters at less than ten days' notice. Zero Hour follows Question Hour, is an Indian innovation and finds no mention in the Rules of Procedure.

A no-confidence motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha, needs the support of at least 50 members and need not state any reason; an adjournment motion also needs 50 members and is likewise available only in the Lok Sabha.

Anti-defection — Tenth Schedule, inserted by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985. The 91st Amendment Act, 2003 deleted the exemption for a 'split' by one-third of the legislature party, leaving only a merger by two-thirds. Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) upheld the Schedule but held the presiding officer's decision subject to judicial review.

Public Accounts Committee — 22 members: 15 elected by the Lok Sabha and 7 by the Rajya Sabha; term one year; first set up in 1921; its Chairman has been drawn from the Opposition by convention since 1967; it examines the audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General.

Estimates Committee — 30 members, ALL elected from the Lok Sabha; no Rajya Sabha representation; term one year; constituted in 1950 on John Mathai's recommendation; the largest of the parliamentary committees and known as the 'continuous economy committee'; it examines estimates only after the Budget has been voted.

Committee on Public Undertakings — 22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha; created in 1964 on the recommendation of the Krishna Menon Committee; strength raised from 15 to 22 in 1974.

There are 24 Departmentally Related Standing Committees, each with 31 members — 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha; 16 are serviced by the Lok Sabha Secretariat and 8 by the Rajya Sabha Secretariat. Introduced in 1993 with 17 committees and restructured to 24 in 2004; a Minister cannot be a member.

Committee on the Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes — 30 members (20 Lok Sabha + 10 Rajya Sabha); Committee on Empowerment of Women — 30 members (20 + 10); Joint Committee on Offices of Profit — 15 members (10 + 5).

Business Advisory Committee — 15 members in the Lok Sabha with the Speaker as Chairman; 11 members in the Rajya Sabha with the Chairman presiding. The Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions is a Lok Sabha committee of 15 members.

Articles 148-151 — Comptroller and Auditor General; his audit reports on the Union accounts are submitted to the President, who causes them to be laid before each House of Parliament under Article 151, after which they stand referred to the Public Accounts Committee.

Article 169 — Parliament may by law create or abolish a Legislative Council in a State if the Legislative Assembly first passes a resolution by a majority of the total membership of the Assembly AND by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting; such a law is not deemed to be an amendment under Article 368, and Parliament is not bound to act on the Assembly's resolution.

Articles 102 and 191 lay down disqualifications for membership; under Article 103 the question is decided by the President after obtaining the opinion of the Election Commission, and his decision is final.

questions.q: Under which Article does the Constitution declare that there shall be a Parliament for the Union consisting of the President and two Houses?
questions.exp: Article 79. The President is an integral part of Parliament though he does not sit in either House.

questions.q: The maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha as laid down in the Constitution is
questions.exp: Article 80 — 238 representatives of the States and Union Territories plus 12 members nominated by the President, making a maximum of 250. The present actual strength is 245.

questions.q: The twelve members nominated by the President to the Rajya Sabha are chosen for their special knowledge or practical experience in
opts: literature, science, art and social service
literature, science, sports and social service
science, art, education and social service
literature, law, art and social service
questions.exp: Article 80(3). This provision is borrowed from the practice of nominating distinguished persons to second chambers; a nominated member gets six months to join a political party.

questions.q: The nomination of two members of the Anglo-Indian community to the Lok Sabha was discontinued by
questions.exp: The 104th Amendment Act, 2019 allowed Article 331 to lapse with effect from 25 January 2020, while extending reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes by another ten years.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Rajya Sabha:
I. It is not subject to dissolution.
II. One-third of its members retire on the expiry of every second year.
III. Its members representing a State are elected by the elected members of that State's Legislative Assembly by proportional representation with a single transferable vote.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Articles 80 and 83. The Rajya Sabha is a continuing chamber; the term of an individual member is six years.

questions.q: The minimum age prescribed for membership of the Rajya Sabha is
questions.exp: Article 84(b) prescribes 30 years for the Council of States and 25 years for the House of the People.

questions.q: The quorum to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament is
opts: one-tenth of the total number of members of the House
one-fifth of the total number of members of the House
one-sixth of the total number of members of the House
one-fourth of the total number of members of the House
questions.exp: Article 100(3). If there is no quorum the presiding officer must adjourn the House or suspend the sitting.

questions.q: The maximum permissible interval between two sessions of Parliament is
questions.exp: Article 85(1) requires that six months shall not intervene between the last sitting in one session and the first sitting in the next. Parliament must therefore meet at least twice a year.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the duration of the Houses of Parliament:
I. The Lok Sabha continues for five years from the date appointed for its first meeting.
II. During a Proclamation of Emergency its term may be extended by Parliament by law for one year at a time.
III. Such an extension cannot continue beyond a period of six months after the Proclamation ceases to operate.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Article 83(2). The term of the Fifth Lok Sabha was extended twice during the Emergency of 1975-77 — the only occasion on which this power has been used.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Article)   List-II (Provision)
A. Article 89   1. Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People
B. Article 93   2. Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council of States
C. Article 100   3. Powers, privileges and immunities of Parliament and its members
D. Article 105   4. Voting in Houses, vacancies and quorum
questions.exp: Article 94 deals with vacation and resignation of the office of Speaker and Article 96 with the Speaker not presiding while a resolution for his removal is under consideration.

questions.q: A resolution for the removal of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha must be passed by
opts: a simple majority of the members present and voting
a majority of all the then members of the House, after 14 days' notice
a two-thirds majority of the total membership of the House
a two-thirds majority of the members present and voting
questions.exp: Article 94(c). This 'effective majority' is also used for removing the Deputy Speaker, and the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT a function of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
opts: Certifying whether a Bill is a Money Bill
Presiding over a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament
Deciding questions of disqualification on the ground of defection
Deciding questions of disqualification arising under Article 102(1)
questions.exp: Under Article 103 the question of disqualification under Article 102(1) is decided by the President after obtaining the opinion of the Election Commission, and he must act according to that opinion.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Speaker of the Lok Sabha:
I. He exercises a vote only in the case of an equality of votes.
II. He presides over the House while a resolution for his own removal is under consideration.
III. He continues in office even after the dissolution of the Lok Sabha, until immediately before the first meeting of the new House.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Article 96 expressly bars the Speaker from presiding while a resolution for his removal is under consideration, though he may speak, take part and vote — except that he has no casting vote on such a resolution.

questions.q: A Money Bill is defined in which Article of the Constitution?
questions.exp: Article 110 lists the matters, such as the imposition of a tax and the appropriation of moneys out of the Consolidated Fund of India, that make a Bill a Money Bill. Article 109 lays down the special procedure for such Bills.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding a Money Bill:
I. It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha and only on the recommendation of the President.
II. The Rajya Sabha must return it within fourteen days with or without its recommendations.
III. The President may return a Money Bill to the Lok Sabha for reconsideration.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The President can either give or withhold assent to a Money Bill but cannot return it, because the Bill is introduced only with his prior recommendation.

questions.q: Whether a Bill is a Money Bill or not is finally decided by
opts: the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
questions.exp: Article 110(3) and 110(4): the Speaker's decision is final and his certificate is endorsed on the Bill when it is transmitted to the Rajya Sabha and presented to the President.

questions.q: The provision for a joint sitting of the two Houses to resolve a deadlock over a Bill is contained in
questions.exp: Article 108. The joint sitting is summoned by the President and presided over by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha; a Bill is passed by a majority of the total number of members of both Houses present and voting.

questions.q: A joint sitting of the two Houses of Parliament may be convened in respect of all of the following EXCEPT
opts: an ordinary Bill passed by one House and rejected by the other
a Bill on which the two Houses have disagreed over amendments
a financial Bill other than a Money Bill
questions.exp: Article 108 excludes both Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills, since each House must separately pass an amendment Bill by the special majority prescribed in Article 368.

questions.q:
Arrange the following Bills, in respect of which joint sittings of the two Houses of Parliament were held, in the correct chronological order:
I. Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill
II. Dowry Prohibition Bill
III. Prevention of Terrorism Bill
questions.exp: Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill (1978) and Prevention of Terrorism Bill (2002) — the only three joint sittings held so far.

questions.q: The Budget is described in the Constitution as the 'Annual Financial Statement' under
questions.exp: Article 112 requires the President to cause a statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government for every financial year to be laid before both Houses; the word 'Budget' does not occur in the Constitution.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Union budgetary process:
I. Demands for grants are submitted to and voted upon only by the Lok Sabha.
II. Expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India is not submitted to the vote of Parliament.
III. The Rajya Sabha may reject the Appropriation Bill.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: An Appropriation Bill is a Money Bill, so the Rajya Sabha can neither reject nor amend it and must return it within 14 days. Charged expenditure under Article 112(3) can be discussed but not voted.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Device)   List-II (Effect)
A. Policy cut   1. Reduction of the demand by Rs 100
B. Economy cut   2. Reduction of the amount of the demand to Re 1
C. Token cut   3. Reduction of the demand by a specified amount
D. Vote on account   4. Advance grant to meet expenditure pending the passing of the Appropriation Bill
questions.exp: A policy cut expresses total disapproval of the policy underlying the demand; a token cut ventilates a specific grievance within the sphere of the Government of India.

questions.q: The corpus of the Contingency Fund of India, as enhanced by the Finance Act, 2021, presently stands at
questions.exp: The Contingency Fund is constituted under Article 267 and the Contingency Fund of India Act, 1950; the corpus was raised from Rs 500 crore to Rs 30,000 crore in 2021 and remains at that figure as of 2026. It is held by the Finance Secretary on behalf of the President.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The Consolidated Fund of India and the Public Account of India are provided for in Article 266.
II. The Contingency Fund of India is placed at the disposal of the Prime Minister.
III. No money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India except under an appropriation made by law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Article 267 places the Contingency Fund at the disposal of the President, not the Prime Minister, to enable advances for unforeseen expenditure pending authorisation by Parliament.

questions.q: The total membership of the Public Accounts Committee of Parliament is
questions.exp: The Public Accounts Committee has 22 members — 15 elected by the Lok Sabha and 7 by the Rajya Sabha — elected annually by proportional representation with a single transferable vote. A Minister cannot be a member.

questions.q: The Public Accounts Committee consists of
opts: 15 members from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha
20 members from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
22 members, all from the Lok Sabha
21 members from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
questions.exp: First set up in 1921 under the Government of India Act, 1919, the Committee examines the appropriation accounts and the audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General.

questions.q: The Estimates Committee of Parliament consists of
opts: 30 members, all elected from the Lok Sabha
15 members, all from the Lok Sabha
questions.exp: The Estimates Committee is the only financial committee with no Rajya Sabha representation. Constituted in 1950 on the recommendation of the then Finance Minister John Mathai, it is the largest parliamentary committee.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Estimates Committee:
I. It is the largest of the parliamentary committees.
II. It has no member from the Rajya Sabha.
III. It examines the estimates only after they have been voted by Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Because it works on estimates already voted, the Committee is described as a 'continuous economy committee'; it suggests economies in expenditure and improvements in organisation and administrative efficiency.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Committee)   List-II (Year of first constitution)
A. Public Accounts Committee   1. 1993
B. Estimates Committee   2. 1921
C. Committee on Public Undertakings   3. 1950
D. Departmentally Related Standing Committees   4. 1964
questions.exp: The Committee on Public Undertakings was set up in 1964 on the recommendation of the Krishna Menon Committee; the standing committee system began in 1993 with 17 committees, restructured into 24 in 2004.

questions.q: The Committee on Public Undertakings consists of
opts: 15 members, all from the Lok Sabha
22 members — 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha
30 members — 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
31 members — 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
questions.exp: The Committee began in 1964 with 15 members; the strength was raised to 22 in 1974. Like the Public Accounts Committee, it is chaired by a Lok Sabha member and its term is one year.

questions.q: Each Departmentally Related Standing Committee of Parliament consists of
opts: 45 members — 30 from the Lok Sabha and 15 from the Rajya Sabha
22 members — 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha
31 members — 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
30 members — 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
questions.exp: There are 24 such committees, 16 serviced by the Lok Sabha Secretariat and 8 by the Rajya Sabha Secretariat. A Minister cannot be a member, and their recommendations are advisory.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Committee)   List-II (Total membership)
A. Estimates Committee   1. 22
B. Committee on Public Undertakings   2. 30
C. Departmentally Related Standing Committee   3. 31
D. Joint Committee on Offices of Profit   4. 15
questions.exp: The Joint Committee on Offices of Profit has 15 members — 10 from the Lok Sabha and 5 from the Rajya Sabha. The Committee on the Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes has 30 members (20 + 10).

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about parliamentary committees is NOT correct?
opts: The Estimates Committee has no member from the Rajya Sabha
A Minister cannot be elected as a member of a Departmentally Related Standing Committee
The Public Accounts Committee examines the audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General
The Committee on Public Undertakings consists of 30 members
questions.exp: The Committee on Public Undertakings has 22 members. It examines the reports and accounts of public undertakings and the CAG's reports on them, but not matters of major government policy or day-to-day administration.

questions.q: By convention, the Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee has been appointed from the Opposition since
questions.exp: Since 1967 the Speaker has appointed a senior member of the Opposition as Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee, strengthening its role as a watchdog over executive spending.

questions.q: The audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General relating to the accounts of the Union are laid before Parliament under
questions.exp: Article 151(1): the CAG submits his reports to the President, who causes them to be laid before each House. They then stand referred to the Public Accounts Committee.

questions.q: The provisions relating to disqualification of members on the ground of defection are contained in
questions.exp: The Tenth Schedule was inserted by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985. The Ninth Schedule protects specified laws from judicial review, the Eleventh lists 29 panchayat subjects and the Twelfth 18 municipal subjects.

questions.q: The exemption from disqualification available in the case of a 'split' in a legislature party was deleted by
questions.exp: The 91st Amendment removed paragraph 3 of the Tenth Schedule, so a defection is now protected only by a merger in which not less than two-thirds of the members of the legislature party agree.

questions.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the decision of the Speaker or Chairman under the Tenth Schedule is subject to judicial review?
opts: Ravi S. Naik v. Union of India
Jagjit Singh v. State of Haryana
G. Viswanathan v. Speaker, Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly
questions.exp: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) upheld the Tenth Schedule but struck down the finality clause, holding that the presiding officer acts as a tribunal and his order is open to judicial review on limited grounds.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. A no-confidence motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha and requires the support of at least 50 members.
II. Zero Hour is not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure of the Lok Sabha.
III. An adjournment motion can be moved in the Rajya Sabha as well.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The adjournment motion, which involves an element of censure, is available only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha cannot make use of this device.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Parliamentary device)   List-II (Feature)
A. Starred question   1. Answered orally, supplementary questions permitted
B. Unstarred question   2. Answered in writing, no supplementary questions allowed
C. Short notice question   3. Relates to a matter of urgent public importance and is asked at less than ten days' notice
D. Half-an-hour discussion   4. Raised on a matter of sufficient public importance already answered in the House
questions.exp: Question Hour, the first hour of a sitting, is regulated by the Rules of Procedure; Zero Hour, which follows it, is an Indian innovation of the 1960s with no mention in the Rules.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about Question Hour and Zero Hour is NOT correct?
opts: Question Hour is the first hour of a sitting of the House
Zero Hour starts immediately after Question Hour
Zero Hour is an Indian innovation not found in the Rules of Procedure
Question Hour is not regulated by the Rules of Procedure of the House
questions.exp: Question Hour is expressly regulated by the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business; it is Zero Hour that is informal and unmentioned in the Rules.

questions.q: Under Article 169, Parliament may create or abolish a Legislative Council in a State if the Legislative Assembly of that State passes a resolution by
opts: a simple majority of the members present and voting
a two-thirds majority of the total membership of the Assembly
a majority of not less than three-fourths of the members present and voting
a majority of the total membership of the Assembly and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting
questions.exp: Article 169(1). This is the 'special majority' of the Article 368 type. The abolition of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council in 1985 and its revival in 2007 followed this route.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 169 of the Constitution:
I. Parliament may by law provide for the creation or abolition of a Legislative Council in a State.
II. Such a law is not deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368.
III. Parliament is bound to act upon a resolution passed by the State Legislative Assembly.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The Assembly's resolution is only a condition precedent; Parliament retains full discretion and may decline to legislate, as has happened with several State proposals.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of Article and financial provision is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Article 266 provides for the Consolidated Fund of India and the Public Account of India; the Contingency Fund of India is provided for in Article 267.

questions.q:
Arrange the following stages in the enactment of the Union Budget in their correct sequence:
I. Voting on demands for grants
II. Presentation of the Annual Financial Statement
III. Passing of the Appropriation Bill
IV. General discussion
questions.exp: Presentation, general discussion, scrutiny by the departmental standing committees, voting on demands for grants, the Appropriation Bill and finally the Finance Bill complete the budget cycle.

chapters.title: Judiciary: Supreme Court, High Courts and Judicial Review
factsheet: Article 124 — establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court. The original strength was a Chief Justice and 7 other judges; it was raised in stages to 34 in 2019 and to 38 (the Chief Justice of India + 37 judges) by the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2026.
The Supreme Court was inaugurated on 28 January 1950, replacing the Federal Court of India created under the Government of India Act, 1935; the first Chief Justice of India was H. J. Kania.

Article 124(3) — qualifications: citizen of India AND either five years as a judge of a High Court, or ten years as an advocate of a High Court, or a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion. No minimum age is prescribed; a Supreme Court judge retires at 65, a High Court judge at 62 (Article 217).

Article 124(4) — removal by the President after an address by each House supported by a majority of the total membership of that House AND by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting, in the same session, on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. The procedure is governed by the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.
No judge of the Supreme Court has ever been removed; the motion against Justice V. Ramaswami failed in the Lok Sabha in 1993 when the ruling party abstained.

Article 126 — acting Chief Justice; Article 127 — ad hoc judges; Article 128 — attendance of retired judges at the sittings of the Supreme Court; Article 224A — retired judges at the sittings of High Courts.

Article 129 — the Supreme Court is a court of record with power to punish for contempt of itself; Article 215 makes the same provision for High Courts. Truth was made a valid defence by the Contempt of Courts (Amendment) Act, 2006.
Article 130 — the seat of the Supreme Court is Delhi, or such other place as the Chief Justice of India may, with the approval of the President, appoint.

Jurisdiction: Article 131 original (federal disputes, exclusive), Article 132 appeal in constitutional matters, Article 133 civil, Article 134 criminal, Article 134A certificate, Article 136 special leave to appeal, Article 137 review, Article 143 advisory.

Article 141 — the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within the territory of India; Article 142 — power to pass any decree necessary for doing complete justice; Article 144 — all civil and judicial authorities must act in aid of the Supreme Court.

Article 143 — the President may refer a question of law or fact of public importance under clause (1), and the Court MAY decline to answer; on a dispute arising out of a pre-Constitution treaty under clause (2) the Court MUST give its opinion. The opinion is advisory and not binding on the President. The 1993 Ram Janmabhoomi reference was returned unanswered.

In November 2025 a five-judge Constitution Bench headed by Chief Justice B. R. Gavai answered the Presidential Reference on the assent of Bills, holding that courts cannot fix timelines for the Governor or the President under Articles 200 and 201 and rejecting the concept of 'deemed assent'.

Writs — habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto — are issued by the Supreme Court under Article 32 and by High Courts under Article 226. Article 32 is itself a fundamental right and was called 'the heart and soul of the Constitution' by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar.

Article 226 is wider than Article 32 because a High Court can issue writs not only for the enforcement of fundamental rights but also 'for any other purpose'; the 15th Amendment Act, 1963 extended its reach to authorities outside the High Court's territorial jurisdiction where the cause of action arises within it.

Judicial review is nowhere defined in the Constitution; it flows from Articles 13, 32, 131-136, 143, 226, 227, 245, 246 and 372. Article 50, a Directive Principle, requires separation of the judiciary from the executive.

Collegium: First Judges Case (S. P. Gupta, 1981) gave primacy to the executive; the Second Judges Case (1993) created the collegium; the Third Judges Case (In re Special Reference, 1998) fixed the collegium at the CJI plus his four senior-most colleagues for Supreme Court appointments and the CJI plus two for High Court appointments.

The 99th Constitutional Amendment Act and the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014 were struck down on 16 October 2015 in the Fourth Judges Case for violating the independence of the judiciary, a basic feature. The proposed NJAC comprised the CJI, the two senior-most Supreme Court judges, the Union Law Minister and two eminent persons.

There are 25 High Courts in India; the Andhra Pradesh High Court at Amaravati, created on 1 January 2019, is the 25th. Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were established in 1862 under the Indian High Courts Act, 1861, Calcutta being the first; the Allahabad High Court (1866) has the largest sanctioned judge strength.

Article 214 — a High Court for each State; Article 231 — a common High Court for two or more States or Union Territories; Article 222 — transfer of a judge from one High Court to another; Article 224 — additional and acting judges.

Article 217 — a High Court judge must have held judicial office in India for ten years or have been an advocate of a High Court for ten years; there is NO 'distinguished jurist' category for High Courts.

Article 227 — power of superintendence of a High Court over all courts and tribunals within its territorial jurisdiction, except courts and tribunals constituted under any law relating to the armed forces.

Article 233 — district judges are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court; a person not already in service must have been an advocate for at least seven years. Article 235 vests control over the subordinate judiciary in the High Court.

Articles 323A and 323B, inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, provide for administrative tribunals and tribunals for other matters; only Parliament can legislate under Article 323A, while both Parliament and State Legislatures can act under Article 323B. The Central Administrative Tribunal was set up under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985.

L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) — judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 is part of the basic structure, and decisions of tribunals are subject to scrutiny by a Division Bench of the High Court concerned.

Article 39A — equal justice and free legal aid, inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976; it is the constitutional basis of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 (in force from 9 November 1995) and of the National Legal Services Authority.

The award of a Lok Adalat is deemed to be a decree of a civil court, is final and binding, and no appeal lies against it. National Legal Services Day is observed on 9 November. A Permanent Lok Adalat for public utility services is set up under Section 22B with pecuniary jurisdiction up to Rs 1 crore.

Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 (in force from 2 October 2009) — mobile courts at the intermediate panchayat level presided over by a Nyayadhikari having the status of a Judicial Magistrate of the first class.

Amendability line: Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) upheld amendment of fundamental rights; Golaknath (1967) reversed this; Kesavananda Bharati (1973), decided by a 13-judge bench by 7:6, laid down the basic structure doctrine.

Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) first used the basic structure to strike down a constitutional amendment; Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment and held the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles to be a basic feature; S. R. Bommai (1994) made a Proclamation under Article 356 justiciable.

Article 21 expansion — fair, just and reasonable procedure (Maneka Gandhi, 1978), speedy trial (Hussainara Khatoon, 1979), livelihood (Olga Tellis, 1985), education (Unni Krishnan, 1993), privacy (K. S. Puttaswamy, 2017, nine-judge bench). Public interest litigation was pioneered by Justices P. N. Bhagwati and V. R. Krishna Iyer, with locus standi relaxed in S. P. Gupta (1981).

questions.q: The Supreme Court of India was inaugurated on
questions.exp: The Court began functioning on 28 January 1950, two days after the Constitution came into force, replacing the Federal Court of India set up under the Government of India Act, 1935. H. J. Kania was the first Chief Justice of India.

questions.q: The original strength of the Supreme Court, as fixed by the Constitution, was
opts: a Chief Justice and 7 other judges
a Chief Justice and 10 other judges
a Chief Justice and 13 other judges
a Chief Justice and 17 other judges
questions.exp: Article 124(1) fixed the strength at eight judges in all and empowered Parliament to increase it by law, which it has done repeatedly.

questions.q: The sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court of India was raised to 38 judges by
opts: the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019
the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2026
questions.exp: The 2019 amendment had raised the strength from 31 to 34. The 2026 amendment, passed by Parliament in August 2026, raised it to the Chief Justice of India plus 37 other judges, the position as of September 2026.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the qualifications for appointment as a judge of the Supreme Court:
I. Service as a judge of a High Court for at least five years is one of the prescribed qualifications.
II. A person who is, in the opinion of the President, a distinguished jurist may be appointed.
III. The Constitution prescribes a minimum age of 45 years.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Article 124(3) prescribes no minimum age and no fixed period of experience beyond the three alternatives; the third alternative, that of a distinguished jurist, has never been used.

questions.q: A judge of the Supreme Court of India holds office until he attains the age of
questions.exp: Article 124(2). A High Court judge retires at 62 under Article 217. Questions about a judge's age are decided by the President after consulting the Chief Justice of India.

questions.q: The address for the removal of a judge of the Supreme Court must be supported in each House of Parliament by
opts: a majority of the total membership of that House and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting
a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of that House
a simple majority of the members present and voting
a majority of not less than three-fourths of the members present and voting
questions.exp: Article 124(4); both requirements must be satisfied in the same session, and the grounds are limited to proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

questions.q: The procedure for the removal of a judge of the Supreme Court is regulated by
opts: the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956
the Judicial Standards and Accountability Act
questions.exp: Under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 the presiding officer constitutes a three-member committee to investigate the charge. No judge has ever been removed; the motion against Justice V. Ramaswami failed in the Lok Sabha in 1993.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Article)   List-II (Provision)
A. Article 129   1. Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
B. Article 136   2. Supreme Court to be a court of record
C. Article 141   3. Special leave to appeal
D. Article 143   4. Law declared by the Supreme Court to be binding on all courts
questions.exp: Article 137 confers the power of review and Article 142 the power to pass any decree necessary for doing complete justice.

questions.q: The power of the Supreme Court to pass any decree necessary for doing complete justice in any cause pending before it is contained in
questions.exp: Article 142. It was used, for example, to transfer the Bhopal gas leak settlement and in the Ayodhya land dispute; the Court has held that it cannot be used to override an express statutory provision.

questions.q: The original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 131 extends to
opts: disputes between the Government of India and one or more States
appeals from the High Courts in constitutional matters
the transfer of cases from one High Court to another
references made by the President on questions of law
questions.exp: Article 131 covers federal disputes between the Centre and States or between States, and is exclusive. It does not extend to disputes arising out of a pre-Constitution treaty, agreement or sanad.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court:
I. The Supreme Court may refuse to give its opinion on a reference made under Article 143(1).
II. The opinion given by the Supreme Court on a Presidential reference is binding on the President.
III. The Supreme Court returned the Ram Janmabhoomi reference of 1993 unanswered.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The opinion under Article 143 is advisory and does not bind the President; on a dispute under Article 143(2) relating to a pre-Constitution treaty, however, the Court is obliged to give its opinion.

questions.q: In November 2025 a five-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court answered a Presidential Reference under Article 143 relating to
opts: the timelines for the grant of assent to Bills by Governors and the President
the validity of the reservation for economically weaker sections
the reservation of seats for women in legislatures
questions.exp: The Bench headed by Chief Justice B. R. Gavai held that courts cannot prescribe timelines for a Governor or the President under Articles 200 and 201 and rejected the concept of 'deemed assent' (opinion delivered on 20 November 2025).

questions.q: Which one of the following writs is issued to secure the release of a person who has been unlawfully detained?
questions.exp: Habeas corpus means 'to have the body of'. It can be issued against both public authorities and private individuals, unlike mandamus, which lies only against a public authority.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Writ)   List-II (Meaning or purpose)
A. Mandamus   1. 'We command' — directing a public authority to perform its public duty
B. Prohibition   2. Issued by a higher court to a lower court to stop proceedings exceeding its jurisdiction
C. Certiorari   3. 'To be certified' — transferring a case to itself or quashing the order of a lower court
D. Quo warranto   4. 'By what authority' — questioning a person's claim to a public office
questions.exp: Prohibition is preventive and lies only against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies; certiorari is both preventive and curative and, since 1991, also lies against administrative authorities affecting rights.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Article 226 is wider in scope than Article 32 because writs under it can be issued for purposes other than the enforcement of fundamental rights.
II. The right guaranteed by Article 32 can be suspended only as otherwise provided for by the Constitution.
III. Article 32 was described by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar as the heart and soul of the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Article 32 is itself a fundamental right and the Supreme Court cannot refuse relief under it, whereas the writ jurisdiction of a High Court under Article 226 is discretionary.

questions.q: The writ jurisdiction of a High Court under Article 226 extends to
opts: only the territory in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, in all cases
its territorial jurisdiction and also to any authority outside it if the cause of action arises within its jurisdiction
the whole of India in every case
matters relating to fundamental rights only
questions.exp: This extension was made by the 15th Amendment Act, 1963 through the insertion of clause (1A), later renumbered as Article 226(2).

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of Article and provision relating to the High Courts is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Article 214 — High Court for each State
Article 217 — Appointment of a judge of a High Court
Article 222 — Transfer of a judge from one High Court to another
Article 227 — Establishment of a common High Court for two or more States
questions.exp: A common High Court for two or more States or Union Territories is provided for in Article 231; Article 227 confers the power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals within a High Court's jurisdiction.

questions.q: How many High Courts are there in India?
questions.exp: The Andhra Pradesh High Court at Amaravati, created on 1 January 2019 on the bifurcation of the Hyderabad High Court, is the 25th. Several High Courts have jurisdiction over more than one State or Union Territory.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (High Court)   List-II (Year of establishment)
A. Calcutta High Court   1. 1866
B. Allahabad High Court   2. 1862
C. Rajasthan High Court   3. 2019
D. Andhra Pradesh High Court at Amaravati   4. 1949
questions.exp: Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were all established in 1862 under the Indian High Courts Act, 1861. The Rajasthan High Court was inaugurated on 29 August 1949 at Jodhpur, with a bench later added at Jaipur.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the judges of the High Courts:
I. A person who has held judicial office in the territory of India for at least ten years is qualified for appointment.
II. A distinguished jurist may be appointed a judge of a High Court.
III. A judge of a High Court holds office until he attains the age of 62 years.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Article 217(2) recognises only two qualifications — ten years' judicial office or ten years' practice as an advocate of a High Court. The 'distinguished jurist' category exists only for the Supreme Court under Article 124(3)(c).

questions.q: A judge of a High Court may be transferred from one High Court to another by the President under
questions.exp: Article 222; the transfer is made after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, who under the Third Judges Case must consult a collegium of four senior-most Supreme Court judges plus the Chief Justices of the two High Courts concerned.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the subordinate judiciary:
I. District judges are appointed by the Governor of the State in consultation with the High Court.
II. Control over the district courts and the courts subordinate to them is vested in the High Court.
III. A person not already in the service of the Union or the State is eligible for appointment as a district judge if he has been an advocate for at least seven years.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Articles 233 and 235. Control by the High Court covers posting, promotion and the grant of leave to persons belonging to the judicial service of the State.

questions.q: The collegium system for the appointment of judges was evolved by the Supreme Court in
questions.exp: The Second Judges Case (Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India, 1993) held that 'consultation' with the Chief Justice of India means concurrence and created the collegium.

questions.q: For the appointment of a judge of the Supreme Court, the collegium consists of the Chief Justice of India and
opts: the four senior-most judges of the Supreme Court
the two senior-most judges of the Supreme Court
the three senior-most judges of the Supreme Court
all the judges of the Supreme Court
questions.exp: This was settled by the Third Judges Case (In re Special Reference No. 1 of 1998). For a High Court appointment the Chief Justice of India consults his two senior-most colleagues.

questions.q: The National Judicial Appointments Commission was declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in
questions.exp: On 16 October 2015 the Court struck down the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act and the NJAC Act, 2014 by 4:1 for violating the independence of the judiciary, a basic feature of the Constitution.

questions.q: Which one of the following was NOT a proposed member of the National Judicial Appointments Commission?
opts: The Union Minister of Law and Justice
questions.exp: The NJAC was to consist of the Chief Justice of India as chairperson, the two senior-most Supreme Court judges, the Union Law Minister and two eminent persons nominated by a committee of the Prime Minister, the CJI and the Leader of the Opposition.

questions.q: The doctrine of basic structure of the Constitution was propounded by the Supreme Court in
opts: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
questions.exp: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) was decided by a bench of 13 judges, the largest ever constituted, by a majority of 7:6. It held that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot destroy its basic structure.

questions.q:
Arrange the following cases in the correct chronological order:
I. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
II. Golaknath v. State of Punjab
III. Minerva Mills v. Union of India
IV. Shankari Prasad v. Union of India
questions.exp: Shankari Prasad (1951), Golaknath (1967), Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Minerva Mills (1980). Sajjan Singh (1965) falls between the first two and followed Shankari Prasad.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Case)   List-II (Principle laid down)
A. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India   1. The procedure established by law under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable
B. S. R. Bommai v. Union of India   2. A Proclamation issued under Article 356 is subject to judicial review
C. Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan   3. Guidelines against the sexual harassment of women at the workplace
D. K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India   4. The right to privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21
questions.exp: Vishaka (1997) arose out of the gang rape of Bhanwari Devi, a saathin of the Women's Development Programme in Rajasthan; the guidelines were replaced by the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the judicial expansion of Article 21:
I. The right to livelihood was read into Article 21 in Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation.
II. The right to a speedy trial was recognised in Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar.
III. The right to privacy was declared a fundamental right by a nine-judge bench in 2017.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Other rights read into Article 21 include the right to a clean environment, to health, to shelter, to legal aid and, in Common Cause (2018), to die with dignity through a living will.

questions.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable?
opts: A. K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
questions.exp: Maneka Gandhi (1978) overruled the narrow reading in A. K. Gopalan (1950) and introduced the American idea of due process into Article 21, linking Articles 14, 19 and 21 as a golden triangle.

questions.q: Equal justice and free legal aid is enshrined in which Article of the Constitution?
questions.exp: Article 39A, a Directive Principle inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, is the constitutional basis of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 and of free legal aid to the poor.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The Legal Services Authorities Act was enacted in 1987 and came into force in 1995.
II. An award of a Lok Adalat is deemed to be a decree of a civil court and is final.
III. An appeal against an award of a Lok Adalat lies to the High Court.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: No appeal lies against a Lok Adalat award; the aggrieved party may only initiate fresh litigation. The Act came into force on 9 November 1995, observed as National Legal Services Day.

questions.q: A Permanent Lok Adalat set up for public utility services has pecuniary jurisdiction up to
questions.exp: Section 22B of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, inserted in 2002, created Permanent Lok Adalats; the pecuniary limit was raised from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore in 2015. Its award is binding even if the parties fail to reach a settlement.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Institution)   List-II (Governing statute)
A. Lok Adalat   1. Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008
B. Gram Nyayalaya   2. Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987
C. Central Administrative Tribunal   3. Commercial Courts Act, 2015
D. Commercial Court   4. Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985
questions.exp: Gram Nyayalayas are mobile courts at the intermediate panchayat level presided over by a Nyayadhikari having the status of a Judicial Magistrate of the first class; the Act came into force on 2 October 2009.

questions.q: Articles 323A and 323B, which provide for administrative and other tribunals, were inserted by
questions.exp: Only Parliament can provide for administrative tribunals under Article 323A, whereas tribunals for other matters under Article 323B may be created by Parliament or by a State Legislature.

questions.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 is part of the basic structure and that decisions of tribunals are subject to scrutiny by a Division Bench of the High Court?
opts: S. P. Sampath Kumar v. Union of India
Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra
Union of India v. R. Gandhi
L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India
questions.exp: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) struck down the clauses excluding the High Courts' jurisdiction over tribunals, ending the position taken in S. P. Sampath Kumar (1987).

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the Supreme Court is NOT correct?
opts: The Supreme Court is a court of record under Article 129
The Constitution expressly defines the expression 'judicial review'
The seat of the Supreme Court is Delhi or such other place as the Chief Justice of India may appoint with the approval of the President
Truth was made a valid defence in contempt proceedings by an amendment to the Contempt of Courts Act in 2006
questions.exp: The expression 'judicial review' is nowhere used or defined in the Constitution; the power is inferred from Articles 13, 32, 131-136, 143, 226, 227, 245, 246 and 372.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of case and principle is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Curative petition — Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra
Public interest litigation and relaxation of locus standi — S. P. Gupta v. Union of India
Basic structure first applied to strike down a constitutional amendment — Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
Balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles held a basic feature — Golaknath v. State of Punjab
questions.exp: It was Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) that held the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles to be a basic feature, while striking down Sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The opinion tendered by the Supreme Court under Article 143 of the Constitution is not binding on the President.
Reason (R): An opinion under Article 143 is advisory in nature and is not a judgment delivered in the exercise of the Court's judicial power.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.exp: The advisory opinion has high persuasive value and is ordinarily followed, but it neither binds the President nor operates as a binding precedent under Article 141.

chapters.title: Centre-State Relations, Emergency, Schedules and Amendments
factsheet: Legislative relations Centre-State: Articles 245-255. Union List originally 97 subjects, State List 66, Concurrent List 47 (7th Schedule).
Art. 248 + Entry 97 of Union List = residuary powers of legislation vest in Parliament.
Art. 249 - Rajya Sabha resolution by 2/3 of members present and voting lets Parliament legislate on a State List subject in national interest for 1 year (renewable).
Art. 250 - Parliament may legislate on State List during a National Emergency; such law lapses 6 months after the emergency ends.
Art. 252 - two or more State Legislatures request Parliament to legislate; Art. 253 - to implement international treaties/agreements. Art. 254 - repugnancy.
42nd Amendment (1976) moved 5 subjects State List to Concurrent List: education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, administration of justice.

Financial: Art. 268 duties levied by Union but collected/appropriated by States; Art. 269 taxes levied and collected by Union, assigned to States; Art. 269A GST on inter-State supply; Art. 270 taxes levied and distributed; Art. 271 surcharge (Union alone).
Art. 275 statutory grants-in-aid (charged on Consolidated Fund of India); Art. 282 discretionary grants; Art. 280 Finance Commission; Art. 293 State borrowing.
Art. 246A + Art. 279A (101st Amendment, 2016) - GST and GST Council; chair = Union Finance Minister; Centre 1/3 and States 2/3 of votes; decisions by 3/4 weighted majority.
Art. 262 - inter-State river water disputes; Inter-State River Water Disputes Act 1956 and River Boards Act 1956.

Art. 263 - Inter-State Council; set up by Presidential Order on 28 May 1990 on the recommendation of the Sarkaria Commission (1983, report 1988); Prime Minister is Chairman. Punchhi Commission on Centre-State relations: 2007, report 2010.

Zonal Councils - 5, created by the States Reorganisation Act 1956 (statutory, not constitutional); Union Home Minister is common Chairman; Rajasthan is in the Northern Zonal Council. North Eastern Council is separate (NEC Act, 1971).
Art. 301-307 - freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse; Art. 304(b) State restrictions need the President's previous sanction.
