questions.exp: The scheme gives an interest-free loan of up to Rs 50,000 to street vendors and informal sector workers in urban areas; the central counterpart for street vendors is PM SVANidhi.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Indira Gandhi Shahri Rozgar Guarantee Yojana — Urban wage employment
Mukhyamantri Yuva Sambal Yojana — Unemployment allowance
Indira Gandhi Shahri Credit Card Yojana — Interest-free loan to street vendors
Rajasthan Mission 2030 — Free coaching for unemployed youth
questions.exp: Rajasthan Mission 2030 was a vision document exercise for the state's development goals, not a coaching scheme.

questions.q: The Indira Rasoi Yojana of Rajasthan has been renamed as:
questions.exp: The Indira Rasoi Yojana was renamed the Shree Annapurna Rasoi Yojana on 5 January 2024; it serves subsidised meals under the slogan 'Koi Bhookha Na Soye' (as of 2026).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Indira Rasoi Yojana (now Shree Annapurna Rasoi Yojana):
I. It was launched on 20 August 2020.
II. Its guiding slogan was 'Koi Bhookha Na Soye'.
III. Meals were initially served at Rs 8 per plate.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The scheme was launched on 20 August 2020 under the slogan 'Koi Bhookha Na Soye' with a meal priced at Rs 8 per plate, the balance being met by state subsidy; it was renamed Shree Annapurna Rasoi Yojana in January 2024.

questions.q: The Annapurna Food Packet Yojana of Rajasthan provides free food packets to:
opts: Families holding ration cards under the National Food Security Act
Only families below the poverty line in urban areas
questions.exp: Launched in 2023 through Mahangai Rahat Camps, the scheme distributes free monthly food packets containing pulses, oil, sugar, salt and spices to NFSA ration-card families.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Scheme)   List-II (Year of commencement)
A. Indira Rasoi Yojana   1. 2024
B. Indira Gandhi Shahri Rozgar Guarantee Yojana   2. 2020
C. Jan Aadhaar Yojana   3. 2022
D. Lado Protsahan Yojana   4. 2019
questions.exp: Indira Rasoi 2020, Indira Gandhi Shahri Rozgar Guarantee Yojana 2022, Jan Aadhaar 2019 and Lado Protsahan Yojana 2024.

questions.q: The Mukhyamantri Kisan Mitra Urja Yojana of Rajasthan provides:
opts: A subsidy of up to Rs 1,000 per month on farm electricity bills
Free electricity connections to all farmers
questions.exp: Launched on 17 July 2021, the scheme gives a subsidy of up to Rs 1,000 per month (Rs 12,000 a year) on the electricity bills of agricultural consumers.

questions.q: The Rajasthan Kisan Kalyan Kosh is:
opts: A dedicated corpus fund for farmer welfare schemes
An insurance fund for crop loss
A market intervention fund of the mandi board
questions.exp: The Rajasthan Kisan Kalyan Kosh was set up in 2020-21 as a dedicated corpus to finance farmer welfare initiatives in the state.

questions.q: The Mukhyamantri Krishak Sathi Yojana of Rajasthan provides:
opts: Compensation for accidental death or injury of farmers and farm labourers
questions.exp: The Krishak Sathi Yojana compensates farmers and agricultural labourers for death or disability caused by accidents while doing agricultural work, including at mandis.

questions.q: The Jan Aadhaar number issued in Rajasthan consists of how many digits?
questions.exp: The Jan Aadhaar is a 10-digit family identity number, distinct from the 12-digit Aadhaar number issued by UIDAI; its motto is 'One Number, One Card, One Identity'.

questions.q: The Jan Aadhaar Yojana of Rajasthan replaced which earlier scheme?
questions.exp: Jan Aadhaar, launched on 18 December 2019 and implemented from 1 April 2020, replaced the Bhamashah Yojana (2008; relaunched 15 August 2014) as the state's family identity and DBT platform.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Jan Aadhaar Yojana of Rajasthan:
I. It is a family-based identity document in which a woman is normally the head of the family.
II. It serves as the single platform for delivery of state government scheme benefits.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.exp: Jan Aadhaar registers the family as a unit with an adult woman of the household as the head, and is the single identity used for direct benefit transfer under state schemes.

questions.q: The Jan Soochna Portal of Rajasthan, launched on 13 September 2019, is significant because it:
opts: Was India's first portal for proactive disclosure of scheme information under the RTI Act
Was the first state portal for online tax payment
questions.exp: The Jan Soochna Portal was the first of its kind in India, giving citizens suo motu access to scheme and beneficiary information in the spirit of Section 4(2) of the RTI Act, 2005.

questions.q: The delivery of citizen services and scheme applications in Rajasthan takes place mainly through which network of kiosks?
questions.exp: e-Mitra kiosks are Rajasthan's citizen service delivery network, used for pension applications, scheme registration, bill payment and certificates, all linked to Jan Aadhaar.

questions.q:
Arrange the following welfare initiatives of Rajasthan in the correct chronological order of their commencement:
I. Jan Aadhaar Yojana
II. Indira Rasoi Yojana
III. Mukhyamantri Rajshri Yojana
IV. Lado Protsahan Yojana
questions.exp: Mukhyamantri Rajshri Yojana (2016), Jan Aadhaar Yojana (2019), Indira Rasoi Yojana (2020) and Lado Protsahan Yojana (2024).

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Jan Aadhaar — Family identity number of Rajasthan
Jan Soochna Portal — Proactive disclosure of scheme information
questions.exp: The Bhamashah Yojana was launched in 2008 and relaunched on 15 August 2014; the scheme launched in 2019 was Jan Aadhaar.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the delivery of welfare benefits in Rajasthan:
I. Jan Aadhaar is used for authentication of beneficiaries under state schemes.
II. Social security pensions are applied for through e-Mitra kiosks.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.exp: Jan Aadhaar authentication and e-Mitra kiosks together form the delivery backbone for Rajasthan's welfare schemes, including social security pensions.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the Rajasthan Minimum Guaranteed Income Act, 2023 is NOT correct?
opts: It guarantees 125 days of employment in a year
It provides for an annual increase of 15 per cent in social security pensions
It covers both rural and urban households
It guarantees a minimum monthly cash transfer of Rs 5,000 to every family
questions.exp: The Act does not provide a universal cash transfer of Rs 5,000 a month; it guarantees employment, a minimum pension of Rs 1,000 a month and an annual 15 per cent pension increase.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Scheme)   List-II (Implementing department)
A. Mukhyamantri Rajshri Yojana   1. Devasthan Department
B. Palanhar Yojana   2. Women and Child Development Department
C. Varishth Nagrik Tirth Yatra Yojana   3. Labour Department
D. Shubhshakti Yojana   4. Social Justice and Empowerment Department
questions.exp: Scheme-to-department matching is a standard RPSC pattern: Rajshri (WCD), Palanhar (Social Justice & Empowerment), Tirth Yatra (Devasthan) and Shubhshakti (Labour Department's construction workers board).

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Programme)   List-II (Administering agency)
A. Social security pensions   1. Rajasthan Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Board
B. Anganwadi network   2. Social Justice and Empowerment Department
C. Nirman Shramik Sulabhya Awas Yojana   3. Tribal Area Development Department
D. Schemes in the Scheduled Areas   4. Women and Child Development Department
questions.exp: Social security pensions are run by the Social Justice and Empowerment Department, anganwadis by the Women and Child Development Department, construction workers' housing by the BOCW Welfare Board and Scheduled Area schemes by the TAD Department.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Scheme)   List-II (Beneficiary)
A. Shubhshakti Yojana   1. Street vendors and informal workers
B. Indira Gandhi Shahri Credit Card Yojana   2. Daughters of registered construction workers
C. Mukhyamantri Kisan Mitra Urja Yojana   3. Educated unemployed youth
D. Mukhyamantri Yuva Sambal Yojana   4. Agricultural electricity consumers
questions.exp: Scheme-to-beneficiary matching: Shubhshakti (construction workers' daughters), Shahri Credit Card (street vendors), Kisan Mitra Urja (farm power consumers) and Yuva Sambal (unemployed youth).

questions.q: Which one of the following schemes of Rajasthan is NOT primarily aimed at women or girls?
questions.exp: The Mukhyamantri Kisan Mitra Urja Yojana subsidises farm electricity bills for agricultural consumers; the other three are schemes for women and girls.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Annapurna Food Packet Yojana and the Shree Annapurna Rasoi Yojana of Rajasthan:
I. The Food Packet Yojana distributes free monthly packets of essential commodities.
II. The Rasoi Yojana serves cooked meals at a subsidised price.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.exp: The Annapurna Food Packet Yojana gives free monthly packets of pulses, oil, sugar, salt and spices to NFSA families, while the Shree Annapurna Rasoi Yojana (formerly Indira Rasoi) serves cooked meals at a subsidised rate.

chapters.title: Physics in Everyday Life
factsheet: Seven SI base units: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature), mole (amount of substance), candela (luminous intensity).
Derived SI units: newton = kg m/s2 (force); pascal = N/m2 (pressure); joule = N m (work, energy); watt = J/s (power); hertz (frequency); coulomb (charge); volt, ohm, farad, tesla, weber, henry.
Units of pressure: pascal, bar, torr, atmosphere, mm of mercury (1 atm = 1.013 x 10^5 Pa = 760 torr = 76 cm of Hg = 1.013 bar).

Unit traps: light year and parsec measure DISTANCE (1 parsec = 3.26 light years); barn = area; knot = speed; decibel = sound level; dioptre = power of a lens; poise = viscosity; Chandrasekhar limit = mass.
1 horsepower = 746 watt. 1 kilowatt-hour (Board of Trade unit) = 3.6 x 10^6 joule. Angstrom = 10^-10 m; nanometre = 10^-9 m; fermi = 10^-15 m.
Scalars: mass, speed, distance, work, energy, power, temperature, density, pressure. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, impulse, torque, weight.

Newton's laws: first = law of inertia (seat belts, dusting a carpet, passenger lurching in a bus); second = F = ma = rate of change of momentum; third = action-reaction (rocket, recoil of a gun, swimming, walking).

Conservation of linear momentum explains the recoil of a gun and jet or rocket propulsion. Impulse = force x time = change in momentum, which is why air bags, sand pits and a cricketer's follow-through reduce injury.
g = 9.8 m/s2 at sea level; maximum at the poles, minimum at the equator; ZERO at the centre of the earth; g on the Moon = 1/6 of that on Earth. Mass is the same everywhere, weight is not.

Escape velocity of Earth = 11.2 km/s; of the Moon = 2.38 km/s (why the Moon has no atmosphere); orbital velocity of a near-earth satellite is about 7.9 km/s. Weightlessness in an orbiting spacecraft or a freely falling lift occurs because body and vehicle fall together, not because gravity is absent.

Geostationary satellite: circular equatorial orbit at about 36,000 km (35,786 km), period 24 hours, used for communication and meteorology. Polar and sun-synchronous orbits (about 800-900 km) are used for remote sensing.

Pascal's law (pressure transmitted equally in an enclosed fluid) - hydraulic press, hydraulic brakes, hydraulic jack. Archimedes' principle (upthrust) - ship, submarine, hydrometer, lactometer. Bernoulli's principle (fast flow means low pressure) - aerofoil lift, atomiser, chimney draught, two boats drawn together.
Atmospheric pressure at sea level = 76 cm of mercury = 1.013 x 10^5 Pa; measured by a barometer (Torricelli). It falls with altitude, so water boils below 100 C on hills - hence the pressure cooker.

Surface tension: spherical raindrops, floating needle, insects walking on water, capillary rise in a wick and in soil; soap and detergent LOWER surface tension. Surface tension decreases as temperature rises.
Viscosity of a LIQUID decreases with rise in temperature; viscosity of a GAS increases with temperature. Units: poise (CGS), pascal-second (SI).

Water: specific heat 4.2 J/g/K, the highest among common liquids - used as a coolant and it moderates coastal climate. Latent heat of fusion of ice = 80 cal/g (336 J/g); latent heat of vaporisation of water = 540 cal/g (2260 J/g), which is why steam burns worse than boiling water.
Anomalous expansion of water: density is maximum at 4 C, so ice floats and lakes freeze from the top downwards, allowing aquatic life to survive.

Heat transfer: conduction (solids), convection (fluids - land and sea breeze), radiation (needs no medium - Sun to Earth). A thermos flask blocks all three: vacuum stops conduction and convection, silvering stops radiation, cork stopper reduces conduction.

Refrigeration and sweating cool by evaporation - the refrigerant absorbs latent heat as it vaporises. A bimetallic strip (unequal expansion of two metals) is the thermostat in irons, geysers and fire alarms.

Sound needs a material medium; there is no sound in vacuum. Speed of sound is greatest in solids, least in gases; about 332 m/s in air at 0 C. Audible range 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; above this is ultrasonic, below it infrasonic.

Ultrasound uses: SONAR (sea depth, submarines), sonography, echocardiography, lithotripsy (breaking kidney stones), detecting flaws in metal castings, cleaning. Bats and dolphins use echolocation. Minimum distance for a distinct echo = 17.2 m. A stethoscope works by MULTIPLE REFLECTION of sound.

Doppler effect = apparent change of frequency due to relative motion (radar speed guns; red shift of receding galaxies). Loudness depends on amplitude, pitch on frequency, quality (timbre) on waveform.

Optics shortcuts: blue sky and red sunset = scattering (short wavelengths scatter most); mirage, sparkle of diamond and optical fibre = total internal reflection; twinkling of stars and seeing the Sun before actual sunrise = atmospheric refraction; rainbow = refraction + dispersion + internal reflection in raindrops.

Vision defects: myopia - concave lens; hypermetropia - convex lens; presbyopia - bifocal lens; astigmatism - cylindrical lens; cataract - the eye lens turns cloudy owing to changes in its protein, corrected surgically. Power of a lens (dioptre) = 1 / focal length in metres; a concave lens has negative power.

Convex mirror - rear-view mirror (erect, diminished, wide field). Concave mirror - vehicle headlight, torch, shaving mirror, dentist's mirror, solar cooker. Periscope uses plane mirrors or total-internal-reflection prisms. LASER = Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation (monochromatic, coherent).

Electromagnetic spectrum in increasing order of wavelength: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. TV remote controls use INFRARED; microwave ovens use microwaves; UHF radio waves travel as space waves.

Electricity: Ohm's law V = IR; Indian household supply is 220 V, 50 Hz AC; appliances are wired in PARALLEL; ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel. A fuse is a thin low-melting-point tin-lead wire connected in SERIES in the LIVE wire.

Faraday's electromagnetic induction runs the generator or dynamo; Lenz's law gives the direction of the induced current. A transformer works on MUTUAL INDUCTION and only with AC. Fleming's left-hand rule - motor; right-hand rule - generator. A photovoltaic cell converts solar energy directly into electrical energy.

Modern physics: photoelectric effect explained by Einstein (Nobel 1921); X-rays discovered by W. C. Roentgen (first Physics Nobel, 1901); radioactivity by Henri Becquerel; neutron by James Chadwick. Alpha = helium nucleus, beta = electron, gamma = electromagnetic wave (most penetrating). Superconductivity (zero resistance, Meissner effect) was found by Kamerlingh Onnes in mercury, 1911.

Nuclear reactors use controlled FISSION of uranium-235 with heavy water or graphite as MODERATOR and cadmium or boron rods as CONTROL rods; the Sun's energy comes from nuclear FUSION of hydrogen into helium.

questions.q: Which one of the following is a base unit in the International System of Units (SI)?
questions.exp: The candela (luminous intensity) is one of the seven SI base units, along with metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin and mole. Newton, pascal and joule are derived units.

questions.q:
Consider the following units:
I. bar
II. pascal
III. torr
IV. atmosphere
Which of the units given above are units of pressure?
questions.exp: All four measure pressure. One atmosphere equals 1.013 x 10^5 pascal, which is 760 torr, 76 cm of mercury and about 1.013 bar.

questions.q: One horsepower is approximately equal to
questions.exp: 1 HP = 746 W. The watt, the SI unit of power, is one joule per second.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Unit)   List-II (Physical quantity)
A. Dioptre   1. Viscosity
B. Poise   2. Power of a lens
C. Becquerel   3. Radioactivity
D. Tesla   4. Magnetic flux density
questions.exp: Dioptre measures the power of a lens (the reciprocal of the focal length in metres), poise measures viscosity, becquerel measures radioactivity and tesla measures magnetic flux density.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a unit and the physical quantity it measures is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: A light year is the distance travelled by light in one year, that is, a unit of DISTANCE. One parsec equals 3.26 light years.

questions.q: Which one of the following is a scalar quantity?
questions.exp: Speed has magnitude only and is therefore a scalar. Impulse, torque and momentum all have direction and are vectors.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Newton's first law of motion:
I. It is also known as the law of inertia.
II. A standing passenger in a moving bus tends to fall forward when the bus stops suddenly.
III. The mass of a body is a measure of its inertia.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. The first law states that a body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion unless acted upon by an external force, and inertia increases with mass.

questions.q: The propulsion of a rocket is based on
questions.exp: Hot gases ejected backwards exert an equal and opposite forward reaction on the rocket, which is Newton's third law of motion.

questions.q: When a bullet is fired from a gun, the gun recoils backwards. This is a direct consequence of
questions.exp: The total linear momentum of the gun-and-bullet system is zero before firing, so the forward momentum of the bullet is balanced by the backward momentum of the gun.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The value of acceleration due to gravity is zero at the centre of the earth.
II. The escape velocity from the surface of the earth is about 11.2 km per second.
III. The value of g is greater at the equator than at the poles.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: I and II are correct. Because the earth bulges at the equator, g is minimum at the equator and maximum at the poles, so statement III is wrong.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about a geostationary satellite:
I. Its orbital period is 24 hours.
II. It is placed in a circular orbit above the equator at a height of about 36,000 km.
III. It is the preferred orbit for remote sensing satellites.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: I and II are correct. Remote sensing satellites use low polar or sun-synchronous orbits of about 800 to 900 km; the geostationary orbit is used mainly for communication and meteorology.

questions.q: An astronaut inside an orbiting spacecraft experiences weightlessness because
opts: there is no gravitational force at that height
the astronaut and the spacecraft are both in a state of free fall
the mass of the astronaut becomes zero in orbit
there is no air resistance in space
questions.exp: Gravity is very much present in orbit; the sensation of weightlessness arises because the astronaut and the spacecraft fall around the earth together, so there is no normal reaction on the astronaut.

questions.q: A coolie carrying a load on his head walks on a level platform. The work done by him against gravity is
opts: equal to the weight multiplied by the distance walked
zero, because the force and the displacement are mutually perpendicular
questions.exp: Work equals force multiplied by displacement multiplied by the cosine of the angle between them; here the upward force and the horizontal displacement are perpendicular, so the work done against gravity is zero.

questions.q: One kilowatt-hour, the commercial unit of electrical energy, is equal to
questions.exp: 1 kWh = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3.6 x 10^6 joule. It is also called the Board of Trade unit and is what a domestic electricity meter records.

questions.q: The working of a hydraulic brake in an automobile is based on
questions.exp: Pascal's law states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished in all directions; it is used in hydraulic brakes, hydraulic lifts and hydraulic presses.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a device and the principle on which it works is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: A pressure cooker works because an increase in pressure raises the boiling point of water; surface tension plays no part in it.

questions.q: Food is cooked faster in a pressure cooker because
opts: the cooker lowers the boiling point of water
the increased pressure inside raises the boiling point of water
the specific heat of water increases inside the cooker
loss of heat by radiation is completely stopped
questions.exp: Trapped steam raises the pressure inside, and since the boiling point of water rises with pressure, water boils above 100 degrees Celsius and food cooks faster. On hills, where atmospheric pressure is low, water boils below 100 degrees Celsius.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Instrument)   List-II (Measures)
A. Lactometer   1. Purity of milk
B. Hydrometer   2. Atmospheric pressure
C. Barometer   3. Relative density of a liquid
D. Anemometer   4. Wind speed
questions.exp: A lactometer is a hydrometer calibrated for milk; a barometer measures atmospheric pressure and an anemometer measures wind speed.

questions.q: Two boats moving side by side in the same direction tend to be drawn towards each other. This is explained by
questions.exp: Water between the boats flows faster and therefore exerts less pressure than the water on the outer sides, so the boats are pushed together. The same principle gives an aeroplane wing its lift.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT an effect of surface tension?
opts: The nearly spherical shape of a freely falling raindrop
The floating of a greased steel needle on water
The rise of kerosene in the wick of a lamp
The operation of a hydraulic jack
questions.exp: A hydraulic jack works on Pascal's law. The other three are classic consequences of surface tension and the related phenomenon of capillarity.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Mercury is depressed in a fine glass capillary tube instead of rising in it.
II. Oil rises in the wick of a lamp by capillary action.
III. The surface tension of a liquid increases with rise in temperature.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: I and II are correct. Surface tension DECREASES as temperature rises, one reason why hot water with detergent cleans better than cold water.

questions.q: With a rise in temperature, the viscosity of a liquid
questions.exp: Heating weakens the intermolecular attraction in a liquid, so it flows more easily. In contrast, the viscosity of a GAS increases with temperature.

questions.q: Water is used as a coolant in automobile radiators mainly because it has
opts: a very high specific heat capacity
questions.exp: Water has a specific heat of about 4.2 joule per gram per kelvin, the highest among common liquids, so it absorbs a large quantity of heat for a small rise in temperature.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The latent heat of fusion of ice is about 80 calorie per gram.
II. The latent heat of vaporisation of water is about 540 calorie per gram.
III. The temperature of ice rises steadily while it is melting at atmospheric pressure.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: I and II are correct. During a change of state the temperature stays constant because the heat supplied is used to break intermolecular bonds; this is also why a burn from steam is worse than one from boiling water.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Everyday observation)   List-II (Explanation)
A. Land and sea breeze   1. Convection
B. The handle of a metal spoon kept in hot tea becomes warm   2. Conduction
C. Warmth felt while sitting in front of a fire   3. Radiation
D. Vacuum between the double walls of a thermos flask   4. Prevents conduction and convection
questions.exp: Land and sea breezes are convection currents arising from the high specific heat of water; radiation, unlike the other two modes, needs no material medium, which is how heat reaches the earth from the sun.

questions.q: The cooling produced in a domestic refrigerator is essentially due to
opts: absorption of latent heat when the liquid refrigerant evaporates
questions.exp: The refrigerant evaporates in the coils inside the cabinet and absorbs latent heat from the contents; the compressor then compresses the vapour and the condenser rejects that heat outside.

questions.q: Ice floats on water and a lake freezes from the surface downwards because water
opts: has a very high latent heat of fusion
attains its maximum density at 4 degrees Celsius
is a poor conductor of heat
has a very high surface tension
questions.exp: This anomalous expansion means water at 4 degrees Celsius sinks while colder water and ice remain on top, so aquatic life survives beneath a frozen surface.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements relating to heat and thermometry is NOT correct?
opts: A thermos flask has a vacuum between its double walls to check conduction and convection
The walls of a thermos flask are silvered to reduce loss of heat by radiation
A bimetallic strip works as a thermostat because two metals expand unequally on heating
Mercury is used in thermometers because it has a very high specific heat
questions.exp: Mercury is preferred because it expands uniformly, conducts heat well, is opaque and does not wet glass; its specific heat is in fact low.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about sound:
I. Sound cannot travel through vacuum.
II. The speed of sound is greater in solids than in gases.
III. The loudness of a sound depends on its frequency.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: I and II are correct. Loudness depends on AMPLITUDE; frequency determines pitch, while the waveform determines quality or timbre.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about ultrasonic waves:
I. Their frequency is above 20,000 hertz.
II. They are used in SONAR to measure the depth of the sea.
III. They are used to break kidney stones in lithotripsy.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. Ultrasound is also used in sonography, echocardiography, cleaning delicate parts and detecting internal flaws in metal castings; bats and dolphins navigate by echolocation.

questions.q: A stethoscope works on the principle of
questions.exp: Sound from the patient's body is repeatedly reflected inside the tubes of the stethoscope and is thus carried to the doctor's ears with very little loss of intensity.

questions.q: The apparent change in the frequency of the whistle of a train as it approaches and then recedes from an observer is called
questions.exp: The Doppler effect arises from relative motion between source and observer; the same principle is used in radar speed guns and in measuring the red shift of receding galaxies.

questions.q: A distinct echo is heard only if the reflecting surface is at a minimum distance of about
questions.exp: The ear retains a sound sensation for about 0.1 second; with the speed of sound about 344 metre per second the sound must travel 34.4 m to and fro, so the reflector must be at least 17.2 m away.

questions.q: The blue colour of a clear sky is due to
opts: scattering of sunlight by the molecules of the atmosphere
reflection of light by air molecules
total internal reflection in the atmosphere
dispersion of sunlight by dust particles
questions.exp: Shorter wavelengths such as blue are scattered far more strongly than longer ones by air molecules. Above the atmosphere there is no scattering, so an astronaut sees a black sky.

questions.q:
Arrange the following electromagnetic radiations in increasing order of wavelength:
I. Gamma rays
II. X-rays
III. Visible light
IV. Radio waves
questions.exp: In increasing order of wavelength the electromagnetic spectrum runs gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves and radio waves; frequency and photon energy decrease in the same direction.

questions.q:
Arrange the following colours of the visible spectrum in increasing order of their wavelength:
I. Red
II. Yellow
III. Green
IV. Violet
questions.exp: The visible spectrum in increasing order of wavelength is violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red. Violet is deviated the most by a prism and red the least.

questions.q: The waves used in a common television remote control are
questions.exp: A remote control uses an infrared light-emitting diode to send coded pulses to the receiver on the television set. Infrared lies just beyond the red end of the visible spectrum.

questions.q: Stars appear to twinkle whereas planets generally do not. The twinkling of stars is caused by
opts: total internal reflection in the atmosphere
diffraction at the pupil of the eye
questions.exp: Continuously changing atmospheric refraction makes the apparent position and brightness of a point-like star fluctuate; planets are extended sources, so the fluctuations average out.

questions.q:
Consider the following phenomena:
I. Formation of a mirage on a hot road.
II. Sparkling of a cut diamond.
III. Transmission of light through an optical fibre.
Which of the above are examples of total internal reflection?
questions.exp: All three depend on total internal reflection. Diamond has a refractive index of about 2.42 and a critical angle of only about 24 degrees, so light is reflected repeatedly inside it before emerging.

questions.q: Optical fibres, widely used in telecommunication and in endoscopy, work on the principle of
questions.exp: Light entering the optically denser core strikes the cladding at an angle greater than the critical angle and is repeatedly totally internally reflected along the length of the fibre.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Defect of vision)   List-II (Corrective lens)
A. Myopia   1. Convex lens
B. Hypermetropia   2. Concave lens
C. Presbyopia   3. Cylindrical lens
D. Astigmatism   4. Bifocal lens
questions.exp: In myopia the image forms in front of the retina and needs a diverging (concave) lens; in hypermetropia it forms behind the retina and needs a converging (convex) lens.

questions.q: A convex mirror is preferred as the rear-view mirror of a vehicle because it always forms
opts: a real, inverted and magnified image
a virtual, erect and diminished image with a wide field of view
a real, erect image of the same size
a virtual, inverted and magnified image
questions.exp: A convex mirror always gives an erect, diminished virtual image and covers a much wider field of view than a plane mirror of the same size.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of an optical device and the mirror or lens used in it is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Short-sightedness, or myopia, is corrected with a CONCAVE (diverging) lens; a convex lens is used for long-sightedness or hypermetropia.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the formation of a rainbow:
I. It involves refraction, dispersion and internal reflection of sunlight in water droplets.
II. It is always seen in the part of the sky opposite to the sun.
III. In a primary rainbow the red colour appears on the outer edge.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. Sunlight entering a raindrop is dispersed, internally reflected once and refracted again as it emerges towards an observer whose back is to the sun.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about domestic electric supply in India:
I. The supply is alternating current at 220 volt and 50 hertz.
II. Domestic appliances are connected in parallel.
III. A voltmeter is connected in series with the appliance whose voltage is to be measured.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: I and II are correct. A voltmeter, having very high resistance, is always connected in PARALLEL; an ammeter, having very low resistance, is connected in series. Parallel wiring lets each appliance get the full 220 volt and work independently.

questions.q: An electric fuse is a safety device that is
opts: connected in parallel with the appliance in the neutral wire
a thick wire of high melting point placed in the earth wire
a thin wire of low melting point connected in series in the live wire
a device that cuts off supply by creating an earth connection
questions.exp: The fuse wire, usually a tin-lead alloy of low melting point, melts and breaks the circuit when the current exceeds a safe value, protecting appliances against short circuits and overloading.

questions.q: The metal body of an electrical appliance is earthed in order to
opts: increase the current supplied to the appliance
provide a low-resistance path to the ground so that a person touching it is not shocked
convert alternating current into direct current
questions.exp: If the live wire touches the metal casing, the earth wire carries the leakage current safely to the ground and the resulting large current blows the fuse.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about a transformer:
I. It works on the principle of mutual induction.
II. It can be used with direct current as well as with alternating current.
III. A step-up transformer increases the voltage and decreases the current.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: A transformer needs a continuously changing magnetic flux and therefore works only with alternating current, so statement II is wrong.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Device)   List-II (Energy conversion)
A. Electric motor   1. Electrical energy into mechanical energy
B. Dynamo   2. Mechanical energy into electrical energy
C. Microphone   3. Sound energy into electrical energy
D. Electric bulb   4. Electrical energy into light and heat energy
questions.exp: A dynamo or generator works on Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction; Fleming's right-hand rule applies to the generator and the left-hand rule to the motor.

questions.q: A photovoltaic (solar) cell directly converts
questions.exp: A photovoltaic cell is a semiconductor device, usually silicon based, that converts sunlight straight into direct-current electricity; a solar cooker, by contrast, converts solar energy into heat.

questions.q: A material that offers zero electrical resistance below a certain critical temperature is called
questions.exp: Superconductivity was discovered by Kamerlingh Onnes in mercury in 1911; superconductors also expel magnetic flux, an effect called the Meissner effect that is used in magnetic levitation.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Scientist)   List-II (Discovery / explanation)
A. W. C. Roentgen   1. X-rays
B. Henri Becquerel   2. Radioactivity
C. James Chadwick   3. Photoelectric effect
D. Albert Einstein   4. Neutron
questions.exp: Roentgen discovered X-rays in 1895 and received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901; Einstein received the 1921 Nobel Prize for explaining the photoelectric effect.

questions.q: The energy radiated by the sun is produced by
opts: nuclear fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium
questions.exp: In the sun's core, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium and release enormous energy; the fission of uranium-235 is what powers a nuclear reactor on earth.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about a nuclear reactor is NOT correct?
opts: It produces energy by the controlled fission of uranium-235
Heavy water and graphite are used as moderators
Cadmium and boron rods are used as moderators to slow down neutrons
The moderator slows down fast neutrons so that they can cause further fission
questions.exp: Cadmium and boron rods are CONTROL rods that absorb neutrons to regulate the chain reaction; moderators such as heavy water and graphite slow the neutrons down.

questions.q: Among the alpha, beta and gamma radiations emitted by radioactive substances, the most penetrating is
questions.exp: Alpha particles (helium nuclei) are stopped by a sheet of paper, beta particles (electrons) by a few millimetres of aluminium, while gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic waves needing thick lead or concrete.

chapters.title: Chemistry in Everyday Life
factsheet: Common name - chemical name - formula: baking soda = sodium hydrogencarbonate = NaHCO3; washing soda = sodium carbonate decahydrate = Na2CO3.10H2O; caustic soda = sodium hydroxide = NaOH; caustic potash = KOH.

Quicklime = calcium oxide = CaO; slaked lime = calcium hydroxide = Ca(OH)2; limestone / marble / chalk = calcium carbonate = CaCO3; gypsum = CaSO4.2H2O; plaster of Paris = CaSO4.(1/2)H2O (gypsum heated to about 100 C).
Bleaching powder = calcium oxychloride = CaOCl2, made by passing chlorine over dry slaked lime; used for bleaching and for disinfecting drinking water.

Vitriols: blue vitriol = CuSO4.5H2O; green vitriol = FeSO4.7H2O; white vitriol = ZnSO4.7H2O; oil of vitriol = concentrated H2SO4. Epsom salt = MgSO4.7H2O; Glauber's salt = Na2SO4.10H2O; hypo (photographic fixer) = sodium thiosulphate Na2S2O3.5H2O.

Other everyday names: dry ice = solid carbon dioxide; laughing gas = nitrous oxide N2O; marsh gas = methane CH4; sal ammoniac = NH4Cl; saltpetre = KNO3; borax = Na2B4O7.10H2O; potash alum = K2SO4.Al2(SO4)3.24H2O; milk of magnesia = Mg(OH)2; heavy water = D2O.
Aqua regia = 3 parts concentrated hydrochloric acid to 1 part concentrated nitric acid; it dissolves gold and platinum.

Acids in daily life: formic (methanoic) acid - ant and nettle sting; acetic acid - vinegar; citric acid - lemon and orange; lactic acid - curd and sour milk; oxalic acid - tomato and spinach; tartaric acid - tamarind; malic acid - apple; hydrochloric acid - gastric juice.

pH: 7 is neutral at 25 C; below 7 acidic, above 7 basic. Tooth decay starts when mouth pH falls below 5.5; human blood pH is 7.35-7.45. Antacids such as milk of magnesia and baking soda neutralise excess stomach acid; a bee sting (acidic) is treated with baking soda and a wasp sting (alkaline) with vinegar.

Rusting = hydrated ferric oxide Fe2O3.xH2O; it needs BOTH oxygen and moisture. Prevention: painting, greasing, galvanisation (zinc coating), tinning (kalai - a tin coating on brass and copper utensils), electroplating, alloying, cathodic protection.

Alloys: brass = copper + zinc; bronze = copper + tin; german silver = copper + zinc + nickel (contains NO silver); duralumin = aluminium + copper + magnesium + manganese; solder = lead + tin; stainless steel = iron + chromium (about 18%) + nickel (about 8%) + carbon; gunmetal = copper + tin + zinc; bell metal = copper + tin (about 78:22); nichrome = nickel + chromium + iron; magnalium = aluminium + magnesium; invar = iron + nickel (low expansion); amalgam = any alloy containing mercury.

Ores: bauxite - aluminium; haematite (Fe2O3) and magnetite (Fe3O4) - iron; galena (PbS) - lead; cinnabar (HgS) - mercury; zinc blende (ZnS) and calamine (ZnCO3) - zinc; copper pyrites (CuFeS2) and malachite - copper; pitchblende - uranium; monazite - thorium; argentite - silver; rock salt - sodium.

Atomic structure: electron - J. J. Thomson; proton - Goldstein/Rutherford; neutron - James Chadwick. Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers; isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers.

Periodic table: Mendeleev arranged elements by increasing atomic MASS; the modern periodic law (Moseley) uses ATOMIC NUMBER. Group 1 = alkali metals, group 2 = alkaline earth metals, group 17 = halogens, group 18 = noble gases. Fluorine is the most electronegative element; caesium is among the most electropositive.

Mercury is the only metal liquid at room temperature; bromine is the only non-metal liquid at room temperature. Sodium and potassium are stored under kerosene. Graphite is a non-metal that conducts electricity.

Carbon allotropes: diamond (hardest natural substance, each carbon bonded to FOUR others, non-conductor), graphite (layered, soft, lubricant, conducts electricity because of one free electron per atom), fullerene C60 (buckminsterfullerene, football-shaped), graphene (single layer), carbon nanotubes.

Catalysts: Haber process for ammonia - finely divided IRON; contact process for sulphuric acid - vanadium pentoxide V2O5; hydrogenation of vegetable oil into vanaspati - NICKEL; Ostwald process for nitric acid - platinum.

Gases: air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen by volume. Argon (with nitrogen) fills incandescent bulbs; helium fills balloons and airships and is used in diving mixtures; neon glows red in advertising signs; ozone (O3) in the stratosphere absorbs ultraviolet radiation; carbon dioxide is used in fire extinguishers and as dry ice.

Fuel gases: CNG - mainly METHANE; LPG - mainly BUTANE and propane, with ethyl mercaptan added as an odorant; biogas / gobar gas - mainly methane; water gas = CO + H2; producer gas = CO + N2; coal gas = H2 + CH4 + CO. Hydrogen has the highest calorific value of all fuels.
Calcium carbide with water gives ACETYLENE (ethyne), used in oxy-acetylene welding and misused for artificial ripening of fruit; ethylene (ethene) is the natural ripening hormone.

Polymers: thermoplastics soften on heating and can be remoulded (polythene, PVC, polystyrene, nylon, PET, teflon); thermosetting plastics set permanently (bakelite, melamine). Nylon is a synthetic NON-cellulosic fibre; rayon is regenerated cellulose. Vulcanisation = heating natural rubber with SULPHUR (Charles Goodyear).

Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids made by saponification of oils with alkali; they do not lather in hard water (Ca and Mg salts). Synthetic detergents are alkyl benzene sulphonates and work even in hard water. Cleaning works through micelle formation and lowering of surface tension.

Cement: made from limestone and clay; gypsum (2-3 per cent) is added to SLOW DOWN the setting. Concrete = cement + sand + gravel + water; reinforced cement concrete uses steel bars. Glass is mainly silica (SiO2); borosilicate (Pyrex) glass resists heat; cobalt oxide gives blue glass.

Fertilisers: urea CO(NH2)2 has the highest nitrogen content among solid fertilisers, about 46 per cent; DAP supplies nitrogen and phosphorus; muriate of potash is potassium chloride; superphosphate supplies phosphorus.
Explosives: gunpowder = potassium nitrate + charcoal + sulphur; TNT = trinitrotoluene; RDX = cyclonite; dynamite = nitroglycerine absorbed in kieselguhr, invented by Alfred Nobel.

Batteries: dry cell (zinc-carbon) and lead-acid storage battery (lead, lead dioxide, sulphuric acid) in vehicles; lithium-ion cells power mobile phones, laptops and electric vehicles; a fuel cell converts the chemical energy of hydrogen and oxygen directly into electricity, giving water as the only product.

Food adulteration: argemone seed oil in mustard oil (causes epidemic dropsy); metanil yellow in turmeric and pulses; brick powder in chilli powder; chicory in coffee; melamine in milk; papaya seeds in black pepper. Common preservatives: sodium benzoate, sodium metabisulphite, salt, sugar, vinegar (acetic acid).

Drugs: analgesic relieves pain (aspirin, paracetamol; morphine is a narcotic analgesic); antipyretic reduces fever (paracetamol); antibiotic kills or checks micro-organisms (penicillin, discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928); antiseptic is applied to LIVING tissue (Dettol, tincture of iodine) while a disinfectant is used on NON-LIVING objects (phenol, chlorine); antacid neutralises stomach acid.

Radioisotopes: carbon-14 - dating of fossils and archaeological material; cobalt-60 - cancer radiotherapy; iodine-131 - thyroid disorders; phosphorus-32 - agricultural and leukaemia studies; sodium-24 - tracing blood circulation and detecting leaks in underground pipelines; uranium-235 - nuclear fission.
Sublimation (solid straight to vapour): camphor, naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride, dry ice. Plasma is the fourth state of matter; the Bose-Einstein condensate is the fifth.

questions.q: The chemical formula of baking soda is
questions.exp: Baking soda is sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO3. On heating it releases carbon dioxide, which makes cakes rise; it is also used as a mild antacid and in soda-acid fire extinguishers.

questions.q: Plaster of Paris is obtained by
opts: treating limestone with dilute hydrochloric acid
heating gypsum to about 100 degrees Celsius
passing chlorine over dry slaked lime
questions.exp: Gypsum (CaSO4.2H2O) heated to about 373 K loses three-quarters of its water of crystallisation to give plaster of Paris, CaSO4.(1/2)H2O, which sets into a hard mass when mixed with water.

questions.q: Bleaching powder, used for disinfecting drinking water, is prepared by
opts: heating limestone in a lime kiln
passing chlorine over dry slaked lime
questions.exp: Chlorine passed over dry calcium hydroxide gives bleaching powder, CaOCl2. It is used for bleaching cotton and paper pulp and for making drinking water safe.

questions.q: Aqua regia, which can dissolve gold, is a mixture of
opts: concentrated sulphuric acid and concentrated nitric acid in the ratio 3 : 1
concentrated nitric acid and concentrated hydrochloric acid in the ratio 3 : 1
dilute hydrochloric acid and dilute nitric acid in equal volumes
concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated nitric acid in the ratio 3 : 1
questions.exp: Aqua regia, literally royal water, is three parts concentrated hydrochloric acid to one part concentrated nitric acid; it dissolves noble metals such as gold and platinum.

questions.q: Heavy water, used as a moderator in nuclear reactors, is chemically
opts: water containing dissolved calcium and magnesium salts
questions.exp: Heavy water is D2O, in which ordinary hydrogen is replaced by its isotope deuterium. It slows down fast neutrons without absorbing them, which is why it is used as a moderator.

questions.q: Vinegar, which is used as a food preservative, is a dilute aqueous solution of
questions.exp: Table vinegar contains about 5 to 8 per cent acetic acid (ethanoic acid). The acidic medium checks the growth of spoilage micro-organisms, which is why it is used for pickling.

questions.q: Calcium carbide, sometimes misused for the artificial ripening of fruit, reacts with water to produce
questions.exp: Calcium carbide with water gives acetylene (ethyne), which mimics the natural ripening hormone ethylene. Its use on food is banned in India because commercial carbide carries traces of arsenic and phosphorus.

questions.q: Fullerene, an allotrope of carbon shaped like a football, contains
questions.exp: Buckminsterfullerene, C60, has sixty carbon atoms arranged in twenty hexagons and twelve pentagons. Graphene and carbon nanotubes are other modern carbon forms.

questions.q: Graphite can be used as a lubricant as well as an electrode because
opts: its layers slide over one another easily and it has free electrons that conduct electricity
it is the hardest allotrope of carbon
each of its carbon atoms is bonded to four other carbon atoms
it is chemically inert to all acids and alkalis
questions.exp: In graphite each carbon atom is bonded to only three others, leaving one free electron for conduction, and the hexagonal layers are held by weak forces so they slip over each other.

questions.q: The hardest naturally occurring substance known is
questions.exp: Diamond, an allotrope of carbon in which every atom is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid three-dimensional network, tops the Mohs scale at 10.

questions.q: The most electronegative element in the periodic table is
questions.exp: Fluorine is the most electronegative element and also the most reactive non-metal; electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group.

questions.q: An ordinary incandescent electric bulb is filled with
questions.exp: These chemically inert gases prevent the tungsten filament from burning away and reduce its evaporation, thereby prolonging the life of the bulb.

questions.q: The ozone layer in the stratosphere is important because it
opts: absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation from the sun
absorbs infrared radiation emitted by the earth
supplies oxygen to the upper atmosphere
reflects radio waves back to the earth
questions.exp: Ozone (O3) shields living organisms from ultraviolet-B radiation. Chlorofluorocarbons deplete it, and the Montreal Protocol of 1987 was adopted to phase out ozone-depleting substances.

questions.q: Which one of the following gases is commonly used in fire extinguishers?
questions.exp: Carbon dioxide is heavier than air and does not support combustion, so it blankets the fire and cuts off oxygen; it also leaves no residue on electrical equipment.

questions.q: Which one of the following is a synthetic, non-cellulosic fibre?
questions.exp: Nylon is a synthetic polyamide made wholly from petrochemicals. Cotton and jute are natural cellulosic fibres, while rayon is regenerated cellulose and is therefore cellulosic.

questions.q: Brass utensils are coated with a thin layer of which metal, a process traditionally called kalai, to prevent contamination of food by copper?
questions.exp: Tinning gives a chemically inert lining so that acidic food does not react with the copper of the brass. Brass itself is an alloy of copper and zinc.

questions.q: An amalgam is an alloy in which one of the constituents is always
questions.exp: Any alloy of a metal with mercury is called an amalgam; dental amalgam, for example, contains mercury with silver and tin.

questions.q: Stainless steel is an alloy of iron with
questions.exp: Typical stainless steel contains about 18 per cent chromium and 8 per cent nickel besides iron and a little carbon; the chromium forms a protective oxide film that resists rusting.

questions.q: German silver, widely used for utensils and ornamental ware, is an alloy of
questions.exp: German silver contains no silver at all; it owes its silvery appearance to nickel. It is also called nickel silver.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Alloy)   List-II (Chief constituents)
A. Brass   1. Copper and tin
B. Bronze   2. Lead and tin
C. Solder   3. Copper and zinc
D. Duralumin   4. Aluminium, copper, magnesium and manganese
questions.exp: Bronze is the copper-tin alloy of the Bronze Age; duralumin, being light and strong, is used in aircraft bodies.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of an alloy and its constituents is NOT correctly matched?
opts: German silver — Copper, silver and nickel
questions.exp: German silver is an alloy of copper, zinc and nickel and contains no silver whatsoever.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Ore)   List-II (Metal obtained)
A. Bauxite   1. Aluminium
B. Cinnabar   2. Mercury
C. Galena   3. Lead
D. Zinc blende   4. Zinc
questions.exp: Cinnabar is mercuric sulphide, galena is lead sulphide and zinc blende is zinc sulphide; haematite and magnetite are the chief ores of iron.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at ordinary room temperature.
II. Bromine is the only non-metal that is liquid at ordinary room temperature.
III. Sodium is stored under water to prevent it from being oxidised.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Sodium and potassium are stored under KEROSENE, because they react violently with water and even with moist air. Statements I and II are correct.

questions.q: Rust formed on iron articles is chemically
questions.exp: Rust is Fe2O3.xH2O and its formation requires BOTH oxygen and moisture; that is why iron does not rust in dry air or in air-free water.

questions.q: Galvanisation is the process of coating iron or steel with a thin layer of
questions.exp: Zinc protects iron even when the coating is scratched, because zinc is more reactive and corrodes in preference to iron, a form of sacrificial protection.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the rusting of iron is NOT correct?
opts: Rust is chemically hydrated ferric oxide
Rusting of iron requires both oxygen and moisture
Galvanisation is the coating of iron with a layer of zinc
Rusting is a physical change that can be reversed simply by heating the article
questions.exp: Rusting is a chemical change, an oxidation reaction, and cannot be reversed by heating; the metal is actually consumed.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Stainless steel does not rust in moist air.
Reason (R): The chromium present in stainless steel forms a thin, adherent oxide film that protects the metal underneath.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.exp: The chromium oxide layer is self-repairing, so even a scratched surface re-passivates. This is why stainless steel cutlery and surgical instruments resist corrosion.

questions.q: Which one of the following is used in mobile phones, laptops and electric vehicles as a rechargeable source of electricity?
questions.exp: Lithium-ion cells offer high energy density and are rechargeable. Lead-acid batteries are used in vehicles for starting, and a fuel cell converts hydrogen and oxygen directly into electricity, giving only water as a by-product.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The pH of a neutral solution at 25 degrees Celsius is 7.
II. Tooth decay begins when the pH of the mouth falls below about 5.5.
III. An acidic solution has a pH greater than 7.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: An acidic solution has pH LESS than 7. Toothpastes are mildly basic in order to neutralise the acid produced by bacteria in the mouth.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Acid)   List-II (Natural source)
A. Formic acid   1. Sting of an ant
B. Lactic acid   2. Tamarind
C. Citric acid   3. Curd
D. Tartaric acid   4. Lemon
questions.exp: Oxalic acid occurs in tomato and spinach, malic acid in apples and hydrochloric acid in the gastric juice of the stomach.

questions.q:
Arrange the following in increasing order of their pH value:
I. Milk of magnesia
II. Gastric juice
III. Sodium hydroxide solution
IV. Pure water
questions.exp: Gastric juice is strongly acidic (pH about 1.2 to 3), pure water is neutral at 7, milk of magnesia is a weak base at about 10 and sodium hydroxide solution is strongly basic at about 14.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Common name)   List-II (Chemical name)
A. Quicklime   1. Calcium oxide
B. Slaked lime   2. Calcium hydroxide
C. Marble   3. Calcium carbonate
D. Plaster of Paris   4. Calcium sulphate hemihydrate
questions.exp: Quicklime slaked with water gives slaked lime, and a solution of slaked lime is limewater, which turns milky with carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a common name and the substance it denotes is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Hypo is sodium thiosulphate (Na2S2O3.5H2O), used as a fixer in photography and for removing chlorine from bleached fabric.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Common name)   List-II (Chemical formula)
A. Glauber's salt   1. Na2CO3.10H2O
B. Washing soda   2. CuSO4.5H2O
C. Blue vitriol   3. MgSO4.7H2O
D. Epsom salt   4. Na2SO4.10H2O
questions.exp: Green vitriol is FeSO4.7H2O and white vitriol is ZnSO4.7H2O, while oil of vitriol is concentrated sulphuric acid. Hypo, the photographic fixer, is sodium thiosulphate.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
II. The modern periodic law states that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic number.
III. The elements of group 17 of the periodic table are called alkali metals.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: Group 17 elements are the HALOGENS; group 1 elements are the alkali metals. Mendeleev's original table was based on atomic mass, which Moseley replaced with atomic number.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the allotropes of carbon:
I. Diamond and graphite are both allotropes of carbon.
II. Graphite conducts electricity whereas diamond does not.
III. In diamond each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three other carbon atoms.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: In DIAMOND each carbon atom is bonded to FOUR others in a rigid tetrahedral network, leaving no free electron; in graphite each atom is bonded to three, leaving one free electron for conduction.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Industrial process)   List-II (Catalyst used)
A. Haber process for ammonia   1. Finely divided iron
B. Contact process for sulphuric acid   2. Vanadium pentoxide
C. Hydrogenation of vegetable oil   3. Nickel
D. Ostwald process for nitric acid   4. Platinum
questions.exp: The hydrogenation of vegetable oil over nickel converts liquid oils into solid vanaspati and is a classic example of catalysis in the food industry.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Hydrogen is the lightest element known.
II. Nitrogen makes up about 78 per cent of the atmosphere by volume.
III. Liquid nitrogen is used as a refrigerant for preserving biological material.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. Liquid nitrogen boils at about minus 196 degrees Celsius and is used for cryopreservation of semen, blood and tissues.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The main constituent of compressed natural gas (CNG) is methane.
II. Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) is mainly a mixture of butane and propane.
III. Ethyl mercaptan is added to LPG so that a leak can be detected by its smell.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. LPG and CNG are both odourless in their pure state, so a strong-smelling mercaptan is deliberately added as a safety measure.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a fuel gas and its chief constituents is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Producer gas — Carbon monoxide and nitrogen
Water gas — Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide
Coal gas — Hydrogen, methane and carbon monoxide
questions.exp: Water gas is a mixture of carbon monoxide and HYDROGEN, obtained by passing steam over red-hot coke; it is also called synthesis gas.

questions.q: Among the following fuels, the highest calorific value belongs to
questions.exp: Hydrogen has a calorific value of about 150 kilojoule per gram, far higher than any other fuel, and it burns to give only water; storage and transport, however, remain difficult.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT a thermoplastic?
questions.exp: Bakelite, made from phenol and formaldehyde, is a thermosetting plastic: once moulded it cannot be softened and reshaped by heating. Melamine is another thermosetting plastic.

questions.q: Vulcanisation, which makes natural rubber harder and more elastic, involves heating it with
questions.exp: Charles Goodyear's process forms sulphur cross-links between the polymer chains, so vulcanised rubber resists heat, wear and organic solvents; it is used for vehicle tyres.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids.
II. Soaps do not form a good lather with hard water.
III. Synthetic detergents work effectively even in hard water.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. Hard water contains calcium and magnesium ions that form an insoluble scum with soap, whereas the calcium and magnesium salts of detergents remain soluble.

questions.q: A small quantity of gypsum is added to cement in order to
opts: slow down the rate of setting
questions.exp: Without gypsum, Portland cement would set almost immediately on mixing with water, leaving no time for placing and finishing the concrete.

questions.q: The chief constituent of ordinary glass is
questions.exp: Soda-lime glass is made by fusing silica (sand) with sodium carbonate and calcium carbonate. Borosilicate or Pyrex glass, which contains boron oxide, withstands sudden temperature changes.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Urea has the highest nitrogen content among solid nitrogenous fertilisers, about 46 per cent.
II. Muriate of potash is chemically potassium chloride.
III. Di-ammonium phosphate supplies both nitrogen and phosphorus to the soil.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. Excessive use of nitrogenous fertiliser causes nitrate leaching into groundwater and eutrophication of surface water bodies.

questions.q: Gunpowder is a mixture of
questions.exp: In gunpowder the potassium nitrate acts as the oxidiser while charcoal and sulphur are the fuel. Dynamite, invented by Alfred Nobel, is nitroglycerine absorbed in kieselguhr.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Argemone seed oil is a common adulterant of mustard oil.
II. Metanil yellow is used to adulterate turmeric powder and pulses.
III. Sodium benzoate is used as a chemical preservative in food.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: All three are correct. Adulteration of mustard oil with argemone oil causes epidemic dropsy, and metanil yellow is a non-permitted coal-tar dye.

questions.q: Morphine, obtained from opium, is classified as
questions.exp: Morphine relieves severe pain by acting on the central nervous system and is habit forming, so it is regulated as a narcotic. Aspirin and paracetamol are non-narcotic analgesics.

questions.q: The antibiotic penicillin was discovered by
questions.exp: Fleming observed in 1928 that the mould Penicillium notatum inhibited bacterial growth; he shared the 1945 Nobel Prize with Florey and Chain, who purified the drug.

questions.q: The essential difference between an antiseptic and a disinfectant is that
opts: an antiseptic kills bacteria while a disinfectant only checks their growth
an antiseptic is a natural product while a disinfectant is synthetic
an antiseptic is applied to living tissue while a disinfectant is used on non-living objects
an antiseptic is taken orally while a disinfectant is applied externally
questions.exp: Dettol and tincture of iodine are antiseptics for wounds and skin; phenol and chlorine compounds are disinfectants for floors, drains and instruments. Dilute phenol acts as an antiseptic while concentrated phenol is a disinfectant.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a drug and its category is NOT correctly matched?
questions.exp: Aspirin is an analgesic and antipyretic, not an antibiotic; it is also used in low doses as a blood thinner.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:
List-I (Radioisotope)   List-II (Use)
A. Carbon-14   1. Detection of thyroid disorders
B. Cobalt-60   2. Determining the age of fossils
C. Iodine-131   3. Treatment of cancer
D. Sodium-24   4. Detection of leaks in underground pipelines
questions.exp: Carbon-14, with a half-life of about 5730 years, is used for radiocarbon dating; phosphorus-32 is used as a tracer in agricultural research.

questions.q: Which one of the following substances sublimes, that is, changes directly from the solid to the vapour state?
questions.exp: Camphor, naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride and dry ice all sublime. Sublimation is used to separate such solids from non-volatile impurities.

chapters.title: Biology: Cell, Tissues and the Human Body
factsheet: Cell theory: M.J. Schleiden (1838, plants) and Theodor Schwann (1839, animals); 'Omnis cellula e cellula' added by Rudolf Virchow (1855).
Robert Hooke coined the term 'cell' in 1665 from cork; Anton van Leeuwenhoek first saw living cells; Robert Brown discovered the nucleus (1831).
Mitochondrion - 'powerhouse of the cell'; double membrane, inner membrane folded into cristae; own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes; Krebs cycle + oxidative phosphorylation.
Ribosome - site of protein synthesis; 70S in prokaryotes (50S + 30S), 80S in eukaryotes (60S + 40S); mitochondria and chloroplasts carry 70S.
Lysosome - 'suicide bag' (Christian de Duve); hydrolytic enzymes at acidic pH. Golgi apparatus (Camillo Golgi) - packaging, secretion, lysosome formation.
Plastids: chloroplast (photosynthesis, grana + stroma), chromoplast (colour), leucoplast (storage). Chlorophyll contains magnesium; haemoglobin contains iron.
Plant cell exclusive: cellulose cell wall, large central vacuole, plastids. Animal cell exclusive: centriole/centrosome (absent in higher plants), prominent lysosomes.
Mitosis - equational, somatic, 2 identical diploid cells. Meiosis - reductional, gamete-forming, 4 haploid cells; crossing over occurs in pachytene of prophase-I.
Energy value: carbohydrate 4 kcal/g, protein 4 kcal/g, fat 9 kcal/g. Enzymes are proteins (except ribozymes) and lower activation energy.
DNA double helix - Watson and Crick, 1953; A=T two hydrogen bonds, G(triple bond)C three; RNA has uracil in place of thymine and ribose sugar.
Five-kingdom classification - R.H. Whittaker, 1969 (Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia); binomial nomenclature - Carolus Linnaeus (genus + species).
Photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2; light reaction in grana/thylakoid, Calvin (dark) reaction in stroma; evolved O2 comes from photolysis of water.
Plant hormones: auxin - apical dominance; gibberellin - stem elongation/bolting; cytokinin - cell division; abscisic acid - 'stress hormone', stomatal closure; ethylene - gaseous, fruit ripening.

Digestion: ptyalin (salivary amylase) on starch; pepsin + HCl in stomach; rennin in infants; bile from liver has no enzyme but emulsifies fat; trypsin, amylase and lipase from pancreas; maximum absorption in small intestine (villi).
Liver - largest gland (about 1.5 kg); makes bile and urea, stores glycogen. Pancreas is a mixed (heterocrine) gland. Appendix is a vestigial organ.
Respiration: 12 pairs of ribs; diaphragm + intercostal muscles; tidal volume about 500 ml; O2 carried as oxyhaemoglobin, most CO2 as bicarbonate in plasma.

Heart: 4 chambers, cardiac muscle; SA node in right atrium is the pacemaker; 'lub' = closure of atrioventricular valves, 'dub' = closure of semilunar valves; normal BP 120/80 mm Hg; resting rate about 72/min.
William Harvey described the circulation of blood. Blood pressure is measured by sphygmomanometer; ECG records electrical activity of the heart.

Blood: plasma about 55%; RBC 4.5-5.5 million/microlitre, anucleate in mammals, lifespan 120 days, formed in red bone marrow, destroyed in spleen ('graveyard of RBCs'); platelets 1.5-4.5 lakh/microlitre.
Blood groups discovered by Karl Landsteiner (1901; Nobel 1930). O = universal donor, AB = universal recipient; AB plasma has no anti-A/anti-B antibody, O plasma has both.

Rh factor - named after the Rhesus monkey (Landsteiner and Wiener, 1940). Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive foetus risks erythroblastosis foetalis, usually from the second pregnancy; prevented by anti-D immunoglobulin.

Excretion: nephron is the structural and functional unit (about 10 lakh per kidney); Bowman's capsule + glomerulus = Malpighian corpuscle; humans are ureotelic; urea is made in the liver (ornithine cycle); ADH (vasopressin) controls water reabsorption.

Nervous system: neuron is the longest cell; adult brain about 1300-1400 g; cerebrum largest (intelligence, memory, will); cerebellum - balance and coordination; medulla oblongata - heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure; hypothalamus - temperature, hunger, thirst.
Humans have 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves; reflex action is mediated by the spinal cord through a reflex arc.

Endocrine: pituitary is the 'master gland'; GH deficiency - dwarfism, excess in childhood - gigantism, in adults - acromegaly; thyroxine needs iodine (goitre, cretinism, myxoedema); parathormone regulates calcium; calcitonin is from the thyroid.

Adrenal cortex - cortisol and aldosterone (deficiency: Addison's disease); adrenal medulla - adrenaline, the 'emergency/fight-or-flight hormone'; islets of Langerhans - insulin (beta cells), glucagon (alpha cells); ADH deficiency causes diabetes insipidus.
Skeleton: 206 bones in an adult (about 300 at birth); femur is the longest bone, stapes of the middle ear the smallest; skull 22 bones; gluteus maximus is the largest muscle, stapedius the smallest.
Muscle types: skeletal (striated, voluntary), smooth (unstriated, involuntary), cardiac (striated, involuntary, non-fatiguing).

Eye: rods contain rhodopsin and work in dim light, cones give colour vision; yellow spot (fovea) has maximum visual acuity; blind spot has no photoreceptors. Ear ossicles - malleus, incus, stapes; cochlea for hearing, semicircular canals for balance.

Human evolution: Australopithecus -> Homo habilis ('handy man', first tool maker) -> Homo erectus -> Homo neanderthalensis -> Homo sapiens; humans have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs), XX female and XY male.

questions.q: The term 'cell' was coined by which scientist?
questions.exp: Robert Hooke coined the word 'cell' in 1665 after observing thin slices of cork under his microscope. Robert Brown discovered the nucleus in 1831.

questions.q: The dictum 'Omnis cellula e cellula' (every cell arises from a pre-existing cell) was given by
questions.exp: Rudolf Virchow (1855) extended the cell theory of Schleiden and Schwann by establishing that new cells arise only from pre-existing cells.

questions.q: Which cell organelle is known as the 'powerhouse of the cell'?
questions.exp: The mitochondrion generates ATP through the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. It has a double membrane, an inner membrane folded into cristae, and its own circular DNA.

questions.q: Which of the following cell organelles is called the 'suicide bag' of the cell?
questions.exp: Lysosomes, discovered by Christian de Duve, contain hydrolytic enzymes that can digest the cell itself; hence the name suicide bag.

questions.q: Ribosomes found in prokaryotic cells are of which type?
questions.exp: Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes (50S + 30S subunits). Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, but mitochondria and chloroplasts also carry 70S ribosomes.

questions.q: Cellulose is the chief structural constituent of which of the following?
questions.exp: The plant cell wall is made chiefly of cellulose. Fungal cell walls contain chitin and bacterial cell walls contain peptidoglycan.

questions.q: Meiosis in a diploid cell results in the formation of
questions.exp: Meiosis is a reduction division producing four haploid daughter cells from one diploid cell; it is the basis of gamete formation.

questions.q: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes takes place during which sub-stage of meiosis?
questions.exp: Crossing over occurs at the pachytene stage of prophase-I, mediated by the enzyme recombinase; chiasmata become visible later at diplotene.

questions.q: The approximate energy value of one gram of fat is
questions.exp: Fat yields about 9 kcal per gram, more than double that of carbohydrate or protein (about 4 kcal/g each); alcohol yields about 7 kcal/g.

questions.q: Which nitrogenous base is present in RNA but absent in DNA?
questions.exp: RNA contains uracil in place of the thymine of DNA, and its sugar is ribose instead of deoxyribose.

questions.q: How many hydrogen bonds are present between guanine and cytosine in a DNA double helix?
questions.exp: Guanine pairs with cytosine through three hydrogen bonds, while adenine pairs with thymine through two; this is why G-C rich DNA has a higher melting temperature.

questions.q: The five-kingdom system of classification of living organisms was proposed by
questions.exp: R.H. Whittaker (1969) proposed the five kingdoms - Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia - using cell structure, body organisation, nutrition and reproduction as criteria.

questions.q: In the system of binomial nomenclature, the first word of a scientific name denotes the
questions.exp: In binomial nomenclature, given by Carolus Linnaeus, the first word is the genus (capitalised) and the second the species (in lower case); the name is italicised.

questions.q: The oxygen released during photosynthesis in green plants comes from
questions.exp: Oxygen is released by the photolysis (splitting) of water during the light reaction, as proved by experiments using heavy-oxygen labelled water.

questions.q: The dark reaction (Calvin cycle) of photosynthesis takes place in which part of the chloroplast?
questions.exp: The light reaction occurs on the thylakoid membranes of the grana, while the Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma, the fluid matrix of the chloroplast.

questions.q: Which plant hormone is chiefly responsible for the ripening of fruits?
questions.exp: Ethylene is the only gaseous plant hormone; it hastens fruit ripening and senescence. Auxin causes apical dominance and gibberellin causes stem elongation.

questions.q: Which enzyme present in human saliva begins the digestion of starch?
questions.exp: Ptyalin, or salivary amylase, converts starch into maltose in the mouth. Pepsin acts on protein in the stomach and trypsin is a pancreatic protease.

questions.q: Bile secreted by the liver is stored in which organ?
questions.exp: Bile is produced in the liver and stored and concentrated in the gall bladder. Bile contains no digestive enzyme; it emulsifies fat and makes the medium alkaline.

questions.q: The pacemaker of the human heart, the sino-atrial node, is located in the
questions.exp: The sino-atrial (SA) node lies in the wall of the right atrium and initiates each heartbeat; the atrio-ventricular node lies in the inter-atrial septum.

questions.q: The circulation of blood in the human body was first described by
questions.exp: William Harvey described the circulation of blood in 1628. Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO blood groups in 1901.

questions.q: Which blood group is known as the universal donor?
questions.exp: Group O red cells carry neither A nor B antigen, so they are not agglutinated by the recipient's anti-A or anti-B antibodies; O-negative is the true universal donor. Group AB is the universal recipient.

questions.q: The Rh factor present in human blood derives its name from
questions.exp: Karl Landsteiner and A.S. Wiener identified the antigen in 1940 in the Rhesus monkey (Macaca mulatta), hence 'Rh' factor. About 93-95 per cent of Indians are Rh-positive.

questions.q: The average lifespan of a human red blood corpuscle is about
questions.exp: A human RBC survives about 120 days; it is produced in the red bone marrow and destroyed mainly in the spleen, which is therefore called the graveyard of RBCs.

questions.q: The structural and functional unit of the human kidney is the
questions.exp: Each human kidney contains roughly one million nephrons. The Bowman's capsule together with the glomerulus forms the Malpighian corpuscle.

questions.q: In the human body, urea is chiefly synthesised in the
questions.exp: Urea is formed in the liver by the ornithine (urea) cycle from ammonia and carbon dioxide, and is then excreted by the kidneys; humans are therefore ureotelic.

questions.q: Which endocrine gland is called the 'master gland' of the human body?
questions.exp: The pituitary (hypophysis), lying in the sella turcica at the base of the brain, secretes trophic hormones that regulate other endocrine glands; it is itself controlled by the hypothalamus.

questions.q: Insulin is secreted by which cells of the human pancreas?
opts: Alpha cells of the islets of Langerhans
Beta cells of the islets of Langerhans
Delta cells of the islets of Langerhans
questions.exp: Beta cells of the islets of Langerhans secrete insulin, which lowers blood glucose; alpha cells secrete glucagon, which raises it. Insulin deficiency causes diabetes mellitus.

questions.q: The number of bones in the body of a normal adult human being is
questions.exp: An adult human has 206 bones; a newborn has about 300, many of which fuse during growth. The axial skeleton has 80 bones and the appendicular 126.

questions.q: Which is the smallest bone in the human body?
questions.exp: The stapes (stirrup) of the middle ear is the smallest human bone; the femur (thigh bone) is the longest.

questions.q: Vision in dim light in the human eye is due to which photoreceptors?
questions.exp: Rod cells contain the pigment rhodopsin (visual purple) and are responsible for scotopic or dim-light vision; cones contain iodopsin and give colour vision.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the mitochondrion:
I. It is bounded by a double membrane whose inner membrane is folded into cristae.
II. It possesses its own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes.
III. The Calvin cycle of photosynthesis takes place in it.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.exp: The Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma of the chloroplast, not in the mitochondrion. The semi-autonomous nature of mitochondria (own DNA, 70S ribosomes) supports the endosymbiotic theory.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the human heart:
I. It is a four-chambered organ made of cardiac muscle.
II. The sino-atrial node is situated in the left atrium.
