questions.exp: Put B at the origin: A is at (0, 3) and C at (4, 0). The distance is sqrt(4^2 + 3^2) = 5 km. Since A is B's father and B is C's father, C is A's grandson.

questions.q: P's house is 8 km West of Q's house, and R's house is 6 km North of Q's house. P is the brother of Q and Q is the mother of R. What is the shortest distance between P's house and R's house, and how is P related to R?
questions.exp: With Q at the origin, P is at (-8, 0) and R at (0, 6); the distance is sqrt(64 + 36) = 10 km. P is the brother of R's mother, i.e. R's maternal uncle.

questions.q: Starting from her home, Z walks 5 km North to reach the home of X, who is her father, and then 5 km East to reach a temple. Y, the wife of X, is Z's ____ and the temple lies in which direction from Z's home?
questions.exp: X is Z's father and Y is X's wife, so Y is Z's mother. Taking Z's home as origin, the temple is at (5, 5), which is North-East of her home.

questions.q: A man walks 12 km North, turns right and walks 9 km, turns right and walks 12 km, and turns right again and walks 15 km. How far and in which direction is he from the starting point?
questions.exp: N12 -> (0,12), E9 -> (9,12), S12 -> (9,0), W15 -> (-6,0). He is 6 km due West of the starting point.

questions.q: From a point, a man walks 5 km South, 5 km East, 5 km North and 5 km East. What is his distance and direction from the starting point?
questions.exp: The 5 km South and 5 km North cancel each other; the two eastward legs add to 10 km. He is 10 km due East of the start.

chapters.title: Ranking, Seating Arrangement and Logical Venn Diagrams
factsheet: RANKING: rank from the bottom = (total) - (rank from the top) + 1. The +1 is because the person is counted at both ends.
When both ranks are of the SAME person, total = (rank from one end) + (rank from the other end) - 1.
When the two ranks are of DIFFERENT persons and they do not overlap, number between them = total - (rank of first from left) - (rank of second from right).
Shifting: if a person moves k places to the right, the new position from the left = old position + k; from the right it decreases by k.
After two persons interchange seats, each takes over the other's old position - convert the new rank into the old person's rank first.
COMPARISON PUZZLES: write one single inequality chain (A > B > C ...) instead of separate pairs; the tallest is at one end, the shortest at the other.
LINEAR ROW FACING NORTH: the persons' right is towards your right as you read the row; left is towards your left.
LINEAR ROW FACING SOUTH: everything reverses - the persons' right is towards your LEFT. Write the row once and mentally flip it.
'X sits third to the left of Y' means exactly two persons sit between them; 'n persons sit between X and Y' means the gap is n+1 seats.
Start a row puzzle from the clue that fixes an END seat or the exact MIDDLE seat; those clues have the fewest possibilities.
Use a fixed number of blank dashes equal to the number of seats and slide the largest block of clues along it.
DOUBLE ROW: row 1 facing North and row 2 facing South sit opposite each other, so the two rows' left-right senses are mirror images.
In a double row, if X faces Y then the person to X's right faces the person to Y's left.
CIRCULAR TABLE, ALL FACING THE CENTRE: the neighbour in the clockwise direction is on a person's LEFT and the anti-clockwise neighbour is on the RIGHT.
CIRCULAR TABLE, ALL FACING OUTWARD: exactly the reverse - clockwise is the RIGHT and anti-clockwise is the LEFT.
Fix one person's seat as the reference point and place everyone else relative to it; a circle has no absolute position, only relative order.
In a circle of n persons the seat exactly opposite is n/2 seats away (defined only for even n).
Number of persons between X and Y counted clockwise = (clockwise gap) - 1; counted the other way it is n - (clockwise gap) - 1.
SQUARE TABLE, one person per corner facing the centre: 'diagonally opposite' means two corners away, which is also 'second to the left' and 'second to the right'.
FLOOR PUZZLES: always draw floor 1 at the bottom and the top floor at the top; 'above' means a larger floor number.
'Only k persons live between X and Y' fixes the gap but not which of the two is higher - test both cases before rejecting.
DAY / MONTH PUZZLES: treat the days or months as numbered slots 1 to n and convert every 'before/after' clue into a difference of slot numbers.
Always verify a finished arrangement by reading every clue once more; a puzzle with a valid but second solution means a clue was mis-read.
LOGICAL VENN: if every A is a B, draw A wholly inside B. If some A are B, draw two partly overlapping circles. If no A is a B, draw two separate circles.

Three fully nested circles (e.g. Jaipur - Rajasthan - India) is the standard 'nested' pattern; two separate circles inside a bigger one (Table - Chair - Furniture) is the standard 'co-ordinate' pattern.
TWO-SET FORMULA: n(A or B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A and B); those in neither = Total - n(A or B).
THREE-SET FORMULA: n(A or B or C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A and B) - n(B and C) - n(A and C) + n(A and B and C).
Exactly one of three = sum of singles - 2(sum of pairwise) + 3(all three). Exactly two of three = sum of pairwise - 3(all three).
In set questions the pairwise figures normally INCLUDE the people who take all three, unless the paper says 'only'.

questions.q: In a class of 40 students, Ravi's rank from the top is 12th. What is his rank from the bottom?
questions.exp: Rank from the bottom = total - rank from the top + 1 = 40 - 12 + 1 = 29th. Remember that the person himself is counted once from each end, hence the +1.

questions.q: In a queue, Meena is 10th from the front and 15th from the back. How many persons are there in the queue?
questions.exp: When both ranks are of the same person, total = (rank from front) + (rank from back) - 1 = 10 + 15 - 1 = 24. Meena is counted twice, so one is subtracted.

questions.q: In a row of 40 boys, Suresh is 12th from the left end and Rakesh is 18th from the right end. How many boys sit between Suresh and Rakesh?
questions.exp: Rakesh's position from the left = 40 - 18 + 1 = 23rd. Suresh is 12th from the left. Boys between them = 23 - 12 - 1 = 10.

questions.q: In a row of 30 children, Aman was shifted 4 places to the right, after which he became 12th from the right end. What was his original position from the left end?
questions.exp: After the shift his position from the left = 30 - 12 + 1 = 19th. He had moved 4 places to the right, so originally he was 19 - 4 = 15th from the left.

questions.q: Rahul is 15th from the top and 20th from the bottom in a class. How many students are there in the class?
questions.exp: Total = 15 + 20 - 1 = 34, subtracting one because Rahul himself is counted in both the counts.

questions.q: In a row of children, Nita is 7th from the left end and Radha is 9th from the right end. When they interchange their places, Nita becomes 11th from the left end. How many children are there in the row?
questions.exp: After the exchange Nita occupies Radha's original seat, which is 11th from the left and 9th from the right. Total = 11 + 9 - 1 = 19.

questions.q: In a class of 45 students, Kamal's rank is 12th from the top. Naveen's rank is 6 ranks below Kamal's. What is Naveen's rank from the bottom?
questions.exp: Naveen's rank from the top = 12 + 6 = 18th. His rank from the bottom = 45 - 18 + 1 = 28th.

questions.q: In a row of 21 girls, when Seema was shifted two places towards the left she became 8th from the left end. What was her earlier position from the right end?
questions.exp: Her new position is 8th from the left, so her earlier position was 8 + 2 = 10th from the left. From the right end that is 21 - 10 + 1 = 12th.

questions.q: Among five friends A, B, C, D and E: A is taller than B but shorter than C; D is taller than C; E is shorter than B. Who is the tallest of them all?
questions.exp: The conditions give E < B < A < C < D, a single consistent order. D, being above C who is above everyone else, is the tallest.

questions.q: Five boxes P, Q, R, S and T have different weights. P is heavier than S, R is heavier than P, Q is heavier than R and T is lighter than S. Which box is the third heaviest?
questions.exp: The order from lightest to heaviest is T < S < P < R < Q. Counting from the heaviest: Q (1st), R (2nd), P (3rd). So P is the third heaviest.

questions.q:
Seven friends A, B, C, D, E, F and G are sitting in a straight row facing North. The following information is known about their seating:
D sits third to the right of A.
E sits second to the left of G.
C and E sit next to each other.
F sits second to the right of B.
Who is sitting at the extreme right end of the row?
questions.exp: Working through the clues fixes exactly one arrangement, from left to right: C, E, A, G, B, D, F. The person at the extreme right end is therefore F.

questions.q:
Seven friends A, B, C, D, E, F and G are sitting in a straight row facing North. The following information is known about their seating:
D sits third to the right of A.
E sits second to the left of G.
C and E sit next to each other.
F sits second to the right of B.
Who sits third to the left of B?
questions.exp: The unique arrangement from left to right is C, E, A, G, B, D, F. B occupies the fifth seat, so the third seat to his left is the second seat, occupied by E.

questions.q:
Six persons P, Q, R, S, T and U sit in a straight row facing South. (For a person facing South, the printed row runs from that person's right to that person's left.) The following facts are known:
U sits immediately to the right of P.
S sits third to the left of Q.
R is not an immediate neighbour of T.
R sits at the extreme left end of the row.
Who sits at the extreme right end of the row?
questions.exp: Since all face South, the person's right corresponds to the printed left. The clues yield one arrangement, printed left to right: T, Q, U, P, S, R. Hence the extreme right end (of the persons) is occupied by T.

questions.q:
Six persons P, Q, R, S, T and U sit in a straight row facing South. (For a person facing South, the printed row runs from that person's right to that person's left.) The following facts are known:
U sits immediately to the right of P.
S sits third to the left of Q.
R is not an immediate neighbour of T.
R sits at the extreme left end of the row.
How many persons sit between S and Q?
questions.exp: The unique arrangement, printed left to right, is T, Q, U, P, S, R. S and Q occupy the 5th and 2nd printed seats, so exactly two persons sit between them.

questions.q:
Eight students A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H are seated in a straight row facing North. It is known that:
C sits third to the right of H.
G is not an immediate neighbour of E.
H is not an immediate neighbour of F.
Only one person sits between G and H.
D sits at the extreme left end of the row.
C is not an immediate neighbour of G.
Two persons sit between B and F.
G sits third to the left of A.
Who is sitting exactly between H and F?
questions.exp: The clues admit only one seating, from left to right: D, G, B, H, A, F, C, E. H is in seat 4 and F in seat 6, so the student between them is the one in seat 5, namely A.

questions.q:
Eight students A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H are seated in a straight row facing North. It is known that:
C sits third to the right of H.
G is not an immediate neighbour of E.
H is not an immediate neighbour of F.
Only one person sits between G and H.
D sits at the extreme left end of the row.
C is not an immediate neighbour of G.
Two persons sit between B and F.
G sits third to the left of A.
Which of the following pairs occupies the two extreme ends of the row?
questions.exp: The unique arrangement from left to right is D, G, B, H, A, F, C, E, so the two ends are held by D and E.

questions.q:
Five persons V, W, X, Y and Z sit in a row facing North, and the following is known:
W sits second to the right of V.
X and Z sit next to each other.
Only one person sits between X and V.
Who sits exactly in the middle of the row?
questions.exp: Only one arrangement satisfies every clue, from left to right: X, Z, V, Y, W. The middle (third) seat is occupied by V.

questions.q:
Five persons V, W, X, Y and Z sit in a row facing North, and the following is known:
W sits second to the right of V.
X and Z sit next to each other.
Only one person sits between X and V.
Who sits immediately to the right of Y?
questions.exp: The unique order from left to right is X, Z, V, Y, W. As everybody faces North, the right of a person is the next seat towards the printed right, so the person immediately to Y's right is W.

questions.q:
Ten persons are seated in two parallel rows of five each. A, B, C, D and E sit in the first row facing North, while P, Q, R, S and T sit in the second row facing South, and each member of the first row faces exactly one member of the second row. The following is known:
A sits immediately to the right of C.
Three persons sit between C and D.
Only one person sits between A and B.
Only one person sits between T and R.
C faces S.
R sits third to the left of Q.
Who faces B?
questions.exp: The clues admit only one seating. First row (left to right): C, A, E, B, D; second row (left to right): S, Q, T, P, R. B is the fourth from the printed left in row 1, so the person facing him is the fourth from the printed left in row 2, i.e. P.

questions.q:
Ten persons are seated in two parallel rows of five each. A, B, C, D and E sit in the first row facing North, while P, Q, R, S and T sit in the second row facing South, and each member of the first row faces exactly one member of the second row. The following is known:
A sits immediately to the right of C.
Three persons sit between C and D.
Only one person sits between A and B.
Only one person sits between T and R.
C faces S.
R sits third to the left of Q.
Who sits at the extreme right end of the second row?
questions.exp: The unique seating is: First row (left to right): C, A, E, B, D; second row (left to right): S, Q, T, P, R. The second row faces South, so their right is the printed left; the person at their extreme right end is S.

questions.q:
Ten persons are seated in two parallel rows of five each. A, B, C, D and E sit in the first row facing North, while P, Q, R, S and T sit in the second row facing South, and each member of the first row faces exactly one member of the second row. The following is known:
A sits immediately to the right of C.
Three persons sit between C and D.
Only one person sits between A and B.
Only one person sits between T and R.
C faces S.
R sits third to the left of Q.
How many persons sit between C and D in the first row?
questions.exp: In the unique arrangement the first row reads C, A, E, B, D from left to right. C is first and D is fifth, so three persons sit between them.

questions.q:
Ten persons are seated in two parallel rows of five each. A, B, C, D and E sit in the first row facing North, while P, Q, R, S and T sit in the second row facing South, and each member of the first row faces exactly one member of the second row. The following is known:
A sits immediately to the right of C.
Three persons sit between C and D.
Only one person sits between A and B.
Only one person sits between T and R.
C faces S.
R sits third to the left of Q.
Who sits immediately to the right of Q in the second row?
questions.exp: The second row reads S, Q, T, P, R from the printed left. Since this row faces South, a person's right is towards the printed left, so the person immediately to Q's right is S.

questions.q:
Eight friends P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W are sitting around a circular table facing the centre. The following information is known:
S sits immediately to the right of P.
W sits second to the right of Q.
V sits third to the left of W.
T sits fourth to the left of U.
T sits third to the left of S.
Who sits third to the right of Q?
questions.exp: The clues fix a single seating. Clockwise order: S, P, W, T, Q, V, R, U (and back to S). For a person facing the centre the right side is the anti-clockwise direction, so three seats anti-clockwise from Q brings us to P.

questions.q:
Eight friends P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W are sitting around a circular table facing the centre. The following information is known:
S sits immediately to the right of P.
W sits second to the right of Q.
V sits third to the left of W.
T sits fourth to the left of U.
T sits third to the left of S.
Who is sitting exactly opposite W?
questions.exp: With eight persons evenly placed, the seat opposite any person is four seats away. Clockwise order: S, P, W, T, Q, V, R, U (and back to S). Four seats from W gives R.

questions.q:
Eight friends P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W are sitting around a circular table facing the centre. The following information is known:
S sits immediately to the right of P.
W sits second to the right of Q.
V sits third to the left of W.
T sits fourth to the left of U.
T sits third to the left of S.
How many persons sit between T and V when counted clockwise starting from T?
questions.exp: In the unique seating the clockwise order is S, P, W, T, Q, V, R, U. Moving clockwise from T we pass exactly one person before reaching V.

questions.q:
Six persons A, B, C, D, E and F are seated around a circular table facing the centre. It is known that:
B is not an immediate neighbour of C.
B sits third to the left of A.
C sits second to the right of D.
E sits fourth to the right of F.
Who sits immediately to the left of E?
questions.exp: The clues give exactly one seating. Clockwise order: A, D, F, B, E, C (and back to A). Facing the centre, the left neighbour is the next person clockwise, which is C.

questions.q:
Six persons A, B, C, D, E and F are seated around a circular table facing the centre. It is known that:
B is not an immediate neighbour of C.
B sits third to the left of A.
C sits second to the right of D.
E sits fourth to the right of F.
Who is sitting exactly opposite B?
questions.exp: For six persons round a table the seat opposite any person is three seats away. Clockwise order: A, D, F, B, E, C (and back to A), so the person opposite B is A.

questions.q:
Five persons K, L, M, N and O are sitting around a circular table facing the centre. The following is known:
N sits second to the right of O.
M sits immediately to the right of K.
Who sits second to the left of L?
questions.exp: Only one seating fits. Clockwise order: K, N, L, O, M (and back to K). Facing the centre, moving to a person's left means moving clockwise, so two seats clockwise from L is M.

questions.q:
Five persons K, L, M, N and O are sitting around a circular table facing the centre. The following is known:
N sits second to the right of O.
M sits immediately to the right of K.
Who sits immediately to the right of O?
questions.exp: Clockwise order: K, N, L, O, M (and back to K) is the unique solution. The right of a person facing the centre is the anti-clockwise neighbour, which for O is L.

questions.q:
Six persons P, Q, R, S, T and U are seated around a circular table but all of them are facing outward, away from the centre. (For a person facing outward the clockwise neighbour is on the right and the anti-clockwise neighbour is on the left.) It is known that:
T sits fourth to the left of S.
T sits third to the left of Q.
U sits immediately to the right of R.
Who sits third to the left of R?
questions.exp: The clues give one seating only. Clockwise order: P, T, R, U, Q, S (and back to P). Facing outward, a person's left is the anti-clockwise side, so three seats anti-clockwise from R is S.

questions.q:
Six persons P, Q, R, S, T and U are seated around a circular table but all of them are facing outward, away from the centre. (For a person facing outward the clockwise neighbour is on the right and the anti-clockwise neighbour is on the left.) It is known that:
T sits fourth to the left of S.
T sits third to the left of Q.
U sits immediately to the right of R.
Who sits second to the right of T?
questions.exp: Clockwise order: P, T, R, U, Q, S (and back to P) is the unique arrangement. Facing outward, the right is the clockwise side, so two seats clockwise from T gives U.

questions.q:
Six persons P, Q, R, S, T and U are seated around a circular table but all of them are facing outward, away from the centre. (For a person facing outward the clockwise neighbour is on the right and the anti-clockwise neighbour is on the left.) It is known that:
T sits fourth to the left of S.
T sits third to the left of Q.
U sits immediately to the right of R.
Who is sitting exactly opposite P?
questions.exp: Whether the persons face inward or outward, the seat opposite a person in a circle of six is three seats away. Clockwise order: P, T, R, U, Q, S (and back to P), so U sits opposite P.

questions.q:
Four persons A, B, C and D are sitting at the four corners of a square table, one at each corner, all facing the centre of the table. It is known that:
B sits immediately to the right of D.
B sits third to the right of C.
Which of the following pairs sits diagonally opposite each other?
questions.exp: At a square table the person diagonally opposite is two corners away. Clockwise order: A, C, B, D, so A and B sit diagonally opposite each other (and so do the remaining two).

questions.q:
Four persons A, B, C and D are sitting at the four corners of a square table, one at each corner, all facing the centre of the table. It is known that:
B sits immediately to the right of D.
B sits third to the right of C.
Which of the following gives the correct clockwise order of the four persons?
questions.exp: Applying the clues to the four corners leaves exactly one possibility. Clockwise order: A, C, B, D.

questions.q:
Six persons L, M, N, O, P and Q are seated around a rectangular table, all facing the centre, with two persons on each of the longer sides and one person on each of the shorter sides. Treating the seats as going round the table, the following is known:
O sits third to the right of N.
Q sits immediately to the right of M.
P sits second to the left of O.
Who sits immediately to the right of M?
questions.exp: Going round the table there is only one possible order. Clockwise order: L, P, N, Q, M, O. Facing the centre, a person's right is the anti-clockwise neighbour, so the person immediately to M's right is Q.

questions.q:
Five persons A, B, C, D and E live on five different floors of a building. The lowest floor is numbered 1 and the topmost floor is numbered 5. The following is known:
B and D live on adjacent floors.
E lives two floors above C.
B lives two floors above A.
Who lives on the topmost floor?
questions.exp: The clues leave only one possible allotment: floor 1 - C; floor 2 - A; floor 3 - E; floor 4 - B; floor 5 - D. Hence D lives on floor 5.

questions.q:
Five persons A, B, C, D and E live on five different floors of a building. The lowest floor is numbered 1 and the topmost floor is numbered 5. The following is known:
B and D live on adjacent floors.
E lives two floors above C.
B lives two floors above A.
Who lives on the third floor?
questions.exp: The unique allotment is floor 1 - C; floor 2 - A; floor 3 - E; floor 4 - B; floor 5 - D, so the third floor is occupied by E.

questions.q:
Six persons P, Q, R, S, T and U live on six different floors of a building, the lowest floor being numbered 1 and the topmost floor 6. The following is known:
P lives three floors below S.
Only one person lives between P and Q.
R lives two floors below P.
P lives immediately below T.
How many persons live between P and Q?
questions.exp: The allotment is fixed uniquely as floor 1 - R; floor 2 - U; floor 3 - P; floor 4 - T; floor 5 - Q; floor 6 - S. P is on floor 3 and Q on floor 5, so exactly one person lives between them.

questions.q:
Six persons P, Q, R, S, T and U live on six different floors of a building, the lowest floor being numbered 1 and the topmost floor 6. The following is known:
P lives three floors below S.
Only one person lives between P and Q.
R lives two floors below P.
P lives immediately below T.
Who lives immediately above T?
questions.exp: The unique allotment is floor 1 - R; floor 2 - U; floor 3 - P; floor 4 - T; floor 5 - Q; floor 6 - S. T is on floor 4, so the person immediately above him, on floor 5, is Q.

questions.q:
Seven persons A, B, C, D, E, F and G live on seven different floors of a building. The lowest floor is numbered 1 and the topmost floor is numbered 7. It is known that:
B and G live on adjacent floors.
A lives two floors below C.
Two persons live between G and E.
G lives immediately below D.
F lives two floors below G.
Who lives on floor number 5?
questions.exp: There is exactly one arrangement consistent with the clues: floor 1 - F; floor 2 - B; floor 3 - G; floor 4 - D; floor 5 - A; floor 6 - E; floor 7 - C. Floor 5 is occupied by A.

questions.q:
Seven persons A, B, C, D, E, F and G live on seven different floors of a building. The lowest floor is numbered 1 and the topmost floor is numbered 7. It is known that:
B and G live on adjacent floors.
A lives two floors below C.
Two persons live between G and E.
G lives immediately below D.
F lives two floors below G.
How many persons live above D?
questions.exp: In the unique arrangement floor 1 - F; floor 2 - B; floor 3 - G; floor 4 - D; floor 5 - A; floor 6 - E; floor 7 - C, D lives on floor 4, so three persons live on the floors above him.

questions.q:
Five persons P, Q, R, S and T visit a museum on five different days of the same week, from Monday to Friday, one person per day. It is known that:
R visits the museum two days after P.
T visits the museum two days after S.
Q visits the museum immediately after R.
Who visits the museum on Wednesday?
questions.exp: Only one schedule satisfies all the clues: Monday - S; Tuesday - P; Wednesday - T; Thursday - R; Friday - Q. Wednesday belongs to T.

questions.q:
Five persons P, Q, R, S and T visit a museum on five different days of the same week, from Monday to Friday, one person per day. It is known that:
R visits the museum two days after P.
T visits the museum two days after S.
Q visits the museum immediately after R.
On which day does R visit the museum?
questions.exp: The unique schedule is Monday - S; Tuesday - P; Wednesday - T; Thursday - R; Friday - Q, so R visits on Thursday.

questions.q:
Six candidates A, B, C, D, E and F have their examinations in six different months of the same year - January, February, March, April, May and June - one candidate per month. It is known that:
C has the examination two months before B.
A has the examination three months before E.
A has the examination immediately after D.
In which month does C have the examination?
questions.exp: The clues fix a single schedule: January - D; February - A; March - F; April - C; May - E; June - B. C's examination therefore falls in April.

questions.q:
Six candidates A, B, C, D, E and F have their examinations in six different months of the same year - January, February, March, April, May and June - one candidate per month. It is known that:
C has the examination two months before B.
A has the examination three months before E.
A has the examination immediately after D.
How many candidates have their examination between the examinations of A and E?
questions.exp: The unique schedule is January - D; February - A; March - F; April - C; May - E; June - B. A appears in February and E in May, so two candidates (March and April) fall between them.

questions.q: Which of the following best represents the relationship between the three classes: Doctors, Men and Human beings?
opts: Three circles that do not touch one another
Two intersecting circles for Doctors and Men, both lying wholly inside a larger circle for Human beings
A circle for Men lying inside a circle for Doctors, and that inside a circle for Human beings
A circle for Doctors lying inside a circle for Men, and that inside a circle for Human beings
questions.exp: Some doctors are men and some are women, so Doctors and Men only partly overlap. Both classes are entirely contained in the class of Human beings.

questions.q: Which of the following best represents the relationship between Pigeon, Bird and Dog?
opts: A circle for Pigeon inside a circle for Bird, with a separate circle for Dog outside both
Three separate circles that intersect one another
A circle for Bird inside a circle for Pigeon, with Dog intersecting Bird
A circle for Dog inside a circle for Bird, with Pigeon separate
questions.exp: Every pigeon is a bird, so Pigeon lies wholly within Bird. No dog is a bird and no dog is a pigeon, so Dog is a wholly separate circle.

questions.q: Which of the following best represents the relationship between Jaipur, Rajasthan and India?
opts: Jaipur and Rajasthan intersecting, both inside India
A circle for Jaipur inside a circle for Rajasthan, which in turn lies inside a circle for India
A circle for Rajasthan inside a circle for Jaipur, which in turn lies inside a circle for India
questions.exp: Jaipur is entirely within Rajasthan and Rajasthan is entirely within India, so the three form completely nested circles from smallest to largest.

questions.q: Which of the following best represents the relationship between Table, Chair and Furniture?
opts: Two separate circles for Table and Chair, both lying wholly inside a larger circle for Furniture
Two intersecting circles for Table and Chair, both inside Furniture
A circle for Chair inside a circle for Table, both inside Furniture
questions.exp: No table is a chair, so the two classes are disjoint; but both are kinds of furniture, so both lie completely inside the class Furniture.

questions.q: Which of the following best represents the relationship between Boys, Girls and Students?
opts: A circle for Students inside both Boys and Girls
Three circles all intersecting one another
Two separate circles for Boys and Girls, each of which partly overlaps a third circle for Students
Two separate circles for Boys and Girls, both lying wholly inside Students
questions.exp: No boy is a girl, so those two circles are disjoint. Some boys and some girls are students while others are not, so Students overlaps each of them only partly.

questions.q: In a class of 60 students, 35 play cricket, 25 play hockey and 10 play both games. How many students play neither game?
questions.exp: Students playing at least one game = 35 + 25 - 10 = 50. Therefore those playing neither = 60 - 50 = 10.

questions.q: In a survey of 100 persons, 65 read newspaper A and 45 read newspaper B, while 20 read both. How many persons read at least one of the two newspapers?
questions.exp: By the inclusion-exclusion rule, n(A or B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A and B) = 65 + 45 - 20 = 90.

questions.q: In a group of 80 persons, 50 like tea and 40 like coffee. If every person likes at least one of the two drinks, how many like both?
questions.exp: Since nobody is left out, n(A or B) = 80. Then n(A and B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A or B) = 50 + 40 - 80 = 10.

questions.q: Out of 200 students, 100 study Mathematics, 90 study Physics and 80 study Chemistry. 40 study both Mathematics and Physics, 35 both Physics and Chemistry, 30 both Mathematics and Chemistry, and 20 study all three subjects. How many students study none of these three subjects?
questions.exp: By inclusion-exclusion for three sets: 100 + 90 + 80 - 40 - 35 - 30 + 20 = 185 study at least one subject. Hence 200 - 185 = 15 study none of them.

questions.q: In a survey of 120 households, 60 use brand X, 55 use brand Y and 50 use brand Z. 25 use both X and Y, 20 use both Y and Z, 22 use both X and Z, and 10 use all three brands. How many households use exactly one of the three brands?
questions.exp: Number using exactly one = (sum of singles) - 2(sum of pairwise) + 3(all three) = 165 - 2(67) + 3(10) = 165 - 134 + 30 = 61.

chapters.title: Shapes, Figure Counting, Mirror and Water Images, Embedded Figures
factsheet: Mirror image (lateral inversion) = reflection about a VERTICAL axis; water image = reflection about a HORIZONTAL axis.
Capitals unchanged in a MIRROR image: A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y (11 letters).
Capitals unchanged in a WATER image: B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X (9 letters).
Unchanged in BOTH mirror and water image: H, I, O, X. Digits unchanged in both: 0 and 8.
Mirror image of a word = write the word backwards, then mirror each letter; the letter ORDER always reverses.
Mirror image of a clock time = 11:60 minus the given time (use 12:00 if the time is exactly 12:00).
Water image of a clock time = 18:30 minus the given time (subtract 12 hours if the answer exceeds 12:00).
Rectangle (or square) + both diagonals = 8 triangles. Square + both diagonals + both mid-lines = 16 triangles.
Rectangle + both diagonals + ONE mid-line = 12 triangles. Triangle + all three medians = 16 triangles.
Triangle with n cevians drawn from ONE vertex to the opposite side: number of triangles = C(n+2, 2).
Joining the midpoints of a triangle's sides gives 4 small triangles; total in the figure = 5.
Equilateral triangle with each side divided into n parts and lines drawn parallel to all sides: n=2 gives 5 triangles, n=3 gives 13, n=4 gives 27.
Rectangles in an m x n grid = C(m+1, 2) x C(n+1, 2). Chessboard (8x8) = 36 x 36 = 1296 rectangles.
Counting method for triangles: count the smallest regions first, then triangles made of 2, 3, 4 ... of them, and finally the whole figure.
Regular polygon: number of diagonals = n(n-3)/2; sum of interior angles = (n-2) x 180 degrees; each exterior angle of a REGULAR polygon = 360/n.
Given each interior angle A of a regular polygon, n = 360 / (180 - A).
Dice: a cube face touches 4 faces and is opposite the 5th. If a number is adjacent to four given numbers, the sixth number is opposite it.
Standard dice: numbers on opposite faces add up to 7, i.e. the pairs are 1-6, 2-5, 3-4.
Two views of a dice with the SAME face on top: the other four numbers lie around it; a quarter turn matching one pair also matches the other, giving both pairs of opposites.
Two views with ONE face common but in different positions: the two faces that never appear together in any single view are opposite each other.
Painted cube cut into n^3 smaller cubes (all six faces painted): 3 faces painted = 8 (always the corners); 2 faces = 12(n-2); 1 face = 6(n-2)^2; 0 faces = (n-2)^3.
Check: 8 + 12(n-2) + 6(n-2)^2 + (n-2)^3 = n^3. At least one face painted = n^3 - (n-2)^3.
If only two OPPOSITE faces of a cube are painted and it is cut into n^3 cubes: exactly one face painted = 2n^2, two faces = 0.
Paper folding: n folds double the layers each time, so one punch after n folds gives 2^n holes; k punches give k x 2^n holes.
A punch made ON a fold line gives fewer holes than 2^n, because the layers meet at that line.
Embedded / hidden figure questions: count the number of line segments and closed regions of the target shape and match them piece by piece.
Classification of quadrilaterals: square, rectangle and rhombus are parallelograms; a trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides and is usually the odd one out.

questions.q: A rectangle ABCD is drawn and both of its diagonals AC and BD are drawn. How many triangles are there in the figure in all?
questions.exp: The two diagonals cut each other at the centre O. Smallest triangles: AOB, BOC, COD, DOA = 4. Triangles made of two of these, i.e. the halves of the rectangle: ABC, BCD, CDA, DAB = 4. Total = 4 + 4 = 8.

questions.q: A square is drawn. Both its diagonals are drawn, and also the two lines joining the midpoints of opposite sides. How many triangles are there in the figure in all?
questions.exp: All four lines pass through the centre O, cutting the square into 8 smallest triangles. Adding pairs that merge across a corner gives the 4 triangles AOB, BOC, COD, DOA; adding further gives the 4 half-squares ABC, BCD, CDA, DAB. Total = 8 + 4 + 4 = 16.

questions.q: A rectangle is divided by both its diagonals and also by the straight line joining the midpoints of its two longer sides. How many triangles are formed in all?
questions.exp: The mid-line passes through the centre O, so it splits only the top and bottom triangles. Smallest triangles = 6 (two on top, two at the bottom, one on each side). Adding pairs gives the 2 triangles AOB and COD; the four half-rectangles ABC, ABD, BCD, ACD give 4 more. Total = 6 + 2 + 4 = 12.

questions.q: In a triangle all three medians are drawn. How many triangles are there in the resulting figure?
questions.exp: The three medians meet at the centroid G and cut the triangle into 6 smallest triangles of equal area. Larger ones: ABG, BCG and CAG (each made of 2 small ones) = 3; the six halves ABD, ADC, BCE, BEA, CAF, CFB (each made of 3 small ones) = 6; and the whole triangle = 1. Total = 6 + 3 + 6 + 1 = 16.

questions.q: A square is drawn with one diagonal and with both the lines joining the midpoints of opposite sides. How many triangles are there in the figure?
questions.exp: The diagonal AC and both mid-lines pass through the centre O. On one side of AC the mid-lines cut off the two small triangles A-P-O and C-Q-O (P, Q being midpoints of AB and BC); on the other side they cut off two more. That is 4 small triangles. The diagonal also splits the square into the two halves ABC and ACD. Total = 4 + 2 = 6.

questions.q: A square is drawn with both its diagonals and with the line joining the midpoints of one pair of opposite sides. The total number of triangles in the figure is
questions.exp: This is the same configuration as a rectangle with both diagonals plus one mid-line: 6 smallest triangles + 2 (the two halves that the mid-line splits) + 4 half-squares = 12.

questions.q: From one vertex of a triangle, two straight lines are drawn to two different points on the opposite side. How many triangles are formed in all?
questions.exp: The opposite side now carries 4 points (2 end-points + 2 interior points). Every pair of these points, joined to the apex, gives one triangle, so the count is C(4,2) = 6.

questions.q: From one vertex of a triangle, three straight lines are drawn to three different points on the opposite side. The number of triangles in the figure is
questions.exp: The opposite side carries 2 + 3 = 5 points. Number of triangles = C(5,2) = 10.

questions.q: The midpoints of the three sides of a triangle are joined to one another. How many triangles are there in the figure so obtained?
questions.exp: Joining the three midpoints cuts the triangle into 4 small congruent triangles. Adding the original triangle itself gives 4 + 1 = 5. (The medial triangle's own three sides create no further triangle.)

questions.q: Each side of an equilateral triangle is divided into three equal parts and lines are drawn through these points parallel to the three sides. How many triangles are there in the whole figure?
questions.exp: Upward-pointing triangles: 6 of unit size + 3 of side 2 + 1 of side 3 = 10. Downward-pointing triangles: 3 of unit size. Total = 10 + 3 = 13.

questions.q: A square is divided into 9 equal smaller squares by two horizontal and two vertical lines. How many squares of all sizes are there in the figure?
questions.exp: Squares of side 1 unit = 9; of side 2 units = 4; of side 3 units = 1. Total = 9 + 4 + 1 = 14. (General rule: for an n x n grid, total squares = 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2.)

questions.q: A square is divided into 16 equal smaller squares. The total number of squares of all sizes in the figure is
How many squares of all sizes are there on a standard 8 x 8 chessboard?
questions.exp: Total = 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + 8^2 = 8 x 9 x 17 / 6 = 204. (The 1296 is the count of rectangles, not squares.)

questions.q: A rectangle is divided into 6 equal parts by two lines parallel to its length and one line parallel to its breadth, forming a 3 x 2 arrangement of small rectangles. How many rectangles of all sizes are there in the figure?
questions.exp: There are 4 vertical lines and 3 horizontal lines. Any 2 verticals and any 2 horizontals bound one rectangle: C(4,2) x C(3,2) = 6 x 3 = 18.

questions.q: How many rectangles (including squares) of all sizes are there on a standard 8 x 8 chessboard?
questions.exp: A chessboard has 9 horizontal and 9 vertical lines. Choose 2 of each: C(9,2) x C(9,2) = 36 x 36 = 1296.

questions.q: Which one of the following capital letters looks exactly the same as itself in a plane mirror placed vertically beside it?
questions.exp: A letter is unchanged by lateral inversion only if it has a vertical axis of symmetry. T does; F, G and J do not. The full set of such capitals is A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y.

questions.q: Which one of the following capital letters remains unchanged in its mirror image?
questions.exp: W has a vertical axis of symmetry, so lateral inversion leaves it unaltered. B, C and E have a horizontal axis of symmetry instead, so they are unchanged in a water image, not in a mirror image.

questions.q: In the word MOUNTAIN, how many letters remain unchanged in their mirror image?
questions.exp: Mirror-invariant capitals are A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y. In M-O-U-N-T-A-I-N the letters M, O, U, T, A and I qualify (6 letters); the two N's do not.

questions.q: Choose the correct mirror image of the word REASONING when the mirror is held vertically to its right.
questions.exp: Lateral inversion reverses the order of the letters. Reading REASONING backwards letter by letter gives G-N-I-N-O-S-A-E-R.

questions.q: A clock seen in a mirror shows the time as 3:40. What is the correct time?
questions.exp: Mirror time and true time add up to 11:60 (i.e. 12:00). So true time = 11:60 - 3:40 = 8:20.

questions.q: A wall clock actually shows 4:50. What time will its image in a plane mirror show?
questions.exp: Mirror image of a clock time = 11:60 minus the time. 11:60 - 4:50 = 7:10.

questions.q: Which one of the following words reads exactly the same in its mirror image?
questions.exp: For a word to be unchanged, every letter must be mirror-symmetric AND the word must read the same backwards. TOOT uses only T and O and is a palindrome, so it qualifies. MOTOR, HIM and AXE fail on one or both counts.

questions.q: Which one of the following capital letters remains unchanged in its water image?
questions.exp: A water image is a reflection about a horizontal axis, so only letters with a horizontal axis of symmetry survive: B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X. D qualifies; A, V and T are mirror-symmetric instead.

questions.q: In the word CHOICE, how many letters remain unchanged in their water image?
questions.exp: Water-invariant capitals are B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X. Every letter of C-H-O-I-C-E belongs to this set, so all 6 letters are unchanged and the water image also reads CHOICE.

questions.q: Out of the capital letters A, B, H, M, O and X, how many remain unchanged in their water image?
questions.exp: Water-invariant capitals are B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X. From the given six, B, H, O and X qualify; A and M are mirror-symmetric, not water-symmetric. Hence 4.

questions.q: Which group of capital letters remains unchanged in BOTH the mirror image and the water image?
questions.exp: Mirror-invariant set: A H I M O T U V W X Y. Water-invariant set: B C D E H I K O X. Their intersection (letters with both a vertical and a horizontal axis of symmetry) is H, I, O, X.

questions.q: A square sheet of paper is folded exactly in half, and the folded sheet is folded exactly in half once more. A single hole is then punched through all the layers at a point not lying on any fold. On unfolding, how many holes will the sheet have?
questions.exp: Each fold doubles the number of layers: after 2 folds there are 2^2 = 4 layers, and one punch pierces every layer, giving 4 holes.

questions.q: A sheet of paper is folded in half three times in succession and one hole is punched through the folded sheet. How many holes will there be when the paper is unfolded?
questions.exp: Number of layers after n folds = 2^n. Here n = 3, so 2^3 = 8 layers and hence 8 holes.

questions.q: A square sheet is folded in half twice and then two separate holes are punched through the folded sheet. On unfolding, the number of holes will be
questions.exp: Two folds give 2^2 = 4 layers. Each punch makes 4 holes, so 2 punches make 2 x 4 = 8 holes.

questions.q: A cubical dice has its six faces numbered 1 to 6. If the face bearing 1 is adjacent to the faces bearing 2, 3, 4 and 5, which number lies on the face opposite to 1?
questions.exp: A face of a cube touches exactly four faces and is opposite to the fifth. Since 1 touches 2, 3, 4 and 5, the only number left is 6, so 6 is opposite 1.

questions.q: On a standard dice the numbers on any two opposite faces add up to 7. If the face showing 2 is on top, what number is on the face at the bottom?
questions.exp: Opposite faces sum to 7, so the face opposite 2 bears 7 - 2 = 5.

questions.q:
Two positions of the same dice are shown below.
Position I: top face 1, front face 2, right face 3.
Position II: top face 1, front face 4, right face 5.
Which number lies opposite the face bearing 2?
questions.exp: In both positions 1 is on top, so 2, 3, 4 and 5 all lie on the four side faces around 1 and 6 must be opposite 1. Rotating from Position I to Position II by a quarter turn about the vertical axis takes 2 to 4's place and 3 to 5's place, so 2 and 4 lie on opposite side faces, and so do 3 and 5. Hence 4 is opposite 2.

questions.q:
Two positions of the same dice are shown below.
Position I: top face 1, front face 2, right face 3.
Position II: top face 2, front face 4, right face 5.
Which number lies opposite the face bearing 3?
questions.exp: The two positions are consistent with exactly one dice, in which the opposite pairs are (1, 5), (2, 6) and (3, 4). Hence 4 lies opposite 3.

questions.q:
Two positions of the same dice are shown below.
Position I: top face 1, front face 2, right face 3.
Position II: top face 3, front face 5, right face 4.
Which number lies opposite the face bearing 1?
questions.exp: These two views are consistent with exactly one dice, whose opposite pairs are (1, 5), (2, 4) and (3, 6). Hence 5 lies opposite 1.

questions.q:
Two positions of a cube whose faces are marked A, B, C, D, E and F are given below.
Position I: top face A, front face B, right face C.
Position II: top face A, front face D, right face E.
Which letter is on the face opposite to C?
questions.exp: A is on top in both positions, so F must be at the bottom, opposite A. The quarter turn about the vertical axis that carries B to D's place carries C to E's place, so B is opposite D and C is opposite E.

questions.q: A cube painted on all its six faces is cut into 64 identical smaller cubes. How many of the smaller cubes have exactly two faces painted?
questions.exp: 64 = 4^3, so the cube is 4 units on a side. Cubes with exactly two painted faces lie along the edges but not at the corners: 12 edges x (4 - 2) = 12 x 2 = 24.

questions.q: A cube is painted on all faces and then cut into 125 identical smaller cubes. How many smaller cubes have exactly one face painted?
questions.exp: 125 = 5^3, so the side is 5 units. One-face cubes are the interior of each face: 6 x (5 - 2)^2 = 6 x 9 = 54.

questions.q: A painted cube is cut into 27 identical smaller cubes. How many of them have three faces painted?
questions.exp: Only the corner cubes show three painted faces, and a cube always has 8 corners, whatever the number of cuts. Hence 8.

questions.q: A cube painted on all its faces is cut into 64 identical smaller cubes. How many of the smaller cubes have no face painted at all?
questions.exp: 64 = 4^3. Unpainted cubes form the inner block of side (4 - 2) = 2, so their number is 2^3 = 8.

questions.q: A cube painted red on all faces is cut into 27 identical smaller cubes. How many of these have at least one face painted red?
questions.exp: Only the single cube at the centre of the 3 x 3 x 3 block is untouched by paint, so 27 - 1 = 26 smaller cubes have at least one painted face.

questions.q: A cube is painted only on its top and bottom faces, the four side faces being left unpainted. It is then cut into 64 identical smaller cubes. How many smaller cubes have exactly one face painted?
questions.exp: The cube is 4 x 4 x 4. Only the top layer and the bottom layer touch paint, and since the two painted faces are opposite, no small cube can get two painted faces. Each layer has 4 x 4 = 16 cubes, so 2 x 16 = 32 cubes have exactly one painted face.

questions.q: How many diagonals does a regular octagon have?
questions.exp: Number of diagonals of an n-sided polygon = n(n - 3)/2. For n = 8 this is 8 x 5 / 2 = 20.

questions.q: What is the sum of all the interior angles of a hexagon?
questions.exp: Sum of interior angles = (n - 2) x 180 degrees. For n = 6 this is 4 x 180 = 720 degrees.

questions.q: Each interior angle of a regular polygon measures 144 degrees. How many sides does the polygon have?
questions.exp: Each exterior angle = 180 - 144 = 36 degrees. Number of sides = 360 / 36 = 10.

questions.q: Three of the following four figures are alike in a certain way and one is different. Which one is different?
questions.exp: A rhombus, a square and a rectangle are all parallelograms, i.e. both pairs of opposite sides are parallel. A trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides, so it is the odd one out.

chapters.title: Numeracy I: Ratio, Proportion, Partnership, Percentage, Profit & Loss, Interest
factsheet: Simple interest: SI = P x R x T / 100; Amount = P + SI. Compound interest: A = P(1 + R/100)^n and CI = A - P.
Half-yearly compounding: rate R/2, periods 2n. Quarterly: rate R/4, periods 4n. CI always exceeds SI for n > 1.
DIFFERENCE between CI and SI for 2 YEARS = P(R/100)^2 = P x R^2 / 10000. (Asked in RAS Pre 2018, 2021, 2023 and 2024.)
DIFFERENCE between CI and SI for 3 YEARS = P x R^2 x (300 + R) / 10^6 = P(R/100)^2 x (3 + R/100).
From the 2-year difference D: P = D x (100/R)^2, and R = 100 x square root of (D/P).
SI doubles a sum when SI = P, so rate = 100/T; triples it when SI = 2P, so rate = 200/T. At CI, if a sum doubles in t years it becomes 4 times in 2t and 8 times in 3t years.
Population after n years = P(1 + r/100)^n; depreciation = P(1 - r/100)^n. Growth or decline over unequal years multiplies the separate factors.
Instalments at CI: each instalment x satisfies x/(1+r)^1 + x/(1+r)^2 + ... = debt (present-value method).
Successive percentage change of a% then b%: net = a + b + ab/100 (use a negative sign for a fall).
An x% rise followed by an x% fall always gives a NET FALL of x^2/100 per cent, never zero.
If price rises by x%, consumption must fall by 100x/(100 + x) per cent to keep the expenditure unchanged.
If A is x% more than B, then B is 100x/(100 + x) per cent less than A. If A is x% less than B, B is 100x/(100 - x) per cent more than A.
Profit % and loss % are ALWAYS calculated on the cost price unless stated otherwise: Profit% = (SP - CP)/CP x 100.
SP = CP(100 + p)/100; CP = 100 x SP/(100 + p); for a loss replace (100 + p) by (100 - l).
Marked price and discount: SP = MP(100 - d)/100. Two successive discounts d1 and d2 equal a single discount of d1 + d2 - d1d2/100.
Marking m% above cost and giving d% discount gives profit % = m - d - md/100.
Selling two articles at the SAME price, one at +x% and one at -x%, always gives a net LOSS of x^2/100 per cent.
If CP of x articles = SP of y articles, then profit % = (x - y)/y x 100 (a loss if y > x).
Dishonest dealer selling at cost price with a false weight: gain % = error/(true value - error) x 100.
A profit of p% on the cost price equals 100p/(100 + p) per cent of the selling price.
Ratio a : b : c -- divide a total in the ratio by giving each share (its part / sum of parts) x total.
Proportion a : b :: c : d means ad = bc. Mean proportional between a and b = square root of ab; third proportional to a, b = b^2/a; fourth proportional to a, b, c = bc/a.
To combine a : b and b : c, scale both so that b matches, then read off a : b : c.
Rule of ALLIGATION: (quantity of cheaper)/(quantity of dearer) = (dearer price - mean price)/(mean price - cheaper price). Water is taken at zero cost.
Repeated replacement: if y litres are drawn from x litres of pure liquid and replaced with water, n times, the liquid left = x(1 - y/x)^n.
Mixing equal quantities of two mixtures: add the component fractions directly (e.g. 4/5 and 3/5 milk give 7 parts milk to 3 parts water).
To change a mixture from a : b to a : c by adding only the second liquid, keep the first quantity fixed and compute the new second quantity.
Partnership: profit is divided in the ratio of (capital x time) for each partner; a working partner's salary or commission is deducted first and the balance shared.

questions.q: What is the difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on Rs 10,000 for 2 years at 5% per annum, interest being compounded annually?
questions.exp: SI = 10000 x 5 x 2 / 100 = Rs 1,000. Amount at CI = 10000 x (1.05)^2 = Rs 11,025, so CI = Rs 1,025. Difference = 1025 - 1000 = Rs 25. Shortcut: difference for 2 years = P(R/100)^2 = 10000 x (0.05)^2 = Rs 25.

questions.q: The difference between compound interest and simple interest on a sum of Rs 8,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum is
Find the difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on Rs 16,000 for 3 years at 5% per annum.
The difference between compound interest and simple interest on Rs 10,000 for 3 years at 10% per annum is
The difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on a certain sum for 2 years at 4% per annum is Rs 32. What is the sum?
questions.exp: For 2 years, difference = P(R/100)^2. So 32 = P x (4/100)^2 = P x 0.0016, giving P = 32 / 0.0016 = Rs 20,000.

questions.q: The difference between compound interest and simple interest on Rs 10,000 for 2 years is Rs 144. The rate of interest per annum is
questions.exp: Difference for 2 years = P(R/100)^2, so 144 = 10000 x (R/100)^2. Hence (R/100)^2 = 0.0144, R/100 = 0.12 and R = 12% per annum.

questions.q: The difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on a sum for 3 years at 10% per annum is Rs 62. The sum is
questions.exp: For 3 years, difference = P x R^2 x (300 + R) / 10^6 = P x 100 x 310 / 1000000 = 0.031P. So 0.031P = 62 and P = Rs 2,000.

questions.q: What is the difference between compound interest and simple interest on Rs 25,000 for 2 years at 8% per annum?
A vessel contains 100 litres of pure milk. 20 litres of milk is drawn out and replaced by water. This operation is performed once more. How much pure milk is left in the vessel?
questions.exp: After each replacement the milk left = previous milk x (1 - 20/100). So milk after 2 operations = 100 x (4/5)^2 = 100 x 16/25 = 64 litres. General rule: milk left = x(1 - y/x)^n.

questions.q: A vessel holds 64 litres of pure milk. 16 litres is taken out and replaced by water; the same operation is repeated once more. What is the ratio of milk to water in the vessel finally?
In what ratio must water be mixed with milk costing Rs 32 per litre so that the mixture is worth Rs 24 per litre?
questions.exp: Water costs Rs 0 per litre. By alligation, water : milk = (32 - 24) : (24 - 0) = 8 : 24 = 1 : 3.

questions.q: A milkman buys milk at Rs 40 per litre, mixes water with it and sells the mixture at Rs 40 per litre, thereby gaining 25%. Find the ratio of water to milk in the mixture.
questions.exp: Since he gains 25% while selling at Rs 40, the cost of one litre of the mixture = 40 / 1.25 = Rs 32. By alligation between water (Rs 0) and milk (Rs 40) at a mean of Rs 32, water : milk = (40 - 32) : (32 - 0) = 8 : 32 = 1 : 4.

questions.q: Vessel A contains milk and water in the ratio 4 : 1 and vessel B contains them in the ratio 3 : 2. Equal quantities from the two vessels are mixed. What is the ratio of milk to water in the new mixture?
questions.exp: Take 5 litres from each vessel. From A: 4 litres milk, 1 litre water. From B: 3 litres milk, 2 litres water. Total milk = 7, total water = 3, so the ratio is 7 : 3.

questions.q: A mixture of 60 litres contains milk and water in the ratio 2 : 1. How much water must be added to make the ratio of milk to water 1 : 1?
questions.exp: Milk = 60 x 2/3 = 40 litres, water = 20 litres. For a 1 : 1 ratio the water must also become 40 litres, so 40 - 20 = 20 litres of water must be added.

questions.q: 40 litres of a mixture contains milk and water in the ratio 3 : 1. How much water should be added so that the ratio becomes 3 : 2?
questions.exp: Milk = 40 x 3/4 = 30 litres, water = 10 litres. Milk stays 30 litres, so for a 3 : 2 ratio the water must be 30 x 2/3 = 20 litres. Water to be added = 20 - 10 = 10 litres.

questions.q: In what ratio must rice costing Rs 30 per kg be mixed with rice costing Rs 45 per kg so that the mixture is worth Rs 36 per kg?
questions.exp: By the rule of alligation, (quantity of cheaper) : (quantity of dearer) = (45 - 36) : (36 - 30) = 9 : 6 = 3 : 2.

questions.q: Two numbers are in the ratio 3 : 5. If 4 is added to each of them, the ratio becomes 5 : 7. What is the smaller number?
questions.exp: Let the numbers be 3x and 5x. Then (3x + 4)/(5x + 4) = 5/7, so 21x + 28 = 25x + 20, giving 4x = 8 and x = 2. The numbers are 6 and 10; the smaller is 6.

questions.q: Rs 1,200 is divided among A, B and C in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7. What is C's share?
questions.exp: Total number of parts = 2 + 3 + 7 = 12. One part = 1200/12 = Rs 100. C gets 7 parts = Rs 700.

questions.q: Two numbers are in the ratio 5 : 8 and their difference is 36. What is the larger number?
questions.exp: Let the numbers be 5x and 8x. Then 8x - 5x = 3x = 36, so x = 12. The numbers are 60 and 96; the larger is 96.

questions.q: What is the mean proportional between 9 and 64?
questions.exp: The mean proportional between a and b is the square root of ab. Here it is the square root of 9 x 64 = 576, which is 24.

questions.q: What is the third proportional to 8 and 12?
questions.exp: If x is the third proportional then 8 : 12 :: 12 : x, so 8x = 144 and x = 18. In general the third proportional to a and b is b^2/a.

questions.q: What is the fourth proportional to 4, 9 and 12?
questions.exp: If x is the fourth proportional then 4 : 9 :: 12 : x, so 4x = 108 and x = 27.

questions.q: If a : b = 2 : 3 and b : c = 4 : 5, then a : c is
questions.exp: Make b common: a : b = 2 : 3 = 8 : 12 and b : c = 4 : 5 = 12 : 15. Hence a : b : c = 8 : 12 : 15 and a : c = 8 : 15.

questions.q: Rs 5,900 is divided among A, B and C in such a way that A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 5 : 6. What is A's share?
questions.exp: Make B common: A : B = 15 : 20 and B : C = 20 : 24, so A : B : C = 15 : 20 : 24 with 59 parts in all. One part = 5900/59 = Rs 100, so A gets 15 parts = Rs 1,500.

questions.q: A and B invest Rs 12,000 and Rs 16,000 respectively in a business for the same period. If the total profit at the end of the year is Rs 7,000, what is B's share?
questions.exp: Since the time is the same, profit is shared in the ratio of capitals: 12000 : 16000 = 3 : 4. B's share = 7000 x 4/7 = Rs 4,000.

questions.q: A invests Rs 5,000 for 12 months and B invests Rs 6,000 for 8 months in the same business. If the profit is Rs 18,000, what is A's share?
questions.exp: Profit is shared in the ratio of capital x time: A = 5000 x 12 = 60,000 and B = 6000 x 8 = 48,000, i.e. 5 : 4. A's share = 18000 x 5/9 = Rs 10,000.

questions.q: A and B start a business with capitals in the ratio 3 : 2. A withdraws his entire capital at the end of 6 months while B continues for the whole year. If the annual profit is Rs 14,000, what is B's share?
questions.exp: Capital x time: A = 3 x 6 = 18 units, B = 2 x 12 = 24 units, so the profit ratio is 18 : 24 = 3 : 4. B's share = 14000 x 4/7 = Rs 8,000.

questions.q: A, B and C invest Rs 20,000, Rs 15,000 and Rs 25,000 respectively in a partnership for one year. If the total profit is Rs 24,000, what is C's share?
questions.exp: The capital ratio is 20000 : 15000 : 25000 = 4 : 3 : 5, a total of 12 parts. One part = 24000/12 = Rs 2,000, so C gets 5 parts = Rs 10,000.

questions.q: A and B invest Rs 30,000 and Rs 20,000 respectively. A is the working partner and receives 10% of the profit for managing the business; the rest is divided in the ratio of their capitals. If the annual profit is Rs 20,000, what does A receive in all?
questions.exp: A's management fee = 10% of 20000 = Rs 2,000. The remaining Rs 18,000 is divided in the ratio 30000 : 20000 = 3 : 2, so A gets 18000 x 3/5 = Rs 10,800. A's total = 2000 + 10800 = Rs 12,800.

questions.q: A starts a business with Rs 8,000. After 4 months B joins him with Rs 9,000. At the end of the year the profit is Rs 21,000. What is A's share?
What is 15% of 640?
If the price of a commodity rises by 25%, by what percentage must a family reduce its consumption so that its expenditure on the commodity remains unchanged?
questions.exp: Required reduction = 100 x R/(100 + R) = 100 x 25/125 = 20%. Check: if 100 units at Re 1 cost Rs 100, then at Rs 1.25 the family can buy only 80 units, a 20% cut.

questions.q: The price of an article is increased by 20% and the new price is then increased by a further 10%. What is the net percentage increase?
questions.exp: Net change = a + b + ab/100 = 20 + 10 + (20 x 10)/100 = 32%. Check: 100 becomes 120, and 120 becomes 132.

questions.q: The price of an article is first increased by 20% and then decreased by 20%. The net effect on the price is
questions.exp: Net change = a + b + ab/100 with a = +20 and b = -20, giving 20 - 20 - 400/100 = -4%, i.e. a 4% decrease. (Rule: an x% rise followed by an x% fall always gives a net fall of x^2/100 per cent.)

questions.q: A man's salary of Rs 25,000 is first increased by 10% and then the increased salary is reduced by 10%. What is his final salary?
questions.exp: After the rise: 25000 x 1.10 = Rs 27,500. After the cut: 27500 x 0.90 = Rs 24,750. (Equivalently, a net fall of 10^2/100 = 1%, i.e. Rs 250.)

questions.q: A's income is 25% more than B's income. By what percentage is B's income less than A's?
questions.exp: Let B = 100, then A = 125. B is less than A by 25, which as a percentage of A is 25/125 x 100 = 20%. Formula: 100x/(100 + x).

questions.q: In an election between two candidates, the winner secured 60% of the valid votes and won by a margin of 1,200 votes. What was the total number of valid votes polled?
questions.exp: The winner got 60% and the loser 40%, so the margin is 20% of the total. Thus 20% of the total = 1,200, and the total = 1200 x 100/20 = 6,000 votes.

questions.q: A student scored 30% of the maximum marks and failed by 20 marks. If the pass mark is 35% of the maximum, what are the maximum marks?
questions.exp: The shortfall of 20 marks equals 35% - 30% = 5% of the maximum. So 5% of the maximum = 20, and the maximum = 20 x 100/5 = 400 marks. (Pass mark = 140.)

questions.q: The population of a town is 20,000 and it increases at the rate of 10% per annum. What will the population be after 2 years?
The value of a machine costing Rs 50,000 depreciates at 10% per annum. What is its value after 2 years?
If 60% of A is equal to 40% of B, then A : B is
An article bought for Rs 400 is sold for Rs 500. What is the profit percentage?
questions.exp: Profit = 500 - 400 = Rs 100. Profit % = (Profit / CP) x 100 = 100/400 x 100 = 25%. (Profit percentage is always taken on the cost price.)

questions.q: An article costing Rs 250 is sold for Rs 200. What is the loss percentage?
By selling an article for Rs 690 a shopkeeper earns a profit of 15%. What is the cost price of the article?
An article whose cost price is Rs 1,200 is sold at a loss of 20%. What is the selling price?
The marked price of an article is Rs 1,000 and two successive discounts of 20% and 10% are allowed. What is the selling price?
questions.exp: SP = 1000 x 0.80 x 0.90 = Rs 720. (Equivalent single discount = 20 + 10 - 200/100 = 28%.)

questions.q: A shopkeeper buys an article for Rs 300, marks it 25% above the cost price and then allows a discount of 10% on the marked price. What is his profit percentage?
questions.exp: Marked price = 300 x 1.25 = Rs 375. Selling price = 375 x 0.90 = Rs 337.50. Profit = Rs 37.50, so profit % = 37.5/300 x 100 = 12.5%.

questions.q: A man sells two articles at Rs 1,200 each. On one he gains 20% and on the other he loses 20%. What is his overall gain or loss?
questions.exp: CP of the first = 1200 x 100/120 = Rs 1,000; CP of the second = 1200 x 100/80 = Rs 1,500. Total CP = Rs 2,500 against a total SP of Rs 2,400, so there is a loss of Rs 100. (Rule: selling two items at the same price with equal % gain and loss always gives a loss of x^2/100 per cent, here 4%.)

questions.q: If the cost price of 20 articles is equal to the selling price of 16 articles, what is the profit percentage?
questions.exp: Let the CP of one article be Re 1. Then SP of 16 articles = CP of 20 articles = Rs 20, so SP of one article = 20/16 = Rs 1.25. Profit % = 0.25/1 x 100 = 25%. Formula: (x - y)/y x 100 = (20 - 16)/16 x 100.

questions.q: A dishonest dealer sells his goods at the cost price but uses a weight of 800 g in place of 1 kg. What is his gain percentage?
questions.exp: He pays for 800 g but charges for 1000 g. Gain % = error/(true value - error) x 100 = 200/800 x 100 = 25%.

questions.q: By selling an article for Rs 900 a man loses 10%. At what price should he sell it to gain 10%?
A shopkeeper marks his goods 40% above the cost price and then allows a discount of 25% on the marked price. What is his profit percentage?
questions.exp: Take CP = Rs 100. Marked price = Rs 140 and SP = 140 x 0.75 = Rs 105. Profit = Rs 5 on Rs 100, i.e. 5%.

questions.q: A trader sold an article at a profit of 15%. Had he sold it for Rs 90 more, his profit would have been 25%. What is the cost price of the article?
questions.exp: The extra Rs 90 corresponds to the extra profit of 25% - 15% = 10% of the cost price. So 10% of CP = 90 and CP = Rs 900.

questions.q: A profit of 25% on the cost price is equal to what percentage of the selling price?
questions.exp: Take CP = Rs 100, then profit = Rs 25 and SP = Rs 125. As a percentage of the selling price the profit is 25/125 x 100 = 20%.

questions.q: What is the simple interest on Rs 6,000 at 8% per annum for 3 years?
At what rate of simple interest will a sum of money double itself in 8 years?
questions.exp: To double, the interest must equal the principal, so SI = P. From P = P x R x 8/100 we get R = 100/8 = 12.5% per annum.

questions.q: At what rate of simple interest will Rs 2,500 amount to Rs 3,000 in 4 years?
The simple interest on a certain sum for 5 years at 6% per annum is Rs 1,800. What is the sum?
In how many years will Rs 4,000 yield a simple interest of Rs 1,200 at 10% per annum?
A sum of money at simple interest amounts to Rs 2,400 in 3 years and to Rs 2,800 in 5 years. What is the sum?
questions.exp: The interest for 2 years = 2800 - 2400 = Rs 400, so the interest for 1 year = Rs 200 and for 3 years = Rs 600. Principal = 2400 - 600 = Rs 1,800.

questions.q: At what rate per cent per annum of simple interest will a sum become three times itself in 20 years?
questions.exp: To become three times, the interest must be twice the principal, so SI = 2P. From 2P = P x R x 20/100 we get R = 200/20 = 10% per annum.

questions.q: What is the compound interest on Rs 10,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years, compounded annually?
Find the amount on Rs 8,000 at 5% per annum compound interest for 2 years.
What is the compound interest on Rs 12,000 at 10% per annum for 3 years, compounded annually?
questions.exp: Amount = 12000 x (1.1)^3 = 12000 x 1.331 = Rs 15,972. CI = 15972 - 12000 = Rs 3,972. (Simple interest would have been only Rs 3,600.)

questions.q: What is the compound interest on Rs 8,000 for 1 year at 10% per annum when the interest is compounded half-yearly?
questions.exp: For half-yearly compounding, halve the rate and double the number of periods: 5% for 2 periods. Amount = 8000 x (1.05)^2 = Rs 8,820, so CI = Rs 820 (against Rs 800 if compounded annually).

questions.q: A sum of money placed at compound interest doubles itself in 5 years. In how many years will it become four times itself?
questions.exp: In 5 years the sum becomes 2P; in the next 5 years that 2P again doubles to 4P. So it takes 5 + 5 = 10 years. (In general, becoming 2^k times takes 5k years.)

questions.q: The value of a machine bought for Rs 10,000 depreciates at 20% per annum. What is its value at the end of 2 years?
If a sum of Rs 6,000 fetches a compound interest of Rs 2,640 in 2 years, what is the rate of interest per annum?

The cash price of a television set is Rs 12,000. Under an instalment scheme a buyer pays Rs 4,000 at once and Rs 4,200 at the end of each of the next two years. How much more than the cash price does he pay in all?
questions.exp: Total paid = 4000 + 4200 + 4200 = Rs 12,400. Excess over the cash price = 12400 - 12000 = Rs 400.

questions.q: A debt of Rs 2,100 is to be repaid in two equal annual instalments at 10% per annum compound interest. What is the amount of each instalment?
questions.exp: If each instalment is x, its present value is x/1.1 for the first year and x/(1.1)^2 for the second. So x/1.1 + x/1.21 = 2100, i.e. x(110 + 100)/121 = 2100, giving 210x = 2100 x 121 and x = Rs 1,210. (Check: 1210/1.1 = 1100 and 1210/1.21 = 1000, which add to 2,100.)

chapters.title: Numeracy II: Mensuration, Averages, Statistics, Data Interpretation, Probability
factsheet: Square: perimeter 4a, area a², diagonal a√2, area from diagonal = d²/2. Rectangle: perimeter 2(l+b), area lb, diagonal √(l²+b²).
Triangle: area = ½ × base × height; Heron's formula = √[s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)], s = (a+b+c)/2; equilateral of side a: area = (√3/4)a², height = (√3/2)a.
Parallelogram: area = base × height (NO ½). Rhombus: area = ½ d1 d2. Trapezium: area = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × distance between them.
Circle: circumference 2πr, area πr². Sector of angle θ: arc = (θ/360)·2πr, area = (θ/360)·πr² = ½ × arc × r. Semicircle perimeter = πr + 2r.
Path w metres wide OUTSIDE a rectangle l×b: area = 2w(l+b) + 4w². Path INSIDE: area = 2w(l+b) − 4w². Crossing roads of width w: w(l+b) − w².
Cube: volume a³, total surface area 6a², lateral 4a², diagonal a√3. Cuboid: volume lbh, TSA 2(lb+bh+hl), diagonal √(l²+b²+h²).
Cylinder: volume πr²h, curved SA 2πrh, total SA 2πr(r+h). Cone: volume ⅓πr²h, curved SA πrl, total SA πr(l+r), slant l = √(r²+h²).
Sphere: volume (4/3)πr³, surface area 4πr². Hemisphere: volume (2/3)πr³, curved SA 2πr², total SA 3πr². Use π = 22/7 with radii that are multiples of 7.
Effect of change: if every linear dimension changes by k, length ×k, area ×k², volume ×k³. Side +20% → area +44%; edge +50% → surface +125%, volume +237.5%.
Two-dimension percentage rule: net change = x + y + xy/100 (use a minus sign for a decrease). +20% and −20% together give −4%, not zero.
Average = sum ÷ number of items. Average of first n natural numbers = (n+1)/2; of first n odd numbers = n; of first n even numbers = n+1.
Weighted average = (n1a1 + n2a2)/(n1 + n2) — never average two group averages directly unless the groups are equal in size.
Replacement rule: if the average of n items changes by d when one item is replaced, new item = old item ± n·d. Inclusion rule: new member = new average + n × (rise).
Average speed for EQUAL DISTANCES at speeds x and y = 2xy/(x+y) (harmonic mean) — never (x+y)/2. For equal TIMES the average is (x+y)/2.
Mean of grouped data = Σfx/Σf. Median: arrange in order; n odd → ((n+1)/2)th value; n even → mean of (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th. Mode = most frequent value.
Empirical relation for a moderately skewed distribution: Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean. Range = maximum − minimum (a measure of dispersion).
nPr = n!/(n−r)! (order matters); nCr = n!/[r!(n−r)!] (order does not); nC0 = nCn = 1, nCr = nC(n−r), nC1 = n, nC2 = n(n−1)/2.
Word with repeated letters: arrangements = n!/(p!q!…). BANANA = 6!/(3!2!) = 60. Handshakes/lines/chords among n points = nC2; number of diagonals of an n-gon = n(n−3)/2.
Probability P(E) = favourable ÷ total, 0 ≤ P ≤ 1; P(not E) = 1 − P(E). Coins: n coins → 2ⁿ outcomes; exactly r heads → nCr/2ⁿ.
Two dice → 36 outcomes. Number of ways to get a sum: 2→1, 3→2, 4→3, 5→4, 6→5, 7→6, 8→5, 9→4, 10→3, 11→2, 12→1. Doublets = 6, so P(doublet) = 1/6; P(sum 7) = 1/6, the most likely sum.
Pack of 52 cards: 4 suits × 13; 26 red (hearts, diamonds) and 26 black (spades, clubs); 12 face cards (J, Q, K), 4 aces; red face cards = 6.
Drawing without replacement uses combinations: P(both black from 4W, 5B) = 5C2 ÷ 9C2 = 10/36 = 5/18. With replacement it would be (5/9)².
Speed conversion: 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s; 1 m/s = 18/5 km/h. Train past a pole → own length; past a platform/bridge → length + length of platform.
Relative speed: opposite directions → add the speeds; same direction → subtract. Boat: downstream = u + v, upstream = u − v.
Time and work: if A takes x days and B takes y days, together they take xy/(x+y) days. Always work with ONE DAY'S work (1/x), never subtract the days themselves.
M1D1H1/W1 = M2D2H2/W2 (men–days–hours). Pipes: filling is +1/x, emptying is −1/y; with a leak the net rate is 1/x − 1/y.

Calendar odd days: ordinary year 1, leap year 2; 100 years 5, 200 years 3, 300 years 1, 400 years 0. Count 0 = Sunday, 1 = Monday … 6 = Saturday. A leap year is divisible by 4, but a century year must be divisible by 400.
Month odd-day codes (Jan–Dec): 0,3,3,6,1,4,6,2,5,0,3,5. The calendar of a year repeats after 400 years; 26 January 1950 was a Thursday, 15 August 1947 a Friday.

Clock: angle = |30H − 5.5M| degrees (take 360 − x if the result exceeds 180). Hour hand 0.5°/min, minute hand 6°/min, relative gain 5.5°/min. Hands coincide 11 times in 12 hours, are opposite 11 times, and are at right angles 22 times.

questions.q: The perimeter of a square field is 48 cm. What is its area?
questions.exp: Perimeter of a square = 4 × side, so side = 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm. Area = side² = 12 × 12 = 144 cm². (Taking side = 48 ÷ 2 = 24 cm by mistake gives 576 cm², and squaring the perimeter itself gives 2304 cm².)

questions.q: A rectangular field is 24 m long and 18 m broad. What will it cost to fence it once at the rate of ₹15 per metre?
questions.exp: Fencing is done along the perimeter. Perimeter = 2(l + b) = 2(24 + 18) = 2 × 42 = 84 m. Cost = 84 × 15 = ₹1,260. (Using the area 24 × 18 = 432 m² instead of the perimeter gives ₹6,480.)

questions.q: The base of a triangle is 18 cm and the corresponding height is 14 cm. Its area is:
questions.exp: Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height = ½ × 18 × 14 = ½ × 252 = 126 cm². (Forgetting the ½ gives 252 cm²; adding the two numbers gives 32.)

questions.q: The sides of a triangle are 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm. Its area is:
The area of a parallelogram whose base is 15 cm and corresponding height 8 cm is:
questions.exp: Area of a parallelogram = base × height = 15 × 8 = 120 cm². Unlike a triangle there is NO ½ here; halving gives the wrong value 60 cm². (46 cm is the perimeter-type trap 2(15+8).)

questions.q: The parallel sides of a trapezium are 22 cm and 14 cm and the perpendicular distance between them is 9 cm. Its area is:
questions.exp: Area of a trapezium = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × distance between them = ½ × (22 + 14) × 9 = ½ × 36 × 9 = 162 cm². (Omitting the ½ gives 324 cm²; using the difference 22 − 14 gives 36 cm².)

questions.q: The circumference of a circle of radius 7 cm (take π = 22/7) is:
questions.exp: Circumference = 2πr = 2 × (22/7) × 7 = 44 cm. (154 cm² is the AREA πr² of the same circle, and 88 cm is the circumference of a circle of radius 14 cm, i.e. what you get if you double the radius by confusing it with the diameter.)

questions.q: The diameter of a circle is 28 cm. Its area (take π = 22/7) is:
questions.exp: Radius = diameter ÷ 2 = 28/2 = 14 cm. Area = πr² = (22/7) × 14 × 14 = 22 × 2 × 14 = 616 cm². (Using the diameter 28 as the radius gives 2464 cm² — the commonest error; 88 cm is the circumference.)

questions.q: The area of a sector of a circle of radius 21 cm with central angle 120° is (take π = 22/7):
questions.exp: Area of a sector = (θ/360) × πr² = (120/360) × (22/7) × 21 × 21 = (1/3) × 1386 = 462 cm². (1386 cm² is the whole circle; 44 cm is the arc LENGTH (θ/360) × 2πr.)

questions.q: A rectangular field is 50 m long and 40 m wide. A path 3 m wide is laid all around it on the outside. The area of the path is:
questions.exp: Outer rectangle = (50 + 2×3) × (40 + 2×3) = 56 × 46 = 2576 m². Inner field = 50 × 40 = 2000 m². Path = 2576 − 2000 = 576 m². Shortcut: 2w(l + b) + 4w² = 6(90) + 4(9) = 540 + 36 = 576 m² — dropping the four corner squares 4w² gives the classic wrong answer 540 m².

questions.q: If each side of a square is increased by 20%, by what percentage does its area increase?
questions.exp: Take side = 100, so area = 10000. New side = 120, new area = 14400. Increase = 4400, i.e. 4400/10000 × 100 = 44%. Shortcut for two dimensions: x + y + xy/100 = 20 + 20 + 400/100 = 44%.

questions.q: The volume of a cube whose edge is 7 cm is:
questions.exp: Volume of a cube = a³ = 7 × 7 × 7 = 343 cm³. (294 is the total surface area 6a² = 6 × 49, and 49 is only a².)

questions.q: A cuboid measures 12 cm × 8 cm × 5 cm. Its total surface area is:
questions.exp: Total surface area = 2(lb + bh + hl) = 2(12×8 + 8×5 + 5×12) = 2(96 + 40 + 60) = 2 × 196 = 392 cm². (480 cm³ is the VOLUME l×b×h; 196 is the bracket without doubling.)

questions.q: The volume of a cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm is (take π = 22/7):
questions.exp: Volume = πr²h = (22/7) × 7 × 7 × 10 = 22 × 7 × 10 = 1540 cm³. (440 cm² is the curved surface area 2πrh and 748 cm² is the total surface area 2πr(r + h).)

questions.q: The curved surface area of a cylinder of radius 14 cm and height 20 cm is (take π = 22/7):
questions.exp: Curved surface area = 2πrh = 2 × (22/7) × 14 × 20 = 2 × 44 × 20 = 1760 cm². (12320 cm³ is the volume πr²h; forgetting the 2 gives 880.)

questions.q: A cone has radius 7 cm and vertical height 24 cm. Its curved surface area is (take π = 22/7):
questions.exp: First the slant height: l = √(r² + h²) = √(49 + 576) = √625 = 25 cm. Curved surface area = πrl = (22/7) × 7 × 25 = 550 cm². (704 cm² is the TOTAL surface area πr(l + r) = 550 + 154; 1232 cm³ is the volume.)

questions.q: The volume of a cone of radius 3 cm and height 7 cm is (take π = 22/7):
questions.exp: Volume of a cone = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3) × (22/7) × 9 × 7 = (1/3) × 198 = 66 cm³. (Forgetting the 1/3 — i.e. using the cylinder formula — gives 198 cm³; a cone is exactly one-third of the cylinder on the same base and height.)

questions.q: The surface area of a sphere of radius 21 cm is (take π = 22/7):
questions.exp: Surface area of a sphere = 4πr² = 4 × (22/7) × 21 × 21 = 4 × 22 × 63 = 5544 cm². (1386 cm² is only πr², and 38808 cm³ is the volume (4/3)πr³.)

questions.q: The total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 7 cm is (take π = 22/7):
questions.exp: A solid hemisphere has a curved part 2πr² plus a flat circular face πr², so total = 3πr² = 3 × (22/7) × 49 = 3 × 154 = 462 cm². (Leaving out the flat face gives 308 cm²; 616 cm² is the full sphere 4πr².)

questions.q: If each edge of a cube is increased by 50%, the total surface area of the cube increases by:
questions.exp: Let the edge be 2 units, so surface area = 6 × 2² = 24. New edge = 3 units, new surface area = 6 × 3² = 54. Increase = 54 − 24 = 30, i.e. 30/24 × 100 = 125%. (Surface area varies as the SQUARE of the edge: 1.5² = 2.25, i.e. 225% of the old — which is an increase of 125%, not 225%.)

questions.q: The average of 5 numbers is 27. If one of the numbers, 35, is removed, the average of the remaining numbers is:
questions.exp: Sum of the 5 numbers = 5 × 27 = 135. After removing 35 the sum = 135 − 35 = 100 and 4 numbers remain. New average = 100 ÷ 4 = 25.
